**FOLIO 144**

**About Ursina Torella**

<note>original: "cisse legat"</note> ...had read. When news was brought to her <note>This refers to Queen Semiramis of Assyria, a common historical comparison for female warriors</note> that the city of Babylon had revolted against her, she—just as she was, with her hair undone, for she happened to be parting her locks at the time—did not finish her hair or end her campaign until she had recaptured the rebellious city through great courage in battle. In this same way, the illustrious **Ursina**, this warrior woman <term>virago: a woman of great spirit and "masculine" strength, used as high praise in the Renaissance</term>, attacked the Venetian fleet with such great and effective force that within a short span of time she utterly routed them. In that battle, more than five hundred Illyrians <note>original: "Illyrij", referring to soldiers from the Dalmatian coast serving Venice</note> were lost. Nevertheless, the victory was somewhat bloody for her own side, as she lost some of her own men. This woman was tireless in the fight, rushing here and there as a primary leader, substituting fresh troops for the weary in the battle line against the enemy. There are some who affirm that many were killed by her own hand, as her weapons were stained with much blood. Because of this successful action, not only **Guastalla** but also **Boretto** <note>original: "Burelluz"</note> were recovered. When news of this victory was brought to her husband and to **Filippo, Duke of Milan** <note>Filippo Maria Visconti, who reigned 1412–1447</note>, immense joy and great gladness were celebrated throughout his entire principality, by all the cities, castles, and towns. It is said that Duke Filippo attributed so much to this woman's courage that he felt no failure needed to be feared after such a victory. Many other famous deeds and exploits of this woman, quite similar to these, could be commemorated by us here, but we intentionally omit them for the sake of brevity.

She bore three children for her husband: **Christoforo**, the eldest, and **Pietro**, both excellent in arms and distinguished by physical prowess and skill; and a daughter, **Antonia**, who later married **Pier Maria Rossi** <note>original: "petromarie rubeo", the Count of San Secondo</note>. Antonia was in no way inferior to her mother in greatness of spirit. For once, when the city of Parma—agitated by certain criminals—had defected from **Francesco Sforza**, Duke of Milan, and was being governed by the people under a claim of "liberty," Antonia was moved to action. She set out from her own territory with many armed men and entered the city amidst great tumult. She soon recaptured it and, having placed a strong garrison within the recovered city, restored it to Francesco Sforza. 

And so this illustrious warrior, **Ursina**, was always vigorous in undertaking great matters, and yet always preserved her womanly dignity. She reached the final day of her old age with the brilliance of her most famous name and the glory of her own deeds and those of all her kin. Departing this life in the year... <note>The text cuts off here at the start of the date</note>

-> # **Regarding Joan, the French Maid** <-

Since from her childhood she had spent a great part of her life among the flocks, where she spent her time with her companions pasturing the livestock, she often practiced running. She would run frequently here and there, and sometimes while running she would seize a spear in her hand like a brave knight <term>eques — literally a horseman or knight</term> and strike the trunks of trees with very powerful blows. Often she would even manfully mount some of the mares that were grazing in the herd, and with a spear tucked under her arm, she would deliver strong blows while running. Those who watched her were filled with great pleasure and admiration. Through such exercises, the woman emerged very strong.

For she was indeed of short stature, with a rustic face and black hair, but very strong in her whole body. She preserved her virginity unsullied throughout her whole life and stood out as a primary guardian of her religion. Her speech was light enough, according to the custom of the women of that country, but her sound character greatly distinguished it with honor. Her sense was so upright and so whole that she was believed to have been brought up or nourished in a place where the highest wisdom and every form of counsel seemed to flourish.

At that time, therefore, Henry, King of the English <note>Henry VI of England</note>, had brought a terrible war upon Charles, the seventh of that name, King of the French <note>Charles VII</note>. He had taken from him the greater part of his kingdom and was already attacking Orleans, the primary city of his kingdom, with the greatest force. The siege of that city was daily most grievous because it was surrounded on all sides, nor did any way appear by which such a siege could be broken. Indeed, all the hope of the kingdom turned upon that city; if it were lost, it seemed that it was all over for the whole kingdom of France. 

In this difficulty of affairs and anguish of mind, the King was driven by uncertainty; nor could he find any plan to follow by any reasoning. Then, while these things were happening, it occurred that this maiden (while pasturing the flocks) fell asleep in a very humble chapel to avoid the rain. At that time, she seemed in her sleep to be warned by God, who had revealed himself to her. It is said she was then only in her tenth year <note>original: "decimum... agebat annum." While historical records usually place her first visions at age 13, this author suggests an earlier start to her mystical experiences.</note>. Moved by this warning, she immediately left the flock she was pasturing and went into the camp...

**On Joan the Maid and Queen Isabella**

<note>original: "dite virtutis mulier/idigne occisa est."</note> This woman of great virtue was unworthily killed. After many years, King Charles himself <note>Charles VII of France, whom Joan helped crown at Reims.</note>—a truly excellent King—having recovered the city of Reims, ordered a bronze cross, a most prominent and gilded one, to be placed in that spot where <term>Joan the Maid</term><note>original: "Janna pulcella." Joan of Arc was known during her life as "La Pucelle" (The Maid).</note> had been so atrociously burned, as a monument and a tribute to her maidenly honor. Later, King Louis <note>Louis XI.</note>, succeeding his father, took the unworthy death of such a great <term>heroine</term><note>original: "viraginis." In this context, it refers to a woman of masculine strength or spirit, a "warrior-woman."</note> very poorly. It is said he obtained from the Roman Pope, Pius II, the appointment of two legal experts to be sent to France to re-examine her life and her trial with greater diligence. When they finally arrived in France, they immediately summoned the two surviving false advisors and judges. After they had accurately and carefully reviewed the entire case, they clearly discovered that this most innocent woman had been falsely condemned and that everything brought against her—specifically the accusations of poisoning and <term>magic arts</term><note>Witchcraft.</note>—had been fabricated. On the contrary, her entire life was found to be so consistently aligned with her noble deeds that she had never committed anything that could violate religion in any way. For these reasons, both of the surviving judges were sentenced to the same death penalty they had pronounced upon the innocent virgin years before. To this condemnation it was added that the bones of the two other judges, who were already dead, were to be dug up from their graves and similarly burned with fire. In the place where this heroine had been burned, a temple was to be built; from the remainder of the confiscated goods of the condemned judges, a daily sacrifice <note>A daily Mass for the soul.</note> was instituted there for the honor of the Highest God and for the atonement of the deceased woman. Thus, in this manner, every honor was restored to this admirable woman. Because of these merits and her unheard-of deeds, this Joan the Maid rightly comes to be included by us among the <term>Famous Women</term><note>A reference to the tradition of "De Mulieribus Claris" (Concerning Famous Women).</note>.

¶ On Queen Isabella, wife of King René. Chapter 158.

[An illuminated initial 'I' decorated with floral patterns] Isabella, the most illustrious and (if I may say so) holy Queen, wife of the renowned and excellent René of <term>Anjou</term><note>A powerful French noble house.</note>.

[A woodcut illustration shows a queen standing in a fenced garden, wearing a crown and holding a scepter, representing her authority and virtue.]

In the year 1449 after the birth of Christ, she passed away in Naples with the greatest praise for her name. She was certainly the most beautiful of all the women of her century, and no less outstanding in intellect than in greatness of soul; she was just, merciful, generous to all, affable, and most devoted to divine matters, as well as being exceptionally eloquent. Her modesty was so great that it seemed almost unheard of; she was adorned with such shamefastness <note>Virtuous modesty.</note> and was so conspicuous and venerable in her appearance that many said she was a divine rather than a human woman. While she was wonderfully decorated with many other good skills and gifts of the soul, she was said to be most highly distinguished by her singular prudence. This was seen especially in her gaining of the <term>Neapolitan kingdom</term><note>original: "parthenopeo regno," referring to Naples.</note> and in her administration of it, through which she certainly achieved immortal glory among her other accomplishments. We should know at this point that when the Kingdom of Naples was left without its rulers Louis and Joanna, the leading men of the kingdom immediately sent to France to summon this woman’s husband, King René—the brother of the late King Louis—to take up the title of the kingdom...

**Concerning Blessed Helen of Udine**
->very useful to her whole Neapolitan kingdom.<- <note>original: "toti suo regno neapolitano vtilissima"</note>

**On the blessed Helen of Udine: of the order of hermits. Chapter 158.**

[A hand-colored woodcut illustration of a woman in a religious habit (blue cloak over a red dress, white wimple) standing in a landscape and holding an open book.]

<margin>**The town of Udine.**</margin> Helen of Udine, a most religious sister of penance of our Order of Hermits of the Divine Augustine <note>The Augustinian Order, named for Saint Augustine of Hippo.</note>, departed to heaven with no uncertain faith amid the ranks of celestial spirits—as attested by scripture—in the year of the Christian Nativity 1458, in the same town of her birth, having been made illustrious by many virtues and miracles. This town is Udine, where this holy woman Helen drew her origin; it is a notably preeminent, very wealthy, and heavily populated place in Italy, in the region of Japedia or Friuli <note>original: "foro iuliano"</note>, which, as it is commonly said, was founded by the Dukes of Austria.

<margin>**Parents.**</margin> In this distinguished town, therefore, Helen, this most religious matron, received from her most noble parents both her nourishment and the sustenance of her whole life, and finally (so to speak) the reward of a most blessed life. Her noble and excellent parents, Valentine and Elizabeth, having raised the girl at home with all diligence until her fifteenth year, saw that she—being of a noble spirit—had adopted their excellent way and manner of living, namely: religion, faith, piety, honor, and all-encompassing integrity and modesty. 

<margin>**Antonio her husband.**</margin> Since she was a girl of remarkable beauty, they married her to Antonio Cavalcati, a citizen of Udine, a man certainly not unworthy in either virtue or fortune. This spouse Antonio, Helen—by her singular goodness and prudence, as well as her excellent character and natural modesty—attracted to love her in a wonderful way for as long as he lived; she was always most lovable and dear to God and to all her parents and friends. It is well known that there were never any quarrels or discords between them, but the greatest peace and perpetual conjugal love. 

<margin>**Note.**</margin> When the Lord took him away from her through death, she grieved for him with such tears and wailing that she herself almost died as well. Indeed, she considered his loss to be the most bitter of all, and therefore it was a most agonizing torment to her. (For it is difficult for women to lose beloved husbands without great sorrow, and to endure that very sorrow without receiving some exceptional consolation). Therefore, after he died, Helen, his most worthy spouse, proposed and promised to God—who granted her grace—to lead her life thereafter chastely, piously, and holily, and to educate and instruct her children with all diligence.

<margin>**She receives the habit.**</margin> Finally, after some years, having listened carefully to the holy teachings of preachers—and especially those things which they are accustomed to use as encouragement for the religious life—this woman of burning faith and devotion, as if pricked by spurs and set on fire, soon rose up against all vanity. She established her footing, having first received the divine virtues and having tasted a little of the sweetness of Christ and religion. She exulted and rejoiced that she had sent her husband ahead of her through death. <note>A common hagiographic trope where the death of a spouse is seen as a liberation to pursue a spiritual calling.</note> For this reason, strengthened and confirmed by mature deliberation, she received the habit of our religion in the House of Saint Lucy, belonging to the Order of Hermits in her town...

FOLIO 147

->Concerning the Blessed Helen of Udine<-
<note>Helen of Udine (c. 1396–1458) was a widow who became an Augustinian tertiary. She is known for her extreme forms of penance and devotion to the Passion of Christ.</note>

dedicated to the divine Aurelius Augustine, she received it humbly and most religiously. And having <margin>On humility</margin> received it, because she excelled in no virtues more than in charity and humility, the more she approached God through her holy habit and good works, the further she considered herself to be from virtue, merit, pardon, and divine grace. Here, she particularly humbled herself before the holy angel-preacher of God, who came from the town of San Severino in Picenum <note>original: "ex sancti Seuerini oppido in piceno oriūdo." This likely refers to a specific spiritual advisor or friar from the Marche region of Italy.</note>, her spiritual father; she submitted herself to him and other religious of both sexes, humbly and suppliantly entreating their prayers. And as much as she was able from her own resources, she pleaded for the mercy of God through almsgiving. <margin>On alms</margin> Thus, first of all, she wonderfully adorned the house of her order with all her jewelry, in gold and silver, and with garments both of silk and gilded fabric, which were at her free disposal. Then she took special care of the sick, the poor, and others oppressed by want; she sustained them continually according to the greatness of her means, and served them herself when there was need, preparing stews and foods. To all these people she was always gentle, affable, very approachable, and generous; in no way did she ever present herself as a mistress, but rather as a servant. In her whole life, she always maintained such modesty of face and speech that she never spat out or uttered a reckless word. <margin>Abstinence</margin> And although she was always content with small and cheap food, after receiving the habit and making her profession of the rule, she chastised herself with such incredible abstinence that for six continuous years she abstained from meat, eggs, cheese, wine, and oil; most days she spent fasting, content with bread and water. Sometimes she was sustained by the roots of herbs. Often she would even mix into her food either dirt, or ash, or certainly cold water. And since she fasted for the most part until evening, as night approached, she would eat a raw apple as if it were a luxurious meal. She also drank vinegar mixed with gall <note>original: "Accetuz aut cum fele mixtum." A direct imitation of the drink offered to Jesus on the Cross.</note> out of consideration for the drink of Jesus Christ. And when she was asked by some why she practiced such a harsh—not to say cruel—kind of life, she is said to have replied that she had entered religion under the condition that she might abolish the sins she had committed through repentance, fasting, the distribution of alms, and continual prayer. For a continual <margin>Memory of Christ’s passion</margin> memory of the passion of Christ persevered within her. Thus, in place of necklaces and pectoral bands and other womanly ornaments, she did not cease to contemplate the charity of the Lord with which he loved us, and his weariness, his fasting, the pillar, the scourges, the thorns, and the harsh cross. Impelled by the memory of these things, she would cruelly strike her body every day with iron disciplines <note>term: iron disciplines; small whips or scourges made of metal chains used for self-flagellation.</note>. At night, and sometimes during the day, she wore a crown made of needles upon her head; and so that nothing of the Passion should be lacking to her, she commanded her maidservant to tie Helen's hands behind her back and, with a rope inserted around her neck, drag her through the entire house in the manner of the Jews <note>A reference to the traditional depiction of Jesus being dragged during his arrest and trial.</note>. Knowing, moreover, that prayer has the greatest power for achieving sanctity of life and performing all other things rightly, <margin>On prayers</margin> this Saint Helen was daily and particularly intent and assiduous in it, with tears. Through prayer she inspected herself, and contemplated herself as if in a mirror. With it, she pursued the enemy devil and subdued the flesh to the spirit. What strength her most ardent prayers had, and what praise they deserved, her immense deeds and most famous miracles have declared. For very often the unconquered and most powerful God allowed himself to be conquered and compelled by her. Indeed, Blessed Helen always held that same excellent virtue of prayer in her heart; it drew her away, as it were, from human things and carried her into heaven, and bore her through every beautiful and sublime thing. Because of this, she was very often filled with the greatest joys—joys so vast that sometimes no senses seemed to remain in her. Her voice...

**On the Blessed Helen of Udine**

Her bed was usually the bare ground. Not a single day passed that she did not receive the bread of salvation <note>original: "viaticum salutis," referring here to the Holy Eucharist or Communion</note>; and she always did so with tears. Once she had received it, she would spend an hour in mourning and weeping, as was her custom. Knowing also that the blessed Jerome had commanded that "reading should follow prayer, and prayer should follow reading," she used such study as the daily food for her soul. <margin>Her reading habits.</margin> Indeed, she did not read just anything, but only those things that might feed, enlighten, and set her soul on fire with spiritual sweetness. There were two books in particular that she read: one which they call the *Mirror of the Cross*, and another titled *On Humility*. Like the virgin Cecilia, she constantly carried the Gospel of Christ in her heart, for which she spent time every day in divine conversation. Her tears flowed especially from her contemplation of God’s blessings and the passion of Jesus Christ; they were like nectar to her day and night, even as it was said to her, "Where is your God?" <note>A reference to Psalm 42:3</note>. From these reflections, the fires of the Holy Spirit certainly stole into her, through which—like a most beloved daughter of adoption—she constantly cried out, "Abba, Father!" <note>original: "Abba pater," a Greek/Aramaic expression of intimacy with God the Father</note> Finally, in all things, she greatly loved solitude and privacy. <margin>Her solitude.</margin> And wherever she turned alone, offering there the living sacrifice of her heart, she always cried out and said: "How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and even faints for the courts of the Lord." <note>A translation of Psalm 84:1-2</note> She sang psalms with her mind and with her spirit. And everywhere in her mouth resonated a new song, which no one is permitted to sing except those who have been redeemed from the earth as firstfruits for God and the Lamb. <note>A reference to Revelation 14:3-4</note> Finally, regarding her frugality and her incredible abstinence in food, her endurance of vigils and labors, and her many other divine virtues, enough has now been said according to the measure of my limited knowledge. <margin>Concerning her obedience.</margin> 

Now, however, it is worthwhile to explain her prompt obedience, which extends the vow of such religious professions. In this virtue, indeed, this blessed woman laid the foundations of all her other virtues. For, inflamed by the divine spirit, she was moved by the fact that the living and truly worthy sacrifice—more precious than any treasure—is that in which the human will itself is offered up. She was moved by the fact that our Lord Jesus Christ, though he was in the form of God, truly emptied himself, so that by his example all Christian followers might fearlessly do the same: namely, that they might discipline their souls under the yoke of obedience with joy. Therefore, this virtue of obedience of which we speak, this excellent handmaid of Christ observed purely and simply from the beginning to the end of her life, always as if she were a new convert <term>neophyte: literally a "new plant," referring to someone newly dedicated to a religious life</term> in Christ. By listening to the voice of her spiritual father and other superiors, she was ready at hand, never making any distinction between their commands. She never considered any of the tasks enjoined upon her to be heavy. She knew that if she obeyed the father placed over her, she also obeyed her Savior, who said: "He who hears you, hears me; and he who rejects you, rejects me." <note>Luke 10:16</note> She certainly believed that without obedience, the life of religious people is empty, and religion itself is hollow. And therefore, in all things, she always placed obedience first; she admonished everyone to do the same and always asked it of them. She also affirmed this: that whoever accurately and perfectly <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail," a Latin idiom for precision</note> kept the commands of their superiors would understand that not only could they not perish, but no snares of the devil or any harmful weapons would hurt them. 

This holy matron Helen endured countless diabolical temptations and persecutions until the end. She very often wrestled with these, and she was even affected by many blows from them. <margin>Diabolical temptations.</margin> For, so that the old enemy <note>The Devil</note> might lead Helen into ruin, once when she was praying at night in her oratory, he climbed onto the roof of her house with a great noise and let out such a horrendous voice that it seemed as though the roof were being torn down. <meta>This page continues the life of Blessed Helen of Udine (1396–1458), focusing on her spiritual combat against demonic temptations, her physical sufferings, and her holy death. She was a member of the Augustinian Third Order.</meta>

# **Concerning Blessed Helen of Udine Folio 148**

She was struck by no terror because of this. But as she persisted more urgently in her prayers—since he <note>Referring to the devil/adversary</note> had been unable to strike fear into her—he beat her most harshly with whips. And so it happened that blessed Helen turned to flight, and he followed in her footsteps. Sometimes the ancient enemy even began to infest her so that she might throw herself headlong from a window or bring death upon herself with a noose. But by the impression of the Savior's sign <note>The Sign of the Cross</note>, she soon turned him to flight. Often the cunning enemy tried to lead her to his will by appearing in the form of an angel.

This holy woman had an excellent custom: she would always set out before dawn <note>original: "ante Lucanum"</note> to the church <note>original: "templum"</note> of Saint Lucy. A certain river which flows past the town had to be crossed by her via a bridge; when she arrived there once, she was thrown into the water by the malignant enemy. Because of this, she was nearly swallowed by the waters. But by the grace of Christ, she was brought to the bank completely soaked. In this way, she proceeded to the church itself to be present for the solemnity of the Mass. 

How many times she was beaten by him with rods; how many times dashed against a stone; how many times her bones were broken so that she could no longer help herself with any limb. But Almighty and merciful God, for whom she bore these things with an unconquered spirit, never missed an opportunity to help her. 

Finally, since Paul says, *"Strength is made perfect in weakness"* <margin>Concerning patience in sicknesses.</margin> [2 Corinthians 12:9], so that God might make her more blessed through bodily infirmities, and offer her help in those same persistent trials as if to a most dear daughter, just as he promises in the Psalm: *"I am with him in tribulation; I will deliver him and glorify him"* [Psalm 91:15]. For three years, He willed her to be vexed by a most heavy disease; nevertheless, Saint Helen always bore this with a most level mind, honoring God with the highest praises for it. And when many, moved by piety, strove to console her, she responded that such a kind of consolation would be superfluous. Her state was to endure most constantly those things which Christ willed. 

Now the glorious Helen had won the victory over the adversary and all evils, so that a most magnificent triumph could be decreed for her, since she had been gifted by the Lord with a most ample reward. For while she was persisting in prayer, Christ presented himself to her in all his joy, together with his most holy Mother the Virgin, the blessed father Augustine, and Nicholas of Tolentino <note>An Augustinian saint famous for his asceticism</note>, and bestowed upon her the greatest and most incredible pleasure. Therefore, for three years, the Lord had tested her in the great fire and anvil of infirmity, so that she might shine and glow like the purest gold—to be formed into a heavenly vessel with every bit of rust expelled—and this blessed woman had labored all the time of her life in every good work. And like a good soldier of Christ, she had constantly held and strenuously performed the aforementioned deeds (which I have placed here before the eyes of all). 

Now that the race was run, so that she might reach the triumph for which she always longed, the Prior of the monastery of Saint Lucy of her Order was summoned—since she was always nourished and cherished in the lap of Holy Mother Church—to witness that she would depart in the faith of Christ. <margin>Her last rites.</margin> She received from him the Confession, the Viaticum <note>The final reception of the Eucharist</note>, and the rest of the sacred rites in the customary way and most religiously, with the brothers standing by. Equipped with these protections, she could depart more safely. 

Finally, when she had passed the sixty-second year of her life, <margin>Her death</margin> lying upon the bare ground, on the second of April <note>original: "quarto nonas Aprilis"</note> in the year of our salvation 1458, from this present dying life, filled indeed with all evils, her most innocent, beautiful, and graceful soul slipped from her body, as if from mortal darkness, and she sent it to Him whom she always worshipped and loved in faith and charity, our Lord Jesus Christ: Where she now truly lives, and shall live forever, in that life which [knows no] death.

# Concerning the Blessed Helen of Udine

...knows none. Therefore, I pray to the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who raised this **blessed matron Helen** to such high degrees of virtue, that he might deign—through the greatest merits of her intercession—to grant to me, his unworthy servant and a sinner, the privilege of following in her final footsteps. When her soul had departed from her body, and the women had taken counsel regarding the washing of it, they immediately and with great care inspected the body, which was covered in sores. <margin>Wounds</margin> <note>original: "uclera"; these wounds were likely pressure sores or signs of her extreme asceticism.</note> These had occurred for the reason that she had lain upon the ground for so many years. When they had placed her upon the bier according to custom, and had set a crucifix upon her breast, suddenly <margin>Miracles</margin> Helen lifted her head up, so much so that it could never afterwards be lowered. 

Thus, if we wished to recount her immense virtues—such as her prudence, her divine talent, her learning, her most ready tongue, her courtesy, her amiability, her humility, her devotion and her taste for divine things, the integrity of her modesty, her exceptional abstinence, and her self-rejection—we would surely be undertaking an inextricable task. 

Therefore, our blessed Helen was invited—indeed, even received—to the wedding of holy religion, where the wedding songs of the new bride of the Lamb are celebrated daily. Being distinguished by her wedding garment, she immediately wished to sit in the lowest place, according to the teaching of our Savior Jesus Christ, who said: *“When you are invited to a wedding, sit down in the lowest place, so that when the one who invited you comes, he may say, ‘Friend, move up higher.’”* <note>A reference to the Gospel of Luke 14:10.</note> And for that reason, at the end, she was ordered by the master of the feast—our Lord Jesus Christ—to move up higher, where she was made one of that number to whom it is said through the Prophet: *“Rise up after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow.”* <note>Psalm 127:2; interpreted here as a reward for earthly suffering.</note> 

Therefore, we must consider that the oracle of the divine mouth has flowed down to us from the example of this holy, heroic woman: *“The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force.”* <note>Matthew 11:12; a common medieval reference to the intense spiritual effort required for sanctity.</note> I, who have published this life of the blessed woman, pray that I may seek this kingdom with desire and reach it in deed through the mercy of God; to the great founder of that kingdom himself I bow my knee, and to her who even now celebrates her triumph with him, and reigns and shall reign for ages of ages. Amen. 

¶ There are many signs and miracles performed by her both before and after death, which drive me to this opinion: <margin>Miracles and her commemoration</margin> that I do not doubt in the least that she is enrolled among the ranks of the saints with her spouse, Christ our Lord. From these, I shall include two. 

First, a certain citizen of Udine named Helenus Calceretus, when he was most heavily oppressed by the <term>comitial disease: a historical term for epilepsy, so-called because the Roman assemblies (comitia) would be dissolved if someone suffered a seizure</term>, was restored to his former health through her intercessions. 

Also, a certain woman of Udine named Benevenuta, when she had produced no fruit from her marriage for three years, was held in contempt and was beaten by her husband. Suffering this poorly, she fled to her kin and explained to them what the underlying cause was, saying she had fled from her husband because he treated her badly. She claimed that after she married him, she never had a single happy day, and that she was afflicted with great sorrow because she was being punished and struck without fault. She affirmed she would never return to him. 

For this reason, many most honorable matrons gathered to Benevenuta, warning and pleading with her to be careful and not to expose herself to contempt and infamy. When Benevenuta would not accept their advice, the blessed Helen ordered her to be called to her. “Let no doubt hold you, my daughter,” she said. “Your husband will undoubtedly receive children from you. Return into favor with him. Place your hope and indubitable faith in God. He will indeed respond to your wishes.” Scarcely a year passed when she gave birth to a girl; this was accomplished through the prayers of Helen.

FOLIO 149
On Angela Nogarola <note>The text reads "Mugarola," a variant spelling of the noble Nogarola family of Verona.</note>

¶ On the most learned Angela Nogarola. Chapter 159.

[A woodcut illustration of a woman, Angela Nogarola, seated in a study. She is wearing a veil and a long gown, and is writing at a desk. The room is filled with books on shelves and on the desk.]

**A**ngela Nogarola, a native of Verona, was a woman of the highest learning. In the era when the pious second of that name, the Roman Pontiff <note>Pope Pius II (reigned 1458–1464), born Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, who was himself a famous humanist scholar.</note>, presided in the Chair of Peter, she lived in Verona, her distinguished city of birth—which stands out among the other cities of Cisalpine Gaul <note>The Roman name for Northern Italy.</note>. She was regarded as the most illustrious and famous of women for the great glory of her virtues and her skill in the arts of poetry and oratory.

Indeed, she was primarily known as the wife of the noble Antonio Nogarola, a most splendid <term>Golden Knight</term> <note>A title of nobility often bestowed by the Pope or the Holy Roman Emperor.</note> and the excellent Antonio who commanded the fortified and warlike town of Arco. She was a woman of truly charming and elegant physical form, a beauty which her own celebrated learning made even more radiant to everyone. She was, moreover, especially kind, approachable, and of the finest character, highly praised for the glory of her modesty. Her speech was most sweet, always abounding in the most beautiful examples <note>original: "exemplis" — historical or moral anecdotes used to illustrate a point</note>, and extremely pleasant to her listeners.

Sacred literature <note>original: "Diuine littere" — referring to theology and the Bible.</note> greatly delighted this woman; she frequently set these subjects into verse, using every kind of poetic meter, which was considered quite marvelous for a woman to achieve. Among other proofs of her erudition, she composed several <term>Eclogues</term> <note>Pastoral poems, a genre made famous by Virgil.</note> with such great skill that they could, without insult, be compared to the writings of the aforementioned most learned Roman woman <note>Likely referring to Falconia Proba, a 4th-century poet who wrote a life of Christ using verses from Virgil.</note> who composed <term>Centos</term> <note>A poem made up of verses or passages from other authors, rearranged in a new order.</note> as has been said. 

And although she was born into a most noble family, she also showed great diligence in managing her household affairs, administering everything in its proper order with an excellent example of conduct. Indeed, she always managed all things prudently and with the highest judgment. Though she lived amidst great wealth, she is remembered for using it honorably and liberally, enjoying the great goodwill of all, both her neighbors and her relatives. She was also equally intent on divine matters, being regarded as merciful, charitable, and very pious. 

She was, above all, modest, chaste, and exceedingly temperate. To these virtues and graces she added this: throughout her entire life, she preserved her husband’s goodwill—from the time she married until the very end of her life—keeping it healthy and inviolate, and living always with the highest devotion. Finally, when the end of her life arrived, it is certain she met death happily from that illness by which almost all others are accustomed to pass, having left behind for posterity many monuments of no small learning and many examples of her other virtues.

## About Maria, Marchioness of Montferrat

**M**aria, the second of that name in this work, was the illustrious wife of William, Marquess of Montferrat. <note>William VIII, Marquess of Montferrat (1420–1483).</note> In the year 1463 after the birth of Christ, while still a very young woman, she died in childbirth in her city of Casale Monferrato <note>Original: "Casale sancti Euuasii," referring to the patron saint of the city, Evasius.</note> in Cisalpine Gaul <note>An ancient name for Northern Italy.</note> to the immense grief of the people. Her virtues were so great that she is rightly included by us among famous women.

->[Illustration: A woman in a yellow gown with red sleeves, pointing upward toward heaven. She is surrounded by a scroll that reads "**HE SHALL BE EXALTED**" <note>Latin: *Exaltabitur*</note> at the top and "**HE SHALL BE HUMBLED**" <note>Latin: *Humiliabitur*</note> at the bottom.]<-

She was first and foremost the daughter of Charles, Prince of Susa and grandson of the King of Navarre. They say she was a woman of such virtue, such excellence, and such generosity that it cannot be easily explained in words. These qualities are greatly desired in rulers, both men and women alike. She particularly applied herself to the study of literature, in which she found incredible pleasure; but the reading of "heavenly literature" <note>Meaning the Holy Scriptures or sacred texts.</note> was especially close to her heart. From these teachings, she had learned to display a certain religious devotion and holiness in every gesture and word. She was so humane, so kind, so merciful, and finally so generous that from her earliest years, she was spoken of honorably and frequently throughout all of Gaul. In every matter, she provided for others with extreme liberality, using her kindness wherever she could. So great was the sweetness of her character, and so approachable was she, that she treated everyone as if they were her brothers or sisters. Until the time of her marriage, she lived among other women, and she was so humble and easy-going that she did not seem like the daughter of a great prince, but rather like a servant of a common man.

When she finally set out from Transalpine Gaul <note>The region of France across the Alps from Italy.</note> to Italy to be brought to her husband, many followed her in a manner almost like a triumphal procession; thus, throughout her entire journey, she was held in high regard and remained conspicuous. Truly, it cannot be told—nor indeed can it be recalled without many tears—how much the people grieved, especially the poor, at her departure. In their sorrow, they cried out, saying: "Oh, most miserable are we! Our every refuge and all our protection now, even now, deserts us. Who will now and hereafter bring us help in our most difficult times and necessities? Who will aid us in our hardships? Who will lift us up when we lie low in our calamities? Where do you leave us, our only hope?" 

After she reached our Italy and her most magnificent wedding was celebrated in her city of Alba, her greatness and magnificence were wonderfully revealed. For when she was about to dismiss all those who had accompanied her to her husband—specifically over four hundred people, including princes, nobles, and those of lower birth—she honored every single one of them with the most magnificent generosity, according to their rank. She gave them gems and all kinds of other most precious things. She left nothing for herself except a very thin gold chain which she wore around her neck for the sake of decorum, so that she would not let anyone depart from her without a gift. This unheard-of magnificence is celebrated with great fame in both Montferrat and Gaul to this very day.

# Concerning Maria, Marchioness of Montferrat, and Senebria Sambara.

The accounts of these women are recorded here. Indeed, under her husband and throughout his entire principality, Maria achieved no less glory or praise than she had previously earned under her father. For she showed herself equally courteous, approachable, and exceedingly kind toward everyone; but she was especially devoted to the poor. She comforted them all through both word and deed, acting as their advocate and protector. These virtues ought to be considered all the more commendable in her because—<note>original: "pace talium natalium"</note> with all due respect to those of such noble birth—few people of such character and nature are found today. 

To these ornaments of her character, this was also added: whenever she visited the towns, castles, and villages of her principality, it was her particular custom that if any petition was offered to her—one that might show a poor person in need of some assistance—she would always carry the offered document in her hand or keep it safely in the fold of her gown <note>original: "in suo sinu"; literally "in her bosom," referring to the pocket-like space in the bodice of a dress.</note>. Nor would she ever dismiss anyone from her presence until she had successfully provided for the needs of the one imploring her help.

This quality also stood out in her, worthy of eternal praise: she was never so softened by any pleasures that she could forget her subjects. For she always desired to have a company of women in her society—including both noblewomen and the most honorable matrons, as well as young maidservants—with whom she conducted herself with such modesty and sweetness of manner that no word ever left her mouth that could be justly criticized. Furthermore, her wisdom and talent were so great among all her servants and subjects that no one could ever guess who was dearer or more favored in her heart. For she behaved so equally with everyone that no woman could ever boast of being more favored, nor could any complain that she was loved less than others. 

This wise and most excellent young woman lived only three years with her husband, from which marriage she bore two daughters. One of them, named Margaret, married Ludovico, the Marquess of Saluzzo <note>Margaret of Montferrat (1484–1532) married Ludovico II of Saluzzo.</note>; she is said to be still living. But alas, during the birth of the second girl, Maria departed from this life. Her death was certainly a cause of the greatest grief and sorrow, not only for her husband but also for all her courtiers and the entire populace; they mourned her for a long time with nearly infinite tears, sadness, and devotion, as if she were the mother of them all.

**FOLIO 151**
**Concerning Isotta Nogarola, the Most Learned Virgin**
**¶ Chapter 163. On the learned virgin Isotta Nogarola of Verona.**

[An illustration of the scholar Isotta Nogarola. She sits in a high-backed chair at a desk covered with an ornate cloth. She is dressed in a modest, high-necked gown and a veil, signifying her religious devotion and status as a "secular nun." Her study is filled with books—some stacked on the floor, others shelved behind her—representing her vast erudition. Two arched windows look out onto a quiet landscape.]

Isotta, the virgin Nogarola and sister of the aforementioned Ginevra <note>Ginevra Nogarola (1417–1472) was also a noted humanist, though she gave up her studies after marriage; Isotta remained a scholar for life.</note>, was a woman of the highest learning. In the year 1466 from the birth of Christ, she passed away in her home city of Verona, having lived her entire life in celibacy. Indeed, led by a love for virginity, she wished to remain entirely separate from the bond of marriage, even though she was incessantly courted by many great men. Neither her kinsmen, nor her relations, nor her friends could ever move her from this laudable purpose of hers. And so that she might ward off all the burdens of marriage and idleness (of which nothing seems more ruinous to me), she devoted herself in every way to the study of letters. In these studies she certainly excelled so much that the dignity and antiquity of those ancient virgins—whom the past had honored with eternal praise—clearly seemed to have been reborn in her. For this reason, she was said to surpass all women of her time in various kinds of literature. Indeed, her talent, her learning, and the splendor of her chaste body—as well as her abstinence, frugality, prayers, and all her other virtues—were revered by all.

She was celebrated as being especially serious, so that in learning she could deservedly be compared with the learned women of antiquity. This is confirmed by her most brilliant orations, which she had sent to several Roman Popes: to Nicholas V <note>Pope Nicholas V (reigned 1447–1455), a founder of the Vatican Library.</note> and Pius II <note>Pope Pius II (reigned 1458–1464), a famous humanist scholar himself.</note>, and especially to that Council which it is well known the latter held at Mantua <note>The Congress of Mantua in 1459, called to plan a crusade against the Ottoman Empire after the fall of Constantinople.</note>. For she persuaded and exhorted—with the strongest arguments and proofs, and not without a great abundance of examples—both the Popes and the most Reverend Cardinals of the Holy Church and Christian princes against the Turk, who was striving to overturn the Christian name and religion. <margin>Isotta's oration to the Great Pope.</margin> This oration indeed displayed such learning, and such brilliance and eloquence, as anyone could certainly express in words. Because of this woman’s learning and her excellent manner of speaking, one cannot say how much praise and honor she received.

For the Cardinal of Nicaea <note>Cardinal Bessarion (1403–1472), a Greek scholar and influential churchman who was a key figure in the revival of Greek letters in Italy.</note>, a Greek excelling in both languages <note>original: "vtraque lingua" — referring to Greek and Latin, the mark of a true Renaissance scholar.</note> and who also had the greatest experience in divine teachings, was immediately moved with a certain admiration upon hearing that oration. In order to acknowledge in person the woman whose admirable style of speaking he had recognized, he wished to travel to Verona. Indeed, it seemed scarcely credible that any woman of his time could be found who stood out with such great erudition and eloquence. Having seen and heard her, he judged it a divine rather than a human feat; thus he admired her for her virtues, and the virtues themselves within her, to the great praise of God and his own edification.

She clearly touched upon not only the studies of humanity <term>Studia humanitatis: the Renaissance curriculum of grammar, rhetoric, history, poetry, and moral philosophy.</term> but also philosophy, nor was she ignorant of Sacred Theology. <margin>Isotta’s Dialogue.</margin> Among other things, she composed an "Altercation"—that is, a dialogue—with the governor of her city, Ludovico Foscarini, a Venetian patrician and a man exceptionally cultured in letters. In this work, the question was asked whether Adam, our first-formed father, or Eve sinned more by transgressing the command of the Lord <note>original: "vtrum Adam prothoplastus noster plus peccaverit quam Eva." This famous debate challenged the traditional view that women were more to blame for the Fall.</note>. In this debate, she defended Eve, while he defended Adam. This truly excellent work pleases many people greatly because they find in it a certain "new theology" combined with refinement and eloquence. She was also very well-versed in the Old and New Testaments...

# Of Isotta Nogarola and Isabella of Naples

It is well known that she had learned almost all of them. Moreover, she was equally studious of the works of the four Doctors <note>The "Four Doctors of the Church" refers to the great early Christian theologians: Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, and Gregory the Great.</note> and others. Scarcely anything was said by her that she did not immediately support with the testimony of Father Augustine. She also always held the divine Jerome in her hands, either because of his eloquence, which delighted her, or because he wrote more than the other doctors to holy virgins. Indeed, it could not be described how perfectly and consummately learned this Isotta was—a virgin and a truly exceptional woman. She also stood out for her inexpressible bodily dignity and was endowed with the best morals. Her manner of dress was always like that of a widow’s habit, which she kept and wore for her whole life. Having reached thirty-eight years of age, she shone in every part of her life with the greatest gentleness and grace; she was so influential not only among those who knew her personally but even those who had never seen her, such was the power of her fame and her reputation for excellent virtues. And so at last this most learned virgin Isotta reached the end of her most accomplished life, heaped with almost every praise.

### Concerning Isabella, wife of King Ferdinand. Chapter 164.

**I**sabella, Queen of Naples, the second of that name, the most chaste wife of the most excellent King Ferdinand, died in this year—which is the fourteen hundred and sixty-fifth year of our salvation—at her royal city of Naples on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April <note>original: "quartodecio chalēdas Aprilis." This corresponds to March 19, 1465.</note>. To the great misfortune of the wretched, she passed away and was carried in a royal funeral to be buried in the church of Saint Peter Martyr. She was truly a conspicuous woman, distinguished by innumerable virtues. She was primarily the granddaughter of the Prince of Taranto, whom King Alfonso <note>Alfonso V of Aragon, who conquered Naples.</note> strove with all zeal to join in marriage to his son [Ferdinand], so that he might strengthen the kingdom for his son more and more, being greatly moved especially by her beauty and virtues. For she excelled in an extraordinary beauty, as great as could be said of any woman. Indeed, she had a royal appearance by nature, so that by her look alone she could easily be judged a queen by everyone. 

<margin>Woodcut illustration of a queen seated in a garden, holding a scepter, with a city in the background.</margin>

She was highly eloquent, endowed with the greatest sweetness of speech; she was exceptionally affable, with chaste manners and full of all modesty. She took great delight in learned and well-mannered men. Worthy women and women of noble character were very dear to her and held great influence with her. From her palace, she prudently removed impure men and those of little sense; but those whom she had learned excelled in character and gravity, she caused to be summoned to her with all zeal and expense, holding them truly dear and welcome. No less did she call to herself women and virgins already of marriageable age, who were especially dear to her. She took care that they were excellently instructed in divine and human matters, with whom she often eased her cares with the most honorable relaxations. Many people, seeing and understanding this excellent way of life, asserted that her royal house was not a palace, but rather a place of religion <note>Meaning a convent or a holy house.</note>. Her clothing and the care of her body were signs of the highest modesty. Thus, before she obtained the title of Queen, she ruled in Calabria with her husband Ferdinand; but after she found the name of Queen, she maintained it with greater diligence and zeal—

...with all zeal, the King restored the Kingdom of Naples to a better and more tranquil state; for from that time forward he reigned with greater glory. ### Chapter 165: Concerning Bona Lombarda, a woman vigorous in arms.

[A woodcut illustration depicts Bona Lombarda standing in a natural landscape. She is dressed in a long, flowing gown but carries a sword in her left hand, signaling her dual identity as a woman and a warrior. Two hunting dogs stand faithfully at her side.]

Bona Lombarda was born in the Valtellina <note>A valley in the Alps</note> in the territory of the city of Como (located near Lake Como), which is subject to the rule of Milan in Cisalpine Gaul <note>Northern Italy</note>. In the year of our salvation 1468, after she had become famous for many deeds in military glory, she departed this life most Christianly in the Peloponnesian town of Methone <note>Modern-day Modon, Greece</note> due to a flow from her bowels <note>likely dysentery</note>. She was a woman born of obscure and low-born parents, as will be explained below. This famous woman was first a mistress and later joined in legal marriage to Pietro Brunoro of Parma, a most skilled leader in military affairs. When he was leading his troops through that Valtellina (which the ancients called Raetia), he saw her—then a very young girl herding flocks in the fields. She was quite unattractive <note>original: "deformem"</note>, of a dark complexion and short stature, but very vigorous. She was playing with her other companion girls (who were also herding flocks) when he snatched her from the road and ordered her to be brought with him. As a form of recreation, he ordered her to be dressed in changing fashions, sometimes in women’s clothing and sometimes adorned in men’s garments. Even in that adolescent age of hers, he sometimes put her in charge of his mules and his hunting dogs. Nevertheless, even though he seemed to hold her in contempt in every way, she was nonetheless held by an incredible love and devotion for this Pietro Brunoro. For that reason, she always endured all labors, necessities, and hardships with an equal mind. And therefore, on every journey, she showed herself a tireless companion to her lord Pietro Brunoro, for whom and with whom she eventually traveled all the way to King Alfonso in Naples. During that same time, this same Pietro Brunoro was serving as a mercenary with Francesco Sforza (then a Count) against King Alfonso. Then King Alfonso himself acted so that Pietro Brunoro [would leave] Francesco...

as she suffered more severely day by day, she ordered two very devout religious men to be summoned to her: to whom, as a true Christian, she entrusted the entire care of her soul. I thought that the virtue of this magnificent woman, so admirable, should be joined here among the honors of other famous women who were to be remembered. Although she was born in a humble place and to obscure parents, she may serve as an example to other women who excel in noble birth and are enflamed by their lineage to emulate the ornaments of virtue, from which all honor and all true praise proceed.

**B**ianca Maria, the best woman among the women of our age, was the wife of Francesco Sforza, Duke of the <term>Insubrians</term> <note>An ancient name for the people of the Milan region</note>, and the only daughter of Duke Filippo Maria [Visconti]. She was certainly a woman most perfect in every part; indeed, her divine and human virtues were such that she ought to have been free not only from death but from any suspicion of death. First of all, she was an exceedingly beautiful woman with a tall body, a becoming and lovely face, whiter than any snow, with bright and rosy cheeks...

...with an outstanding and singular grace, as anyone can notice from her portrait printed here. <note>This text originally appeared alongside a woodcut illustration of the Duchess.</note> Her eyes were also large and black, with a certain sparkling brilliance and splendor. She was, moreover, in both fact and name, truly "White" <note>original: "blancha" — the author is making a play on her name, Bianca, which means "white" or "pure" in Italian.</note>, surpassing the whole female sex in dignity and more beautiful in her radiant purity. 

For so great was the modesty of her mind that no one could tell which was greater: her internal chastity or the purity of her physical body, both of which everyone always revered and admired. Her words were not only modest but full of all propriety. However, she sometimes used wit and jests in her speech, though without offending anyone and to the delight of all her listeners. She was clearly a follower of our Savior's command, which says: "Vengeance is mine, and I will repay." <note>original: "Mihi vindictā ꝛ ego retribuā" — a reference to the biblical passage in Romans 12:19.</note> 

Everything, according to the measure of her human fragility and in her most Christian way, she always referred back to her Creator, whom she knew rewards most generously beyond human merits. She was, furthermore, so calm and gentle that she never turned away anyone who wished to approach her, even at inconvenient times, and required no middleman to grant an audience. On the contrary, she listened to everyone with such attention and ease that she seemed to embody the kindness of a most gracious divinity. 

Nothing was more sacred than her word; for whatever she had once promised, she would rather die than fail to carry out. Nor was she (as most women are said to be) greedy for collecting or hoarding money; rather she was most liberal, most pious, and most generous. She never wished to keep any private wealth <term>peculium — private savings or property</term> for herself; instead, she most freely distributed all the income she received from her vast estates to those who deserved it according to their rank. 

She provided dowries from her own funds to almost countless noble girls who might otherwise have fallen into ruin for lack of money, allowing them to be honorably married. She restored, enlarged, adorned, or enriched many monasteries, both for women and for men, in Milan and elsewhere. Nor should it be passed over in silence that when the city of Piacenza was given over to the soldiers to be sacked <note>This refers to the siege and brutal sack of Piacenza in 1447 by the troops of Francesco Sforza, Bianca's husband.</note>, the monasteries of the holy nuns were saved by her intervention and prayers, allowing many virgins to remain in their unstained modesty. Indeed, she never wanted any servant of God to be excluded from her charity. She also took great care for the poor who had died, as well as her own deceased, for whom every year without fail...

### FOLIO 156

### On Battista of Urbino and Queen Margaret

When it happened that her husband returned home from his business, it is said that he, wondering at the order and sequence of affairs she had established in managing the household, remarked: "It no longer seems to me that I am entering my own home, but surely a convent of religious men." 

At last, when a most acute fever finally seized her—from which sickness she understood entirely that she was to die and that no remedies could overcome the illness—being a woman of prudent and great spirit, she resolved to submit to death with a level mind and to welcome its coming. This was so even though she had not yet passed her twenty-sixth year and was flourishing in the flower of her age. <note>Battista Sforza died at only 25 or 26 years old, shortly after giving birth to her son and heir, Guidobaldo.</note> 

Wherefore, as a most religious woman devoted to the Christian faith, she soon underwent all the Christian rites. Finally, calling her husband to her side, she said: "I beg you, my dearest prince and my sweetest husband, if ever I have offended you in anything, or was less than obedient to you, that you might deign to most piously forgive me." Then, continuing, she said: "I earnestly commend my soul and our common children to you." Raising her eyes and hands at last, she followed with a blessing upon everyone as best she could. 

By these words, which clearly declared such a pious soul, the entire court and the Prince, her husband, were moved to great weeping, piteous tears, sobs, and groans. After a short space of time had passed, she died; she was carried out by her husband in a most magnificent funeral. 

A few days after her funeral rites, the Illustrious husband himself honored the deceased with a new and unheard-of kind of distinction. Every rite which religious men are accustomed to use to appease God was performed. For this honor, so new and unheard-of for such a funeral, ambassadors arrived from nearly all of Italy, with almost four hundred horses, for these solemn rites. Among them was the Reverend Giovanni Antonio Campano, <note>original: "Joannesantonius Campanus"</note> a Bishop sent by the Supreme Pontiff Sixtus IV. He delivered a funeral oration on the praises and life of this woman of admirable virtue, which was most elegant, before all those standing by. <note>Giovanni Antonio Campano was a famous humanist scholar and poet who served as a diplomat for the papacy.</note>

FOLIO 159

## On Barbara Gonzaga
<note>The original text uses the spelling "Songyaga," a variant for the Gonzaga family of Mantua. This refers to Barbara of Brandenburg (1422–1481), wife of Ludovico III Gonzaga.</note>

In her appearance, she possessed a lively and sharp intellect. Her speech was both prudent and serious, always seasoned with a certain kindness. She stood out for her restrained life, her incredible modesty, and a certain memorable generosity. She was a lover of peace, sparing no labor if she could remove all quarrels and discord. She carried herself with a certain excellence of mind and exceptional judgment. In the administration of her royal court, she was more elegant and splendid than can be described. She was always effective and ready in her affairs. She pursued greed as if it were the worst poison. In her company and retinue were numbered both young maidens and matrons of noble birth, who were no less distinguished by their honorable character and total modesty; she took great delight in their company. 

In all her practices, following the custom of holy virgins, she frequently visited religious temples and monasteries, bestowing much upon them with a generous hand. She was an example to her people in all truly praiseworthy actions; nor did she fail to choose a life of abstinence, as God granted her, showing and proposing a model for correct living. She was considered kind in listening and very generous. As much as was in her power, she did not allow anyone to leave her presence unless they were happy and had their wishes granted. 

Furthermore, she held all those endowed with honorable character and virtue in high regard—as much as is rightly owed to good and serious men. When she saw such men coming toward her, she would immediately be the first to meet them most urbanely and would lift them up with her hands. Nor would she allow anyone to speak with her with their head uncovered <note>original: "sine tegumento capitis." This was a sign of humility; she insisted her subjects put their hats back on rather than remaining bareheaded in deference to her rank.</note>, taking one or another by the hand, celebrating this as a sign of great and true love. She had this phrase frequently in her mouth: that although she excelled in rank, she nevertheless considered everyone to be her brothers by birth. She was wonderfully affable to everyone, rejecting no one and scorning no one. 

Her diet was primarily sober, and she did not display any of the German customs in her food or drink <note>Barbara was a member of the German House of Hohenzollern; the author suggests she adopted Italian moderation over the perceived excesses of her homeland.</note>. She felt the greatest pleasure if she encountered a woman of honorable character; conversely, she was not a little indignant if she found one who was immodest or less than honorable. 

Since she was a most fertile woman, she bore five males for her husband: the first, named Federico, succeeded his father in the ruler-ship. The second was Gianfrancesco, excellent in physical stature and no less prudent in every matter, who served in the military with great glory. The third was Francesco, a Cardinal-Deacon and an apostolic senator. She gave birth to a fourth, Rodolfo, a most strenuous soldier who was killed in the year of our salvation 1485 at Parma in a most fierce conflict and battle against Charles VII, fighting with an unconquered spirit <note>The text likely contains a historical error here. Rodolfo Gonzaga actually died in 1495 at the Battle of Fornovo (near Parma) fighting against the forces of Charles VIII of France, not Charles VII.</note>. She brought forth a fifth, Ludovico, the Bishop of Mantua, a pastor and certainly a most generous prince. 

Among her daughters, the first was called Susanna, who dedicated herself to religion because of a hunchback <note>original: "gibositatem." Physical deformities often led noble families to place daughters in convents during this period.</note>. The second was Dorothea, a most beautiful girl who died while betrothed. The third was Cecilia, numbered among the holy nuns. The fourth was Barbara, who married in Germany. The fifth and last was Paula, likewise joined in marriage to a prince of the Count of Gorizia in Germany. By all of these children, she was most excellently honored with all piety and filial love. She survived for three years after the death of her husband; that time was spent in the highest reputation and for the benefit of that principality, as she was a most illustrious woman.

**FOLIO 160**

**On Hippolita and Catherine, Countess of Forlì**

...of whom one died before she passed away; the other was named Ferdinand, later called the second king of that name in the realm <note>Ferdinand II of Naples, also known as Ferrandino</note>. Her daughter, named Isabella <note>Isabella of Aragon, Duchess of Milan</note>, is now the widow of the late Gian Galeazzo, Duke of the Insubrians <note>Latin: Insubrium; referring to the people of Milan</note>; she is very similar to our grandmother in all kinds of virtues and most worthy of being remembered. Her patience, strength of spirit, and piety were so great that she seemed to surpass all others in those same qualities. 

Her son Ferdinand, who later became king, once—while still a young man—tried to show the great strength of his body. While he was spurring a large and fierce horse to make it clear a great distance in a single jump, he fell to the ground and was nearly crushed by the animal. He lay there as if lifeless for several days. Upon seeing this accident, his mother judged that he would surely die. As a woman of great faith and devotion, she immediately fled to divine aid. She requested the prayers of all the religious orders throughout almost her entire kingdom, placing much faith in their intercession. Finally, while leaning over her son’s body, as no hope of recovery was shown—indeed, many signs of death were present—she left him with many tears so that she would not witness his passing. She shut herself alone in her bedchamber. With her hair loosened <note>A traditional gesture of intense mourning or supplication</note>, she prostrated herself before the image of the Blessed and most Glorious Virgin. With tearful words, she pleaded, prayed, and entreated that her son might be mercifully granted back to her in health. She remained there prostrate with a torn heart until his spirit (so to speak) returned to his body. 

Seeing this most remarkable miracle, those standing by with lights <note>likely candles or torches used during a death watch</note> were stunned with joy; many ran to the mother’s chamber to announce it, nearly breaking down the door. Hearing the news, the pious mother flew to her son and covered him with the sweetest kisses and most devoted tears. Affected by such an inestimable blessing, those present could not contain their own tears. Moved by this unexpected joy and the mother’s goodness, she gave immense thanks to the most Blessed Virgin for as long as she lived afterward. 

Not long after these events, she was seized by an abscess in the head. Its force was so great that it brought her life to an end when she was forty-two years old. It is recorded that she performed all the duties of the Christian religion, as becomes a Christian woman. She was carried out in a royal funeral, as was fitting for such a great matron and such a model of modesty. It seemed right to recount her beauty and character here among other noteworthy women, to serve as an example to all who wish to be studious lovers of divine and human virtues.

**FOLIO 162**

**On Leonora of Este, Duchess**

...not <note>original: "nō" — the sentence likely begins on the previous page with "she was not only..."</note> [only...] but also quite god-fearing. And where reason or necessity demanded, she showed herself to be familiar, humane, affable, and pious. She was extremely mindful of favors and most grateful to those who had contributed something to her, whether in material goods or in effort. She constantly cultivated justice and loved innocence very much. She exercised the greatest liberality toward the poor, especially those whom a sense of shame <note>The text refers to the "shame-faced poor," those who have fallen from status and are too embarrassed to beg.</note> prevented from begging; she often assisted by providing dowries so that young virgins could be joined in legitimate marriages. She greatly pursued and hated avarice as if it were the worst poison.

¶ Indeed, I confess, and I call my God to witness, that I intend to praise nothing in this <term>heroic woman</term> <note>original: "viragine" — in this period, the term "virago" was a high compliment, describing a woman who possessed "manly" courage and strength of spirit.</note> except what was truly her own. And to conclude briefly: this most chaste and wise woman possessed such grace and wisdom that in the governance of such a great realm, even among the slanderous people of these turbulent times, I may say she never received any reproach or obscene rumor concerning her conduct toward her neighbors. For very often that teaching of the Gospel was before her mind: "Be," it says, "well-doing and benevolent toward your adversary while you are on the way with him, lest perhaps he place a scandal before your soul." <note>A paraphrase of Matthew 5:25.</note> And therefore nothing unpleasant was ever heard about her. 

For she was adorned with such chastity and integrity that she never wished to speak or listen to anyone within her large house and the crowd of people without a witness being present. She always desired to have grave matrons in her company, knowing that from the wantonness of young girls, the character of their mistresses is often judged, and that one is delighted by the company of such people. Her diet was especially frugal, and it would not be easy to recount her fasts in this place, or to fully explain her abstinence and other such signs of her beauty and true holiness. 

And among other things, this was greatest and most worthy of memory in her: that like Saint Cecilia, the most holy Roman virgin, it was often discovered that she wore the harshest garments <note>original: "asperrimas vestes" — likely a hair shirt, a garment of rough animal hair worn against the skin as a form of penance.</note> next to her flesh beneath her soft outer clothing (just as it was found her divine mother had also done). This she did to repress the desires of the body and all its delays. But we cannot fully relate her continuous prayers to immortal God, which she offered for her own safety and that of her family; all these things excelled in this woman. For these reasons, she often frequented sacred places and visited the temples of the saints. 

Her greatest pleasure was especially in the company of the most grave and excellent men, and learned preachers. There seemed to be an incredible passion in her for divine eloquence; for that reason, she desired to visit monasteries not only of women but also of men. There, as far as her nature allowed, she would question learned men about the Holy Scriptures, and she did not immediately agree with them; on the contrary, she moved questions, not to be contentious, but so that by seeking she might learn the solutions to them. 

Nor was this <term>heroic woman</term> only concerned with the best discipline of her citizens—so that all, both women and men, might be formed to the best morals and the best institutions of well-ordered cities—but also that the religious men and women who were there, living less than religiously, might be transferred to a more laudable way of life. Thus, after many monasteries in her city had been restored by her in this way—in which the servants of Christ might live apart and work in all holiness of character and integrity of life—such incorrupt discipline continues in her cities to this day. 

Since she was incredibly dedicated to divine things, so that nothing was omitted by her that pertained to fostering religion, she constantly supported many religious virgins with her own goods and wealth. Moreover, she took the greatest care in educating her children, whom she saw to it were instructed in every discipline of morals; and especially Alfonso <note>Alfonso I d'Este (1476–1534), who would later become Duke of Ferrara.</note>, her eldest son, whom she had instructed in every kind of virtue, so that when he became a prince, he would know how to rule others and command them. 

¶ And although this illustrious Leonora was a woman of unheard-of virtue in all things, and was held to be excellent in her whole life...

<meta>This page continues the biographical sketches of the Pico della Mirandola family, focusing here on Bianca Maria d'Este (1440–1506), the wife of Galeotto I Pico. It transitions from a general introduction to her specific virtues and her role as a ruler.</meta>

**On Bianca of Mirandola**

She is illustrious. Indeed, she approaches every single task she must perform with great courage, neglecting no labor, no care, or study; so that as much as she excels others in power, she certainly surpasses them in virtue and industry. For whatever she does or certainly says seems to be derived from virtue; nor is she moved to undertake any task by the "wind" of human praise, always valuing the eyes of God more than those of men. 

Among other things, her praise consists in this: she believes that her own safety, the affection of her kin, her own comforts, or any prayers and tears should never be prioritized over gravity, faith, justice, and constancy of soul. Whatever duties occur to her day by day (as the story goes), she seems to perform them all for the common salvation of souls and the common benefit of her subjects, so much so that she has turned her small <term>state</term><note>The original Latin "rem publicam" here refers to the small Lordship of Mirandola.</note> into a grand one. In whatever matter she is to act or deliberate, she is considered not sluggish, but certainly most diligent; so that in arranging and managing business, she surpasses even her husband and others, not only in prudence but also in diligence. 

Indeed, she has been regarded as a cultivator of her own salvation and that of her people with the greatest eagerness and persistence. She begins with herself, restraining her own new desires, uprooting malice, and cultivating justice in all things. Christian religion is clearly no small care to her, so much so that by her example, her children—both male and female (as will be mentioned below)—should be counted among the best servants of Christ rather than as noble courtiers. And although she may not be noted for extensive literary knowledge or erudition <note>The author implies she was not trained in the deep classical "Humanist" education typical of the era.</note>, nevertheless, since she is a woman of most eminent talent, her speech is always composed when she talks. Even though she speaks in the vernacular tongue <note>original: "vernacula loquatur lingua" — meaning she spoke the local Italian dialect rather than the scholarly Latin of the elite.</note>, her speech is so refined that listeners are often turned to admiration. Her eloquence is mild, possessed of a certain very grave fluency, and she is most familiar to everyone. 

There is, moreover, in her an incredible piety toward the servants and handmaidens of Christ, whom she gathers to her bosom, as it were, with a cheerful countenance; she cherishes and venerates them as if the Son of God himself were present. For these reasons, she has already founded and built two monasteries in her town and restored others, decorating them with gold and silver ecclesiastical ornaments, in which she certainly takes no small delight. 

When Prince Galeotto, her husband, had long tested her natural prudence and noticed how she conducted herself in all secret matters—such that she was more likely to be deceived by fraud than by any cleverness of her own—he entrusted the universal care of his entire <term>principality</term> to her. He asserted and attested that she would administer it more rightly than he, primarily because she is so memorable for her justice and mercy. 

She is, furthermore, a patient and very steadfast woman, as the many insults of fortune have sufficiently shown. Though she has often been shaken by these trials, she has always endured all things with a brave heart; and not only with an unconquered soul, but she even overcame herself to attain glory, knowing it is written: <note>original: "Qui vult venire post me abneget semetipsum, et sequatur me" — a quote from Matthew 16:24.</note> *“If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and follow me.”* Indeed, the life of this woman is full of good examples which certainly compel people to live well and blessedly. 

For she already seems to think nothing of all these inferior goods which mortals are accustomed to soothe themselves with through false delight—such as riches, honors, powers, the pleasures of the senses, and the perverse allurements of glory. Being remarkably fertile, she bore many sons and daughters to her husband, Prince Galeotto. To all of them, both girls and boys, she prescribed a way and form of living—not only by speech, but by example—so that they seemed to have at home what others usually seek from the various books of holy doctors or from any teachers. In her, they found piety, religion, modesty, faith, integrity, liberality, munificence, mercy, civility, and in every fortune, a perpetual constancy of soul and modesty.
