**On Beatrice Sforza and Ginevra Bentivoglio**

It can be observed how some of her daughters, though in the bloom of their youth, were so powerfully driven by the spur and stimulus of such integrity that they turned away from the vanities of this world. With the most fervent passion, they flew toward the banner of Christ <note>original: *Christi vexillum*; a common metaphor for entering a religious order or taking up a life of dedicated Christian service</note> and entered into a life of religious devotion. 

Her eldest son, Giovanni Francesco—a philosopher, a most eloquent orator, and a man deeply learned in many subjects—is likewise in the prime of his youth and physical health. Yet, he has been so moved by the examples and encouragement of his excellent mother that, although he still lives physically in this earthly pilgrimage <note>The author uses "pilgrimage" to refer to the temporary nature of human life on Earth</note>, he and his wife, Joanna, already seem to dwell in their eternal homeland <note>original: *eterna patria*; referring to Heaven</note> through their constant thoughts and deep spiritual longing. 

These two, who are (so to speak) almost dead to this world, devote all their labors in this life to the pursuit of the everlasting one. Like a skilled accountant <note>original: *ratiocinator*; here used to describe someone who wisely calculates the spiritual "profit" or "interest" of their earthly actions for the sake of the afterlife</note>, he manages his affairs as if looking toward a hundredfold return...

# **Concerning Cassandra of Venice, Leaf 165**

Regarding her mastery of the Roman language <note>original: "romani sermonis"; the author refers to Classical Latin</note>, which is seen to bring no small honor to every field of study, all are struck with wonder. They derive great pleasure from the extensive writings of this young woman. Her speech is exceptionally refined, fluent, and distinguished by a profound dignity and modesty. These are the very skills that most clearly adorn her sex: being both wise and modest. Indeed, if anyone should think that the riddles of logic <note>original: "dialectices enigmata"</note>, the overflowing fountains of the Muses, or even the highest heights of the orator’s art could ever be fully grasped by a mortal heart, he must conclude that such a gift was divinely granted to her. 

Her praiseworthy virtue is frequently spoken of in many circles, even by Agostino Barbarigo, the most wise Prince of the Venetians <note>Agostino Barbarigo was the Doge of Venice from 1486 to 1501; his patronage of Fedele was a significant mark of her status.</note>. On one occasion, following his custom of devoting a two-day festival to the celebration of Christmas, he invited all the orators present in Venice and his leading patricians, both women and men. To these festivities, he added a third, even more celebrated day specifically to showcase the learning and erudition of this girl. To demonstrate how much she excelled in genius, he arranged for her to be invited to the holiday banquet. To this same event, he also invited many philosophers and theologians who were present in the city of Venice.

And so, for that festival, the maiden Cassandra arrived dressed in respectable clothing, carrying herself with an incredible sense of maidenly reserve <note>original: "pudorem"; in the Renaissance, this was considered a vital intellectual and moral virtue for women.</note>. There, in the presence of a great number of patricians and learned men, at the command of the aforementioned Prince, she immediately ascended to a prominent place. From there, with a brave and fearless spirit, she delivered a charming oration—a great testament to both her eloquence and her learning. she performed this with such grace of movement and gesture, and finally with such sweetness of voice, that all who were present were filled with the highest pleasure and offered her the greatest praise. Her father was also frequently present, delighted by his daughter’s great virtue.

Afterward, she engaged in a formal debate <note>term: "Disputauit" (Disputation); a formal academic debate where a scholar defends a series of logical or theological propositions against challengers.</note> on proposed questions, both in philosophy and in theology, with those most learned men we mentioned had gathered there. I will remain silent on the subtlety and sharpness of the arguments she used in both proving her points and refuting others while she debated. When the disputation was finished, she presented herself again to the Prince with as much grace as one could possibly describe in a long speech. Indeed, the speech she gave to the Prince was delivered in the common tongue <note>original: "vernacula lingua"; likely referring to Venetian Italian rather than Latin</note> and was highly celebrated by all those standing by.

She has also very often delivered orations at the public University of Padua <note>original: "Gymnasio publico parauino"; Cassandra Fedele famously spoke at Padua in 1487, a rare honor for a woman at the time.</note> to the highest acclaim. In these settings, she displayed such a flow of eloquence as neither the ancient age nor our own has ever seen. Because of this, the name of this most illustrious girl is celebrated with the utmost respect. Furthermore, the letters of this highly accomplished young woman, written to various outstanding men of great dignity and learning, confirm her sweet excellence in speaking. She is also said to be by no means lacking in the art of music. These most noble arts are further perfected and completed by the glory of her supreme maidenly virtue.

But just as our Cassandra has long devoted much labor to Latin and the liberal arts, she has also (since her mind is quite versatile) applied herself most accurately to Greek. And so that her love and study of literature might progress more and more, she has divided her time with diligent care (like a most prudent woman). Specifically, she has begun to work so that her literary studies are not only a source of pleasure and ornament to herself through reading and teaching, but also that she might be seen to benefit others through her writing. From the greatness of her genius, she has begun to forge a certain outstanding short work *On the Order of the Sciences* <note>original: "de ordine scientiarum"</note>, in which she elegantly records the sects of many philosophers. 

Therefore, such is the faithful genius of Cassandra, from which we have gathered these few things out of many. We have chosen to set them forth here so that her fame may be celebrated throughout the entire world. Nor shall her image be consumed by old age or death; we have caused her likeness to be printed here, engraved so that it may endure forever.

**FOLIO 166**

**On Saint Gisela and Saint Cunigunde** <note>original: "Seissilla Et Semigūda"; Seissilla refers to Gisela of Hungary, and Semigunda to Cunigunde of Luxembourg.</note>

...he commanded to be built. From there, through the counsel of his most holy wife, he united several nations into one and mixed them together; she herself provided the source and origin for the power of future things. For these most excellent kings—namely Stephen and Gisela—strove so greatly to turn their people toward the sacrament of baptism after they received it, that the borders of Hungary became much larger than they had ever been before. For they crossed the Danube and added the Slavs, Bosnians, Serbians (also known as Rascians, formerly called Triballians or Moesians), as well as the Vlachs (whom some call Getae and others Transylvanians) to their empire, all the way to the Poles. Truly, there was something great and divine in this woman, that she—a foreigner called to be queen by barbarians—could change everything so quickly, so magnificently, and so holily through her persuasion. Among her other sons, this heroic woman <note>original: "virago"; here used as a term of respect for a strong, capable woman.</note> gave birth to Saint Emeric the king, who succeeded his father in the kingdom and in all virtues, and who also increased the Christian religion in no small measure. After the falling asleep <note>original: "dormitionē"; a traditional way of describing a peaceful death.</note> of King Stephen her husband, who is said to have reigned for thirty-seven years, she herself survived long into her final old age; it is clear that she spent that time in the highest holiness and for the benefit of her people. Therefore, this most holy queen died not by a swift or sudden death, but failing gradually and by a light illness. When she passed away, all the people showed their longing for her life and her holiness at her burial. For immediately, people from the entire kingdom came to the funeral rites with public processions and vows because of her wonderful miracles; then religious men of every rank and dignity carried the bier, while the rest of the crowd—men mixed with women and children—followed with wailing and tears, not as if attending the funeral of a great queen, but as if mourning the parent of all. And so they buried her with worthy honor alongside her husband, King Stephen, in the same tomb in the Basilica of Alba <note>The Basilica of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary in Székesfehérvár, the coronation and burial city of Hungarian kings.</note> which they had built in honor of the most blessed Mother of God; there, both were long renowned for frequent miracles. Thus, even after her death (as often happens to the righteous), greater praise followed her. Furthermore, the calamities of certain later queens made her glory shine even more clearly and illustriously.

**On Saint Cunigunde, virgin Empress and wife of Emperor Henry. Chapter 181.**

[S]emigunda—or, as others prefer, Cunigunde—the Empress and wife of the first Caesar Henry <note>Emperor Henry II (reigned 1014–1024), known for his piety.</note>, a most holy man, was herself holy and a kinswoman of the aforementioned Queen Gisela. Living justly, chastely, and piously in that same age, she was held in high esteem among the Germans, Bohemians, Saxons, and finally all the Italians. This was because, beyond her great religious devotion, she was a kind and very humane woman; she was always easily accessible to the needy, and her court was daily open to the words of all and to those suffering injustice, so that she never rejected the conversation or the necessity of anyone. For this reason, she ignited great devotion toward herself among the common folk and other people of all kinds, so that they submitted themselves to her willingly and with pleasure in all things, and obeyed her words and commands most freely...

**FOLIO 167**

**Of Saint Cunigunde and the Young Lady Trivulzio**

<margin>This describes where the province of Hesse is located.</margin>

Hesse itself is entirely mountainous and cold, situated between the Westphalians and the Franks, stretching north from the Rhine river and joining the province of Thuringia. Furthermore, the monastery there <note>Likely referring to the Abbey of Kaufungen, founded by Cunigunde.</note> is so extremely wealthy in its revenues in our time (as they say) that many German princes seem to aspire to it. In that same monastery, then, this holy virgin Cunigunde <note>original: "Semigunda"</note> lived her life with a pure body, just as an angel might always appear. It is well known that she was always content with lighter and coarser food, plain clothing, and the most humble of bedding and covers. As much as was in her power, she always showed herself most humble among the humble, and she turned her whole self tirelessly toward the common benefit of her holy religion and her nourishing mother church. Finally, having overcome the shipwreck of this life—as is ordained for all people—since she had lived most purely and holily in every part of her life, she departed from this world. When the people heard of her "falling asleep" <note>original: "dormitionem"; a common religious term for a peaceful death.</note> in the monastery, they decreed a public honor for her funeral, acting as if they had never given her anything worthy of her dignity while she lived, but owed her every grace. It was carried, therefore, with great pomp and religious devotion to the church of Bamberg in eastern Franconia, where they buried her at the side of Henry, her most Christian husband. Indeed, the city of Bamberg itself—as mentioned above—is most famous among the Germans and is situated on the river Regnitz. Its cathedral church was founded by her husband, the Emperor Henry, who held many lands; for this reason, the local inhabitants religiously honor the Caesar <note>Referring to the Holy Roman Emperor Henry II.</note> and hold him as a saint. This queen departed on the third day of March to the splendors of heaven, where she holds citizenship with the angels of our mother, the Jerusalem that is above. Later, Pope Innocent IV <note>Pope from 1243–1254.</note> added her to the catalog of saints because of her frequent miracles. Her feast day is held among the Germans on the very day of her death, namely, the fifth day before the Nones of March <note>March 3rd.</note>.

¶ **Of Damisella Trivulzio, a young girl of Milan. The final chapter.**

[A large decorative initial 'D' containing a woodcut portrait of a woman in profile, facing left. She wears an ornate, jeweled headband and a high-collared, patterned dress with a necklace. The background shows a landscape with a castle on a hill and trees.]

**D**amisella <note>The name is likely a Latinization of Damigella, though here she is treated as a contemporary prodigy.</note>, a young girl of Milan, born of the ancient and most noble Trivulzio family in this our elderly age. At fourteen years old, like a second Hortensia <note>A famous female orator of ancient Rome, daughter of Quintus Hortensius.</note>, the Roman orator, she stands out for her exceptional character. Growing through her love of letters and the sweetness of her studies, and already possessing elegance in speaking and an incredible sweetness of voice, she is beginning to shine so brightly in that most populous city that she is considered a marvel rather than a woman. Indeed, from the maternal court, she has been called "Damisella, the best of women." Her most eloquent talent and sharp mind, as well as her passion and love for studies, have been evident from the very cradle (so to speak), so that she promises her noble parents another future wisdom of nobility. For she has a father named John, distinguished by equestrian rank and senatorial office as well as by good literature; her mother, Angela, is equally noble, descended from the powerful Martinengo family of Brescia, and she is herself not without knowledge of letters. These parents, first nurtured by the Muses...

**Concerning the Young Lady Trivulzio**

And they dedicated her to the Muses <note>The "Muses" here refers to a life of classical learning, poetry, and the arts.</note> in the seventh year of her age, handing her over to be nourished by them. Having been brought to masters and various disciplines, she immediately cultivated the first elements of learning and grammatical studies in her childhood with such an ardent spirit that, in a short time, she achieved something admirable for such a tender age—indeed, something truly incredible. For if a book was given to her to read, she would read it immediately, correctly, and appropriately; she expressed every single word so learnedly and clearly <note>original: "eniatum", likely meaning clearly articulated or polished</note> that she moved her listeners to admiration and amazement. Many of them would say: “When her mother gave birth to her, the Muses were surely present at the childbed and touched her lips.” Indeed, all the descendants of that family are born with such talent. And therefore, I believe this heritage has passed down to this girl:

### Concerning the Lady Trivulzio

Nothing escaped her: whether she happened to learn it, or to read or hear it more attentively. Indeed, this was proven by a most certain test in her twelfth year: once, while listening to a very eloquent preacher, she committed everything <note>original: "ad unguem" – literally 'to the nail,' a Latin idiom meaning to do something with perfect precision</note> to her memory so perfectly that upon returning home, she recited it word for word to her parents. She also learned almost innumerable verses in a single day and recited them to her teacher in a certain incredible order. 

But the same thing did not happen to her as often happens to many—and especially to women of quick wit—who do not possess a strong memory; for those who perceive things with labor usually turn out to be more tenacious in keeping them. Nor does she seem content with only Latin literature; she acquired a far from common knowledge of Greek in a short time, so that she now utters harmonious Greek speech. <margin>She learned Greek letters.</margin> We ourselves have seen her familiar letters, which certainly breathed a most sharp wit for a young girl and a very rich learning. 

But her parents do not only strive to present her to the world shining with letters; they already have her distinguished in every kind of moral and life instruction and religion. Furthermore, she was considered (as it is said) to be of such purity and innocence that almost nothing could be found to criticize. Nevertheless, she displays such wisdom that whenever it happens that she is rebuked or admonished by anyone, she seems to bear it all not only bravely, but with joy, and considers it a gain to be corrected by her parents' rebukes. 

From this, the name "Damisella" <note>A title for a young noblewoman, here used almost as a proper name</note> comes from her mother; for I believe she obtained her by divine gift from that excellent matron, and she does not degenerate from her in the least. Rather, she displays the integrity of her mother's whole life in every way. She has always been known to me above others for her lively and deep faith. The happy memory of her remains fixed in my mind as if she were present, as one most proven in every kind of praise. For never do I think of her among the most famous and best women without being greatly moved to wonder—they who have spoken so often of her singular, almost divine virtue, of her religion, her piety, her chastity, her character, and the many other gifts which in her seemed not only supreme, but truly incredible. 

She was, to tell the truth, a certain specimen and fragrant exemplar of many virtues at once. Therefore, I have decided to set forth her life in this place openly. <margin>He recounts the life of Lady Martinengo here.</margin> For thus her most honorable character, her most chaste and innocent life, her constant study toward me, and finally her holiness and religion, so bind me to her that I can do nothing less than commend the praises of her probity to immortality. 

But in explaining her life, I shall not use a pomp of words, but our own rustic style. The lady <term>Damisella</term><note>The author uses this as a title of respect for a high-born woman</note> of whom we now speak was the daughter of Matteo of Sant’Angelo—a man most experienced in arms and general of the Venetian infantry—and the wife of Agostino Martinengo, a most beautiful and excellent youth and most diligent soldier. After she had given birth to four children by him—namely three girls and a son, Cesare—she was left a widow at twenty years old. And since her love for that most noble young man, her husband, was so great, along with her piety and faith, she found no rest for three years; she received no consolation, but daily tears, daily sobs, and deep sighs from her heart, thinking more had been snatched from her than from any other mortal. Her sorrow during that three-year period was such (as I might say)...

# On Damisella Trivulzio

she had remained in mourning: to such an extent that she always kept her ears closed to the remedy and comfort of any friend, until her relative Ursina—the daughter of the great Venetian commander Bartolomeo Colleoni—passed away in a timely death; or rather, at that unexpected funeral, she was seized with terror and began to be torn by the gnawings of conscience. Then, returning to her true self, she began to say to herself (as she afterwards used to relate to me): "Wake up, Damisella, wake up, and finally return to your senses; for tomorrow, perhaps, <margin>Her conversion.</margin> you too will die. Indeed, you are uncertain whether death even now hangs over you." Driven by these stings, she came to me while I was then staying in Brescia—which was the year 1468 after the birth of Christ—and, like a most Christian woman, she wiped clean her conscience with the most soul-healing medicine of a general confession, accompanied by many tears. But I, after the benefit of absolution had been granted to her, began her training as best I could; I directed her, as if leading her by the hand, through the first steps of virtue: toward purity, innocence, and devotion. And soon, <margin>A saying of Ezekiel.</margin> such a sweetness of divine love was brought into her as the Lord promises through Ezekiel: *When I shall be sanctified in you, I will take you from among the nations and gather you to myself; and I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed. And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit will I put in the midst of you; and I will take away the stony heart and give you a heart of flesh.* <note>The author quotes Ezekiel 36:23–26, a passage often used to describe spiritual rebirth.</note> Soon indeed, just like Blesilla <note>Blesilla (364–384 AD) was the daughter of Saint Paula and a follower of St. Jerome; she was famous for her devotion after becoming a young widow.</note>, the daughter of the divine Roman Paula, having been deprived of her husband, she snatched up the standard of the cross. She immediately devoted herself to God the King with the best of faith and a pious, noble soul. And because I, through my persuasion and exhortations, had led her to a contempt for worldly things, she thereafter—out of her truly incredible goodness—wished to have me as a participant and confidant in all her thoughts and counsels, whether I was present or absent. But I began to venerate her virtues and her <margin>An excellent example.</margin> holiness in the greatest measure. This matter filled the ears of the matrons of the entire city of Brescia with immortal joy and inflamed the minds of many in the city to imitate her; so much so that, following her example, they began to wear the most moderate and shortest trains on their dresses. <note>In the 15th century, long, extravagant dress trains were a sign of vanity; Damisella’s choice to shorten hers was a public act of humility that started a local trend.</note> Truly, no praise could be found worthy enough for her other virtues, such as her religion, piety, humility, and many others. <margin>Her frequent communions.</margin> She took communion not just once, but at least nine or ten times a year; and always with singular humility and, as far as could be recognized, with a devout and uplifted mind, always with tears toward God. Every day, in the manner of those in religious orders, she performed the <margin>The Canonical Hours.</margin> Canonical Hours <note>The set of prayers (such as Matins, Vespers, etc.) recited at specific times of the day.</note> in addition to her other private prayers. While all her own relatives often spent their secular lives in games and other most joyful spectacles, <margin>Her solitude.</margin> she, as if withdrawn from all worldly allurements, wished to leave nothing for herself that could move her away from her upright purpose and blessed way of living. Indeed, she considered it more honorable or pleasant to work at some honest labor with her hands after attending to her daily sacred duties. But what shall we say of her constancy and her truly unheard-of fortitude in enduring adversity? <margin>Her immense strength.</margin> This she showed most greatly at the death of Cesare, her only son, at which the entire city of Brescia was surely struck with amazement. Her strength was indeed so great that (if I may say so with everyone's permission) she could be compared to Saint Melania of Rome, the disciple of the divine Jerome, in her admirable fortitude and immense patience. For this excellent Damisella had an only son among her children who was dearer to her than light itself; a youth of extraordinary character and great soul and talent, clearly well-behaved, very refined, and devoted to virtues, whom she loved uniquely as the refuge and solace of her soul. But he, when he had reached his fifteenth year of age: being born to mortality...

**Concerning Lady Trivulzio Folio 169**

...she was piously surrendering and rested in the Lord. At her death, the city was so struck with lamentations as if many of its most distinguished ornaments had been snatched away from human life at once. For this reason, a great crowd of men and matrons gathered to celebrate her funeral. Severinus was present, her spiritual father <note>A priest or monk who provides personal spiritual guidance</note>, a most religious man and a very rich witness; also present were many other solemn members of religious orders and several of the city’s leading citizens. They came so that, by softening her grief, they might apply the strongest remedies to her, or, if necessary, set a limit to her weeping. Yet, they themselves were all unable to restrain their own tears because of their great piety. 

But she, lest she should seem to have no commerce with virtue and nothing in common with reason—and supported by a mighty faith—with her hands folded and her eyes dry and raised toward heaven, spoke these words with an unbroken spirit to God during the funeral, while all the people stood by and listened: "My Lord God, who created and watched over me, a poor little woman <note>original: "misellaz," a diminutive expressing humility</note>, and who took the love of the world away from me and granted me the virtue of patience: I humbly pray that You grant me Your benefits and sweet solaces at this hour. Furthermore, I pray that this most beloved son of mine may live for You, Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all blessed souls live forever. I pray that he may finally rest in You, free at last, secure at last, and at last eternal. I pray, O Lord God, do not remember his sins, but forgive the ignorance of his youth. I pray You, receive him from this humble dwelling into Your most safe rest, so that he may live forever in the splendor of Your saints."

Our Lady <note>The text uses "Damisella," a title for a young noblewoman</note> indeed displayed and declared this extraordinary character of both piety and gravity in that very act. But truly, since enough has now been said of her religion and her other virtues, and of the excellence of her patience and fortitude, we must finally speak of her wonderful appearance and her falling asleep <note>A common euphemism for death in a religious context</note>. 

<margin>

This Lady Martinenga was of distinguished and noble beauty, of moderate stature, and of soft flesh (just as her surviving daughter, Angela, represents her). She always had a lovely and cheerful face, colored with a becoming complexion, interspersed with black eyes and golden hair. And although she had been quite fertile while her husband was living, she afterwards valued chastity so highly that, through her virtue, she not only resisted the nature of her body and all external things, but she almost seemed to have wished for the death of her most loving husband. 

<margin>
Concerning
chastity.
</margin>

Hence, I have no doubt that she would have preferred to die rather than to marry again, even though she was urgently sought in marriage by many nobles. Finally, this best of women, in the year of our salvation 1479, when she had reached the thirty-fourth year of her life (such is the fragile state of humans and a life quick to perish), was extinguished in the month of July <note>original: "quintili," referring to the fifth month of the old Roman calendar, July</note> after an illness of nearly a week. By this departure, this excellent woman escaped the frequent shipwrecks of this life, the changes of fortune, and the frequent narrow straits of her own little body; and, as I hold for certain, she has passed unhindered and free to the sublime joys of the heavenly region.

These indeed are the things which, out of the desire of a most upright soul for our most beloved woman, we have turned over in our minds. We have also briefly sketched this at the end of this volume like an epitaph for all present and future people, so that her holiness and virtues might become known to everyone. No passage of time shall ever snatch her blessed memory from me, nor shall forgetfulness surely erase it, so that she may live for me, her unworthy father. But neither in this place have I been afraid to imitate Saint Jerome, who, while he was consoling his most holy Roman matron Paula on the falling asleep of her daughter Blesilla, did not fear to use these words: *"While the spirit rules these limbs..."* <note>original: "Dum spiritus hos reget artus," a quote from Virgil’s Aeneid often used by Jerome to express eternal remembrance</note>

<meta>This page continues the praise of the Trivulzio family women, specifically focusing on a young girl named Damisella (Damigella) and comparing her to her grandmother of the same name.</meta>

[unclear, possibly XIX] **Lady Damisella Trivulzio** <note>original: "Damisella Triultia." The Trivulzio were a powerful aristocratic family in Milan.</note>

My tongue shall sound her name. My intellect shall labor for her sake. There shall be no page that does not resonate with the name of Blesilla. <note>original: "Blesillam." Blesilla was a 4th-century saint and disciple of St. Jerome, famous for her learning and piety; the author is modeling his praise on Jerome’s letters.</note> I certainly cannot remember her except with singular joy and with the immense praise of our highest God, from whom all good always flows. For I knew what integrity, what modesty, what piety, and what wisdom flourished within her. My purpose is this: that the virtue praised in the grandmother might inspire this granddaughter to pursue noble deeds. For I believe there are no greater stirrings of the soul than to commemorate the praises of one’s ancestors; a practice which has this benefit: it fires the diligent to surpass them and the idle to imitate them.

Therefore, I have no doubt that she will imitate to perfection this grandmother—the elder Damisella, so modest, so pious, and so magnificent, whose illustrious name this granddaughter has inherited; indeed, she will surpass her by far. Distinguished by these virtues, and protected and illuminated on all sides by heavenly armor, she will make the families of her parents even more renowned. Moreover, for this girl already distinguished by the extraordinary gifts of nature, the teachings and examples of her mother (whose speech, gait, and bearing are a lesson in themselves) will be of no small help. For every day, following the example of her mother, they celebrate and read through the canonical hours together without fail, according to the Roman rite. <note>The "canonical hours" are the specific prayers said at set times of the day by clergy and devout laity.</note> 

And as if she were a Sibyl <note>A prophetess of the ancient world.</note> carrying God in her mind, she pours out special little prayers to God with tears every day. And although she appears devoted to literary studies with a most sharp intellect, she does not suffer the same fate as some who seem to excel only in a single art; rather, she shows herself so versatile in performing all womanly tasks that there is nothing she sees that she does not approach with wonder, so that you truly would not know for which use of her intellect nature first produced her. 

Many things could be committed to writing concerning her many gifts and graces, but we have gathered only the more important ones according to custom, and specifically those we judged most necessary for illustrating her name. Because of this, she will live through all ages and be raised up by all kinds of languages, even despite the envy of ignorance. However, for other matrons—even great ones—who grow numb with idleness, there will scarcely be a day's memory; certainly their lives will perish along with their names. 

But if anyone perhaps desires to soothe their eyes and be more sweetly delighted by a mere picture, let them look upon the likeness of this girl truly printed here. <note>This likely refers to a woodcut portrait or illumination included in the original manuscript or book.</note> In which, even if the cheerfulness of her mouth, the movement of her eyes, her vivid color, and the joy of her face are missing, the outlines nevertheless testify to this great fact: that she is a girl of the gentlest character and exceptionally lovable; in whom her whole kindred rejoices, as if in a glowing Rose of the Church. For these reasons, a certain distinguished poet of ours, greatly cheered, elegantly sang these verses, saying:

What are you doing on earth, Damisella Trivulzio? 
Heaven ought to be the home for such intellects. 
But I know what you are doing: you do not gather flowers 
With the spouse of Dis <note>original: "coniuge ditis." This refers to Proserpina, who was kidnapped by Pluto (Dis) while picking flowers. The poet suggests Damisella avoids such worldly vanities.</note>, to be carried off to the Stygian lakes. 
Your care is virtue, and you contemplate a journey to the stars, 
For virtue lifts its companions to the stars. **The End.**

# **Prologue**

¶ **The Prologue of Brother James Philip of Bergamo**, <note>original: "Jacobi philippi Bergomēsis"; Jacobus Philippus Foresti (1434–1520) was an Augustinian monk and historian from Bergamo.</note> of the Order of Hermits of Saint Augustine, to the most sacred **Beatrice of Aragon, Queen of the Hungarians and Bohemians**, regarding the book recently compiled on **Famous and Select Women.** <note>The Latin "sceletisqꝫ" is a scribal abbreviation for "selectisque" (and select).</note>

**Prologue.**

**S**ome time ago, most sacred Queen, we wrote in a more extensive volume about all the kings and various illustrious men, both from older times and the most recent; but also about many women, and about the deeds of the entire world along with the geography of many kingdoms and regions, insofar as the history we were writing required descriptions of those places to make the narrative clearer. This volume we clearly titled the *Supplement of Chronicles*; <note>original: "Supplemēti Titulo"; the *Supplementum Chronicarum* was the author's most famous work, a universal history first published in 1483.</note> and we took care to make this work available to many studious people through the work of printers. That book—for what reason I do not know, unless it is that mortals are quite pleased by things that pique their curiosity—has been received by almost everyone with great affection. However, if anything in those pages has pleased readers, I certainly thought it should not be ascribed to me, but rather I believe we must give thanks to the most bountiful God, from whom always flows whatever excellence human fragility can produce.

From this success, therefore, I was encouraged and kindled with confidence; and I was moved (even though I have been led into old age with a wrinkled brow) by the fact that I have very often turned over in silent thought the outstanding deeds of many women. These include divine figures, beginning with the most glorious **Mary, the Mother of God** herself, and almost innumerable others, both pagans <note>original: "gentilibus"</note> and Christians, even those living down to this age of ours, which is like dregs. <note>original: "nostre fecis etatem"; a common medieval and Renaissance trope suggesting the world was in its final, decaying stage.</note> Some of these women—namely the pagans—decided to devote all their study, wealth, blood, and their very souls, as opportunity required, so that they might surpass others in noble deeds, pass their names down to posterity, and be remembered with perpetual memory. There are also the worshippers of Christ, <note>original: "Christi colis"</note> who acted even more vigorously, bravely, and wisely for the glory of Christ, and acted beyond the expectations of nature. For although a softness of nature was implanted in them, and they were given weak bodies and slow intellects, they nevertheless rose to a manly spirit; <note>In the medieval worldview, "manly" (virilem) was a technical term for spiritual or intellectual strength that transcended the perceived physical weaknesses of women.</note> so that with a famous intellect, an unbroken heart, and conspicuous virtue, they dared to undertake and complete for Christ things very difficult even for men. For these things they certainly deserve to be extolled with the greatest praises. And therefore, lest they themselves be deservedly defrauded of the honor due to them, it first came into my mind from those stories which...

<summary>This prologue introduces Jacobus Philippus Foresti's biographical work on famous women, dedicated to Queen Beatrice of Aragon. The author reflects on his previous success as a historian and explains his motivation to record the virtuous deeds of both pagan and Christian women.</summary>

<keywords>Jacobus Philippus Bergomensis, Beatrice of Aragon, Supplementum Chronicarum, biography of women, Augustinians, Renaissance history, female virtue</keywords>

Nor, indeed, did they say that among women of ancient or more recent times could any suitable comparison ever be found for her.

**Prologue.**

...the unique <note>original: "singularis"; this word is split from the previous page</note> glory not only of women, but also of all Kings. They assert, moreover, that you are by far the most pleasing and most generous, beyond the expectation of all people among other mortals: as indeed the Niece, Daughter, Sister, Paternal Aunt, Cousin, and finally the renowned Wife of so many Kings—all of whom were most skilled in matters of war <term>bellice: relating to warfare and military strategy</term> and very often won most celebrated victories over their enemies. They say besides, that you have so devoted yourself from youth to those most refined studies of letters (which they call the "liberal arts" <term>liberales: the traditional curriculum including grammar, logic, rhetoric, etc., deemed suitable for a free person</term>) that now, whether in history, or certainly in sacred scripture <note>original: "divis litteris," literally "divine letters"</note>, or in any learning whatsoever and even in philosophy itself, nothing at all remains unknown to you. From this it has happened that your speech (according to the opinion of many) is considered most ready and eloquent in every public and private matter.     *   *...nō vtiꝙ vt contra te seuiat (ꝛ tanꝙ carnifex) perdat: sꝫ vt optimus liberatoꝛ cū eisdem sctissimis mulieribus ab oī culpa eximat: ꝛ i perpetuuz muneret.* (...not so that He might rage against you and destroy you like an executioner, but so that as the best deliverer He might free you from all fault along with those same most holy women and reward you forever.)
    *   *Hec dubito qn ꝛ tandē cuz grarū actiōe cū Apostolo dicas. Que cūꝙ scripta sunt equidē optie aiāduerto: ꝙ ad nostrā doctrinā scripta sunt: vt per paciētiā ꝛ consolationē haruz scripturaruz ꝛ nos spem habeamus.* (I do not doubt that you will finally say with gratitude, along with the Apostle: "I observe very well that whatever things were written, were written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of these scriptures we might have hope.") <note>Reference to Romans 15:4.</note>

        "...has certainly acquired eternal glory for you. O good Jesus: what is more exalted than this gift of majesty? What could be more pleasant? Surely the whole world stood amazed. Indeed, for a Woman, this gift was greater than King Attalus bequeathing Asia to the Roman people <note>original: "populo Romano Asyam Attalo Regi condonasse"; King Attalus III of Pergamon famously left his entire kingdom to Rome in his will in 133 BCE.</note>, especially since these gifts were held to be of no less value than all of Asia (so to speak) was then considered to be. Therefore, these gifts of yours, most worthy heroine <note>original: "virago"; here used as a term of high praise for a woman of courage and strength</note>, display your royal greatness. For since you were born and educated for honor and glory, you have seemed to both contemplate and perform all things in a manner above the reach of ordinary humans. Very often also, like the most Christian of women, it is reported that you humbly cleanse your conscience with the most healing medicine of confession. Indeed, you are considered so excellent among us in your nature, virtue, and glory, that our own age can compete in every kind of praise with the most select women of ancient and modern times. Therefore, according to the saying of our Savior, pearls and holy things should be given and dedicated to those such as you, and not to pigs or impure and unclean dogs <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 7:6, "Do not give what is holy to the dogs; nor cast your pearls before swine."</note>. And for that reason, we thought this distinguished work on famous women should be dedicated to your most noble name, deservedly and opportunely in these your adverse fortunes; we undoubtedly predict it will be the most beautiful crown <note>original: "caput", literally "head," but here meaning the crowning achievement or leading example</note> of all famous women, provided that you are not prostrated by your many hardships. And although these writings of mine, these late-night labors <note>original: "lucubrationes"</note>, fall far short of the supreme praise belonging to those works you often hold in your hands—namely the sublime works of the holy Doctors of the Church and of almost countless other most learned men, to which nothing could be added to increase their perfection—nevertheless, even after a rich meal, the simplest little vegetables are appetizing <note>original: "post adipem etiam blādisima oluscula appetibilia sunt"; the author humbly suggests his work is a light "vegetable" side dish compared to the "heavy" theological works the Queen usually reads.</note>. Indeed, I believe without a doubt, most sacred Queen, that if you read through these lives of women with diligent examination, you will lift up your spirit, which currently lies dejected by various troubles. From these lives you will surely recognize that the pious Lord has deprived and rescued you from these momentary and fragile worldly goods as His faithful and dear one; He does so not to rage against you or destroy you like an executioner, but so that, as the best Deliverer, He might free you from all fault along with those same most holy women and reward you forever. I do not doubt that you will finally say with gratitude, along with the Apostle: 'I observe very well that whatever things were written, were written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of these scriptures we might also have hope.' <note>A reference to the New Testament, Romans 15:4.</note> If you do this, no age will ever put an end to your praises, and I, a humble man, will extol the name of a most constant queen with the greatest reverence. Indeed, your renowned gentleness and wisdom, praised by all, is so great—as is your religion and the rectitude of your soul—that the longer I dwell upon them with you, the more readers might interpret a note of diffidence in me. Therefore, now setting a limit for myself, I desire your Majesty to be exhorted: that out of your singular and innate virtue you might most kindly receive this gift of ours, *Famous Women*, and read it often; for if you do, your life will seem secure and even very pleasant, even in the midst of adversities. Farewell, ornament and glory of the female sex and of all Queens."

### Concerning Mary, the ever-virgin: the most glorious mother of God: and queen of the heavens and the angels. ¶ Chapter One

**[The text begins with a large, decorative letter M, within which is a detailed illustration of the Virgin Mary holding the infant Jesus]**

Starting to write here of the most blessed and immaculate ever-virgin **Mary**: mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ—a life most consummate <note>meaning "complete" or "perfected"</note> and most perfect of all: who, in truth, has filled the entire world with every kind of wonderful example. I fear that, overwhelmed by the weight of the praise she deserves, I might reveal the weakness of my own mind rather than representing her inexpressible and divine virtues as is fitting. Since she herself is the Queen of Angels: the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, and the dwelling place of the entire most Holy Trinity: and the gate through which one may enter the heavenly kingdom. May she be, moreover, a pattern of all virtues, a path for the wandering, a standard of all integrity: and a comfort to the destitute, a refuge for the afflicted, and finally, a port of safety for those at sea.

Clearly, she who is so great was created before all ages: and before anyone would dare to imagine. And although she was later fashioned in the flesh among us, she was nonetheless with God before the ages: though not in fleshly substance, yet in full divine arrangement <note>original: *dispositione*; this refers to the theological idea that Mary existed in the mind and plan of God before the creation of the world</note>. For that divine providence, to whom all things are utterly known and present, had foreseen with a light clearer than any other from eternity—before the mass of this world was established or yet to be established—the fall of both angels and men. He foresaw the restoration of the angels through men: and of men through the Son born to Himself...

# On the Virgin Mary

...equal in nature and eternity. Having decreed that the work of redemption and restoration <note>The Latin 'subvectionem' implies a lifting up or supporting of fallen humanity.</note> should be carried out through this same blessing, He also prepared a means that could be most clearly realized, being at once most wise and most beneficent. For when He saw that captive humanity could not be freed except by God, yet that an innocent God <note>original: "Deum innocentem"</note> ought not to satisfy the debt for guilty man <note>The author is explaining the theological necessity of the Incarnation: only a human could pay for human sin, but only God had the power to do so; therefore, the Savior had to be both.</note> without sharing his nature, He established a most beautiful and incomprehensible conjunction—or to speak more truly, a **union**—of both natures. He ordained that His only-begotten Son should assume human nature and live and die among men as the **God-man**. 

When the Divine Mind, in that unspeakable light of His eternity and wisdom, had foreseen all these things, He first conceived <note>The text uses the metaphor "in the most spacious womb of His mind."</note> a Mother for His co-eternal Son. She was perfected by every gift of nature, endowed with every virtue, and brought forth by every gift of His beneficence; in short, He fashioned her to be exactly as it was fitting for the Mother of God to be. Concerning this eternal birth...

<summary>This page explains the theological reasoning for the Incarnation, arguing that God created a "union" of divine and human natures to redeem humanity. It describes the Virgin Mary as being perfectly conceived in the mind of God before the beginning of time to serve as the fitting vessel for His Son.</summary>

<keywords>Virgin Mary, Incarnation, Redemption, God-man, Divine Wisdom, Predestination, Christology</keywords>

**Concerning the Virgin Mary [Folio III]**

Just as adults are accustomed to do, she ascended the fifteen steps of that temple easily and with grace. In memory of this miracle, the Christian religion later celebrated as many psalms, which for this reason are called the <term>Gradual Psalms</term> <note>original: "psalmi graduales." These are Psalms 120–134 in the Bible, also known as the "Songs of Ascent." Tradition tells that the three-year-old Mary climbed the fifteen steps of the Temple in Jerusalem without assistance, symbolizing her spiritual ascent.</note>. For indeed, already in the infancy of his virgin, the Lord was demonstrating through the sign of this miracle how great she was to be and the great work he was already performing.

...the mother of the Only-Begotten. <note>The "Only-Begotten" (Latin: *unigeniti*) refers to Jesus as the unique Son of God.</note> Therefore, receive her in this way, as a entrusted heavenly treasure and the riches of God's divinity. Therefore, Joseph, according to the angel's warning, took this Virgin Mary as his wife; yet he did not know her in any way, but guarded her chastely and purely. Immediately, he also perceived the power of the mystery and a certain magnificent sacrament within her, to which he considered himself unworthy even to draw near. For this reason, profoundly humbling himself before such an ineffable Virgin, he was cautious and greatly feared even to touch the garments of such great holiness.

¶ When the ninth month from the conception of Christ was approaching, Joseph, having taken his wife and the things that were necessary, set out from Nazareth toward the city of Bethlehem, from where he originated, to fulfill the command of the Empire. At that time, Octavian Augustus was holding the monarchy of the entire Roman Empire above all other emperors, fortunate in his justice and religious devotion. Indeed, during his time, a peace was established throughout the whole world, because of which, certainly, it seemed that no longer an iron age, but a **Golden Age** <note>The "Golden Age" (*aureum seculum*) refers to the *Pax Romana*, a long period of relative peace and stability in the Roman Empire.</note> had arisen throughout the world. The fields seemed to rejoice in its sweetest fruit, the seas to be glad, the paths of the cities and the plains to be straight; and all other things exulted with a certain unusual joy. ...he was recognized by his mother at first sight: so that when Mary the mother climbed to a somewhat higher place and recognized her son, she was terrified and remained as if lifeless. Who could describe this most glorious mother prostrate on the ground? What was the cause of her lamentation, or what was the end of such great wailing? Was it love for her son or a lack of faith? Had she not learned about both from his own teaching? Why then did she weep? Why were her eyes wet? Why did she groan so much, and why did she draw such deep sighs? Did she not see that the eyes of all those standing by were cast upon her alone, so that what she did, they also might be permitted to do? Was she not wasting time <note>original: "tempore terrebat," literally "frightening the time," used here to mean losing or struggling with the moment.</note> by weeping, and showing herself to distrust divine goodness? She, to whom the divine mysteries—namely the Incarnation, Passion, Resurrection, and Glorification—seemed so certain? Indeed, she ought to have rejoiced and been glad, because her son’s coming death would be his own glorification. But her weeping was certainly most modest, and full of love rather than distrust. Therefore, in this place where the Virgin collapsed, a chapel was built, which in ancient times was called the shrine of **Saint Mary of the Spasm.** <margin>Saint Mary of the Spasm: why it received this name.</margin> <note>The "Spasm" or "Swoon" of the Virgin refers to a popular medieval tradition where Mary collapsed in agony upon seeing Jesus carrying the cross. A little while later, as the most blessed mother returned to herself, she spoke these words: "O divine and illustrious sight! O unique hope of the world, as you depart from here, to whom do you leave your mother to be comforted? Is this the worthy reward for the labor endured? Is this the prize of the divine ordinance? Certainly it was fitting for the ungrateful Jew to give nothing else—he who was always rebellious to his father and will never be faithful." <note>This passage reflects the sharp anti-Judaic rhetoric common in late medieval and Renaissance devotional literature, characterizing the Jewish people as inherently ungrateful and rebellious.</note> Thus speaking together and shedding tears, they walked the path. There Jesus Christ was laid prostrate on the bare ground, nailed naked to the cross, and raised high from the earth, so that the eyes of the ungrateful Jews might behold that pitiable spectacle. 

When the Virgin mother saw this, she could hardly endure it, but afflicted with grief, she was left as if dead. The women stood around her, comforting her as much as they could in her extreme affliction. But the Virgin, casting her eyes upward not at all, was tortured more and more. Then, having moved as close to the cross as she was able, she opened her mouth thus: "O glorious head, with what a crown do I see you encircled? O hands, whose work are the earth, the sea, and the heavens—what do you hold now? O feet, bringing peace to the world and pardon to sinners, what do you tread upon now? O Son, the middle person of the Trinity, now the companion of thieves! O Cross, show yourself generous to one who entreats you; bend yourself down a little, so that I may be able to kiss the sacred feet of my son!"

Following these very words of Jesus Christ, and as she herself closed her eyes when her time had come, she returned her most holy and immaculate soul to the Lord himself, her son Jesus Christ. Receiving her soul into his divine hands, Jesus himself commanded his apostles that they should bury the most holy Body in the Valley of Jehoshaphat <note>A valley beside Jerusalem, traditionally cited in scripture as the site of the final judgment and, in this tradition, the site of Mary's tomb.</note> and observe it with every care for three days, because he intended to resurrect it entirely and bring it, glorified, into Heaven.

Therefore, the Lord Jesus Christ came to her with such glory and unspeakable splendor, and with songs of incomprehensible melody, that the most holy College of Apostles and all others who stood by the bed of the same Virgin were turned—by the excessive joy from that heavenly sweetness and delight—into a most sweet, indeed almost divine, ecstasy. Then, not long after returning to themselves, they suddenly perceived that the most glorious and undefiled Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, had now departed from human affairs. And nonetheless, she seemed to everyone to be enjoying a most sweet sleep; for although she rested in death, her face was yet most white and her lips most becomingly red, like purple roses. While indeed all the Apostles and the others who stood by the most holy remains, perceiving the appearance of an unusual miracle, immediately prostrated themselves humbly on the ground, adored the most blessed Body, and with tears and holy groans, followed the funeral rites as best they could.

¶ Then Simon Peter <margin>The funeral oration of the blessed Apostle Peter</margin>, who among the Apostles encouraged everyone with both authority and the greatness of his voice, began a proclamation of this kind concerning the most glorious Mother of God:

**On the Blessed Virgin Mary**

Although she has already been shown and revealed to all the unworthy Apostles everywhere on earth, let us nonetheless—as far as is lawful for us—venerate her according to the measure of our own humble state. Let us honor her with whatever praises we can, because as we can clearly perceive and see: she gave glory to the heavens and peace to the earth and its people. Indeed, she shone faith upon the whole world, bringing an end to vices, providing an order for life, and a discipline for the best of morals. Even while she lived in the flesh, she lived beyond the desires of the flesh, for the total fullness of grace was poured into her at once. And although I realize I am not at all fit to offer such praises, nor can I fully express what I feel, I will not cease from praising her with all my heart.

Because the path to salvation for everyone consists in the praises of the Savior himself, I exhort you and admonish you in the Lord Jesus: on this (so to speak) solemnity of the present day, do not cease from the praises of such a virgin. God, the lover of dignity and purity, chose this very virgin for this reason: so that she herself might also be an example of purity for us. As long as she lived, every form of virtue shone back from her as if from a mirror. We have had in her, as it is said, the clearly expressed teachings of all uprightness. What should we first choose, what should we reject, and what should we follow? Her first virtue was the foundation and guardian of all virtues: humility itself, in which our mother gloried. For she said, <note>original: "respexit humilitatem ancille sue"</note> "He has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid; for behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed." <note>This is a reference to the Magnificat, the song of Mary found in the Gospel of Luke 1:48.</note> Therefore, the first incentive to learning is the nobility of the teacher; then comes the reward for the labor, and the fruits of blessedness are obtained.

And so, my dearest ones, if such a great mother has ever pleased you, let the work of her virtue please you also. Her life is an example of discipline, and her morals shall henceforth be the best established customs of the churches, for she surpasses and towers over all others. For this reason, whoever among us desires any help from her must imitate her example. And therefore, my dearest ones, I ask you most earnestly: do not be overly saddened, nor let your heart be troubled, but let us rejoice together. Let us rejoice, I say, because the way to the heavens is now opened to us. From what we now know of this world—by the grace of God and our Lord Jesus Christ—we are no longer merely of this world; for even if the world once deserved to hold us, it could not keep us entirely. Therefore, the Blessed Mary, mother of our Lord, will henceforth be proclaimed far and wide—not only by us, her children, but by all nations—on account of her own immense virtues and frequent miracles. To all who follow the example of such a virgin, heavenly blessedness will eventually and undoubtedly be granted. For she alone is the one who, after God, will strengthen everyone in virtue; she will undoubtedly help those who commend themselves to her by her own merits and prayers.

Indeed, the holy apostle Peter says that the things said to us about her excel all others, for they are divine and unspeakable things: that the most blessed and glorious Virgin brought forth from herself the Word made flesh. Here, then, my dearest ones, are all the things we seek in abundance. Let us direct our minds to her, after God, so that when Christ her son appears at the end of the ages, we also may appear with him in glory. Amen.

There were present at her funeral rites, ready to serve, the holy angels together with the entire Court of Heaven, who promised their festive service. Nor is it a wonder (as Saint Jerome says), for it was his maternal honor, he who was born of her, whom every order of the heavens came to venerate. The Son himself was present, elevated above all, with the seat of the Lord's majesty, so that they might carry her most holy soul—surrounded by hymns and praises—directly to the Throne of the majesty of God. From that place, a most sweet scent emanated, like that which comes only from paradise. The holy women who were present were moved by this and all burst into the most poignant mourning. Then, with the greatest veneration, they prepared themselves with as much care and devotion as they could to lay out the most holy body and place it in the tomb. And so, at last, having been placed most decorously within it, the choir of holy women, the apostles, and many others gathered together.

# Of the Blessed Virgin Mary Folio 11

John the Evangelist, having been sent ahead of Blessed Peter **(carrying the palm sent from heaven)** <note>According to legend, an angel brought Mary a palm branch from Paradise to be carried before her bier as a sign of her victory over death.</note>, was accompanied by holy angels as chosen young men lifted the funeral bier. Thus, they carried her to the tomb in a procession that seemed almost celestial. Before the bier, those holy apostles and several others sang in harmony, chanting psalms and hymns with such marvelous melody that, from the resonance of their singing and the joyful sounds, nearly the entire city of Jerusalem was turned to wonder. Many people flocked from every direction to witness the spectacle. 

However, many of the wicked and troublesome Judeans <note>The text reflects medieval anti-Jewish polemics common in "Transitus" narratives, portraying the local non-Christian population as antagonists to the miracle.</note>, noticing and recognizing that the body being carried out was that of the woman who had given birth to Jesus Christ—who, to his followers, had made himself out to be the Son of God—were greatly disturbed. In a fit of great fury and madness, they rushed upon the group to inflict injury on the holy body of the deceased and to disrupt the apostles from their funeral duties. They conspired among themselves, saying: "If we permit this, it will result in this sect causing a great scandal and no small ruin for us." Thus, as they rioted among themselves, there was a great schism and much confusion.

While they were raging in this manner, behold, one of them, a priest bolder and more insolent than the rest, inflamed by a rabid fury, ran forward to lay a sacrilegious hand upon the holy bier to overturn it immediately. <note>In traditional accounts, this priest is often named Jephonias.</note> As soon as he touched the coffin, by divine judgment, his ill-fated hands stuck fast to the bier. He was cast into great torment and torture, but immediately, recognizing the magnitude of his crime, he turned to repentance. With tears, he began to implore the Apostles for help, begging that they might deign to have mercy on him and pray to God on his behalf. 

The holy apostles said to him: "If you desire to receive the benefit of healing, you must believe with your whole heart that our Lord Jesus Christ is truly the Son of Almighty God; that he was incarnate of the Holy Spirit in the womb of this deceased virgin and born of her, while she remained a virgin. Otherwise, there is no way you can obtain the benefit of health." As soon as he said, "I believe," and adored the body of the Virgin, he immediately regained his former health. He then returned to his people and narrated the miracle, the sequence of events, and the cause of the danger that had befallen him. He persuaded them all that they too should believe entirely in the Lord Jesus Christ and in his most holy parent, the ever-pure and spotless Virgin Mary. For this reason, that entire crowd believed.

The most holy Apostles and all the remaining disciples and women finally arrived in the **Valley of Jehoshaphat** <note>A valley between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives, traditionally identified as the site of the Last Judgment and Mary's tomb.</note>. There, they reverently buried that wondrous and most holy body in a new tomb. That valley is situated between Mount Zion and the Mount of Olives; later, a church was built there by faithful Christians, floored everywhere with marvelous stone. 

After the apostles had committed the most holy body to burial with every rite performed (as was fitting for the Mother of the Savior), they remained there around the tomb for three days, persevering in prayer, awaiting both her resurrection and her assumption. There, after a space of three days, our Lord Jesus Christ came again in joy with all his hosts of angels and a great company of blessed spirits, within a most shining cloud of crystalline color <note>original: "nebulā christalini coloꝛis"</note> which covered the entire tomb of his mother. Its splendor was so great that neither the eyes of the apostles nor those of the holy women could endure it. 

Then the Lord Jesus himself, lifting the stone from the tomb and calling back his sweetest mother from the dead, joined her holy soul to her body once more and raised her up completely. He spoke these most joyful words to her: "Come, queen of the heavens and the angels; come, my undefiled mother; come, my dove, my immaculate one, come; **for now the winter has passed and gone** <note>A quote from the biblical Song of Solomon 2:11, traditionally interpreted by the Church as Christ speaking to the Soul or to Mary.</note>; come, I say, to possess the kingdom of my Father, and to enjoy that immortal blessedness." And since she was of many and great merits...

The Girdle itself, as a testimony of these events, was held in high esteem by the most blessed Apostle Thomas as long as he lived; with it, he also performed incredible miracles. However, at what time or by whom the Girdle of the Blessed Virgin was brought to Italy, we have found recorded nowhere. But now, the noble, spacious, and beautiful Tuscan town of Prato is made famous by this same Girdle, and they venerate it with incredible religious devotion and worship it with faith; and if there is anything for which the town must pray, the inhabitants humbly process with it. <note>The "Sacra Cintola" or Holy Girdle is a famous relic in Prato Cathedral, which tradition says Mary dropped down to St. Thomas during her Assumption as proof of her ascent to heaven.</note> Indeed, the people of Prato consider themselves more fortunate than others, in that they excel others in this regard. Therefore, with such and so great a triumph, our Lord Jesus Christ led his most glorious mother to the starry kingdoms. There also, such an immense light appeared to her at once, as well as the splendor of all the saints and the joy of the exulting spirits, and this was so great that neither tongue, nor mind, nor human intellect would be sufficient to grasp it. There also, being moved with ineffable and incredible joy by her son, our Lord Jesus Christ, she was presented most delightfully to the Father of Lights: He, receiving her joyfully amidst the shared exultation of all the elect, crowned her as the preeminent Queen of Angels, and decreed that she should rule over the heavens, the sea, and the earth. And then indeed, that sweet song began to be sung by everyone in common: "Queen of Heaven, rejoice, alleluia: for He whom you were worthy to bear, alleluia: has risen as He said, alleluia." <note>original: "Regina celi letare alleluia: quia quem meruisti portare alleluia: resurrexit sicut dixit alleluia," a famous liturgical antiphon.</note>

<margin>The final joy of the Blessed Virgin</margin>

And this was her seventh and final joy, the most complete of all: which also stood as a unique celebration in paradise, arising especially from twenty-six prerogatives <note>The author refers to a specific list of 26 virtues or spiritual privileges attributed to Mary in medieval theology</note> with which the blessed Virgin herself had been most worthily endowed and adorned. From which she also carries back the most happy palm [of victory]. The first signs of her singular honor were these: that she was born of royal lineage, then the beauty of divine loveliness, elegance of character, greatest wisdom, and fruitfulness. Likewise, she was commendable for her prudence, then for her justice, for the strengths of the greatest holiness, humility, gentleness, clemency, mercy, charity, faith, and hope. Again, she gloried in the Lord because of her unsullied virginity and chastity, and because of her devotion, grace, and blessedness in all her joys and glory. All these virtues, both collectively and individually, added such a heap of beauty and joy to the same most glorious Virgin among the delights of paradise, that it was truly—wonderful to say—manifest especially in heaven among all the saints and the blessed of God even to this day. Therefore, let us all preach, dearly beloved, and with all the ardor of our hearts, let us magnify the most perfect and admirable life throughout all ages of the most glorious and exceedingly excellent Mother of God, Mary, who was truly a virgin and a martyr, although she ended her life in peace. For she suffered in that part of her being which is usually incapable of suffering <note>The soul; the author argues that her mental anguish was so great it constituted a form of martyrdom</note>; and for that reason, she has been considered more than a martyr. For it is certain that she loved God more than all others, and therefore she grieved more, so much so that the force of the pain of the passion of Jesus Christ pierced through her whole soul; and because she suffered in her mind, she is esteemed by all as even more than a martyr. Just as the Church Militant <term>Church Militant: The community of Christians living on earth, as opposed to the "Church Triumphant" in heaven</term> celebrates anniversary triumphs and most joyful days regarding every single act of her life in the divine offices at their proper times, it keeps frequent memory, which always fills the heavens with glory and the whole world with joy. Indeed, the happiness brought about and commemorated by her stirs great and noble souls toward the palm of victory and holiness. So that we ourselves, through prayers and supplications to her, may be found deserving, and finally after...

# **On the Blessed Virgin Mary — Folio 13**

...the completion of this life: that we may be able to see and contemplate her. For those of us who, because of our unworthiness <note>original: "demeritis," referring to the theological concept of being undeserving of divine favor</note>, have not been granted the chance to see her in this life, let us at least consider her wholeness and her most perfect deeds—those of her eyes, her ears, her tongue, and all her other gestures. Thus, let us compose ourselves, our actions, our speeches, and finally our thoughts, so that at the end of our lives we may be able to see that same most blessed mother, exalted together with all the holy Angels and spirits. Finally, in this place, together with Alan <note>Likely referring to Alan of Lille (c. 1128–1202), a famous French theologian and poet known as "The Universal Doctor."</note>, that most excellent doctor and most devoted foster-son of this holy and undefiled virgin, the fervor of the spirit compels me to say these things to all the faithful:

She is the **star of the sea**, the way of life, the gate of salvation,
The rule of justice, the boundary of piety, the origin
Of virtue, the mother of pardon, and the chamber of modesty.
An **enclosed garden**, a sealed fountain, an olive tree
Bearing fruit, a fragrant cedar, a pleasant paradise.
A sprig of spice, a wine cellar, endowed with
Heavenly liquid, proffering heavenly nectar.
Knowing no thicket of thorns, a flowering rose knowing no fault.
Grace, a fountain, free from mud, a light driving away the clouds.
Hope for the wretched, medicine for the guilty, protection for the blessed.
A return for the exiled, a path for the wanderer, and for the blind
A light; rest for the dejected, a stopping place for the weary.
She wiped away the first falls and the first stain
Of the **first parent** <note>original: "prime parentis," referring to Eve</note>, conquering guilt with virtue.
Restoring what was broken, returning what was taken, repaying
What was lost, restoring what was missing, compensating for what was put to flight.
Giving new joys after evening groans;
After the darkness of death, shining again with the novelty of life.
At whose coming the **golden age** returns to the world:
Piety after crime, grace after guilt, virtue
After vice, peace after hatred, joy after sadness.
As the rose of the thicket compensates for the harshness with its flower,
And as the adopted branch redeems the fruit of the root's love
With its sweetness: so she washes away the crimes of her mother
And, as a daughter, causes her own mother to be born again.
So that the pure one might wash the guilty, the virgin the corrupt, the modest
The shameless, the happy one the wretched, and the humble the proud.
May she wash them, and may her leaves bear life-giving mothers.

Therefore, Queen, hear the prayers of your servant who repents
For the crimes he has committed, and whom the monuments of his sins terrify.
Now, O undefiled Virgin, I commend my soul and body to you,
Though they lack true uprightness. **The End**

# On Eve

## Chapter Two: On Eve, the first mother of all

**E**ve, the first mother of all, was brought forth five thousand one hundred and ninety-nine years <note>This specific date reflects traditional medieval chronologies of the world's age based on the Septuagint version of the Bible.</note> before the birth of Christ our Lord. She was not produced in this valley of miseries as all other mortals are—who are born to toil—nor was she fashioned by the same hammer or anvil <note>original: "eodem malleo: aut incude"; this is a metaphor for human sexual reproduction and the "labor" of birth.</note>. Neither did she enter the world wailing or weak. Rather, as the sacred history of the Book of Genesis tells us, when God Himself—the creator of all and the greatest craftsman—had formed Adam, the first-made man <note>original: "protoplastum," meaning the first-formed.</note>, from the mud of the earth in the field of Damascus <note>A common medieval tradition held that Adam was created in a field near the future site of Damascus before being moved to Eden.</note> and had moved him into the garden of delights, He soon brought her into the light. He drew her from the side of the sleeping Adam by a craftsmanship known only to Himself, making her perfect, most wise, and mature for a husband; she was joyful in her Maker, most beautiful to behold, immortal, and mistress of all things.

<summary>This page describes the unique creation of Eve, the first woman, emphasizing her perfection and divine origin in contrast to the suffering and physical birth of later humans.</summary>
<keywords>Eve, Creation, Genesis, Adam, Garden of Eden, Damascene field, Protoplast, Medieval Chronology</keywords>
