<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Fall of Man, specifically focusing on the transition from the curse of Eve to the promise of Mary. It maintains the theological argument that God uses the very circumstances of the Fall to prepare for humanity's redemption.</meta>

# **Concerning Eve**
## **Folio 14**

She [Eve] drew her husband, whose character was too flexible, into her own opinion and error. He, having tasted the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good and evil with reckless daring, dragged himself and all future generations from eternity and the highest peace into wretched death. He secretly submerged a certain poison into human bodies. This act, namely, divided the single and perfect nature of man into two substances by a certain discord of division. So it was that while the human race was meant to have but one mind—that is, a certain kinship between the soul and the body—through vice (on account of the transgression of that command), he infused into the soul another will, contrary to the nature given to him by God. For this reason, Paul also said: I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind, and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members <note>original: "Video aliam legem in membris meis: repugnantem legi mentis mee: et captivantem me in lege peccati, que est in membris meis"; a citation of Romans 7:23</note>. 

And so, although our parents were most happy under the mercy of the highest God, they immediately received curses upon each of them from the troubled Creator, as the magnitude of the crime demanded. About these we shall speak below. Nevertheless, as He saw that death had been introduced, He soon, like a most pious father, took care to show them the mystery of their salvation. He did this so that, in a new way, the very things which had been the cause of His anger might be seen to be the origin of His mercy as well. Thus, through a secret operation, He manifested that He wished their very weakness to be a proof of virtue; He showed how much He loved them even while they had sinned against Him. 

But God, against all hope, out of the riches of His mercy, finding good in evil and bringing forth piety from wrath, willed that the seed of sinning should result in the fruit of mercy. And although He should have destroyed them and all their descendants on account of their transgression, He promised that they should be restored because of His mercy. At the very time when they deserved punishment, He showed them the proof of salvation. 

In our parent Eve herself, as the Lord spoke, He immediately pledged the help of His mercy to all descendants. He immediately made public a sacrament unknown even to the angels, which was to be fulfilled in the final age: from the earthly Adam, He promised an Adam from heaven. For when He cursed the serpent for its crime, He first commanded it to have the earth for food; then, because the serpent had been the first to cause that death, He added: I will put enmities between you and the seed of the woman. She indeed shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel <note>original: "Et ponam inimicitias inter te et semen mulieris. Ipsa quppe caput tuum calcabit: et tu eius observabis calcaneum"; a variation of Genesis 3:15</note>. 

From these words, even in the woman Eve, it is now implied to us that Mary, the mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, was promised, she who was set against the enmities of the serpent. "I will put," He says, "enmities between you and the woman." He certainly does not say "I put," <note>original: "pono"</note> lest this should seem to pertain only to this Eve here. It is a word of promise—as Saint Jerome <note>Hieronymus, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> reports—which refers to the future: "I will put," He says, "enmities between you and the woman." I speak indeed of that woman who might give birth to the Savior, not she who bore a <term>fratricide</term> <note>referring to Cain, who killed his brother Abel</note>. 

"I will put," He says—that is, "I will raise up a woman"—who will not only listen to you like this Eve, who was easy and too credulous, but even when Gabriel himself brings the message, she will raise a rational inquiry about the novelty of the promise, saying: How shall this be, since I know not a man? <note>original: "Quomodo erit istud: quoniam virum non cognovi"; the Virgin Mary's response to the Angel in Luke 1:34</note>. That holy woman indeed, whom modesty made to tremble at the ears at the vision of the angel, yet whom the fire and constancy of faith—knowing not how to fall—made bold to inquire the reason. And she who had stood silent out of modesty before the one arriving, did not cease out of wonder toward the one making the promise. 

For, anxious about that which was being announced, she inquired. To whom the Angel said: The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you <note>original: "Spiritus sanctus superueniet in te: et virtus altissimi obumbzabit tibi"; from Luke 1:35</note>. Behold, for that is the "seed of the woman" which is not infused into the body as a slave through the act of sexual union, but is found in the womb while the enclosure of virginity remains closed. Therefore, that very "seed" of this most holy virgin was our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to the flesh had no human father. Finally, He added, saying: And...

# **Concerning Sarah**

"She herself shall crush your head." <note>original: "ipsa tuū calcabit caput"; this is a Latin rendering of Genesis 3:15, which medieval theologians often interpreted as a prophecy of the Virgin Mary or Christ defeating the devil.</note> And who could doubt this? For no one except our Lord has crushed the head of the serpent; He alone walked upon **dragons and scorpions** and led all captivity captive. And that which follows: "And you shall lie in wait for his heel"—to what else do we believe this pertains, if not to the future resurrection of man? For we say the "heel" pertains to the final trace of a man. The Lord made Adam and Eve as parents similar to Himself—that is, in His own image. Since He made them so, they shall be similar to Him again when they rise from the dead. For whatever now appears in us that is unlike our Creator is entirely impressed upon us by the sin of the transgression of our first parents. 

Indeed, that lying craftsman <note>The Devil.</note> has, through his deceptions, deformed the living shape of man; he ascribes his own depravity to our members while he corrupts our minds. All of these things shall at last be washed away through the glory of the resurrection, by the Lord's own piety and the glorious intercession of his Virgin Mother. Then, only that which reflects the Creator of all things—as if in a mirror—will shine forth. Thus, the Enemy himself, the inventor of death, shall grieve to see his work destroyed, and man shall finally glory in being whole again. Yet not everyone shall experience this; only the righteous shall be in the light. For we shall all indeed rise again, but we shall not all be changed. The very distinction of persons will surely create a diversity of merit.

Returning then to **Eve**: I say that after she was greatly rebuked, the Lord immediately sent her out from that delightful place <note>Eden.</note> into anxious labors, together with our <term>protoplast</term> <note>From the Greek "first-formed," referring to Adam.</note> clothed in girdles of leaves, amidst mountains and brambles. When they had finally arrived as weary exiles in the field of **Hebron**, that excellent woman (as some believe) began to work the earth with a distaff while her husband turned the soil with a hoe. And there (as **Methodius the Martyr** <note>Methodius of Olympus, a 3rd-century Christian author.</note> writes) she gave birth to one hundred children with unbearable pains. She endured many other labors, cold, and many other inconveniences of this life until her old age. When she finally reached the death foretold to her by the Lord, she was buried in that place where the Lord was crucified, alongside her husband.

## **Chapter Three: Concerning Saint Sarah, Wife of Abraham**

[Large decorative initial S] **Sarah**, a Hebrew woman and wife of the great patriarch **Abraham**, was a woman of unconquerable faith and love toward God and her husband. She was also a woman of remarkable beauty. In the year 1878 <note>original: "septuagesimo octauo supra millesimū ⁊ octigētesimū"; medieval chronologies often dated biblical events from the creation of the world or relative to the birth of Christ.</note> before the coming of Christ our Lord, having lived one hundred and twenty-seven years, she died a most holy death in the province of **Canaan** in Syria. Her husband **Abraham**, a pilgrim in that land, buried her in **Hebron** (with the permission of the Canaanites) after a most pious mourning of his marital love. 

->[Illustration: A woman (Sarah) standing in a landscape, wearing a red cloak over a yellow dress, with a halo, holding an open book.]<-

Once she was dead, the righteous **Abraham** immediately wished to purchase a field there from a certain **Ephron the Hittite** for four hundred shekels of tested money. In this field, he established tombs not only for his deceased wife but also for himself and his descendants. **Sarah** had as her father **Haran**, the son of the patriarch **Terah**; Haran was the brother of **Abraham** and **Nahor**. After their father Haran died among the Chaldeans, leaving behind his son **Lot** and daughters **Sarah** and **Milcah**, **Abraham** took this **Sarah** as his wife, and **Nahor** took **Milcah**. Thus **Sarah** was famous among all the distinguished women of her age, both for her singular form and beauty, and for her devotion to God...

**On Semiramis** **Folio XVII**

By pretending to be her son <note>According to legend, Semiramis disguised herself as her young son, Ninyas, to secure the throne after her husband's death, as the people might not have accepted a woman's rule</note> and through wondrous diligence, she attained royal majesty. # Concerning Juno

**J**uno was the daughter of Saturn and the previously mentioned Ops (or Rhea). In the songs of the poets, she is proclaimed throughout the entire world as the most celebrated among all women tainted by the stain of paganism. <note>original: "gentilitatis labe infectis" — the author uses this phrase to distance the Christian reader from the "error" of worshipping these historical figures as gods.</note> During the time of the patriarch Jacob, her name became most well-known among the heathens. Of her, we can certainly recount her remarkable good fortune rather than report any memorable deed, for she was born at the same birth and raised alongside that Cretan Jupiter (whom the ancients falsely imagined to be the god of heaven). From her infancy, she was sent to the island of Samos, where she was educated with all possible care.

[Illustration: A woman (Juno) standing in a landscape, wearing a crown-like helmet and a blue garment decorated with peacock eyes over a red dress. <note>The peacock is the traditional symbol of Juno; its "eyes" were said to be the eyes of the hundred-eyed giant Argus, placed on the feathers by the goddess.</note> She holds a spear in her right hand. To her right, an open book rests on a stand.]

At last, when she had reached the age of maturity, she was married to her brother Jupiter. This union was attested for many centuries by her statue in the temple of the Samians. For the Samians—thinking it brought no small glory to themselves and their descendants that Juno had been raised and betrothed among them—considered her the queen of heaven and a goddess. So that her memory would not fade, they built a massive and wonderful temple to her. They dedicated it to her <term>Numen (a Latin term for a deity's divine power or presiding spirit)</term> and sculpted her image from the whitest marble in the attire of a young bride, and placed it within their temple. Having married such a great king, and with her fame and empire increasing daily and carrying her name far and wide, she herself achieved a great deal of splendor. Indeed, she was eventually made the "Queen of Heaven" through the fictions of poets and the reckless <note>original: "insana" — meaning "insane" or "excessive."</note> imagination of the ancients.

--- Page 110 ---
**FOLIO XVIII**

**About Isis**

That she was changed into a cow <note>original: "vacca"</note> by Juno, tormented by a gadfly <note>original: "oestrum," a biting fly sent by Juno to harass Io/Isis</note>, and carried in a rapid course to Egypt, where she recovered her human form and was thereafter called Isis, does not differ much from historical truth. For there are those who assert that she was a maiden oppressed by the adulterous Jupiter; because of this crime, and driven by fear of her father, she boarded a ship with some of her followers. This ship had a cow as its figurehead <note>original: "vacha insignem"</note>. Being a woman of great talent and driven by a desire to rule, she sailed with a favorable wind to the Egyptians. 

Having arrived there, she was delighted by the region and settled down. When she discovered that the people of that land were unrefined and uneducated, ignorant of almost all human affairs and living more like beasts than men, she taught them with great labor and renowned industry how to till the earth and commit seeds to the cultivated soil. Eventually, she taught them how to process the harvested crops into food or bread. Furthermore, she gathered those wild and wandering people into a single community and gave them laws so they might live in a civilized manner. 

And—what is far more remarkable in a woman—she invented letters <margin>The original inventor of Egyptian letters</margin> suited to their language and showed the men most capable of learning how to join them in order. These things appeared so marvelous to those unaccustomed to them that they easily believed she had fallen from heaven. For this reason, they established divine honors for her. After her death, however, and by the persuasion of the devil, she rose to such veneration that not only did the Egyptians establish sacred rites for her every year, but the Romans and other nations also built grand temples to her. The husband of this famous woman was King Apis, who ruled with Isis for many years. There are some, however, who say a certain Theglonus was the husband of this Isis, and that he fathered Epaphus by her, who later ruled the Egyptians. Concerning this woman, the ancient poets invented many fictions which do not pertain to history.

**About Ceres, goddess of grain, chapter 9.**

**C**eres, the great queen of the Sicilians and daughter of King Saturn <note>original: "Celi," referring to the lineage of Coelus/Saturn</note>, was held in great esteem among the Sicilians at the same time as the aforementioned Isis. After she was first joined in marriage to Sicanus, the king of the Sicilians, she showed such great talent there that when she had devised the cultivation of fields, she was the first among them to tame oxen <margin>The first inventor of taming oxen</margin>, accustom them to the yoke, and invent the plow <margin>The first inventor of the plow</margin> and the plowshare with which to cut the earth. She was the first to begin committing seeds to the furrows. 

When these had grown into a most ample harvest, she taught them how to remove the grain from the ears, grind it with stones, make bread, and use it for food <margin>The first inventor of bread-making</margin>—teaching people who were accustomed to eating acorns <note>original: "glandibus"</note> and wild fruits. Because of this merit, though she was a mortal woman, the Sicilians considered her the goddess of grain and exalted her with divine honors, believing her to be the daughter of Saturn and Cybele. They say she had only one daughter, Proserpina, by Jupiter, whom Orcus <note>Pluto, the god of the Underworld</note>, the king of the Molossians, stole away in secret. When Ceres had searched for her for a long time, the ancient poets fashioned many fables about it.

## **On Marpesia** **FOLIO 19**

...care which is ours. For, having cast aside the distaff <note>The distaff and wool-baskets were traditional symbols of domestic female labor.</note>, wool-baskets, and other womanly tasks, they hardened the younger girls with hunting, roaming, the taming of horses, the constant labor of arms, archery, and similar exercises. Through these skills, they developed a masculine strength and a fitness by which they not only held the Scythian <note>original: "Cyrios"</note> fields once occupied by their ancestors, but indeed, having acquired a huge part of Europe by right of war, they occupied much of Asia and became formidable to all. 

Truly, lest their strength lack leadership, they appointed **Marpesia** and **Lampedo** as their Queens above others after their husbands had been slain. Under their auspices, they greatly increased their empire. Nor were they anything less than distinguished in military discipline, having divided the provinces between them so that while one remained for the protection of the kingdom, the other, taking a portion of the forces, proceeded to subjugate their neighbors to their empire. And so, by turns, having taken the greatest spoils, they increased their commonwealth for some time. But when Lampedo had finally led the army against the enemies, by a sudden incursion of the surrounding barbarians, Marpesia—being too trusting in herself—was slain along with a portion of her forces, leaving behind some daughters. However, what became of her sister Lampedo is found nowhere. Nevertheless, many assert that these Queens lived long before the time of Jacob, as we also mentioned in the second book of our chronicles.

### **On Hypermnestra, the most excellent wife of King Lynceus. Chapter 11.**

[Woodcut illustration of a woman in a crown and regal dress holding a scepter, standing in a landscape with trees and a castle in the distance.]

**H**ypermnestra, daughter of Danaus, King of the Argives, and wife of King Lynceus, was very famous for her lineage, dignity, and piety during the times of Moses the Prophet. For, as we wrote in the third book of our chronicles, Danaus and Aegyptus <note>original: "egistus"</note> were brothers, notable sons of Belus <note>original: "prisci," likely referring to Belus the Ancient</note>, and preeminent in power. The fortune of their offspring was not equal, even if the number was the same: for Danaus had fifty daughters, and Aegyptus just as many male sons. 

Truly, since Danaus had received an oracle <term>oracle: a divine prophecy, often cryptic</term> that he was to be killed by the hand of a grandson, he was greatly tormented by fear as to whose hands, out of such a great multitude of daughters, he should hold suspect. It happened that all of his daughters were joined in marriage with the sons of Aegyptus. When his daughters were betrothed to his nephews—namely, the sons of Aegyptus—and as Danaus prepared the marriage rites, he strictly warned all his daughters that if they wished for his safety, each one should pierce her husband with a sword on the first night, when she knew him to be bound in heavy sleep. 

All of them, having secretly brought swords into their bedrooms, killed the young men while they were sluggish with wine <note>original: "crapula"</note> at their father’s command. But Hypermnestra alone abstained. She had already turned her heart toward her bridegroom; immediately, as she had seen him, she began to love him. And for this reason, in the manner of a young girl, she felt compassion for him and, with great praise, abstained from the deadly slaughter. She urged the young man to flee, by which he escaped death. But in the morning, while the others applauded the crime they had committed, Hypermnestra alone wept for a time; having been rebuked and shut in prison, she wept for her pious deed for a long while. Truly, after that cruel and ferocious old man had reigned for fifty years, by the just [judgment] of God...

# **On Hypermnestra and Diana**

She could not escape the judgment of the hand of Lynceus, her nephew <note>original: "nepotis"; in this context, Lynceus is her cousin and brother-in-law, though "nepos" often refers to a nephew or grandson</note>, who did not hesitate to spill that harmful blood of hers, which he could have redeemed with the blood of many nephews. Danaus, finally driven and put to flight from his kingdom, crossed the sea into Greece; then, the kingdom of the Argives was occupied by the talent and strength of Lynceus. He reigned there in place of his uncle Danaus, and mindful of the man's cruelty, he slew him with a sword. Having led Hypermnestra out of prison, he joined her to himself in a marriage of higher honor than any other woman, making her a partner in the kingdom. She not only shone as a queen but was made a priestess of Argive Juno, appearing adorned with a double brilliance of splendor. And while her sisters had fallen into foul infamy, she herself, on account of her commendable devotion <note>original: "pietatem"; here meaning duty to her husband and family moral law</note>, sent her name down to us, distinguished and worthy of all praise. But Danaus, who had sought to extend his own trembling years with the blood of so many nephews, stripped himself of a robust and splendid line of descendants and defiled himself with everlasting infamy.

### **¶ On Diana, who is also the Moon: Chapter 12.**

Diana, who is also called the Moon, was the sister of Delphic Apollo and the daughter of the second Jupiter by Latona. She lived during the times of the Egyptian servitude <note>A reference to the period when the Israelites were enslaved in Egypt, used here as a chronological marker</note>—that is, in the year 1596 before the coming of Christ our Lord. She was most highly distinguished at Delphi for her perpetual virginity. And although Cicero, in *The Nature of the Gods*, says there were many Dianas, he writes that this one was the most excellent and famous. To her, all honors are attributed. Because of her love of virginity, she spurned the company of men and sought out the forests, where she devoted much labor to hunting. For this reason, the ancients depicted her with a bow and a quiver. They called her the goddess of the groves and mountains, and they wished her to use a chariot drawn by white deer. Because of this, many virgins followed her in a similar fashion, which led people to say she enjoyed the company and service of Nymphs. They further desired her to be a protector of the roads, and along with the Moon, they called her by many names.

For she was a woman who, in the manner of the nuns <note>original: "sanctimonialium"; Boccaccio compares the ancient followers of Diana to contemporary Christian nuns</note> of our own age, utterly renounced the itch of lust. Therefore, the foolish opinion of the pagans <note>original: "gentilium"</note> called her the Moon, because she seemed to correspond perfectly to the planet of the Moon. ¶ For the Moon, by its coldness, is said to restrain carnal desires and to illuminate the groves and mountains by night with its light; thus, these things were seen as pertaining to the Moon, as if she herself were the Moon. She killed Orion, the son of Neptune, when he wished to violate her. On account of this, sacred sacrifices of human flesh were made to her. She had a wonderful temple at Ephesus, frequented with great crowds and religious devotion. She was also greatly invoked by those in labor, because Servius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> writes that as soon as she was born, she performed the office of a midwife for her mother in the birth of her brother Apollo.

### ¶ Chapter 17: On Medea, Queen of the Colchians

->[Woodcut illustration: A queen, Medea, stands within a rugged landscape, holding a scepter in one hand and a leafy branch in the other, likely a reference to her expertise in herbalism and sorcery.]<-

The life of Medea, Queen of the Colchians—who lived in the times of the aforementioned Sibyl—is certainly not to be counted among the illustrious women. However, I thought it should be written down as a warning for many women who do not know how to restrain their eyes from harmful gazes. For from their impudence, many evils often arise, as we can clearly gather from this lesson. Thus, this Medea was a most cruel example of ancient treachery. She had Aeëtes <note>original: "Oetam"</note>, the most renowned King of the Colchians, as her father, and her mother was Persa, the king's own wife. She was beautiful enough, but wicked in every kind of evil deed. No matter who her teacher might have been, she emerged so fully learned that no one surpassed her. Indeed, she was so familiar with the powers of herbs and fully knew their properties that, by chanting certain spells, she could disturb the sky, summon winds from their caves, stir up storms, stop rivers, and prepare all sorts of poisons at her pleasure. She also knew how to compose elaborate fires <note>A reference to "Greek fire" or magical combustibles</note> for any conflagration, and all such things. 

<margin>The virtue and excellence of Jason</margin>
Nor was her mind at all different from her arts, being far worse; for when her spells failed, she thought nothing of using the sword. She fell ardently in love with Jason the Thessalian, a young man conspicuous in that age for his valor. Jason had been sent to Colchis by his uncle Pelias—who was plotting against his integrity—under the pretext of a most glorious expedition to steal the Golden Fleece. Captured by his excellence, she loved him passionately. To earn his favor, she acted so that a rebellion arose among the inhabitants, inciting war against her father; thus, time was granted for Jason to achieve his vow. What sensible person would even imagine that from a single glance of the eyes, the destruction of a most wealthy king would follow? 

<margin>The wicked deed of the woman</margin>
Therefore, having committed that crime, when she had earned the embraces of the beloved youth, she fled secretly with him, taking her country’s entire wealth with her. Not content with such a great outrage, she turned her cruel mind to something even worse. Thinking that Aeëtes would follow the fugitives, she ordered her young brother Absyrtus <note>original: "Egyaleum"</note>—whom she had brought with her as a companion in this flight—to be butchered on the island of Tomi on the Phasis river, through which the pursuer was to pass. She ordered his limbs to be scattered here and there across the fields, so that while the miserable father collected the scattered remains and [shed] tears over them...

          **Of Orithia, Queen of the Amazons, Chapter 18.**

**O**rithia was the daughter of Queen Marpesia. During the times of the three aforementioned women <note>likely referring to previous Amazon queens</note>, she successfully succeeded her mother in the kingdom of the Amazons.

She was truly a woman distinguished among others by her perpetual virginity and most highly to be commended. When Orithia heard that Theseus, the companion of the expedition, had carried off Hippolyta, she dared to provoke war against all Greece by summoning allies. But on account of dissension, having been deserted by her allies and overcome by the Athenians, she returned to her kingdom; nor is it found what she did further.

# Concerning Argia

[Decorative initial A with floral and geometric patterns] **Argia** was a Greek woman and was born from the lineage of the kings of Argos, the daughter of King Adrastus <note>Adrastus was the King of Argos and one of the leaders of the famous 'Seven against Thebes' expedition</note>. # Concerning Manto                              FOLIO XXIII

### ¶ Chapter 20: Concerning Manto, daughter of Tiresias.

->[Woodcut illustration of a woman (Manto) in a landscape, holding a staff and a shield bearing the likeness of a face.]<-

**Manto**, the daughter of Tiresias—the greatest prophet of the Thebans—lived during the time of Tola, Judge of the Hebrews <note>Tola is a biblical figure from the Book of Judges, traditionally dated to the 12th century BCE</note>, and one thousand two hundred and thirty-seven years before the coming of our Lord Christ. She was highly distinguished and famous for many virtues. Under the mastery and teaching of her father, she possessed a mind so ready and capable that she learned **pyromancy** <term>divination by observing fire</term> and **necromancy** <term>the practice of communicating with the dead</term>—the ancient invention of King Zoroaster—so excellently that in her time no one better understood the movements and heat of flames. She also understood the "murmurings" through which, by some diabolical work, it is said that demonstrations of the future can be known. Furthermore, she knew the fibers and entrails of cattle and other beasts with a sharp intuition. It is believed that she very often used her arts to draw forth <note>original: "spūs imundos" — literally 'unclean spirits'</note> and compelled the shades of the underworld into voices, forcing them to give answers to those who sought them.

Truly, when the Argive kings who had besieged Thebes had fallen in war and occupied the Imperial city, Manto, fearing the new king, fled into Asia <note>Asia Minor, or modern-day Turkey</note>. There, through her powers of divination, she established the shrine of Apollo, which later became very famous, and she gave birth to Mopsus, the renowned diviner; however, it is not known by whom she conceived him. Others, however, holding a different view, say that after the Theban war she wandered for a long time with certain of her companions and finally arrived in Italy. There, joined to a certain Tyberinus, she conceived and gave birth to a son whom they called Cytheonus, though he was called Bianor by some. From there, she herself crossed into Cisalpine Gaul. <margin>The founding of the city of Mantua</margin> When she reached the marshy places bordering Lake Benacus <note>modern-day Lake Garda</note>, she sought a place where she could be most hidden—either to be more free to devote herself to her incantations, or to lead the remainder of her life more securely. She established her seat in the swamp upon a place rising above the waters. Finally, she died and was buried in that same spot. They say that around her tomb, Cytheonus built a small city for his people and called it **Mantua** after his mother’s name. Yet some others affirm differently: namely, that she preserved her virginity unsullied until death, but that she built the city of Mantua herself and named it after her own name.

### ¶ Chapter 21: Concerning Medusa, who had the surname Gorgon.

->[Woodcut illustration of Medusa with snakes for hair and a serpentine lower body, holding a snake.]<-

**Medusa**, the woman who was given the surname of the **Gorgon**, flourished until the time of Tola, Judge of the Hebrews, which was one thousand one hundred and fifteen years before the coming of our Lord Christ. She was the daughter of Phorcus, a very wealthy king, and was the heir along with her four sisters. This king of the Phorcides—the father of this Gorgon whom we mentioned in the third book of our chronicles—had four daughters of extraordinary beauty: Euryale, Stheno, Syllana, and this Medusa. They were so very similar to one another that one could scarcely be distinguished from the other.

--- Page 121 ---
->### About Medusa<-

Among these sisters, there was one kingdom; for this reason, they are imagined to have been one-eyed <note>original: "monocule"</note>, meaning they were of the same appearance and beauty, possessing every kind of loveliness. Her extremely wealthy kingdom was located in the Atlantic Sea, and in that place, she was preferred above her other sisters. She was of such admirable beauty that she not only surpassed all other women of her time, but—as if by some wonderful thing beyond nature—she drew a great many men to come and see her. 
<margin>She did not despise agriculture</margin>
Furthermore, some assert that she was highly skilled in agriculture, and that she obtained the surname "Gorgon" from that pursuit <note>The author is likely making a linguistic connection between "Gorgon" and the Greek *georgos*, meaning farmer.</note>. Through her work and with wondrous wisdom, she not only preserved her ancestral riches but increased them to such an immense degree that those who knew her believed she surpassed all previous kings in her treasures. Thus, through both her extraordinary beauty and her wealth and wisdom, she achieved the widest fame among many nations. Indeed, among others, the news of her spread to the people of Argos by means of famous rumor. Among them was Perseus, the most flourishing of the Achaean youth; having heard such reports, he fell into a state of longing both to see this most beautiful woman and to seize her treasures. And so, having boarded a ship (which had a winged horse named **Pegasus** as its figurehead), he was carried toward the west with marvelous speed. There, using both his prudence and his arms, he captured the queen. Carrying away her gold and all her possessions, and laden with the finest spoils, he returned to his people with joy. From these events, poetic fiction found a place for itself: we read that Medusa the Gorgon was accustomed to turn those she looked upon into stone, and that her hair was turned into snakes by the wrath of Minerva because she had defiled her temple through intercourse with Neptune. The poets say she gave birth to Pegasus, and that Perseus, sitting upon a winged horse, flew into her kingdom and overcame her using the shield <term>aegis: a protective shield or breastplate associated with Athena/Minerva</term> of Pallas. Varro says that Phorcus, the father of this Medusa, was King of the islands of Sardinia and Corsica; when he fought in a naval battle against King Atlas, he was defeated and submerged in the sea, and was called a "Sea God" by the talkative Greeks. Virgil touched upon this in the fifth book of the *Aeneid*, saying: <note>original: "Trithonesque cethi, phorcique exercitus omnis"</note> "And the Tritons of the deep, and all the host of Phorcus."

## About Nicostrata, daughter of Ionius, King of the Arcadians, Chapter 22

**N**icostrata—who was later given the name **Carmentis** among our people—flourished as a most famous prophetess among us Italians during the time of Jair, the judge of the Hebrews. This was in the year one thousand two hundred and twelve before the coming of Christ our Lord. She was indeed the daughter of Ionius, King of the Arcadians; she was not only distinguished by the splendor of her royalty, but was also most learned in Greek letters. She was of such a versatile and extraordinary intellect that she attained a most flourishing reputation for prophecy and was called a very well-known seer. To those who sought her out, she would often reveal many future things through song <note>original: "carmine"</note>; for this reason, she was later named "Carmenta" by the Latins. 

[A hand-colored woodcut illustration of a woman standing in a landscape, holding a bow and arrow in her right hand and a shield with a lion's head in her left.]

She later gave birth to a son, Evander of Arcadia, whom the fables claim was conceived by Mercury (either because he was eloquent and silver-tongued, or because he was a clever man). As some say, when he had by chance killed Euaz—who was his true father—he was driven from his ancestral kingdom. At the persuasion of his mother Nicostrata, who promised great things through her prophecy if he sought the dwelling place she would show him, she became the holy companion of his wandering. And so, having boarded ships with his father and his people...

**FOLIO XXV**

**Of** [left header] **Penthesilea** [center header]

With a favorable wind, she arrived from the Peloponnese at the mouth of the Tiber. Not far from that same place, led by her mother <note>The text refers to Carmenta leading her son Evander</note>, she settled with her people on the Palatine Hill (which he named "Pallanteum" after his son, Pallas). There, she founded the town of Pallanteum. Furthermore, when Carmenta discovered that the indigenous peoples were nearly wild forest-dwellers—even though they had long since learned to sow crops by the gift of Saturn <note>In Roman mythology, the god Saturn was credited with introducing agriculture to Italy</note>—she found they were accustomed to no use of letters, or at most a very slight use of Greek characters. Since she was a woman of versatile and nearly divine intellect, she invented new characters for letters, and taught the people their combinations and sounds. At the beginning, there were sixteen of them.

Then, a certain master of games named Silvius later added the letter *K*. The letter *Q*, however, she considered superfluous. *H* is indeed a letter, but serves as a mark of aspiration <note>A breathy sound rather than a full consonant</note>. The letter *X* is said to have been discovered in the times of our divine father Augustus <note>Original: "Augustini" — this likely refers to Emperor Augustus, though the scribe has used the form for Augustine</note>. At that time, the Latins also borrowed *Y* and *Z* from the Greeks. <margin>The first inventor of Latin letters</margin> And so it is that we use these aforementioned characters even unto this day.

The unrefined Latins, all admiring the prophecy and intellect of this woman, judged her to be no mere woman but a goddess fallen from heaven. For this reason, they celebrated her with divine honors while she lived, and even after her death, they built a shrine in her name at the Capitol where they had first settled. To perpetuate her memory, they even called the adjacent places the "Carmentalia" after her name. I consider not only our Italy, but all of Europe, to be greatly indebted to this nearly divine woman for such a great benefit and such a distinguished gift. Therefore, it is most pious that we should extol her into eternal memory to the best of our ability, so that we may never be justly reproached for ingratitude. 

It is also believed that she was the first woman to give us the faculty of <term>grammar</term> <note>The art of writing and structured language</note>, which our ancestors expanded into a more abundant harvest over time. God was so favorable to these letters that, with the greatest part of the glory taken away from Hebrew and Greek letters, almost all of Europe across its vast stretch of lands has used our Latin script. Through these letters, the infinite and splendid volumes of all the arts are articulated, preserving the deeds of men and the wonders of God in perpetual memory; thus, those things which we ourselves could not see, we may know through their help.

# Concerning Helen

<note>This first section continues the story of Penthesilea from the previous page.</note>

With such great opportunity, and with her abundance of troops, she was easily provoked to descend into the struggle to aid [the Trojans] against the Greeks. Nor did the famous reputation of the Greek princes terrify her; rather, she desired to please Hector with arms and valor more than with beauty, and she very often entered into the battles of crowded armed men. At times she would prostrate them with a spear; at other times she would open a path through those resisting with a sword. Often, she drove turning troops into flight with her bow and performed so many and such great deeds manfully that she eventually drew Hector himself, who was watching, into admiration of her. At last, while this <term>virago</term><note>A woman of masculine spirit or a female warrior.</note> fought alone among the thickest ranks of the enemy—proving herself more than usually worthy of such a lover—many of her own troops were already slain. Having received a fatal wound, she fell, pitiable, in the midst of the Greeks whom she herself had laid low. Others, however, claim that she arrived at Troy only after Hector was already dead, and was slain there in a fierce battle. 

Those who might wonder how women, however well-armed, ever dared to rush against men, should be drawn into admiration: for practice turns into a second nature. By this practice, she and others of her kind were made into "men in arms" far more than those whom nature created as wild males, but whom idleness and pleasure turned into women—or rather, hares wearing helmets.

## Concerning Polyxena, daughter of the aforementioned Queen Hecuba: Chapter XXVI.

**P**olyxena was the daughter of the same Queen Hecuba. She was a maiden of such flowering beauty and elegance that she was able to cast the flames of desire <note>original: "cupidinis"</note> into the stern heart of Achilles, son of Peleus. Through the trickery of her mother Hecuba, Achilles was led alone to a temple at night to meet his death. However, after the Trojan cause and its strength had fallen and Ilion was cast down, Polyxena was led to the tomb of Achilles by Neoptolemus <note>Achilles' son, also known as Pyrrhus</note> as an offering to appease the spirits of his father <note>original: "piaculum manium patris"</note>. There, seeing the fierce youth draw his sword, the delicate young girl—while everyone standing around was weeping—offered her throat with such a steadfast heart and fearless face that the minds of the onlookers were moved no less by admiration for her courage than by pity for her death. Indeed, it is a great and memorable thing that neither her tender age, nor the perceived weakness of the female sex, nor her royal upbringing could crush the great spirit of this maiden even when her fortune changed. For quite often, the hearts of even the most outstanding men fail when facing the sword of a victor and enemy.

## Chapter 30: About Camilla, Queen of the Volscians

**Camilla, Queen of the Volscians**, was born to King Metabus and his wife Camilla <note>Historical sources usually name the mother Casmilla; the author notes below that the daughter's name was altered from the mother's by one letter.</note> during the time of Abdon, Judge of the Hebrews. This was one thousand one hundred years before the coming of our Lord Christ. She was a virgin most worthy of memory who, amidst armed exercises, was struck by a lethal arrow by a certain enemy named Arruns and died to the great loss of her people. She was a virgin of such dignity and praise that Virgil ended the seventh book of the *Aeneid* with a long description in her honor.

->[Illustration: A woodcut depicting Camilla as a Renaissance-style warrior. She wears blue-tinted plate armor and a helmet with a visor. She holds a long spear in her right hand and a shield featuring a "gorgon" or grotesque face in her left. She stands in a grassy landscape with stylized trees.]<-

Her mother the queen died as soon as she had given birth to her. After she died, King Metabus, her father, as a solace to himself, named her Camilla, taken from the mother's name with only one letter removed. From her very birth, fortune was always harsh toward this virgin. For shortly after the mother’s death, King Metabus the father was driven from his kingdom. He carried nothing else with him into the forest except this little daughter, who was dearer to him than all other things. When he had brought her into the woods, he raised her with great labor on the milk of wild animals. When she reached a stronger age, she began to cover her body only with the skins of wild beasts. From then on, she cast away all feminine labors and began to accustom her body to many hardships: such as wielding slings, drawing bows, chasing deer and wild goats, and enduring many other such things.

In this way, she mocked the loves of young men and utterly rejected marriage to powerful nobles, so that she might preserve her virginity whole and inviolate (which she had devoted to the service of Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt and the moon, who required her followers to remain chaste.</note>). The virgin became so accustomed to these exercises that when she was finally recalled to her father’s kingdom with glory, she maintained her vow of virginity with unshaken strength even after obtaining the throne.

Finally, when Aeneas arrived in Italy from Troy and took Lavinia as his wife, a war arose because of this between him and Turnus of the Rutulians. Camilla, favoring the side of Turnus, came to his aid with a great troop of her people. After she had often rushed armed upon the enemy and had killed many of them in a single day of fighting, she was finally struck by an arrow and died while she was greedily pursuing a certain Chloreus <note>original: "corebū"; Chloreus was a priest of Cybele whose golden armor attracted Camilla's attention, leading to her distraction and death.</note>, a priest of Cybele. Her death brought the greatest loss to her people. Therefore, Turnus, whom she had come to help, wishing to praise her after her death and having nothing more to say than to call her a virgin, said: "O virgin, glory of Italy!" <note>original: "O decus Italie virgo"</note>

From this, modern girls can extract an excellent example of chastity and modesty. They can see a virgin who was a law unto herself as an adult, running here and there as she pleased, yet suppressing lust and immoderate appetites through constant labor, fleeing luxuries and softness, and with a most constant soul... <margin>Chapter 4</margin>

## **About Dido, the Finest Queen: Chapter 31**

[An illustration of a crowned queen (Dido) standing, wearing a red and blue gown, holding a scepter in her left hand and a leafy branch in her right hand. To her left is a stylized representation of flames or perhaps a rocky outcrop.]

**D**ido, whose name was previously Elissa, was the daughter of Belus <note>original: "belli"</note>, king of the Phoenicians, and the sister of Pygmalion. She was the wife of Sychaeus, a man of the highest character. In the time of King David <note>The author uses "synchronism," a medieval historical method of aligning pagan mythology with Biblical timelines to provide a sense of historical reality.</note>, she emerged as a supreme example of widowhood.

Therefore, while this girl was of the most striking beauty, after the death of her father Belus, her aforementioned brother Pygmalion joined her in marriage to Sychaeus—also known as Acerbas, a priest of Hercules <note>original: "Sicheo seu Accerbe herculis sacerdoti"</note>. He was a man who was certainly distinguished and very wealthy. Once joined in marriage, they always loved each other most holily <note>or "most devotedly"</note>. However, Pygmalion was more greedy for gold than all other mortals, just as Sychaeus was the wealthiest.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Dido, the legendary founder of Carthage. The previous text likely detailed her flight from Tyre following the murder of her husband, Sychaeus, by her brother Pygmalion.</meta>

**Concerning Dido, Folio 29**

...so that she might appear to her neighbors to be doing nothing out of the ordinary, and so that no one would suspect her of planning any great undertaking. She purchased from the local inhabitants a piece of land on which to establish a home, asking for no more than what could be covered by the hide of an ox. However, using a most clever trick, she immediately ordered the ox hide to be cut into the thinnest possible strips. By doing so, she was able to encompass a far greater area of ground than the sellers had ever imagined. Following the auspicious discovery of a horse’s head <note>An ancient omen signifying that the city would be wealthy and powerful in war.</note>, she founded a most warlike city, which she named Carthage. She called its citadel "Byrsa," after the ox hide. <margin>The founding of the city of Carthage</margin> Her companions in flight, seeing the city’s beginning and Dido’s innumerable treasures, were immediately encouraged; they rose up and began to erect the city walls, temples, a forum, and both public and private buildings. After she had given the people laws and a standard of living, the city suddenly emerged as a remarkable place. Dido herself became famous for her renown: news of her extraordinary beauty, unheard-of virtue, and chastity was carried throughout all of Africa. Because the African men were very prone to lust, it happened that the King of Libya <note>Commonly identified as Iarbas in classical mythology.</note> came to desire her. He demanded her in marriage from the city's leaders, threatening them with a declaration of war if they refused. When she learned of this, having dedicated herself to any fate for the safety of her city and fatherland, she bore the news with difficulty. However, she obtained a delay, promising that she would go to the man at the end of that period. 

When the time came, she built a massive funeral pyre in an elevated part of the city, pretending she was going to appease the spirit of her late husband, Sychaeus. Dressed in funeral black and having prepared various ceremonies and sacrificed many victims, she climbed the pyre. While the citizens stood by, waiting to see what she would do, and once she had performed everything according to her vows, she drew a knife she had hidden under her clothes. Placing it against her most chaste breast, she said: "O dearest citizens, I go to my husband as you wish." Calling upon Sychaeus, she said: "I come to you, most beloved husband, in the underworld." Scarcely having finished these few words, she threw herself onto the knife and into the fire. Though help was offered in vain, she died from her wounds, pouring out her most modest blood. 

Regarding this Dido, the most certain glory of all women, Saint Jerome, in his work *Against Jovinianus*, says: <note>original: "Casta dido carthaginem cõdidit: z pro castitate vitam finiuit quia maluit ardore quam nubere"</note> "Chaste Dido founded Carthage and ended her life for the sake of chastity, for she preferred to burn rather than to remarry." And again, he says that the city’s history ended with similar praise for chastity: when Carthage was captured and set on fire, the wife of Hasdrubal <note>The last commander of Carthage during its fall to Rome in 146 BC.</note>, seeing she was about to be captured by the Romans, took her small sons by each hand and threw herself into the fire of her burning house. 

Therefore, as long as Carthage stood, Dido was held to be a goddess. This was rightly so among those pagan people, for she was a venerable example of inviolate modesty and unbroken widowhood. I wish that Christian widows would deign to consider this: to see a pagan and unfaithful woman, to whom Christ had not yet come and who had no hope of salvation, yet who—solely to obtain a fleeting praise—proceeded toward death with such a persevering soul and brave heart. She inflicted death by her own hand rather than enter a second marriage or allow her most venerable vow of devotion to be violated. Thus, the citizens of Carthage honored their dead Queen Dido with the greatest mourning and grief, granting her not only human honors but divine ones as well. She was regarded not merely as a public mother and queen, but as a renowned deity, and they always worshipped her with the most exquisite sacrifices.

# On Sheba

[Initial N containing a figure of a king or scholar] **Nicaula**, Queen of the Ethiopians, whom the sacred Third Book of Kings <note>original: "tertius Regnorum liber"; in older biblical traditions, 1 Kings was titled 3 Kings</note> names **Sheba**. To her, the Lord also gives testimony in the Gospels: that on the day of judgment she will come with the men of this unbelieving <note>original: "icredibile," likely a transcription error for "incredulae" following Matthew 12:42</note> generation and will condemn them. Because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon—one thousand and nineteen years before the coming of Christ our Lord, which is to say, during the time of King Solomon—she became famous not only for incomparable riches but also for her knowledge and most distinguished character.

[Illustration of a queen, likely the Queen of Sheba, in a landscape]

She was, therefore, the most powerful queen of a certain island of the Nile in Ethiopia called **Meroe** <note>original: "Meroze"</note>. Since she was imbued with all learning and wisdom, hearing frequently through seafaring men <note>original: "per marimaz," likely a corruption of "per maritimos" or "per marinarios"</note> of the wisdom, virtue, and prudence of King Solomon, she was captured by a desire and wonder to see him and arranged to come to Jerusalem. And with a magnificent retinue and having undertaken splendid expense (leaving behind her noble kingdom), she traveled through the Ethiopian and Egyp[tian]...

## On Sheba, Folio 30

...to raise you to the royal height. And to show the affection of her mind, she immediately opened her treasures and offered twenty talents of gold to the king. She also offered an infinite multitude of spices <margin>The first planting of balsam</margin> and many most precious stones. And among other things (as the historian Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> writes in the eighth book of *Antiquities*), she gave certain small trees or roots that "sweat" balsam, which Solomon himself ordered to be planted and cultivated not far from Jerusalem on Mount En-gedi. In return, after receiving even greater gifts from Solomon, she returned to her homeland with the highest praise. Peter Comestor <note>A 12th-century theologian known for his 'Scholastic History,' which combined biblical narrative with secular history and legend.</note> says that this same queen was the Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses; medieval tradition often identified the Queen of Sheba as a "Sibyl" who foresaw the coming of Christ.</note> and a worshiper of God, who foretold the future to Solomon. In his presence, she pointed out a certain piece of wood upon which a man was to be fixed, whose death would bring about the end of Solomon's kingdom—which indeed came to pass. That wood (as they say) is reported to have been found in the **Sheep Pool** <note>The *probatica piscina*, or Pool of Bethesda, known in the New Testament for its healing waters.</note> at the time of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, and from it his cross was fashioned by the Jews. Some say she descended from the kings of the Egyptians and, as was said before, held her kingdom on the island of **Meroë** <note>An ancient city and island on the east bank of the Nile in modern-day Sudan.</note>, where there was such a great abundance of riches that it is believed she exceeded all mortals in this life. This should not seem inappropriate to anyone, for on that island (which is very large), gold, silver, and much iron are dug up, and many different kinds of precious stones are found; ebony wood also grows there. Yet, despite such an abundance of wealth, this most excellent queen did not give herself over to any luxuries, leisure, or feminine softness, but, clinging entirely to virtues, she took care to learn many sciences thoroughly.

And so, this Queen of Sheba is seen to have prefigured the **Universal Church** in all things, which comes from among the Gentile people to hear the wisdom of Solomon—that is, the wisdom of our Lord Jesus Christ, the true King of Peace. She came at first testing him through questions and riddles <note>Original Latin: *enigmata*.</note> which previously seemed unsolvable to her: concerning the knowledge of the true God, the creatures of the world, the immortality of the soul, and the future judgment. These matters—for her (the Church) and for her Gentile teachers and philosophers—had always remained uncertain or doubtful, and she was set free from these doubts by him. She also came to Jerusalem for the "vision of peace" <note>A traditional etymological meaning for the name 'Jerusalem'.</note> with a great multitude and much power. She did not come with only one nation—as the Synagogue did previously, which only held the Hebrews—but she came with the nations of the whole world, bringing gifts worthy of Christ: that is, the **good works** which ascend to God as a sweet fragrance. But she also came filled with gold—representing, without doubt, refined senses and rational disciplines. She also brought a precious stone, by which we can understand the **ornaments of moral character**. With this preparation, therefore, the Queen of Sheba (the Church of Christians) must enter to the peaceful King Christ, and then he opens his heart in the confession and repentance of previous sins. And she told him everything that was in her heart. Because of this, Christ, who is our peace, announced to her all his words, and there was not a single word the King omitted or failed to announce to the Queen of Sheba—that is, the Church gathered from the Gentiles. If we carefully observe the state of the Church and consider its distributions and ordinances, then we will notice how the Queen marveled at all the prudence of Solomon. For indeed, learned men wish for **prudence** to be understood as concerning human affairs, and **wisdom** to be understood as concerning divine matters. She also saw the house which he built—undoubtedly the **mysteries of his Incarnation**. She also saw the food of Solomon, which we should think of as those things about which he himself said: *My food is to do the will of him who sent me, so that I may finish his work.* <note>John 4:34</note> And she saw the order of his servants. And in this also, we should think of and speak of the **Ecclesiastical order**, which resides in the seats of the bishopric and the priesthood...

->**On Athalia**<-                                  **FOLIO 31**

She desired to be queen. To this splendor, after her father Ahab died, her brother Joram—who succeeded his father—added no small amount of splendor to his own throne. Truly, in the course of time, after being tossed about by many misfortunes (her husband being now deceased), she saw her son Ahaziah sitting on his father’s throne. Indeed, when Ahaziah himself died after being struck by an arrow, the bloodthirsty woman—inflamed by the desire for ruling—conceived a memorable crime. Having gathered enough resolve to carry it out, and with womanly piety driven out, she not only failed to shed tears for her dead son, but rather, she would have progressed to even more weeping if she had a womanly heart. Instead, while the earth was still wet with her son's blood, she unleashed swords against the entire Davidic line <note>The descendants of King David</note>, and she raged against them so long that she left no male alive, driving them all to death through wounds. Only one escaped such great cruelty: Joash, the small son of King Ahaziah, was snatched away without her noticing. For Jehosheba <note>original: "Josabeth"</note>, his daughter and formerly the sister of Ahaziah, had secretly taken the child and brought him into the house of Jehoiada the High Priest, her husband, to be protected and raised. And so, through the blood of so many impiously slain, this daring woman ventured to ascend the royal throne as if it were a vacant possession of her own making, and to arrange all royal matters. Thus Athalia shone with the royal diadem; she was indeed a great sight, though more notable for being splattered with purple blood than for royal dignity. Truly, just as she had cruelly raged with the sword against the innocent souls of the Davidic line, so she could feel her own people turn against her as strangers. She could easily have seen her brother Joram, King of Israel, lying in the field of Naboth, surrendered to the dogs through a thousand wounds. Likewise Jezebel, her mother, though dressed in royal ornaments, was thrown down from a tower, trampled by the feet of those running about, and crushed by the wheels of wagons, so that, turned into filth, no trace of her ill-fated body remained. Likewise her seventy brothers were struck down in a single hour at Samaria (by the victor's command <note>Refers to Jehu, who overthrew the house of Ahab</note>), and their heads fixed on poles: outstanding proofs of a singular deed. Likewise all her other kinsmen; not one escaped being pierced by the sword of that same executioner. And finally, lest this bloody and wicked woman should pass unpunished, after she had reigned for seven years (as was said before), through the work of Jehoiada the High Priest, her grandson Joash—whom she thought killed with the others—was raised up as king. She saw herself dragged from the royal seat by servants. And while the people shouted against her, she was led disgracefully by the hands of soldiers to the gate of the mules, shouting and threatening in vain, and there she was foully slaughtered as she deserved. Thus, the guilty woman went to the underworld by no other path than the one she forced the innocent to take. Thus acted Divine Justice, which, though it may delay, does not forget; it acts with more severe punishment upon those whom it has long waited for, yet sees no change in their ways. While we neglect to think on this, we refuse to believe, nor do we care to be amended; we bind ourselves with greater outrages until, when we least expect it, we are swallowed by the storm, and we wretches grieve for our crimes when it is too late. All these things are excerpted from the Fourth Book of Kings <note>original: "quarto regnorum"; known in modern Bibles as 2 Kings</note>, the Second Book of Chronicles <note>original: "secundo paralipomenis"</note>, and the ninth book of the historian Josephus.

### Of Gaia and Sappho

[Woodcut illustration of a queenly figure, Gaia, holding a scepter, with a crown and elaborate dress, standing before stylized trees.]

**G**aia Cyrilla, an Etruscan woman and the most beloved wife of Tarquinius Priscus, King of the Romans, lived during the time of Josiah, King of Judah <note>King Josiah of Judah reigned approximately 640–609 BCE; the text aligns Roman and Biblical chronologies.</note>. That is to say, she most happily entered into the kingdom of the Romans with her husband Tarquinius in the six hundred and twenty-sixth year before the coming of Christ our Lord. 

Because she was a woman of the most outstanding talent, no matter how much she shone with regal splendor or was elevated upon the royal throne, she did not allow herself to succumb to the sluggishness of idleness. On the contrary, she dedicated herself, among other pursuits, to <term>wool-working</term> <note>original: "lanificio." In ancient Rome, spinning and weaving were considered the highest virtues of a noble matron, symbolizing her industry and devotion to the household.</note>. This was a craft I believe was considered so honorable among the Latins of that time that she emerged as an excellent and diligent worker in it. 

As a result, the fame of her name has extended even to the present day. For this reason, she was never without public honor throughout her entire life. Indeed, because she was considered a wonderful and most beloved woman among the Romans for these virtues, it was established by public decree that when new brides first entered [their homes], to the groom... <note>The text likely refers to the traditional Roman wedding chant, "Ubi tu Gaius, ego Gaia" (Where you are Gaius, I am Gaia), attributing the origin of this custom to the virtues of this queen.</note>

## **Chapter 39: About Tamiris, Queen of the Scythians**

**T**amiris <note>Usually known today as Tomyris.</note> was a most illustrious queen of the Scythians <note>The Scythians were nomadic warriors living in the vast steppes of modern-day Ukraine and Southern Russia.</note> during the time of Cyrus, King of the Persians. This was in the five hundred and thirty-ninth year before the coming of our Lord Christ. She was a woman of remarkable nobility and distinction, who subdued the untameable Persians with her arms and ruled over them for many years. It is not established by any authentic author from which parents this woman descended, or to whom she was joined in marriage. Her Scythian kingdom, however, is in a barren place under a frozen stretch of the sky, connected to the Riphean and Hyperborean mountains <note>Ancient geographers used these names for legendary, frigid mountain ranges in the far north.</note>.

->[Illustration: Queen Tamiris stands in a rugged landscape, wearing a crown and holding a scepter as a symbol of her sovereign power.]<-

As we have stated in our second book of Chronicles, the people in that kingdom and on that soil are quite wild and poor; however, they have always remained unconquered. Even when provoked by many wars by the greatest kings, they always stood undefeated. It was against this woman that Cyrus, King of the Persians, moved to war out of a greed for wider dominion, after he had already subjected all of Asia to himself. When Tamiris learned of his arrival, she did not seek hiding places out of fear like a woman, nor did she plead for terms of peace. On the contrary, having gathered her forces, she allowed him to enter her borders, even though she could have resisted him with a focused effort. She judged it far better to crush Cyrus's madness within her own boundaries than to attempt it outside them. When she was certain he had penetrated the interior of the kingdom, she committed a third of her forces to her only young son and ordered him to go forth to fight Cyrus. 

Cyrus, however, having considered the nature of the locations and the customs of the people, heard that the youth was coming with his army. He decided to conquer him by fraud rather than by arms. He left behind a camp filled with wine (which the Scythians did not yet know), feasts, and other delicacies, and then feigned a flight. When the youth entered the empty camp, as if he were a victor and the enemy had been put to flight, he was joyful with his Scythians. Invited not to war but to a feast, they began to gorge themselves on large amounts of food and unknown drinks. Because of this, military discipline dissolved and sleep followed. While they were buried in sleep, Cyrus returned, put the youth and the rest to death, and, as if certain of victory, proceeded further into the country. 

When Tamiris heard of the slaughter of her men, even though she was deeply moved as a widow by the death of her only son, she did not give herself over to tears in a feminine manner. Instead, she comforted herself with a desire for anger and revenge. With her remaining forces, she reckoned that the enemy (clever though he was) could be captured by the same art by which she heard her son had been taken—even if a camp full of drinks were not used. Being familiar with the terrain, she simulated a flight and led the greedy pursuer into a stretch of narrow, rough roads among barren and horrific mountains, depriving him of almost all advantages.

# **Concerning Judith**

[An illustration of Judith standing, holding a curved sword in her right hand and the severed head of Holofernes in her left. She is wearing a long dress with a bodice. In the background, there is a castle or city wall on the left and a tree on the right.]

[Decorated initial J]udith was a Hebrew woman of **great spirit** <note>original: "ingentis animi"</note> and a widow of the holiest and most rare devotion. She remains an eternal example of perfect widowhood and chastity for posterity. During the times of the Judean captivity—that is, in the five hundred and twentieth year before the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ—she performed a most beautiful and memorable work of piety to the honor of her people: the liberation of her city, **Bethulia**. She accomplished a deed so bold that even the most robust and sharp-minded man would surely have been afraid to attempt it.

This woman was, above all, most worthy of remembrance. She was the daughter of a certain noble Hebrew named Merari and the wife of Manasseh, a man of the same tribe. Although she was considered the most striking and beautiful woman of her age, she remained a widow in the very flower of her youth. From then on, she refused to enter into a second marriage <note>original: "secunda vota"</note> out of her love for chastity, judging it honorable enough for a woman to have married once. Consequently, no one could provoke her to a second marriage by any means. Indeed, she spent the rest of her life within the walls of her husband’s chambers, living so holily and chastely that her celebrated widowhood surpassed the praises of all Hebrew matrons of the past.

Therefore, while Judith was leading this most excellent and celibate life, she heard one day that the priests and her fellow citizens intended to surrender their city, Bethulia, to **Holofernes**, the prince of the Persian army <note>Holofernes is traditionally associated with the Assyrians, but early modern texts often conflated eastern empires</note>. Holofernes was fiercely and mindlessly besieging the city, and the leaders planned to hand it over unless help arrived within three days. Moved by her religion and piety for her people, she determined to expose herself to the total danger of death for their liberation.

For this reason, this most modest woman did not demand a large army, nor strong weapons, nor the help of neighboring peoples; instead, she first pleaded for the aid of the Most High God with the greatest faith, tears, and fasting. Then, guided by the hand of the Supreme Craftsman <note>meaning God</note>, she believed she would triumph over the most powerful commander entirely through her own adornments. Therefore, one night, laying aside her garments of widowhood, she anointed her face with oil and bound her hair with a headband <note>term: "mitra" — a traditional head-covering or tiara</note> to deceive Holofernes. Thus, with great bodily finery and incredible beauty—the gates of the city being opened for her—she approached the camp of Holofernes, the leader of the military, as if she were a fugitive, accompanied only by her handmaid.

When she arrived, she shone with such grace of face and charm of her whole body that the judgment of the prince and the others who looked upon her was deceived. For this reason, all the barbarians said she was not a Hebrew or a woman of the earth, but entirely heavenly. Thus, her sandals ravished his eyes, and her beauty made the soul of Holofernes her captive. While his eyes were first snatched away, his mind turned toward sin. Through such incitement and entrapment, the holy Judith, wonderfully adorned, finally possessed the soul and the head of that most cruel enemy in a most glorious fashion. After this heroic woman <note>original: "virago" — used here to denote a woman of masculine strength or courage</note> had slaughtered so great a prince, she was held in such high esteem among the Jews that for all the days of her life she was preferred above all other Jews. She was celebrated with triumphal praise and perpetual proclamations; they held her up as an example to be imitated not only by women but also by men. This was because the Rewarder of her chastity granted her such virtue that she conquered everyone and overcame the unsurpassable.

<margin>The death of Holofernes</margin>

For, with Holofernes killed:

Coriolanus dismissed them back to their fatherland with a harsh response, because of which they were sent a second time but were not received at all. By now, despair had entered the minds of the Romans from every side. 

Then, many weeping matrons <note>socially prominent married women of Rome</note> came to this Veturia, the mother of Coriolanus, and Volumnia, his wife. They succeeded in persuading the now elderly woman to go into the enemy camp, so that she might placate her son with prayers and tears, seeing as the city could no longer be protected by men with arms. She went with his wife, and a great crowd of following women accompanied them. 

When Coriolanus recognized her arrival, even though his heart was filled with pride, he was nevertheless struck with consternation by his mother’s arrival. Rising from his chair, he left the tent and went to meet her, intending to embrace her. Truly, Veturia—holding Coriolanus's wife on one side and his children on the other—did not look upon her son as a mother until she had put aside her maternal devotion and turned to anger. Where she had cast off her status as a suppliant of the city when entering the enemy camp, she instead became a rebuker. With strength stirred up in her weakened chest, she said: 

"Stop your step, you hostile youth! I wish to know before I enter into your embraces: do I come to meet a mother or a captive enemy? I suppose an enemy. Wretched me, that my long life—so desired by mortals—has brought me to this: to see you first condemned to exile and then an enemy of the Republic <note>original: "reyp," an abbreviation for "res publica" or Republic</note>..."

<margin>The Altar of Fortune</margin>

And there are those who say that by a decree of the Senate it was even granted to these same women that they could inherit estates from anyone, which was not permitted before. This great gift has certainly not been diminished for women in our own times; rather, it is preserved with the most tenacious perseverance. Therefore, let women give thanks to this Veturia and exalt her name forever, as often as they adorn themselves with gems, purple, and gold, and as men rise when they approach.

## On Hippo, a most chaste Greek woman: Chapter 44

**H**ippo, a certain noblewoman in Greece, is said to have lived during the time of the aforementioned Veturia. She was famous for a single celebrated deed, and so that its merit and due glory are not lost, I believe it is worth commemorating here as an example for many women. This Hippo, a most chaste woman (as it is said), was captured by chance by enemy sailors. Since she was possessed of great beauty, she perceived that the pirates intended to violate her chastity and honor. She valued the glory of her purity so highly

[Illustration: A woman in a red dress stands in a landscape, holding a long, winding scroll that reads "ONE LIVES LONG" <note>original: "VIVITVR DIVI"</note> and "HVAL" <note>This may be a fragment of a name or a motto</note>.]

<margin>Note how much value women used to place on chastity.</margin>
that, seeing it could only be preserved through death, she did not wait for violence but threw herself headlong into the waves. By this act, her life was taken, but her chastity was saved. Who would not praise such a stern resolution in a woman? She redeemed her chastity with the few years by which her life might have been extended, and in an early death, she acquired for herself eternal glory. The stormy sea could not hide this work of virtue, nor could the deserted shore take it away; instead, it has been kept in the light with its own honor through the perpetual monuments of literature. As for her body, after it had been tossed about for some time by the waves as if in mockery, it was driven by those same waves onto the <term>Erythraean shore<note>Erythrae was an ancient city in Ionia (modern-day Turkey).</note></term> and buried by the coastal people in the manner of a shipwreck victim. Finally, when the report spread from her enemies as to who she was and the cause of her death, the place of her burial was honored by the Erythraeans with the greatest veneration, marked by a massive and long-lasting tomb on the shore as a testament to her preserved honor. This is so we may know that the light of virtue cannot be darkened by any shadows of adverse fortune.

# Concerning the Painter Thamyris <margin>Folio 36</margin>

**T**hamyris <note>original: "Thamiris"; also known in classical sources as Timarete.</note> was a painter outstanding in her own time—the same era as the previously mentioned <note>Referring to Hippo, the subject of the previous chapter, known for her chastity.</note> Hippo—and was held in the highest regard for her distinguished name and her great skill in her craft. She was, in fact, the daughter of an excellent Athenian painter named Micon <note>Micon the Younger, a Greek painter and sculptor of the 5th century BCE.</note>. Such a marvelous talent resided within her that, having set aside the tasks usually expected of women, she most diligently imitated her father's art. She achieved such unique glory and fame in painting—so much so, in fact, that in Ephesus (where the people worshipped Diana <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Artemis; the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.</note> with special honor), a portrait of that same Diana, painted by Thamyris’s own hand upon a wooden panel, was preserved for a very long time as a celebrated work of art. Because this work lasted for many ages, it provided such a powerful testimony to her skill that it was considered highly memorable almost until our own times. It is surely most praiseworthy when we consider the typical occupations of other women.
