# Of Artemisia Page 38

## Of Artemisia, Queen of Caria. Chapter 47.

[Woodcut initial A] **Artemisia**, Queen of Caria, was a woman of vast spirit. During the times of the aforementioned Queen **Esther**, she was the glory of most upright widowhood and a most worthy example for the future of holy marital love. She was indeed the daughter of Hecatomnus, the first king of the city of Caria; she took as her husband **Mausolus**, her brother born of the same father <note>In many ancient royal traditions, including those of Caria, sibling marriage was practiced to keep the bloodline pure and consolidate power.</note>. She loved him so much in life that, surviving him, she could never forget him after his death. His famous monuments stood for a long time. For, as the historian **Valerius Maximus** writes: as soon as her most loving husband had closed his final day, she carried out his corpse with the most exquisite honors. Nor did she allow his collected ashes, after the funeral fires, to be stored away in a golden urn to be preserved; she judged every other vessel to be unsuitable for so beloved a spouse except for her own breast, in which the flames of their old love burned much more than usual after his death. For this reason, she wished to drink all the collected ashes herself <note>Ancient accounts claim she mixed his ashes into her daily drink so that she would literally become his living tomb.</note>, and she consumed the remaining time of her life in tears, until she might go joyfully into death to join her husband. 

Truly, having been made a widow, she performed great deeds. And among other things, according to her excellent and amiable custom for her husband, she erected a distinguished sepulcher. This work was plainly most admirable and sumptuous, because in its artistry and expense it exceeded almost all the buildings in the world; and it stood for a long time as one of the **Seven Wonders of the World**. Indeed, she called this work the **Mausoleum** from the name of her husband, and from which—as if from a more worthy source—the tombs of subsequent kings were named <term>Mausoleums</term> <note>original Latin: "Mauſolea"</note>. <margin>The Mausoleum sepulcher</margin> 

And not only in this was Artemisia to be extolled, but she also excelled greatly in manly strength, boldness, and military discipline; and she adorned the majesty of her name with many triumphs. Because, as we read, after the death of her husband, setting aside her tears for a time, she took up arms twice: first, to protect the safety of her fatherland; second, to maintain her social duty as required. For when Mausolus was dead, and the Rhodians—situated not far from Halicarnassus—were indignant that a woman should rule the kingdom of Caria, they came there with an armed fleet, as if with certain hope of taking possession, to occupy it. 

Indeed, the city of Halicarnassus, overlooking the sea near Icaria, was situated in a naturally fortified place having twin harbors; when the Rhodians had tried to occupy it, they were not only prevented by the cunning of Artemisia, but their own Rhodian city was most fortunately occupied by her. Having gained it, she ordered all their leaders to be slain. Furthermore, as **Justin** writes in the third book of his *Epitomes*, when the Persian King **Xerxes** declared war against the Spartans and Greeks, Artemisia came to the fight with armed ships as requested. And with the land forces of Xerxes already broken, when the fleet of Xerxes and the Athenians under the leader **Themistocles** <note>The OCR reads "Teſtimocle," a common variation for the Athenian general Themistocles.</note> met in naval battle in sight of **Salamis**, Artemisia—with Xerxes watching—encouraging and fiercely driving among her first leaders, seemed as if she had swapped roles with Xerxes. To such an extent that if the spirit of Xerxes had been as bold and robust, his fleet would not have easily turned its back in flight. Truly a great and much...

# On Olympias

Many were the deeds and acts of this Artemisia, which are worthy of admiration. Let these words concerning her suffice.

## On Olympias, mother of Alexander the Great, Chapter 48.

**O**lympias, Queen of the Macedonians, who from her infancy was named **Myrtale** <note>original: "Mistilis"; a name given to her at birth, likely associated with the cult of the mysteries</note>, was established as queen three hundred and fifty years before the coming of Christ our Lord. She became illustrious and renowned for many titles, because she had for a father Neoptolemus, King of the **Molossians** <note>A people of Epirus, in modern-day Greece and Albania</note>. He was of the blood of the **Aeacidae** <note>original: "Eacidarum"; the royal dynasty of Epirus who claimed descent from the hero Achilles</note>, who at that time were considered more splendid than all the rest of Greece, and indeed the whole world. Furthermore, she had as a brother Alexander, King of Epirus; and upon the death of her husband Philip, King of Macedonia, she had a son, **Alexander the Great**. His deeds were so immense that no one was heard of before or would be born in the future who could surpass him in glory. This added no small amount of luster to Olympias—if indeed it is a glory for mothers to have given birth to such outstanding sons.

But that luster was not entirely able to escape being darkened by certain stains that were eventually cast upon it, though Olympias became even more well-known because of them. For in her prime, Olympias was disgraced by the lure of adultery. Scarcely anything more shameful could have happened to a queen. And what was even more foul, it was suspected that Alexander had been fathered through adultery. This suspicion so disturbed Philip that he not only openly said at one time that Alexander was not fathered by him, but he also marked Olympias with the ignominy of divorce and took **Cleopatra** <note>original: "cleopatram"; historical sources identify her as Cleopatra Eurydice, the niece of Philip's general Attalus</note>, the daughter of Alexander of Epirus, as his wife. 

<margin>The outrages of this woman</margin>

How bitterly Olympias took this, she could not hide. For she, who until that day (except for that one stain) had been famous for her royal brilliance, now made herself notorious for various atrocities. It was believed, indeed, that she incited and drove the youth **Pausanias** <note>A member of Philip's royal bodyguard</note>, born of noble and honorable blood, to the murder of her husband Philip—with Alexander also being aware of the plot. For after Pausanias had been executed for killing Philip, his head was found the following morning decorated with a golden crown by the work of Olympias, on the very cross where he had been hung. A few days later, by Olympias's command, his body was taken down and honorably burned according to the Macedonian rite over the remains of Philip, and buried with a funeral procession. Furthermore, the queen commanded that the sword with which Pausanias had killed Philip be placed in the Temple of Apollo under the name **Myrtale**. And as for Cleopatra, who had been brought in over her, Olympias so provoked the wretched woman with words (after first killing her daughter) that she forced her to put her neck in a noose. 

Finally, after her son Alexander had grown great through his many victories and was consumed by poison at Babylon, and after her brother Alexander was slain among the **Lucanians** <note>A tribe in southern Italy</note>, she entered Macedonia from Epirus, despite **Arrhidaeus** <note>Philip's other son and Alexander's half-brother</note>, the King of Macedonia, and his wife Eurydice trying to prohibit her. Supported by the favor of the veteran Macedonians, she alone obtained the kingdom of Macedonia as a royal widow, putting her enemies to death. But when she began to rage like a **wild beast** <note>original: "belua bacaret"; literally "raging like a Maenad or beast"</note> in the slaughter of both nobles and common Macedonians, she was besieged by **Cassander** <note>One of Alexander's generals and rivals</note> in the city of **Pydna** <note>original: "epidua"; a transcription variant of Pydna, where Olympias was famously besieged in 316 BCE</note>.

# Folio 39

## Of Claudia
<note>While the text is titled "De Claudia," the content describes the death of Olympias, mother of Alexander the Great, following her defeat by the Macedonian ruler Cassander in 316 BCE.</note>

She was besieged, and so greatly compelled that, together with the townspeople, through a total lack of all supplies, she fell into famine. Under the weight of this necessity, it was arranged that, once certain conditions were established, she would entrust herself to the protection <note original: "in fidem">The Latin term "fides" implies a formal promise of safety or a hand-over in good faith.</note> of Cassander. However, he, having through deceit incited the friends of those she had previously killed, summoned her to her death after the surrender.

When Cassander had sent ministers of crime into the place where she was being held to kill her, and she, already perceiving that she was to die by the hands of those approaching, stood up fearless between two of her handmaidens. With her garments and hair carefully arranged so that nothing unseemly might be seen as she fell, she neither allowed herself to plead for mercy nor to listen to their words, nor did she let out womanly wails. Instead, she went to meet the assassins and voluntarily offered her body, ready for the wounds, as if she held of little account that which even the strongest of men are usually most terrified of. By that very deed, she proved that she truly was the mother of such an illustrious Emperor <note>original: "egregij Jmperatoris genitricem"; a reference to her son, Alexander the Great.</note>.

# Concerning Irene the Greek, a woman of wondrous painting. Chapter 50.

**Irene** <note>original: "Yrene"</note> was a Greek woman, the daughter and pupil of a certain painter named **Cratinus**. **On Cleopatra, Great Queen of the Egyptians. Chapter 60.**

[Illustration: A portrait of a woman (Cleopatra) wearing a crown and holding a scepter, set against a landscape background.]

**C**leopatra, the great Queen of the Egyptians and daughter of King Ptolemy Auletes <note>original: "Dyonisij Auletes"; he was Ptolemy XII, nicknamed "The Flute-Player."</note>, was a legend to the whole world. In the one hundred and eighty-first Olympiad <note>A four-year period used in ancient Greek dating; this corresponds to roughly 56–52 BCE.</note>—specifically in the forty-ninth year before the birth of our Lord Christ—she seized the Egyptian kingdom through wickedness <note>original: "per nephas"</note> and reigned for twenty-two years. This woman shone with almost no quality except for her royal dignity and the beauty of her face and fame. On the contrary, she became notorious throughout the whole world for her greed, cruelty, and lust. 

To begin from the start of her rule: Ptolemy Auletes, a very close friend of the Roman people (and himself a most disgraceful man), decreed in his will upon his death that his eldest son should rule together in marriage with Cleopatra, his eldest daughter. Because it was a very common disgrace among the Egyptians to exclude only mothers and daughters from marriage <note>A reference to the Ptolemaic custom of sibling marriage, which the author finds scandalous.</note>, this was carried out. 

However, as a lust for reigning burned within Cleopatra, she consumed that same young man—her brother and husband, who was then in his fifteenth year—with poison. Once he was dead, she gained possession of the kingdom alone. Later, when the city of Alexandria had been captured by Caesar, he was delighted by the beauty of this woman. After he had slept with her for many nights and after he had defeated Pompey, he finally granted and confirmed the kingdom to her, as if it were a reward for those nights and pleasures. Her sister Arsinoe was led away so that, with her as a leader, nothing new might be attempted against him. 

Thus, having now obtained the kingdom through a double crime, Cleopatra poured herself into her pleasures. She became like a prostitute for Eastern kings. Greedy for gold and jewelry, she not only stripped her own companions of such things through her craft, but it is also said that she left the temples and sacred houses of the Egyptians empty of their vessels, statues, and other treasures. After Caesar had been killed and Brutus and Cassius defeated, she went to meet Mark Antony as he was entering Syria. She easily captured the man with her beauty and her wanton eyes, and she held him miserably in her love. She led him to such a point that she, who had killed her brother with poison, forced Antony to murder her sister Arsinoe in the Temple of Diana at Ephesus, where the unhappy girl had fled seeking safety, so that any suspicion regarding the kingdom might be removed. This was taken as the first gift from her new lover for their adulteries. And when this wicked woman had learned Antony's character, she did not hesitate to demand the kingdom of Syria and Arabia from him. Indeed, since the primary...

### Concerning Saint Afra

[Woodcut illustration of a female saint (Saint Afra) with a halo, wearing a veil and long robes, holding a book in her left hand. She stands in a landscape with hills and trees.]

**Afra**, the daughter of the martyr Saint Hilaria, entered the heavenly kingdoms while enduring martyrdom for Christ most steadfastly in the city of **Augsburg** <note>original: "Augustana"</note> in **Raetia** <note>A Roman province that included parts of modern-day Bavaria, Switzerland, and Austria.</note> during the reign of the Roman Emperor Diocletian. She was, in fact, of Cyprian descent. Since she was marked by remarkable beauty and devoted to the cult of the goddess **Venus**, she operated a brothel following the instruction of her mother. 

It is said that **Semiramis** <note>original: "semia" – likely referring to the legendary Queen Semiramis, whom medieval authors often blamed for the institutionalization of prostitution to excuse her own reputation</note>, that most unchaste and false goddess of the heathens, devised a wicked foulness so that she might seem to have wiped a little of the blush from her own shameful face and granted herself greater license for lust: she invented the first public houses of prostitution, established brothels, and compelled matrons to enter them. This most cursed custom of the Cypriots has continued—if I may say so—even into our own age. For they were accustomed to send their virgins to the seashores to sleep with strangers, so that they might be seen to have paid the offerings of their future chastity to the goddess Venus and to have sought dowries for their marriages. 

Indeed, Afra maintained this abominable folly here in the city of Augsburg in Raetia. Her detestable impurity and shameful trade as a prostitute caused her Cyprian origin to be forgotten. Even though she cannot be decorated with the most magnificent titles <note>A reference to the "title" of virginity, which Afra lacked, but which was usually required for female saints.</note>, because she so quickly bore martyrdom for Christ with a most ardent and unbroken heart, she ought not to be cheated of her portion of praise. Although she was less than chaste—by the good grace of other famous women—I have judged that she deserves to be described not only among famous women, but as someone who should rightfully be counted among the **holy saints**. 

Thus, while the lost Afra was in the aforementioned city with her handmaids in that wicked trade, **Saint Narcissus**, the bishop, and **Felix**, the deacon, once entered the location of her brothel by mistake while fleeing the persecution of Diocletian. At first, she received him as if he were a base lover. Later, when she recognized him as a bishop of the Christians, she immediately threw herself at his feet with tears and wailing. Her such great <note>The text ends mid-sentence as the narrative of her conversion begins.</note>

# FOLIO XCVI

## **Concerning Saint Afra and Saint Grata**

...[that] the God of the Christians abhors prostitutes; and because He is most just, He has no desire to dwell within such people. <note>original: "deus christianorum meretrices abhorrere." I did not realize that if even modest and gentle men take no joy in such wicked debaucheries, how much more should the gods be strangers to such things. For I have learned that He [is the giver of life] to all..."

**Of Saint Grata**

It is very little known from the historical records how she received the teachings and the emblems <note>referring to the *insignia* or outward signs of faith, such as the cross</note> of the Christian religion. ### Chapter 114: On Saint Helena, Mother of Constantine

**H**elena, the holy mother of Constantine the Great, migrated gloriously to the Lord with innumerable merits at Rome on the eleventh day before the <term>Kalends of June</term><note>May 22nd.</note>, in the year 337 from the birth of Christ, while Pope Julius was presiding in the Chair of Peter. She was, first of all, the most illustrious queen of all Christians, and also a most affectionate parent, as well as an extraordinary brightness of Christian splendor and the most certain witness of good virtues.

According to certain records and those of Saint Ambrose (who calls her a *stable-maid*), <note>original: "stabulariā." St. Ambrose used this term to emphasize her humble beginnings, suggesting she worked at an inn or stable where she met Constantius.</note> she was the daughter of a common man. Others, however, wish her to be the daughter of Coel, King of the English <note>original: "Angloꝫ regis." This refers to the legendary British King Coel, the "Old King Cole" of nursery rhymes.</note>, and a captive from the beginning; I myself am inclined to this view, as it is held by many. As she was a girl of incomparable form and beauty, she married as a virgin the illustrious Constantius, <term>Caesar</term><note>A title for a junior emperor or high ruler in the Roman system.</note> of the entire West. From him (to pass over the others) she conceived and gave birth to that extraordinary beam of the Christian faith, Constantine, surnamed "the Great," and later the renowned Augustus. So great was the brightness and ardor of his faith that he did not only make himself splendid with eternal fame, but he also ennobled and raised up his parents, his unbelieving kin, his fatherland, and all Christians with everlasting glory and triumph.

But this holy woman, Helena, became known throughout the entire world not only for the grace of her happy kingdom and empire, nor for her most serene offspring, her great son, but because of her great passion for divine worship, which led to the discovery of the <term>Trophy of our Salvation</term><note>This refers to the True Cross of Christ.</note>. For it is often said that after she was cleansed in the perennial fountain <note>A poetic reference to baptism.</note> by the holy Pope Sylvester and was perfectly instructed in every mystery of the Incarnation of the Word of God and the Cross, she said: "How shall I consider myself redeemed if the redemption of the Cross itself is not seen?" 

Truly, since the history of this holy heroine is quite a journey, before proceeding further, we must go back a little earlier. As was mentioned above, there are various opinions among famous men regarding the origin of this queen—from what family she was born—but whatever her lineage was, it does not change the history itself. Because of her beauty...

# Concerning Saint Helena

Many assert that she was exceedingly pleasing to Constantius Caesar, <note>original: "Constantio cesari," referring to Constantius Chlorus, the Roman Emperor (reigned 293–306 AD)</note> and that it was by him that she was first taken as a wife. She was indeed of the character of that nation <note>A reference to the inhabitants of Britain; many medieval chronicles claimed Helena was the daughter of a British king, such as King Coel</note> who are for the most part of beautiful and tall stature, with very strong limbs and a fair complexion. There was also a certain miraculous quality in her that seemed beyond nature, so much so that not only the Caesar’s army but also countless other men from every corner of the world would travel even to those remote western regions <note>original: "occidiuis partibus," referring to the western edges of the Roman Empire, specifically Britain</note> just to see her. 

Among her other attributes, her body was of such exceptional height and dignity that those who knew her believed she surpassed any other women of the West, even outshining them in her presence. She was of gentle and charming speech, possessed an eloquent tongue, and excelled all others in her intellect. She shone with the beauty of great prudence and wisdom; and thus, through such goodness...

Helena, who already understood religion rightly <note>Helena was often depicted by medieval chroniclers as being spiritually prepared for Christianity even before her formal conversion</note>, sent word to her son Constantine once he had accepted the Christian faith. The Emperor Constantine, having seen, heard, and understood the messengers from his mother Helena, sent an honorable embassy to Britain as quickly as possible to summon her to Rome. These messengers were to report to his mother not only his happiness, but his perfect health <note>This refers to the legend that Constantine was cured of leprosy through baptism by Pope Sylvester</note>, the most manifest help from heaven, and the innumerable miracles worked by God. They were also to bring her back to him so they could rejoice together. When the news of her son's health reached Helena, it is said she was moved with such great pleasure of soul that the cheerfulness of her face brought joy to those standing around her. At the first news of her son's health (assisted by baptism), Helena conceived such hope in God regarding his excellent life and future integrity that she thought a great heap had been added to her happiness.

Nor indeed did her opinion fail her. They say Helena brought many Jews with her to Rome, and these were indeed very learned. Since we have said that this noble queen drew her origin from Britain, it will not be out of place to mention a few things here about the location of that kingdom. <margin>Concerning the island of Britain.</margin> Britain, then, which is now also called England, took that name from Brutus the Trojan King <note>A reference to the popular medieval myth that Britain was founded by Brutus, a descendant of the Trojan hero Aeneas</note>, though it was first called Albion (from certain white mountains nearby <note>The White Cliffs of Dover</note>). It is the largest island in the ocean; when Julius Caesar finally subdued it to himself, they say he said the Roman Empire had propagated itself beyond the world. According to Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman geographer</note>, it extends 800 miles in length and 300 in width. In it, among other things, London is a very famous town, called *Londinum* by the ancients, a very famous <term>Emporium: a major center of commerce and trade</term> for nearly the whole West, in which trade of all kinds is carried out.

<margin>Helena comes to Rome.</margin> Helena having set out from Britain for Rome, she arrived and, out of the unexpected joy of seeing her most beloved son, she almost reached the point of deathly faintness. Truly her son himself restored her greatly, though even he could not restrain himself from tears. Their words to one another do not seem to me worth relating now. Nevertheless, Constantine himself told his dearest mother of the many benefits bestowed upon him in many ways and unexpectedly by the Lord Jesus Christ. For instance, that a most excellent time had come to him, in which the sun, which had previously been behind a cloud, shone most brightly upon him. First of all, indeed, he was delivered from the greatest dangers through the trophy of the Holy Cross, which had appeared to him as a golden sign in the air <note>The famous vision of the "Chi-Rho" or cross before the Battle of the Milvian Bridge</note>; not only was he delivered, but he victoriously carried off a great triumph over the tyrant <note>The rival Emperor Maxentius</note>. Furthermore, he said that the apostles of Christ, Peter and Paul, appeared to him in a nightly vision, giving him the best advice for recovering his health. Finally, after receiving the grace of health, he—along with all the Roman people—had visibly seen the image of the Savior miraculously depicted on the walls in the Basilica of Saint John the Baptist <note>Now known as the Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran</note>, which he had recently built. 

The Emperor recounted these and many other portents and miracles that had happened to him to his mother. Hearing these things, the solemn mother was violently stunned and stood astonished with a certain miraculous joy; her voice immediately stuck in her throat, and she began to waver in various thoughts between fear and joy. There were present at that time many very learned Hebrews; the most holy Pope Sylvester was also present with an innumerable multitude of people, when these things were seriously recited by the Emperor to his mother Helena. There was much and long debate concerning this. Pope Sylvester, however, wishing to show that the Jewish accusers were false—since they kept asserting that Christians were devoid of reason and persuaded by faith alone, unable to prove anything at all—set aside all quibbling and immediately brought forth the most certain and clear proofs of the Christian faith. With many transparent arguments, he proved that the grace of God and heavenly blessings were bestowed upon Christians through our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God and our Savior. 

For he said: "Listen to me, O Jews, and all you who stand by. Our speech and preaching are not (as our Apostle says) <note>Sylvester is quoting St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 2:4.</note> with the persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power." And again: "We speak wisdom among the perfect; yet not the wisdom of this age, nor of the princes of this world, who are coming to nothing; but we speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery." <note>original: "sapientiam in ministerio absconditam," referencing 1 Corinthians 2:6-7.</note> Furthermore, he said: "Our sufficiency is from God, who has made us fit ministers of the New Testament." 

Finally, Pope Sylvester—with the August son <note>This refers to Emperor Constantine the Great.</note> and his mother <note>Saint Helena.</note> present, along with countless wise men—refuted the objections of the Jews after a long, rational, and most wise debate. <margin>Sylvester and the Jews</margin> He showed that our ancestors, though they had long held to the worship of demons, had paid attention to the Jewish scriptures; because of these, they came to loathe and despise their former rituals. Although they gathered many things from those scriptures that agreed with the Christian religion, they nevertheless refused to imitate the ceremonies and way of life of the Jews themselves. 

But, lest his words should seem to be merely his own invention, as if he had received these things only from his elders or the ancient virtues of the Jews, he set them out in the open before the eyes of everyone, so that the power of his dispute and argumentation might be evident to all. He proved through the very scriptures of the Jews that Christians had been liberated from their former errors. He also proved with many reasons why Christians, while admiring the Jewish scriptures, nonetheless chose to reject the Jewish way of life. 

Lastly, the holy Pope Sylvester himself showed those Jews the nature of the Gospel, and who could properly and sincerely be called "most Christian"—that it was neither a Gentile nor a Jewish way, but a certain new and true religion named after the Savior himself. Indeed, the Pope brought before all who were standing there (who were indeed legalistically stunned) the ancient and primary theologies of all nations, regions, and cities. He presented the proven opinions of all the wise philosophers concerning the gods and the constitution of the world. From these most clear reasons, they were able to recognize whether or not the Christians were right to reject the Jewish rites. When the Jews did not know how to respond to these things, they yielded to the most holy Sylvester and submitted their necks to the yoke of Christianity. 

Helena, however, because of her long-standing acquaintance with the Jews, had some knowledge of the Divine Scriptures and was not ignorant of the Hebrew language. <margin>The Trinity</margin> She proposed questions to the holy Sylvester about the scriptures and demanded the causes and reasons for many passages. <margin>Excellent [explanation]</margin> But he most effectively instructed her and all the others, not only regarding the Divine Scriptures but also concerning the mystery of the most holy Trinity. He declared that God is one, the almighty creator and Father of all things visible and invisible, and that His only Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were created, is true God. Neither did the Father ever have a beginning, nor the Son. They held that the Holy Spirit is also truly God, proceeding from the Father, equal in all things to the Father and the Son: in power, in will, in eternity, and in substance. Nor is there any rank whatsoever in the Trinity; nothing that can be called lower or higher, but the entire Divinity is equal in its perfection. Thus, except for the names which indicate the unique property of the Persons, whatever is said of one Person can most worthily be understood of all three. 

He taught, moreover, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one in substance, but are distinguished only by Their Persons and names. He taught that the Son of God—who possessed eternity without beginning along with the Father and the Holy Spirit—at the end of the ages took up a perfect man of our nature from Mary, ever virgin. And He taught that He truly took upon Himself the passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to human sufferings and physical experiences.</note> of men, yet in such a way that His divinity remained impassible <note>original: "impassibilis"; incapable of suffering or changing.</note>. Whatever the mind can think, and whatever the tongue cannot explain, we must believe happened at that time. Everyone rushed to embrace one another; and for the joy of Christ, not only did the holy prelate Sylvester and his clergy weep, but even the most holy Augustus Constantine did not cease to cry. 

Oh, good Jesus, how auspicious was that day! What great exultation there was in that now-sanctified city. ## Concerning Saint Melania, a Roman Matron. Chapter 117.

[A large decorative initial 'M' containing the letters 'M' and 'A'. To the right is a woodcut illustration of a woman in religious habit, possibly Saint Melania, holding a book and standing in a landscape.]

**M**elania was the finest of Roman matrons, once the daughter of the most noble consul Marcellus. She was a woman of truly beautiful body, and most splendid in her holiness, character, magnificence, integrity, and laudable modesty. Saint Jerome calls her "holy" on account of the merits of her virtue, because there was a certain nobility in all her virtues. The same Blessed Jerome hoped to have a place with her on the day of judgment. In the three hundred and seventy-seventh year of the Christian era—which was the tenth year of the reign of Emperor Valentinian—having left behind her only son Urbanus <note>Historical sources usually name her son Valerius Publicola; Urbanus may be a variant or error in this specific hagiography.</note> as the prefect of the city of Rome, she sailed to Jerusalem for the sake of Christ. There, she stood out to everyone as such a miracle of all virtues, and especially of humility, that she earned the name **Thecla**. <note>Saint Thecla was a famous first-century follower of St. Paul; being called a "new Thecla" was one of the highest compliments for a devout woman.</note> For indeed, beyond the things already mentioned—namely the marks of her nobility—she was to be set before all other Romans of her age for her chastity, humility, and merits. It will be enough to relate a single memorable and almost incredible act of hers to understand her whole life and to pay her the deserved honor.

The same Saint Jerome reports, among other monuments of her passion and faith, that while her husband’s body was still warm and not yet buried, she lost two sons of wonderful promise and future integrity. At this truly cruel news, though she was nearly out of her mind with grief, she did not tear her hair, nor rip her clothes, nor beat her breast according to the custom of the women of this world. Instead, with dry eyes, she stood motionless, and casting herself at the feet of the crucifix as if she were holding [Christ] himself in her hands, she said: "Now, my Lord Jesus Christ, I shall serve you more freely, because you have unburdened me of such a heavy load." <note>original: "honore." While this literally means "honor," it is used here ironically or as a synonym for the "weight" of worldly status.</note> And so that she might utterly trample underfoot all the ornaments of worldly folly, she despised her innumerable riches and, having effectively abandoned her aforementioned son Urbanus, she took up the cross of the Lord as a sign of piety.

She attached herself to the mastery and teaching of Saint Jerome, who took her under his instruction because of her renowned holiness, and he honored her with all veneration as long as he lived. But she, having granted all the possessions she then held to her only son Urbanus, did not cease to pray for the Lord’s mercy in continuous days of fasting and mourning, appearing unkempt and humble in **ashes and sackcloth**. <note>A traditional sign of extreme penance and mourning.</note> In place of customary worldly songs, she chose the psalms; instead of sweet and vain speech, she chose the Gospels; and in place of luxuries, she chose continence; and for a "sweet life," she accepted fasting for the entire duration of her life. And so, in this most excellent way of living, she finally returned her immaculate soul to Christ at Bethlehem.

# Of Queen Mamea and Empress Mamea

[Woodcut illustration of a crowned woman sitting in a landscape, holding a scepter.]

**M**amea, or Mania <note>This refers to Mavia (reigned c. 375–425 AD), a powerful warrior queen of the Saracen (Arab) confederation who rebelled against Rome.</note>, a certain noble young Egyptian <note>In many medieval accounts, "Egyptian" was used loosely for various peoples of the Near East or Saracens.</note> of royal blood, was renowned during the times of the Emperor Valentinian <note>original: "Ualẽtiniani Augusti"</note>. From which parents she drew her lineage, her age, and the names of her parents and husband have been lost to the passage of time. It is nonetheless to be believed that she was born of the most noble and great parents; nor is it certain whether she had any offspring. Thus, after her husband died, she possessed such a great spirit that she not only took up the rule of the nations her husband had governed and restrained through skill and wit, but, her strength increased by the greatness of her soul, she declared an implacable war against the Romans, so much so that she began to be formidable to them. When she had greatly worn down their resources through frequent battles, she also most fiercely devastated the towns of the Palestinian and Arabian borders. When later the Emperor Valens <note>The Eastern Roman Emperor Valens (reigned 364–378 AD), who faced Mavia's revolt.</note> and Lucius the heretic <note>Lucius of Alexandria, an Arian bishop who persecuted the orthodox Nicene Christians.</note> humbly begged her for peace, she was unwilling to grant it unless they designated the most holy hermit, Moses, as bishop for her people. When Lucius had most willingly promised to do this and attempted to carry it out, the holy Moses refused, saying: "O Lucius, all the Catholic Christians <note>original: "x̃piani oēs catholici"</note>, certainly condemned to the mines, banished across various islands, and thrust into prisons, bear witness against you. Therefore, know that unless you permit all those whom you hold condemned to go free, you shall never lay your hands upon me for consecration." Moved by these words, Lucius the <term>pontiff</term> <note>In this context, a high-ranking cleric or bishop.</note> or patriarch, together with the Emperor Valens, immediately recalled all the bishops. And thus, in this manner, they presented the consecrated Moses as a priest to the Queen; and through this, a complete peace was restored to the Roman Empire. They say this woman was favorable to Christians, and that she performed many deeds with a great spirit, and restored many cities that had collapsed from old age, and lost them anew. By what kind of death she died, or what successors she had, I do not remember reading in any books.

She bought bread with only three small coins <note>original: "minutis"</note> which had been given to her as alms. Crossing the river in a small boat, she went into the vast desert. ### Concerning Blesilla, the holy widow of Rome and daughter of Saint Paula. Chapter 192.

[Large decorated initial 'B' containing a figure]
[Illustration: A woman in a red cloak and blue dress with a halo, holding an open book, standing in a landscape. This represents Blesilla, noted for her scholarship.]

**Blesilla**, the noblest of all Roman women, was the child of the most holy matron **Paula** and the sister of the virgin **Eustochium**. She is a most famous example of widowhood. In this year, which is the three hundred and eighty-ninth after the Christian birth <note>389 AD; though historically she died in 384, the text dates her passing here</note>, having left behind a most certain and indelible proof of her religious love for God, she passed from darkness to light at Rome in the company of her holy mother, in the twentieth year of her age. As the divine **Jerome** reports, she received her crown while caught between the fire of a beginning faith and the perfection of her finished work. Truly, because of her great holiness, innocence, mercy, and chastity, as well as her outstanding education in three languages <note>Latin, Greek, and Hebrew</note>, I think she should rightly be counted among the most famous—indeed, the saintly—women. She was also a model of great humility and frugality. Indeed, when she had lost her very powerful and noble husband in the flower of her youth, she immediately followed her mother's example. With the most burning faith, she raised the standard of the cross, appearing to grieve more for her lost virginity than for the death of her husband. Once Blesilla was freed from the bond of marriage, nothing was more important to her than to humble herself through a lowly life and a despised style of dress. Her example of humility was almost unheard of in that age. Just as she was previously adorned with the most precious necklaces, and spent the whole day looking for what she might be lacking...

**Concerning Saint Blaesilla and Saint Asella**

Before the mirror, she used to have her hair parted and arranged by her handmaidens, not just once but many times. Yet afterwards, her head being entirely neglected, it seemed sufficient to her simply to be veiled. Likewise, where once the softest rain seemed harsh to her, she later did not cease to beg and invoke the Lord's mercy—so that He might deign to forgive her sins—praying and praising God upon the bare ground on her knees with tears and incredible fervor. <note>Blaesilla was a young widow who, after a period of worldly vanity, underwent a dramatic religious conversion under the guidance of Saint Jerome.</note> Thus, after her prayers, the psalms would resound; with her neck relaxed, her knees wavering, and her sleepless eyes drooping, her mind—burning with such great ardor—could scarcely be persuaded to rest. Her clothing was always humble. Her belt was not made of gold or set with gems, but was woolen and most pure in its total simplicity, designed so that it could more tightly bind and even cut into her garments. <note>The "cutting" refers to the practice of wearing tight or rough belts as a form of bodily penance or mortification of the flesh.</note> Indeed, the very humility of her clothes did not signify a prideful heart (as is seen in many who are puffed up with spiritual vanity), but rather she said in her inner mind that there was no middle ground between the dress of handmaidens and that of noble ladies, except that she was more easily recognized because she walked with a heavy and more negligent step.

Finally, four months after taking up her holy purpose, she fell into a wasting sickness and burned with fevers for thirty continuous days. She remained so destitute in her whole body from these fevers that her thin neck could scarcely sustain her head and face. Yet she always desired to hold either a Book of the Prophets or the Gospel in her hands, and from the reading of them, she filled her face with tears. At last, when the heat of the fevers parched her holy and weak little body, and she lay half-dead in her small bed, she spoke these final words to those standing around her: "Pray, I ask, to the Lord Jesus, that He forgive me, because I was not able to fulfill what I desired." <note>original: "Orate quaeso dominum Iesum, ut mihi ignoscat, quia quod volebam, implere non valui"</note> And saying these things, the burden of the flesh cast aside, her soul flew to its Author; after a long pilgrimage, she ascended into her ancient possession. <note>Her "ancient possession" refers to the Christian concept of returning to a heavenly home or paradise.</note> Her holy mother wept for her death so much that she herself nearly died. Upon her holy death, Saint Jerome, who was then in Rome and wishing to console her mother, finally used these words: 

"As long as the spirit rules these limbs of mine, my tongue shall resound with Blaesilla. To her my labors shall be dedicated; for her my genius shall sweat. <note>original: "Dum spiritus hos meos reget artus, Blesilla mea resonabit lingua. Illi mei dedicabunt labores: illi sudabit ingenium."</note> There will be no page that does not resound with Blaesilla. Virgins, widows, monks, and priests shall read of her fixed in my mind; and eternal memory shall outweigh the brief space of her life." 

This Blaesilla was of such a tenacious and almost divine intellect, with a most sharp memory and an eloquent tongue, that even at a tender age she devoted so much effort to her studies that she not only learned the Latin and Greek languages perfectly, but also—something all of Greece admired in Origen <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was a prolific early Christian scholar and theologian.</note>—she conquered the difficulties of the Hebrew language in a short time. She learned to pronounce the rattling and broken words so precisely <note>The "rattling and broken words" refers to the distinctive guttural sounds of Hebrew that were often difficult for Latin and Greek speakers to master.</note> that anyone who heard her would have thought she knew no language other than Hebrew.

# Of Saint Asella. Of Saint Euphrosina. Folio 106

When she had asked her mother for a dark garment <note>The Latin *fuscam vestem* refers to the somber, undyed clothing of a mourner or an ascetic, signaling her rejection of colorful noble silks.</note> and could not obtain it, soon, while she was still a tender little child, with an incredible passion she sold a gold chain which she wore around her neck—without her parents' knowledge—and with the price she had a dark dress bought for herself, which she had so desired. She then dressed herself in it. In this humble clothing (having already condemned the worldly life), she dedicated herself to the Lord. 

After her twelfth year had passed, she accepted, held, and fulfilled with the most burning love that which she had chosen by her own will and by the gift of God. She chose for herself a single small cell at the house of her spiritual mother, Marcella, in which she always lived; it was to her a place of both prayer and quiet. There, she treated fasting as a game, and hunger as a banquet and a sumptuous meal. Her food was usually bread and water alone. 

She always conducted herself with such moderation and kept herself so strictly within the secrets of her chamber that she never set foot in public, nor did she ever know the conversation of any man. What is more remarkable, she loved and saw her own sister (also a virgin) only rarely. She also worked with her own hands every day, knowing it is written: **He who does not work shall not eat.** <note>original: "Qui non laborat non manducet" — a reference to 2 Thessalonians 3:10.</note> 

She spoke to her heavenly bridegroom either by praying or by singing psalms. She hurried to the thresholds of the martyrs <note>This refers to visiting the tombs or shrines of saints in Rome.</note> almost without being seen. Although at all times she fasted three or four times a week, during Lent she would link almost all the weeks together with a joyful face. Her bed was often the bare ground. She wore haircloth and sackcloth instead of a soft shirt. 

So great was her perseverance and frequency in prayer that her knees displayed the hardness of camels' skin. <note>A traditional hagiographic image indicating constant kneeling, famously attributed to Saint James the Just.</note> Nothing was more pleasant than her severity, and nothing more severe than her pleasantness. Her speech was brief and serious, seasoned with all edification. Her walk was always the same. Neglected cleanliness and an unrefined garment were her ornaments. 

In this most holy order of living, the virgin Asella reached the fiftieth year of her life in such a way that she never suffered from a stomach ache nor was she tormented by the neglect of her internal organs. Indeed, her skin never gave off any odor, but rather, being always healthy in body and even healthier in soul, she considered her hardships to be delights. In the middle of a bustling city, she found the solitude of the monks. 

And so, after the finished work of her life, she migrated to the heavens as a victor and a heavy-triumphing queen. We have touched upon her most holy life here in a brief discourse for the edification of many, so that widows and virgins may imitate the illustrious and famous Asella, and that married women may honor her, and the harmful may be afraid and confounded—and finally, that all priests may take up the examples of her virtues.

### Of Saint Euphrosina, holy virgin of Alexandria. Chapter 124.

**E**uphrosina of Alexandria, a most illustrious holy virgin and truly worthy of every praise. In the 392nd year from the birth of Christ, not far from the city of Alexandria, in the monastery of Abbot Paphnutius, she passed to the Lord, distinguished by innumerable virtues and miracles. She had a father named Paphnutius, a certain man among the citizens who was venerable in age and nobility, and at that time distinguished in military service—a most Christian father.

# Concerning Saint Euphrosyna

The beauty and character of this virgin were not distinguished by any changeableness; her modesty and maidenly gravity, as well as her greatest learning and eloquence, were so great that they exceeded all human estimation. Since she possessed a most sharp intellect, diligently applying herself to studies from her very adolescence, she progressed so much in liberal and sacred literature through her conversation with holy monks that she was considered excellently learned beyond all others. When the noble father Paphnutius <note>The Latin text spells this "Pamphuntius," a common medieval variation of the name Paphnutius.</note> noticed this, he was moved by inexpressible joy because, beyond her knowledge and eloquence, she excelled in singular honesty, gravity, and holiness. Indeed, this girl was endowed with these virtues alongside the brilliance of her mind and the excellence of her character, such that she seemed admirable to all beyond her age. Because of these innumerable virtues of soul and body, many Alexandrians <note>Citizens of Alexandria, Egypt, where the story is set.</note> who excelled in rank contended importunately to have her given to them in marriage. And when her father had finally promised his daughter Euphrosyna as a wife to one man excelling in both dignity and wealth, he led her one day to the monastery <term>cenobium: a monastery where monks live in community rather than as hermits</term> of certain monks for the sake of greeting and prayer. 

There the virgin remained for three days, contemplating the order of those fathers and their way of life, and said within herself: "Blessed are such men, for while established in this life, they are certainly held to be like angels; and after their departure from this world, they enjoy the reward of eternal life." Immediately her heart seemed to be pierced by the zeal of the love of God. It happened, however, that some days later, the memory of the abbot of that place was to be celebrated—he who had been the founder of that monastery. Therefore, the abbot sent an invitation to the honorable man Paphnutius. But when her father Paphnutius had departed from the house, Euphrosyna called a certain excellent brother and holy man and inquired from him about the number of those brothers, the observance of their fasts, their psalm-singing, and their entire way of living. She said further: "I would wish, my faithful father, to escape from here entirely in male attire, so that through the religious life I might be saved; but I fear my father very much, who desires to celebrate my wedding." But when the holy monk had given her instructions on how to cut her hair and depart, and her father had already set out for the monastery, Euphrosyna, putting aside womanly fear and assuming male attire, secretly went to the monastery where her father was. Bringing five hundred gold coins with her, she pretended that she was a eunuch from the palace, requesting the Abbot to be called Smaragdus <note>Latin for "Emerald."</note>; she immediately received the religious habit. When the Abbot had received her with a willing mind into the religious habit according to custom, he handed her over to Agapitus, a proven monk, to be instructed. Shortly, she gave such effort to vigils, fasts, and very frequent prayers that she was an object of admiration and wonder to all. 

But when the father Paphnutius returned home and did not find his only, most beloved daughter—whom alone he loved wonderfully even above his own life—he was affected by such sorrow that he stubbornly decided to commit suicide. As he was being carried along, raging and headlong, for his mind was already inflamed with excessive ferocity, the sudden and miserable mercy of God was present for him, drawing him back from every impulse of cruelty to saner counsel and restoring his virtue. And when he had sought her everywhere, she could be found nowhere. Therefore Paphnutius went away, sad and mourning, to the abbot, lamenting and beseeching that he might deign to pour out prayers to the Lord for his daughter, so that he might be able to find her. The abbot, as he was of a most pious mind, grieved greatly for the man, and commanded the monks...

After this, when she fell into a wasting illness, her father came to her again, pleading with the most earnest prayers that she might fervently beseech God for his daughter. She said, "Do not be saddened, my lord; it is near at hand that your daughter shall be revealed to you. But I ask that you deign to remain here for three days." 

When these days had passed, and she knew she was about to depart from this life, she called her father to her and said: "Since the end of my life is now at hand, I do not wish to keep you in suspense any longer, nor indeed to leave you in sorrow. I," she said, "am your daughter Euphrosyne. You have seen me now, and at last you are satisfied. But I ask you by my God and I adjure you, do not let anyone touch my body, but whatever is necessary, perform it yourself." And when she had told him everything in order, she gave up her immaculate spirit to God. 

When this matter was publicized and known, everyone with one voice glorified God, who never ceases to perform wonders. There was then one monk who was blind <note>original: "captus oculis"—literally 'seized in the eyes'</note>, who, when he touched the holy little body, immediately regained his sight. Indeed, her father, having seen these miracles, distributed his entire wealth to the poor and took up the religious habit himself. In that place where his daughter had lived <note>original: "decubuerat"—had lain or stayed</note>, he lived for ten years in great austerity of life, and afterwards migrated to the heavenly kingdoms.

## **¶ Concerning Saint Marentia, Patroness of the people of Trent. Chapter 125.**

**M**arentia, the holy patroness of the people of Trent and the parent of Saint Vigilius (the Bishop of the city of Trent), was a Roman matron. During the times of the Emperors <note>original: "Augustorum"—the Augusti</note> Jovinian and Valentinian, and while the most blessed Pope Damasus presided on the Chair of Peter <note>The Papacy</note> in Rome, she was a woman of great soul. Bearing the greatest and most ardent sign of love toward the salvation of her sons, she provided a testament of the most upright faith to those present and to posterity.

# **Concerning Saint Marentia**

...eternal. Although it has not come down to our day from which parents she was born or from what lineage she sprang, it is enough for the praise of her brilliance to know that she was the consort of Marentius, a most powerful Roman patrician <note>A member of the noble ruling class of ancient Rome.</note> distinguished by the rank of praetor—even though he was a pagan. <margin>Vigilius, Claudius, and Maioranus, the sons.</margin> After she had borne him three sons of marvelous character—namely, Vigilius, Claudius, and Maioranus—she ceased to bear children. Being a most Christian mother, she had all of them purified in the bath of baptism from their infancy. Later, once they were somewhat grown, she sent them to Athens (following the custom of their father’s rank) to be steeped in the liberal arts. There, as they were youths of the finest nature and most excellent intellect, they applied themselves to their studies with such great capacity, devoting themselves to all manner of virtues and rational disciplines, that in a short time they were undoubtedly considered most illustrious in every field of knowledge. Finally, having returned home to their parents, they began to apply their entire intellect to the Divine Scriptures.

On account of this, it would be difficult to explain here how Marentia—a most wise, religious, and pious parent—leapt for joy and a kind of divine triumph. She herself was by no means ignorant of fine literature or divine matters; thus, she frequently debated the interpretations of Holy Scripture with her sons, and they would wonderfully compare the teachings of Pythagoras and Socrates <note>Famous Greek philosophers whose ideas were often reconciled with early Christian thought by scholars.</note> among themselves. Because of this, it came to pass that they declared a disregard for worldly affairs and devoted themselves entirely to divine things. They did this so that they might eventually attain glorious immortality with the Lord Jesus Christ and reach a blessed end. 

This was especially true when the glorious mother realized that the city of Rome was a kind of "habitation of demons." Detesting the vices and sins of her husband, she would admonish her sons daily, saying: "I beseech you, my sweetest sons, let us flee from the midst of Babylon! <note>original: "de medio babilonis" — a biblical metaphor for a corrupt or godless city; here referring to pagan Rome.</note> Let us flee, I say, so that each of us may save his soul. Let us not be participants in the sins of our parents, nor receive their plagues, for her sins have reached even unto the heavens."

As mentioned before, she was uncommonly well-educated and refined in her sweet eloquence. She had been diligently instructed by the blessed Pope Damasus and was greatly encouraged in her resolve to live a good and blessed life. She omitted nothing that might lead toward true religion and the light of eternal truth. Thus, by her own encouragement and example, she led all her sons—already skilled in divine letters and inflamed by the grace of the Holy Spirit—to such a loathing <note>original: "nauseam"</note> for this world and such a passion for true religion that she did not fear to steadfastly defend their cause before their father, her husband, who wished to overcome their resolve.

She would say daily to these children <note>original: "pignoribus" — literally "pledges," a poetic Latin term for children as the bond of a marriage.</note>: "Sweetest sons, no man can serve two masters. <note>Matthew 6:24</note> Likewise, one cannot enjoy both present pleasures and future joys. Our Lord says, 'He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters.'" She always said that the love of God and the love of the world were adversaries to each other. Indeed, like a most wise parent, fearing that these earthly things might eventually oppose the virtues and salvation of her sons, she very often set before them and explained that golden teaching of John the Evangelist, <margin>A most excellent teaching</margin> saying: "Sons, take heed and see: for all that is in the world is either the lust of the flesh, or the lust of the eyes, or the pride of life. <note>1 John 2:16</note> I beseech you, turn your minds away from other things for a little while so that you may perceive this more fully. Set yourselves on high, as if in a watchtower, from where..."

...observed with an intuition of those things which are done down here among humans and mortals, a miserable thing to behold. You will see that I begin from the **concupiscence** <note>In a theological sense, this refers to intense worldly desire or lust that leans away from reason.</note> of the flesh: I say, my most beloved sons, you will see that from the smoke of this unchaste flesh even the air has lost its own natural brightness. So great indeed is the power and, so to speak, the "necessity" of this worst of crimes, that it is much easier to strike it out than to avoid it. I come also to the concupiscence of the eyes, by which the holy Evangelist denotes the crime of **avarice** <note>Greed.</note>; which has now taken root in the souls of almost all mortals. It is right to say what even the pagan poets deplore: <note>original: "Viuitur ex rapto/nō hospes ab hospite tutus"</note> *They live on plunder; the guest is not safe from his host.* <margin>The poet says.</margin> Finally, my sons, if you wish to turn your eyes toward the vices of a proud age, surely an infinite number of evils will offer themselves to you. Thus, I dare to say that ambition, greed, and carnal use and luxury possess all the rewards of virtue. Saying these and similar things often and more often, and most frequently repeating them as an excellent mother, she asserted that only eternal things are certainly true, while temporal things are merely "shadows of truth" <note>original: "veresimilia" — things that look like truth but are fleeting.</note> and ought to be altogether despised. She said that one must flee toward eternal things so that evils might be avoided. Wherefore, in order to prove that she had fulfilled her own exhortations through her actions—having already been separated from her husband by divorce <note>In the early medieval context, "divortium" often referred to a legal separation for the purpose of taking up a religious life of celibacy.</note>—she distributed the greater part of the vast riches she had obtained by hereditary right and paternal succession to the poor, and undertook a plan of pilgrimage together with her sons.

She was indeed set on fire with a marvelous ardor, and was continually driven by a certain incredible strength, as if forgetting her sex and the fragility of her body. Not mindful for a single moment of anything pertaining to the world, she deserted her soil and her fatherland. Almost without a retinue, she proceeded eagerly with her sons toward the desert of the holy fathers, despising all earthly things (so to speak) so that she might attain true riches. Finally, this Maxentia, wishing to flee and turn away from the mouths of those who would praise her—and being unable to endure worldly visitations and crowds—decided to leave Rome and its ceremonies with her family. Having first obtained permission and a blessing from the most blessed **Pope Damasus** <note>Damasus I, Pope from 366–384 AD.</note>, she set out joyfully and prepared. She traversed the whole of **Picenum** and **Flaminia** <note>Ancient regions of Italy along the Adriatic and the road to Rome.</note> as well as part of **Lombardy** on her delicate feet; she reverently visited whatever holy places she could reach in those regions. She cheerfully bestowed alms as far as her means permitted.

At that time, those regions were flourishing with most learned and holy men, such as many monks, priests, and hermits. Whenever she entered their lodgings with her sons (scenting their holiness), she would prostrate herself at their feet in their manner and earnestly beg for lessons in salvation from everyone. She always thought she saw Christ in each individual, and if by chance she conferred any act of piety upon them, she rejoiced as if she had conferred it upon the Lord Jesus Christ. Finally, when they had reached the city of **Bergamo** <margin>Bergamo</margin> in Lombardy, and had been kindly received by its citizens and religious persons, they provided many examples of a holy life to those same citizens for many days as most religious persons. Then, being not a little delighted by the kindness of the people and the goodness of the soil—as if they intended to remain there forever—they built several small cells for themselves not far outside the city walls, on the most pleasant **Mount Delimo**. There, removed from worldly disturbances, they led a quiet life for some time in the greatest holiness and integrity of soul; by which life and religious practice they foresaw many future things. Wherefore, even unto this day, that place is called **Mount Saint Vigilius** by the inhabitants. In that place, after their "falling asleep" <note>A traditional Christian term for death.</note>, a church was built by the citizens in honor of the same Saint Vigilius, which remains intact to this day...

# **Concerning Saint Monica**

She took care to refresh the poor with food secretly taken from her home; and very often, moved by a natural piety, she did not fear to bring them into her own house to be fed. Toward all her other relatives, she was nevertheless most obedient. From her very infancy, a certain compassion was seen to grow within her; because of this, she showed a natural affection for loving the poor. She visited the sick with most ardent love and received guests; she washed the feet of the sick and served them as best she could. As a girl of a most gentle nature, she would reprove those who were quarreling and strive to bring them back to a healthy state of peace. 

There was also in her a certain desire for learning. For this reason, she constantly strove to either hear or learn something excellent. Indeed, there seemed to be in her an insatiable desire for learning. Therefore, as much as possible, she followed her most Christian soul in every way of life according to the measure of her capacity; she clung to it, desiring to imitate that soul in every walk of life. The sharpness of her mind was such—as her divine son <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the famous theologian and author of the *Confessions*.</note> relates—that she attained something good every day beyond her years. By this study of knowledge and by her way of life, it came to pass that her mind could never be deceived by any vanities of the world, nor certainly by pleasures or pomp. 

When she was thirteen years old, she was given by her parents as a wife to a noble Carthaginian patrician. She accepted a husband who was still a pagan <note>original: *gentilem*</note>, not by her own will but by the will of her elders; she preferred to proceed safely in a humble station rather than to waver in another state on a precarious footing. Yet, once the marriage was entered into, she thought of nothing else by day or night except that, once the fruit of the marriage was returned <note>A reference to bearing and raising children.</note>, she might attain a state of chastity. And she, a woman of such great character, strove to eventually join her most fierce and pagan husband to her own purpose, not leaving him behind but waiting for him as a companion for her own salvation. This holy wife desired children for no other reason than to leave them to Christ as either Christians or virgins. Nor was her hope deceived; for besides that most holy teacher Augustine, she left behind two daughters, Perpetua and Basilica, distinguished virgins in perpetual virginity. Then, not only for herself but for the entire world, after her sleep and rest <note>A common Christian metaphor for death.</note>, she brought forth to the earth that most brilliant light, the most consummate teacher of the Church. 

Therefore, Monica, having been given to the aforementioned man named Patricius, did not cease to venerate him, serving him as if he were her lord, and striving to win him for the Lord. Indeed, she was very beautiful, wise, lovable, respectful, and modest. She always bore his fits of anger and his injuries in such a way that she never had any quarrel because of them. For she always waited for God's mercy upon him so that, believing in the Lord, he might afterwards be made chaste. And although he was exceedingly hot-tempered, he was nonetheless also outstanding in benevolence. For this reason, she never presumed to resist him when he was angry, not only in deed but not even with a word. But when he was calmed and quiet, she would afterwards, when she saw it was an opportune time, give an account of her actions if there was a need. 

But many matrons, whose husbands seemed gentler, bore the marks of blows <note>Signs of physical domestic abuse.</note> even on their disfigured faces; during friendly conversations, they would criticize the lives of their husbands. Monica, as if in jest, would seriously warn their tongues, which they had filled with too much talkativeness, burdening their husbands with innumerable complaints—that they were overlooked, that they were abandoned, that they were looked down upon, and finally that they were held in no value by their husbands, treated like hired and purchased handmaids. Therefore, she advised them to be mindful of their condition <note>The legal and social status of wives in the late Roman Empire, where women had few rights compared to their husbands.</note>, and that they ought not to be prideful against their lords. But they wondered greatly, knowing what a fierce husband Monica endured, that it had never been heard, nor was there any sign, that Patricius had ever beaten his wife, or that they had ever disagreed for even a single day in a domestic quarrel. And when they asked the cause privately, she taught them her rule, which I mentioned above.

FOLIO 110

# Of Saint Monica

All people, not only the matrons but also the men who knew these things, cried out together and said:
“O woman, worthy to be extolled to heaven with sacred praises!”
Even her mother-in-law, who was at first stirred up against her by the whispers of evil servant-girls, she overcame with such most kind services—persisting in gentleness and patience—that the mother-in-law, of her own accord, revealed to her son the gossiping <note>original: "medias," literally "middle" or "intervening" tongues that sow discord between parties</note> tongues of the maids, by which the domestic peace between herself and her daughter-in-law was being disturbed; and she demanded punishment for them. Thereafter, Monica lived under her mother-in-law for as long as the woman survived, within the limits of her duty <note>original: "subiectionis," referring to the traditional social and domestic submission expected of a daughter-in-law at the time</note>, so peacefully and so holily that she surpassed the praises of all women of the past through her celebrated devotion <note>original: "filiatione," which usually means "sonship" or the state of being a child; here it refers to her conduct as a "daughter" to her mother-in-law</note>. 

Indeed, this venerable Monica was like a most precious gem shining among many gems; and just as the sun’s radiance overwhelms and obscures the small fires of the stars, so did her hum[ility] <note>The Latin text cuts off at "hum-", likely intending "humilitate" (humility), a core virtue in this narrative.</note> [surpass] the virtues and powers of all others...

<summary>This page recounts Saint Monica's virtuous conduct within her household, specifically how her patience and kindness won over her difficult mother-in-law and silenced the gossip of servant-girls. It uses celestial and lapidary metaphors to elevate her sanctity above all other women.</summary>

<keywords>Saint Monica, mother-in-law, domestic peace, humility, hagiography, patience, servant-girls, virtue</keywords>

# On Saint Monica

He speaks thus: Our mother Monica was with us. I had already recognized her natural talent and her spirit—which was set ablaze toward divine matters—through our long daily life together and through careful observation. 

When, indeed, in a certain discussion regarding matters of no small importance <note>This likely refers to the philosophical dialogues Augustine held with his friends and family, specifically "On the Happy Life" (*De Beata Vita*)</note>, which I held with my guests on my birthday <note>Augustine’s birthday was November 13th.</note> and recorded in a small book, her intellect appeared so great to me that nothing seemed more suited to <term>true philosophy</term> <note>In this context, "philosophy" refers to the pursuit of wisdom and the Christian life rather than just academic study.</note>. 

And so, I had resolved in my mind that whenever she had sufficient leisure, I would act to ensure she was not absent from our conversation. Her son <note>The narrator, Augustine, refers to himself here in the third person or as the speaker recording the event.</note> also said that his mother’s philosophy pleased him a great deal; and for that reason, he said, "I gladly hand myself over and entrust myself to you, my mother, as a disciple." 

In all matters, both divine and human, Monica was so attentive that she did not seem to spend even a single moment of her life uselessly. Indeed, a holy fear was always in her heart, like a breast-band <note>original: "pectoralis fascia"</note> that might restrain harmful thoughts. In her mouth also, as if—

<summary>This page describes Saint Augustine's profound respect for his mother Monica's intellectual and spiritual depth, noting her active participation in his philosophical dialogues.</summary>

Folio 111

# On Saint Monica

They say that a holy bishop <note>This refers to Saint Ambrose, the Bishop of Milan, whom Monica frequently petitioned to intervene with her son.</note>, having been importuned by her with great persistence, spoke with a certain prophetic spirit. He said: "Go in peace, woman; for it is impossible that the son of such tears <note>original Latin: "tantarum lachrymarum filius." This became one of the most famous phrases associated with Monica, suggesting that the depth of a mother's grief and prayer guarantees a child's salvation.</note> should perish."

Furthermore, Saint Augustine says the following concerning her: that one day, while she was praying upon a certain wooden rule <note>original: "linea lignea." In Augustine's *Confessions*, he describes Monica having a vision while standing on a wooden measuring-rule or platform, symbolizing the "rule of faith."</note>, an Angel of the Lord appeared to her as she slept most peacefully. The Angel addressed her very kindly with these words: "Monica," he said, "be at ease; for your most pious prayers concerning your son Augustine have earned a hearing before the most merciful Redeemer of the human race. For it shall come to pass that in that heavenly homeland, where all things are full of tranquility and eternal joys, you shall both be there together. Therefore, let nothing sad or mournful remain with you regarding this matter. You must no longer labor and groan over this." Having said these things, the Angel vanished. And holy Monica, from her sleep... <note>The text cuts off here as the page ends.</note>

<summary>This page recounts two pivotal moments of divine encouragement for Saint Monica: the prophetic words of a bishop and a heavenly vision promising that she and her son, Augustine, would be reunited in heaven.</summary>
<keywords>Saint Monica, Saint Augustine, Saint Ambrose, vision, prophecy, conversion, mother's prayers, son of tears</keywords>

The blessed mother rejoiced beyond measure, that the Lord had deigned to make her, who was once sorrowful, joyful and happy.

**About Saint Monica Folio 112**

“Let no concern for this <note>referring to her burial place, as she had previously told her sons she did not care where she was buried as long as she was remembered in prayer</note> disturb you. I only ask this of you: that you remember me at the altar of the Lord in your offerings <note>original: "oblationibus" — referring to the prayers and the celebration of the Mass</note>, wherever you may be.” And so—to use the words of Augustine—on the ninth day of her illness, in the fifty-sixth year of her life and the thirty-third year of her son Augustine, that most religious and pious soul was released from the body, on the Nones of May <note>original: "nouis maij" — May 7th. The Nones was a marker in the Roman calendar</note>. And there she was buried with honor in the Basilica of Saint Aurea the Virgin <note>A martyr's church in Ostia Antica, the port city of Rome</note>. However, it is known that her holy body remained in that place until the year of salvation 1429. But God, who sees all things, wished that the holy body be placed in a more honorable location where it might be more worthily venerated by the followers of Christ. In the time of Pope Martin V <note>Pope from 1417–1431, known for restoring Rome</note>, it was ordered to be moved most honorably to Rome. And placed in the temple dedicated to her son Augustine, under the care of our brothers... <note>The text refers to the Augustinian Friars who maintained the Church of Sant'Agostino in Rome</note>

<summary>This page records the death of Saint Monica in Ostia and the subsequent 15th-century translation of her relics to the Church of Saint Augustine in Rome.</summary>

# Concerning Saint Monica and Saint Fabiola

O, how much we all confess we owe to you:
By whose help such great salvation was restored to the world: <note>The author attributes the "salvation" of the Church to Monica’s persistent prayers for her son, Saint Augustine.</note>
For surely, he would not have returned from the darkness to the sacred lights,
That son himself, converted by your merits.
Unless he had spread his high-sounding doctrines
Throughout the whole world, in so many and such great volumes.
Unless he had struck down so many wicked plagues of error
And so many depraved dogmas by his own genius,
Which strengthened the falling Church
With such vigor—O happy tears and prayers!
O sweet tears, may they conquer honey and honeycombs;
May these sweet prayers conquer everything!
What wonder if our faith and worship had perished,
And all the honor of our religion?
But now, since the pure world holds you,
Having reached the heights of heaven;
Since you have been snatched away from this earthly filth and prison,
You now inhabit more liberated places.
Now, as you look upon our affairs, consult for us better,
And pour out prayers more effectively for our salvation.
Bring help now, you, and succor the failing world;
Succor those in afflicted circumstances and bring help.
All nations entreat you; they pour out their vows to you.
Succor and bring help to all nations.
All the elderly and every age calls upon you.
Whoever calls upon you, bring help to them all.
Especially mothers, as you have experienced such great labors,
Bring help both to your children and to mothers.
The learned call upon you before all others; do not despise the learned,
For no one was more learned than your son; bring them help! <note>original: "Nemo tuo nato doctior." This refers to Saint Augustine, whose intellectual works defined Western Christianity.</note>
Hail, light of mothers! Most holy mother, hail!
O hail, parent who must be sung with eternal praise! Amen.

### ¶ Concerning Fabiola, a Roman matron. Chapter 127.

[Woodcut illustration of a woman (Saint Fabiola) in a brown habit with a white wimple and a yellow halo, holding a blue book, standing in a landscape with green plants and a pinkish sky.]

Fabiola, a most holy widow, the crown and singular glory of Roman matrons, departed to the Lord in Rome with the greatest testimony of her piety and humility, around the year of our salvation 405, before the destruction of the Roman disaster. <note>original: "ante excidium romane cladis." This refers to the Sack of Rome by the Visigoths in 410 AD; Fabiola died just years before this historic catastrophe.</note> Saint Jerome, writing about her admirable life and royal funeral rites, reports that she was a miracle. <note>Saint Jerome was a contemporary of Fabiola and a leading scholar of the early Church; he famously praised her for founding the first public hospital in the West.</note> For first, this venerable Fabiola was descended from the illustrious and noble family of the Fabii. <note>The Fabii were one of the most ancient and powerful patrician families in ancient Rome.</note>

<summary>This page contains a poetic tribute to Saint Monica, praising her role in the conversion of her son Saint Augustine, followed by the beginning of a biography of Saint Fabiola, a noble Roman widow praised by Saint Jerome.</summary>

<keywords>Saint Monica, Saint Augustine, Saint Fabiola, Saint Jerome, Roman Matrons, Fabii family, early Church history, conversion</keywords>
