FOLIO 113

### Concerning Saint Fabiola

She who, after the death of her second husband—whom she had taken while her first was still living, against the strictness of the Gospel <note>Fabiola had divorced an abusive first husband and remarried, a practice the early Church prohibited while the first spouse lived</note>—returned to her true self and showed such contrition for her error to everyone as no one could ever explain in words. For, in order to publicly confess her error, she put on sackcloth <note>a rough garment worn as a sign of mourning or penance</note>, and while all the people watched in the Lateran Basilica <note>The cathedral church of Rome and the seat of the Pope</note>—specifically on the holy day of Easter—she entered dressed in this way. There, in the order of the penitents before the bishops and priests, with her hair disheveled and her hands soiled, she prostrated herself humbly and, with tears, begged for pardon and penance for her errors.

Having finally obtained pardon, as soon as she returned home, she descended from the throne of her luxuries, took up a millstone, and made flour; and with bare feet, she waded through streams of tears and sat upon coals of fire, which by the grace of God served as a refreshment to her. Indeed, she cast away all bodily ornaments and studied to decorate her soul with humility and other most holy virtues, so much so that it is not easily judged whether she, unadorned, or **Quintus Maximus** <note>original: "Q. Maximus" — referring to Quintus Fabius Maximus, the great Roman general and ancestor of the Fabian family</note> in his toga, provided more ornament to the Fabian family.

Therefore, she frequently struck with her fists her own face, through which she had sought to please her second husband; then, despising gems, she did not wish to see linens on her bed and fled from every other ornament. She grieved as if she had committed adultery. Through this, with many expensive remedies, she sought to heal her own wound. After her penance was received by the church, she soon sold all the wealth she could possibly have (which was indeed ample and appropriate for her noble lineage), gathered it into money, and prepared it for the use of the poor.

And first of all, she built a hospice, which is commonly called a <term>hospital</term> <note>original: "hospitale" — at this time, a place for "hospitality" for the poor and sick rather than just a medical clinic</note>. In this place, she gathered and nurtured the sick of all kinds, the poor, and the wretched. In this work, she practiced such acts of piety as have ever been known to be done by anyone. Who would ever believe that a most noble and delicate woman would carry on her own shoulders those languishing from the <term>royal disease</term> <note>original: "morbo regio" — likely referring to jaundice or scrofula, which were considered particularly loathsome</note> and those seized and consumed by excessive stench? She washed the putrid gore and the wounds of the infirm, which certainly no one else would have presumed to do, or even dared to look upon. Furthermore, she offered food with her own hand to "breathing corpses" and performed other similar acts, which no rich person—or even hardly any holy man—could have ever attempted because of the queasiness of the stomach.

What monastery was not sustained by her resources? What naked or paralyzed person was not clothed in her own garments? In this, her festive bounty poured itself out after the manner of the ancient nations <note>referring to the grand public generosity of noble Roman families</note>. But not only in the city of Rome did Fabiola confer these refreshments of piety; she also traveled through several islands and the whole Etruscan sea...

<summary>This page recounts the public penance of Saint Fabiola of Rome for her second marriage and her subsequent devotion to extreme asceticism and the founding of the first public hospital. It emphasizes her transition from a noblewoman of the Fabian line to a humble servant of the sick and wretched.</summary>

<keywords>Saint Fabiola, Lateran Basilica, penance, Roman nobility, Quintus Fabius Maximus, hospital foundation, royal disease, asceticism, Christian charity</keywords>

+̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃̃

->**On Saint Paula**<- **FOLIO 114**

And leaving behind all her children, she set out for Syria with the virgin Eustochium <note>Eustochium (c. 368–420 AD) was Paula’s daughter and a lifelong companion in her ascetic labors; she is also recognized as a saint.</note>, her daughter, who was the companion of her holy purpose and her voyage. There, after she had visited and traveled through many of the sites of the holy fathers <note>This refers to the "Desert Fathers," the early Christian monks and hermits whose spiritual wisdom Paula sought to emulate.</note>, she finally arrived in Jerusalem sitting upon a little donkey. And it is said that she traveled through all the places of our Lord Jesus Christ with such fervor and devotion that, unless she had hurried on to the remaining sites, she could not have been drawn away from the first ones. For immediately, as she arrived before the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, she worshipped it as if she had seen Christ himself hanging there. Entering the tomb of the resurrection, she kissed the stone that the angel had moved from the door of the monument, as well as the holy place where the body of the Lord had lain. Like one thirsting for long-desired waters, she licked the spot with a faithful mouth, so that she seemed to have become completely lost to herself <note>original: "sui ipsius nescia"; this describes a state of ecstatic devotion where she was no longer aware of her own physical presence.</note>. What tears she shed there, how many groans, and what great sorrow she poured out: Jesus is the witness, who sees all things, as is the Father whom she entreated. Departing from there, she climbed up Mount Sion and...

# On Saint Paula

<note>Saint Paula (347–404 AD) was a wealthy Roman widow and a close companion of Saint Jerome. This text describes her ascetic life in Bethlehem after she abandoned her high-society Roman lifestyle.</note>

She abandoned luxuries, saying: "I who once pleased my husband and the world now desire to please Christ in this manner."
<margin>Chastity</margin>
If anyone wished to praise her chastity among such great virtues, it would certainly be superfluous; for even while she was a secular woman, she was an example to all the matrons of Rome. She conducted herself in such a way that the rumors of even the most malicious people never dared to invent anything against her. Indeed, nothing was more merciful than she, nothing more humble, and nothing more gentle. If she saw the poor, she supported them; if she saw the powerful, she encouraged them to do good deeds. Her generosity alone exceeded all moderation. For this reason, even the <term>best fathers</term><note>Likely referring to church leaders or advisors, including Saint Jerome himself.</note> sometimes reproached her for being so profuse in her giving. She would respond by saying: "It is written in the Gospel: 'He who has two tunics, let him give one to the one who has none'" <note>original: "Qui habet duas tunicas: vnā det non habenti"</note>. She introduced many other testimonies of Holy Scripture for this kind of thing with wonderful modesty and very few words. 
<margin>Abstinence</margin>
But her acts of abstinence could not easily be recounted, for they almost exceeded measure. Except on feast days, she scarcely took oil in her food. I say nothing of wine, meat, fish, milk, honey, and eggs, and other foods which are sweet to the taste; she completely abstained from these for as long as she lived. 
<margin>Patience</margin>
Furthermore, her patience was truly greatest against detractors and persecutors. For the Lord had raised up an enemy against her to buffet her <note>This is a biblical allusion to the "thorn in the flesh" mentioned by Saint Paul.</note>, so that she might not exalt herself because of so many and such great virtues. Although she equipped herself against the detractors and the injuries of those raging and speaking ill with the most beautiful testimonies of Holy Scripture, as if with the armor of Christ—and especially against raging envy—by enduring injuries, she mitigated the fury of a rabid heart. For she used to say: "If the devil did not fight everywhere against the servants and handmaidens of God, and if he did not go before those fleeing all places—if he were not held back by the love of holy places—he would have already found me in another part of the world than Bethlehem. Why should I not overcome malice with patience? Why should I not break pride with humility? And to the one who strikes my cheek, I shall offer the other," as Paul said: "Overcome evil with good" <note>original: "Vince in bono malum"</note>. Did not the apostles glory when they suffered insults for the Lord? Did not the Savior himself humble himself, taking the form of a servant, and was made obedient to the Father even unto death—even death on a cross—so that he might save us by his passion? 
<margin>Monastery for women</margin>
After the monastery for men, which she had built at her own expense and handed over to men to inhabit and govern, she likewise built another for women, in which she had gathered many noble and ordinary virgins from various provinces. In this place, she wished all to be joined in work, in food, in all things, and in the psalms. And according to that word of the Psalmist: "Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you," and "at midnight I rose to confess to you." At morning, the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, evening, <term>compline</term><note>The final prayer service of the day in the Christian liturgy.</note>, and at the midnight crowing of the rooster, the psalter was sung in order. In that place, they used linen cloths only for wiping their hands. The separation from men was so great that they were even kept apart from eunuchs. But no one could describe with a pen her excellent way of living in this place, together with the other holy virgins who were with her. In this, she completed the whole course of her life and kept the faith, for which she now enjoys the crown of justice. 
<margin>On her character</margin>
Finally, she regarded heretics as if they were heathens and...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Saint Paula, focusing on her scholarship, her final illness in Bethlehem, and her subsequent death and funeral. It highlights her relationship with Saint Jerome and her daughter Eustochium.</meta>

FOLIO 115
**Concerning Saint Paula**

...to translate into Latin and to explain and compose many things for her. She was of such eminent talent that she learned the Hebrew language, which Jerome himself had learned from his youth with much labor and sweat. Thus, she could sing the psalms in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin equally whenever it was required. At last, this noble woman Paula, after many struggles and labors endured for the love of Christ, fell into a most serious illness. Finally, sensing that she was approaching death, she whispered those verses of the Psalmist as best she could:
*Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place where your glory dwells.* <note>Psalm 26:8 (Vulgate 25:8)</note> And: *How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and even faints for the courts of the Lord.* <note>Psalm 84:1-2 (Vulgate 83:2-3)</note> And: *I have chosen to be an outcast in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.* <note>Psalm 84:10 (Vulgate 83:11)</note> When she was asked by her master and father Jerome why she was silent, why she would not respond, and whether she was in any pain, she replied in the Greek language <note>original: "greco sermone"</note> that she had no distress, but rather beheld all things as tranquil and quiet. After this she became silent, and with closed eyes, as if already despising mortal things, she repeated those verses until her last breath. Holding her finger to her mouth, she traced the sign of the cross upon her lips. And so she returned her holy soul to Christ her Savior in the presence of bishops, priests, and almost innumerable monks. <margin>The death of Paula.</margin>

When this most holy woman died, there was no wailing or lamentation as is common among people of the world, but instead crowds began to sound out psalms in various languages. She was carried by the hands of bishops who placed their shoulders beneath the bier, while other prelates carried lamps and wax candles. Others led the choirs of singers into the cave located in the middle of the Church <note>The Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem, where Paula was buried near the site of Christ's birth.</note>. The entire multitude of Palestinian cities gathered for her funeral. What monk hiding in the desert remained in his cell? What virgin remained hidden in the privacy of her chambers? Widows and the poor showed the garments she had provided for them, following the example of Dorcas. <note>A biblical figure (also called Tabitha) known for her charity and for making clothes for the poor; see Acts 9:36-41.</note> The whole multitude of the needy cried out that they had lost both a mother and a nurse.

What is marvelous is that no pallor had changed her face, but such a dignity and gravity filled her features that you would think her not dead, but sleeping. In Greek, Latin, and Syriac <note>original: "Greco Latino Syroq;"</note>, the psalms resounded in order, not only for three days, but until the body was laid beneath the Church and next to the Cave of the Lord. For an entire week, all who had come celebrated the funeral as if it were their own, believing their tears to be their own loss. But the venerable virgin Eustochium, her daughter, like a child being weaned from her mother, could not be pulled away from her parent; she kissed her eyes, clung to her face, embraced the whole body, and cried out that she wished to be buried with her mother.

Indeed, the generosity and faith of this most holy woman were so great that not even a single penny was left to her daughter. It is truly wonderful and incredible to see a woman from a most noble family, once great in wealth, who had given everything away with such faith that she herself reached the very depths of poverty. Certainly, no one gave more to the poor than Paula, who left nothing for herself. And now indeed she enjoys divine riches, and from tiny Bethlehem she has ascended to the heavenly kingdoms. Let these things said of Saint Paula of Rome suffice. Upon her tomb, the blessed Jerome placed this inscription, namely:

*Scipio sired her, the offspring of the Paulian line,*
*Descendant of the Gracchi and Agamemnon's noble stock,*
*In this tomb lies she whom the elders called Paula:*
*Mother of Eustochium, first lady of the Roman Senate,*
*Who followed the poverty of Christ and the fields of Bethlehem. Amen.*

# About Proba

## On the poet Proba, wife of Adelphus. Chapter 119.

[An illustration of a woman, Proba, seated at a desk in a study, writing in a book. She is surrounded by other open books on the desk and on shelves.]

Proba was a woman most worthy of memory for both her actions and her literary reputation. She lived in the age of Prince Honorius <note>Honorius was the Western Roman Emperor from 393 to 423 AD.</note>, specifically in the four-hundred-and-fourteenth year after the birth of Christ. She was highly distinguished for her learning and her Christian faith, and was very well known. Indeed, she was an Italian woman, originating from the town of Orte, and was the wife of a certain illustrious man named Adelphus.

How much she excelled in the liberal studies <note>The "liberal arts" or "liberal studies" were the traditional core of Roman education, including grammar, rhetoric, and logic.</note> can be clearly perceived. Among her other studies, she became so familiar with the poetry of Virgil through such watchful care that she seemed to have his work always before her eyes and in her memory, as evidenced by almost every work she completed. While she was perhaps reading with particularly sharp attention, the thought occurred to her that the entire history of the Old Testament and the sequence of the New Testament could be described using Virgil's smooth, ready, and pithy verses. It is certainly not without wonder that such a sublime consideration entered a woman's mind. But it was far more miraculous that she carried it out.

Giving her effort to this concept, she ran here and there through the *Bucolics*, the *Georgics*, and the *Aeneid* <note>These are the three major works of the Roman poet Virgil.</note>. Plucking sometimes whole lines from one part and sometimes small fragments of meter from another, she reduced them to her own purpose with marvelous skill. She placed the whole lines so aptly and connected the fragments so well—preserving the laws of poetic feet and the dignity of the poem—that only the most expert reader could detect the joins.

Starting from the very beginning of the world, she composed the history found in the Old and New Testaments up to the descent of the Holy Spirit so elegantly that a person unaware of how it was composed would easily believe Virgil had been both a prophet and an Evangelist. From this, it is no less commendable that this woman had a complete or quite full knowledge of the sacred volumes—a thing which, we note with sorrow, happens rarely even to men in our own age.

Furthermore, this excellent woman wished the work she had composed to be called the <term>Cento</term> <note>original: "Centonam." A Cento is a poem made up of verses or passages quoted from other authors, rearranged to form a new story—literally a "patchwork" poem.</note>, a name we use often. And the more we think it worthy of perpetual memory, the less we believe that this woman's celebrated genius could have acquired so much through labor alone. On the contrary, I believe that if her life had been extended by more years, she would have composed other praiseworthy things which, due to the laziness of scribes and much to our loss, have been unable to reach us.

<margin>The Book of the Cento.</margin>

Among these, some believe there were Homeric Centos <note>original: "homeri Centona"</note>, written with the same art and on the same subject matter as those she had written from Virgil, but published using poems taken from Homer. If this is so, it is taken as proof of even greater praise: that she knew Greek literature as learnedly as she knew Latin. But I ask now, what could be more desirable than to hear that a woman scaled the peaks of Maro <note>Maro refers to Publius Vergilius Maro, commonly known as Virgil.</note> and Homer? Let the most learned men behold how she placed and joined these separate parts into an artistic context for her own work. While the profession of sacred letters is distinguished, it is nonetheless arduous and difficult to draw parts from the vast bosom of the sacred volumes, now here and now there, and to bring them together into the sequence of the life of Christ.

# FOLIO 116
## On Saint Marcellina

...to force the words into prose, as she did from a pagan poem. <note>This refers to the poet Proba, who created a "Cento," a poem made of recycled verses from Virgil to tell the story of the Bible.</note> It would have been enough for her—if we consider the traditional customs of women—to occupy herself with the distaff, the needle, and the loom <note>original: "colus et acus atque testrinum." These were the standard tools for spinning and weaving, symbols of domestic labor.</note>, had she wished to be idle as so many others are. But because she wiped away the rust of sluggishness from her mind through her dedication to sacred studies, she has emerged into eternal light.

However, let those who look upon this with a good mind—those who yield to pleasures and idleness, for whom it is a grand thing to sit in a bedroom, wasting irrecoverable time with frivolous fans, and from the earliest morning until the whole night through, often drawing out conversations that are either harmful or empty chatter, or devoting themselves only to vanity—let them certainly take note of how great a difference there is between seeking fame through praiseworthy works and burying one's name along with the corpse, departing from life as if they had never lived.

# CXV 09
## Concerning Saint Marcellina and Saint Marcella

...of her most holy mother, watering her with prayers mixed with weeping, he <note>This refers to Pope Liberius, who historically consecrated Marcellina.</note> solemnly blessed her; and with a veil and other garments of holy religion, he betrothed her, in a certain manner, making her an immaculate bride of Christ Jesus, whom she had longed for with her whole heart. Once initiated and bathed in the pontifical blessing, she strove to show herself such a servant to the King of Kings, Christ the Lord, in the holiness of mind and body, that without doubt she was believed to be already satisfied in heaven, for whom she vigilantly reserved herself undefiled on earth. Truly blessed were the parents who dedicated such a first living gift of their offspring to the living God: through whom their noble posterity was doubled, not diminished. Indeed, to Ambrose, the father of this virgin, were born **Ambrose** and **Satyrus**; supported by these two as if by the rowing of two wings, the virgin of Christ, Marcellina, flew past all earthly things with a swift feather, sighing daily for entry into the heavenly fatherland. Aided by their protection and instructed by their warnings, there was soon nothing of the living world to be found in her. Rather, according to the Apostle, she was **crucified to the world**, and the world itself was crucified to her. <note>original: "mundo crucifixa," a reference to Galatians 6:14.</note> Hence, she sought nothing from the heritage of her entire ancestral possession except a simple habit and meager food. With continuous fasts and frequent vigils, wearing down her supple limbs, she never ceased from intent prayer or the meditation on the divine scriptures. And so it happened: while the care of one <note>Likely referring to Saint Ambrose.</note> continually provided the signs of spiritual banquets to the holy virgin, through the vigilance of the other, the requirements of bodily necessities were provided; her mind, dedicated to God as if in a mirror-stone <note>A "speculari lapide" refers to a transparent stone like mica or selenite, used here as a metaphor for clear, divine contemplation.</note> always intent on divine contemplation, presented herself irreproachable and immaculate before the sight of her heavenly spouse by looking upon herself with circumspection and foresight.

It is certain, therefore, that it was the custom of this venerable virgin to constantly kneel upon the tomb of her dead brother, Satyrus, and commend his holy soul to her Creator with continuous and assiduous prayers; and on that account, she often spent the day entirely without any food, and passed the night without sleep, so much so that she could hardly be pulled away from the sepulcher for a moment. After the death of the divine **Ambrose**, who used to keep watch day and night before the tombs of those brothers, he finally gave up his spirit to God in that same place. His holy body, anointed with spices by the bishop **Simplicianus** <note>Simplicianus was the immediate successor to Saint Ambrose as Bishop of Milan.</note> (the immediate successor of Saint Ambrose), was placed next to his brothers: where, through their intervening merits, he bestows many benefits upon the faithful. We believe that this holy virgin of God, Marcellina, undoubtedly reached His sight, toward whose image and likeness she knew her secret prayer was directed: so that she may pray for me, a sinner, both now and always, in all my affairs and actions, as a gracious presence and helper, and constantly direct my fragile self in the way of justice and piety. Amen.

->#### Concerning Saint Eustochium, a Roman virgin. Chapter 315.<-

[Decorative initial E] **Eustochium** was the daughter of the noble Roman matron **Paula** and the sweetest flower and glory of virginity. # Concerning Saint Ursula
## Concerning Saint Ursula, virgin and martyr. Chapter 136.

**[A large decorative woodcut initial U]** **Ursula**, a virgin and martyr of the most illustrious origin and celebrated character, was a British woman. It is well known that in the year of our Lord 455, she achieved a most glorious martyrdom for the name of Christ, along with eleven thousand Christians of mixed sex—though all are called by the name of "the virgins"—at the famous city of Cologne in Germany. They were killed by the Scythian Huns, a most impure, wicked, and savage people fighting under King Attila. 

**[Woodcut illustration of Saint Ursula standing, holding a banner with a cross, her large cloak sheltering many smaller female figures.]**

Although she might seem to have sought a great name of renown for herself through her radiant blood and the immense beauty of her body, earning a place among famous women, she is judged to have occupied that place far more for another reason. This was not only because of her fervent love for faith and virginity toward God—which the holy virgins of Christ most often possess—but because of the merit of her remarkable audacity and prudence in gathering to herself so many prelates of the Church, most noble royal sons and others, as well as matrons and virgin daughters. Lest this claim seem like a mere slip of our pen <note>original: "a calamo nostro surreptum"</note>, it must be explained in a few words. 

She was the daughter of a certain Maurus, a most Christian King of the Britons, and his equally Christian and most devout wife, Demetria. When her immense and nearly incredible beauty of body and face, her other virtues, and the greatness of her soul were reported to the knowledge of the most powerful King of the English, he was immediately drawn into a love for this consecrated virgin. He began to consider himself blessed if such a great virgin were joined in marriage to his only-begotten son. Likewise, the son himself was so drawn by the love of her extraordinary beauty that he thought nothing else in his vast kingdom was dear or delightful to him except her. 

And so, while the father and son were burning with this desire, they sent solemn ambassadors <note>original: "oratores," meaning envoys or speakers</note> to King Maurus, the father of the virgin, to demand the same virgin as a wife for the great king's son using both flatteries and promises, while adding threats if they should return to their lords empty-handed. 

The King, having received the ambassadors, began to be no little bit anxious, turning many things over in his mind. Firstly, he considered it unworthy to join a daughter marked with the seal of Christ in marriage to a worshiper of idols, and he feared that she herself would never agree to it. Secondly, he dreaded the power of that king. But she, supported by the divine spirit, persuaded her trembling father to grant his assent to the demands, but only with this condition added: that the King of the English himself, along with her father, should provide ten select virgins to her for comfort; and to her and the aforementioned ten most noble select virgins, he should assign a thousand other virgin maidens each <note>A mathematical way of reaching the traditional number of 11,000 companions</note>. Furthermore, after providing several triremes <note>A type of galley or ship with three banks of oars</note>, he should grant her a three-year reprieve <note>original: "indutias," a truce or delay</note> to celebrate the dedication of her virginity according to royal custom. In the meantime, the groom himself, being sufficiently instructed in the faith of Christ, should be baptized. She used this most wise counsel so that, by the difficulty of the proposed condition, she might either turn his mind away from such a marriage, or by such an opportunity, she might...

...so that she might dedicate the virgins together with herself to Christ our Lord. But the young man, now inflamed with an exceeding passion for the virgin, willingly accepted the condition and began to urge his father that he should be baptized immediately; he successfully requested that everything the holy virgin had proposed should be carried out. Meanwhile, the girl’s father, who loved her uniquely, provided her with eunuchs, grave men, and many other nobles, so that she might have in her company their solace and help, which she and her virginal army would require. This most renowned Queen Ursula, beyond her extraordinary physical beauty, was greatly distinguished by her outstanding learning in many idioms and languages. For she spoke so fluently whenever necessary, in whatever language she was questioned, that she seemed to know only that language. Whence, as necessity required, she spoke most elegantly; and again, like a modest virgin, she remained silent when the situation called for it. And since she knew by nature that there is a great power in speech to stir up not only men but to calm all the movements of the soul, she applied herself with the greatest vigilance to eloquence. And since she was beautifully skilled in Latin <note>original: "latinitatem"</note>, she also shone as most eloquent in her speaking. 

How much weight her copious and elegant speech had—perfectly suited for persuasion—she demonstrated in many other matters, but especially in this: that so many virgins of every nation, who were formerly strangers to the faith of Christ, were won for Christ through her preaching. Indeed, how great was the weight of her discourse, how great the torrent, how great the force, and what power was in the genius of that holy virgin! One may see it from this: that she attracted to herself first Pantulus, the Bishop of Basel <note>A legendary early bishop of Basel</note>—a most excellent and learned man—who accompanied her all the way to Rome, and returning from there with her, received the palm of martyrdom alongside them. 

Furthermore, she also drew the Roman Pontiff <note>Historically identified in the Ursula legend as the fictional Pope Cyriacus</note>, several Cardinals, and many most learned prelates of the Church. She also won over the heavenly son of the King of the English, the holy virgin’s own spouse, despite his previous burning desires, and countless other nearly most noble young men. She even attracted Saint Gerasina, the Queen of Sicily and sister <note>original: "germanam"</note> of Saint Ursula’s own mother, who sailed all the way to Britain with her four daughters—Babilla, Juliana, Victoria, and Aurea—and her little son Adrian (who, out of love for his sisters, voluntarily joined the pilgrimage), leaving her kingdom behind just to see and hear Ursula. 

And so it happened that many who previously condemned her in their hearts and made light of her as if she were insane and mad, were forced, even against their will, to follow her and accompany her pilgrimage. Her most holy and burning teachings moved everyone so much that, almost forgetting themselves and shaken to their core, they cast aside the propositions they had long followed. Contrary to the stubborn opinions of their own paganism <note>original: "gentilitatis"</note>, they began to wonderfully praise and extol the woman they had—not without reason—previously hated. 

What should be said of the aforementioned Etherius <note>The Latin text uses "Erithreo" here, a variation of his name</note>, her most illustrious spouse, along with his mother and the virgin Florentina (the spouse’s sister), and Marcellus, the Bishop of Greece, a most accomplished teacher and orator? They even went so far as to expose themselves voluntarily to martyrdom. **Concerning Saint Ursula**

...some things are commanded, some are permitted, and others are advised. Therefore, evil things are forbidden to Christians, good things are commanded, neutral things are permitted, and the perfect path is advised. In those two principles, my dearest sisters, which I have written down first, every sin is included. For in both, the authority of our Lord is contained; it belongs to the one who commands not only to order what is right but also to forbid what is wrong. Generally speaking, the law of Christians mandates justice for all; the Savior, briefly but most fully encompassing this in the Gospel, says: **Whatever you wish that people do to you of good things, these also you should do for them.** <note>This is the "Golden Rule" from Matthew 7:12. The author uses it here as the foundation for the moral life.</note> This means that we should inflict no evil on others and provide everything that is good, because we wish both these behaviors to be observed by others toward ourselves.

<margin>Note.</margin>
Therefore, this sentence holds all Christians entirely by the equal law of command; nor is anyone at all permitted to transgress what has been commanded to all. It is an open contempt of God either to do what is forbidden or to fail to do what is commanded. Moved and taught by these and other instructions of the holy virgin Ursula, all the virgins believed in Christ and all received the sacrament of baptism. Having been baptized and having boarded their ships, by the power of the one God and with a favorable wind blowing, they reached a certain port of Gaul called **Tyella** <note>original: "Tyella"; possibly referring to a port near the mouth of the Rhine or the river Thielle</note>. From there, they finally came to **Cologne** by way of the bed of the Rhine river. There, an angel of the Lord appeared to the holy virgin Ursula and foretold that they would eventually return to this very place in their full number and would receive the crowns of martyrdom from the **Huns** <note>The Huns were a nomadic people whose invasion of Europe is a central element in the legend of Saint Ursula's martyrdom.</note>. 

Following the angel’s instruction, they departed and, sailing toward Rome, they reached **Basel**, a noble city of the Germans. Leaving their **triremes** <term>triremes: ancient galleys with three banks of oars, here used to describe the large ships of the 11,000 virgins</term> there, they all proceeded to Rome on foot. Indeed, their entry into the city of Rome was almost unheard of—a triumphal procession of wonderful devotion—and it was a miracle to all. For such was the order and the most beautiful, religious arrangement of their walking around this Queen and her companions that they turned the eyes of everyone toward them. None of those virgins were dressed in anything but decorous clothing, with their hair flowing loose over their shoulders. No public street, no forum, no portico, and no windows above could hold all the onlookers. Because of the devotion of this spectacle, many people—not only secular citizens but even the most holy bishops and cardinals—went away as if stunned. 

**Cyriacus**, who was then the High Pontiff of the Roman Church and himself a **Briton** by birth, rejoiced greatly at the arrival of the most holy virgin Ursula and her innumerable virgin companions, because some among them were his own kinswomen. For this reason, out of honor for them, he received them with reverence along with the entire Roman clergy. He sheltered them and sustained and fed them with all diligence and care for the space of two years. He also had them accurately and diligently instructed in every teaching of Christian truth, and those among them who had not yet been baptized, he baptized. 

One night, however, the Pontiff was forewarned in a divine vision that he was to receive the palm of martyrdom along with these holy virgins. Therefore, seizing the opportunity—specifically in the second year after the arrival of the holy virgins—Pope Cyriacus gathered a synod and revealed what had been shown to him by the Lord. In front of everyone, he resigned his dignity and his office. But when all the fathers of the college <note>Referring to the College of Cardinals or high clergy</note> protested against him in amazement, saying he was **raving most shamefully** for refusing the papal glory of the general Church just to follow after some **foolish little women** <note>original: "fatuas mulierculas"; a derogatory term used by the clergy in the text to dismiss Ursula's companions</note>, he would by no means yield to their protests. Instead, after **Antherus** was declared pope as his successor, he (being a virgin himself) followed these virgins all the way to the crown of martyrdom. Truly, because he resigned his dignity and the papacy against the will of the fathers, he is recorded least of all in the catalog of popes...

For the power of the Lord is salvation: because God is love: and he who remains in love, remains in God. <note>original: "deus dilectio est" (1 John 4:16). The text begins mid-sentence, concluding an exhortation by Ursula to her followers.</note> Indeed, the tribulations of human death are present, as you see; however, in the face of them, God has called us to eternal joy, so that he may establish us forever in the heavenly inheritance and in royal honor. Thus, be prepared, for we are already called to the crown; and since we have striven to imitate Christ, we shall be fixed in his footsteps. Having set down our burdens, impediments, and the shackles by which the lovers of this world are held—sitting in darkness and the shadow of death—we, now liberated and unhindered, shall be committed to the crucified Lord of majesty. No one can carry his image unless they render themselves naked and dead to this world. 

Exhorted by these and similar words, and all being strengthened and protected by the sign of the cross, each gave the kiss of peace to their neighbor. As they moved toward Cologne, the Barbarians <note>The "Barbarians" here refers to the Huns, who according to legend besieged Cologne and slaughtered the virgins.</note>, rushing upon them like dogs and wolves upon sheep, slew the entire multitude with arrows. 

However, when they came to the most blessed and beautiful Ursula (the others having been slaughtered), the prince <note>Traditionally identified as the leader of the Huns, sometimes named Attila in later versions of the legend.</note>, seeing the great and extraordinary elegance of her beauty, was greatly amazed. Consoling her over the death of the virgins and his army, he promised that he would take her as his wife. But when she utterly rejected him, he, perceiving himself to be held in contempt, immediately snatched up his bow and pierced her with an arrow. By that kind of death, she consummated her martyrdom. 

And so the holy heroine Ursula, with her nearly infinite company, lived a life so beneficial to her homeland of Britain and to all of Germany (as I might say), that even after death she remains of no small use to them—and especially to the city of Cologne <note>original: "Agrippine ciuitati." Cologne was founded as Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium.</note>—where she shall remain in eternal habitation with her followers. Monuments to her virtue have been established throughout the whole world, and she attained a royal tomb in that city where very frequent miracles occur daily. Therefore, the annual celebration for them is dedicated and celebrated by the faithful on the eleventh day before the Calends of November <note>October 21st.</note>. 

However, concerning the timing of the passion of this holy virgin and her aforementioned companions, there has been some ambiguity among illustrious historians. There are those who say she suffered in the times of Alexander, the Roman prince <note>Emperor Alexander Severus.</note>, who ceased to reign in the two hundred and thirty-sixth year of our salvation. But reason does not allow that the blessed Ursula suffered at such a time, since Sicily did not then hold the title of a kingdom, nor did Byzantium; it is more true that she suffered at the time mentioned above. <note>The author is debating the historical "fit" of the legend, arguing that the political titles mentioned in some versions of the story didn't exist in the 3rd century.</note>

**Concerning Saint Scholastica**

[An illuminated woodcut illustration of Saint Scholastica. She is depicted with a halo, wearing a blue habit and a white veil. **S**cholastica the virgin was the full sister of the blessed Benedict, born of the same parents. During the times of the Emperor Justin the Elder <note>Justin I, who reigned from 518–527 AD</note> and Pope John, the first of that name, around the year of our salvation 524, she shone most brightly throughout nearly all of Italy, and especially in the Italian province of Abruzzo, because of the exceptional holiness of her life and her most perfect religious devotion. Indeed, it is well established that this most holy virgin, tracing her origin from the region of Umbria in Italy—which is now called the Duchy of Spoleto—in the very ancient city of Norcia, had most noble parents.

I have decided that she should be placed among the <term>illustrious women</term> <note>original: "claras femias" [claras feminas]. This refers to a literary tradition of collecting biographies of famous women.</note> because of her remarkable and great holiness, and her other famous deeds and miracles. Although I am aware that it is very difficult to find a commendation equal to her virtues and glory, I will nonetheless proceed according to the measure of my own talent, relying most of all on the testimony of the blessed Gregory <note>Saint Gregory the Great, whose *Dialogues* provide the primary historical account of Scholastica’s life.</note>. It would not be at all reasonable for her to receive less praise or fame than others, given that she reached the highest peak of perfect holiness. Whatever this holy virgin did in her religious life, I will recount as briefly as possible. For from her deeds, one may observe her character and wonderful holiness. 

When Saint Scholastica, still in the flower of her youth, had taken up the <term>habit of holy living</term> <note>original: "sancte cōuersatiōis habitū." This refers to the formal adoption of a monastic or religious life.</note> in imitation of her brother Benedict, it was not long after that her most holy way of life became known throughout almost all of Italy. Because of this, a huge number of both virgins and other matrons flocked to her. 

Yet even before this, in her father’s house, while she was still a delicate girl, she was inspired by a certain divine spirit. She showed that she abhorred luxuries and all physical adornment and pleasure. She turned away from her great beauty, in which she greatly excelled, and fled from the finery of young girls. She not only began to severely criticize and disapprove of the lavish feasts, the use of baths, and similar things that were then the custom of living in her wealthy home, but she also frequently had it on her lips that she could in no way gain the kingdom of heaven unless she restored the ancient ways of life of the holy fathers. Moved by these reasons...

FOLIO 125

# Saint Scholastica

...she had begun to restore the harsh and extremely strict ancient dignity and rigor of living to the religious orders. At that time, there were many monks of great authority, both women and men, established in the Church of God. These people, first observing the proposal of the divine Benedict and his sister, attempted to deter them from such a purpose as if they were merely headstrong youths, claiming they were presuming to do something vain and beyond their strength. But when the then-blessed Roman Pontiff, the fourth of that name <margin>Felix</margin> <note>This refers to Pope Felix IV, who reigned from 526–530 AD.</note>, and several other lesser prelates began to exhort the old monks—persuading them to hope for the success of such a reformation of the Rule—they easily acquiesced to the organization of the divine Benedict and his sister Scholastica. This was especially true since Saint Benedict was pressing from the other side, asking them to allow themselves to give up the resources they held for pleasure, pomp, and the pursuit of honor; for he argued it would be impossible for him to satisfy other prelates of the church with riches alone. He suggested that by modesty, religion, and greatness of soul, he could surpass the delights of the many, and that by restoring equality and harmony in holy religion, it would come to pass that they would pursue the name and glory of good and true servants of God.

By these most effective and ardent exhortations of divine Benedict, many of the veteran religious were moved, and they changed their former way of thinking so much that they themselves, burning with a desire for glory and for the reformation of morals, voluntarily encouraged the holy youth Benedict and his sister Scholastica to complete the task. Inspired by a certain divine spirit and a love of integrity, they even urged the holy regulator himself to make haste. Furthermore, having called others together, they opened the plan to other monks through both speech and writing, exhorting them to observe the Rule and to offer their help. They preached the same thing to other women. 

However, at that time, there was a very great abundance of wealth among the nuns <term>sanctimoniales</term> <note>A term for women living a consecrated religious life.</note>, which certainly brought a great deal of difficulty to Saint Benedict in carrying out his work. For because of these riches, the nuns were living a licentious life according to their own will and—if I may say so—their own lusts, just as the Roman Vestals <note>The author compares the nuns to the Vestal Virgins of ancient Rome, who were known for their high social status and luxury, implying the nuns had become secularized and elite rather than humble.</note> were dismissed. Indeed, they wandered curiously through the streets, the marketplaces, and other less-than-honorable places, elegantly dressed and adorned. They reclined in porticoes with wanton and worldly women, speaking and chattering about things which are not permitted. Having jeweled hands, they observed absolutely nothing of those things which they had anciently professed in holy religion; instead, because of their countless riches, they defiled everything with their own pleasures. 

Grieving daily over these evils and outrages, the divine Benedict and the holy virgin sister Scholastica said with the Prophet: "O good Jesus, what is this that we discern? For they have set fire to your sanctuary; they have defiled the dwelling place of your name." <note>original: "Incenderunt enim sanctuarium tuum igni; polluerunt tabernaculum nominis tui." A citation of Psalm 74:7.</note> Therefore, the most blessed virgin Scholastica, moved by piety, took care to pour water over such a great fire with all her might. So that she might ward off the rage of the wolves, she hedged the vineyard of the Lord with the best "thorns" of the Rule <note>The "thorns" represent the protective barriers of strict discipline and monastic regulations.</note>. She wiped away the disgrace of holy religion, about which even infidels were speaking ill. She consulted best for the salvation not only of herself but of those unhappy nuns who were not following the voice of the Bridegroom <note>A traditional reference to Jesus Christ as the "Bridegroom" of the soul or the Church.</note>, and indeed for the salvation of countless future women. From these deeds, the holy virgin Scholastica consecrated her eternal praises and eternal memory.

With matters thus managed for the best according to her purpose, and since everything was now succeeding prosperously for divine Benedict and his sister Scholastica, lest any should dare to oppose what had been started, not long after, certain "pestilent" religious people—inflamed by a diabolical spirit—attempted to subvert everything time and again. They attempted to corrupt that most beautiful and holy Rule (which was perfectly suited to the best customs of Mary) because of the most shameful disease of their own greed. But the holy virgin Scholastica built for herself, first of all, a spiritual house; and she built it not upon sand, but upon firm rock. She laid first the foundations of innocence, upon which she could more easily erect the steep summit of justice, knowing that the greatest part of equity is fulfilled by one who strives to harm no one. Truly, in her state of innocence...

->**Saint Scholastica**<-

In her home, she often sang with the Prophet, saying: "I walked in the innocence of my heart in the midst of my house." <note>original: "Perambulabam in innocentia cordis mei: in medio domus mee" — a reference to Psalm 101:2.</note> Among her sisters established within the monastery walls, she often preached those words of the Prophet, saying: "God did not withhold his good gifts from those who walked in innocence." <note>original: "Non fraudavit eos deus bonis: qui ambulabant in innocentia" — a reference to Psalm 84:11.</note> She said this so that she might completely remove from them all malice, hatred, and envy—which are the seeds most accustomed to causing harm. "In this way, dearest sisters," she said, "may your mind remain vigorous and watchful; for if you live innocently, you will be able to see God even within your fragile bodies." With great effort, she taught those nuns by both word and example to flee all the softness of their sex and to preserve the commitment to the most perfect virginity. 

She further instructed them to follow the <term>Rule</term> <note>The "Rule" refers to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the foundational set of guidelines for Western monastic life.</note> of life, binding their affections to the constant contemplation of the divine through the miraculous lives of holy monks, especially through the precious devotion of the holy <term>Confessors</term> <note>A "Confessor" is a title for a saint who lived a life of profound faith and suffered for it, but did not die a martyr's death.</note>. Finally, she taught them through the examples of the holy martyrs to endure all the adversities of this world and the storms of this perilous sea, along with all the devilish deceits and infestations of demons. 

She further shaped their minds through the obedience of the holy patriarchs and prophets. As for herself, she always held the book of the Gospels in her hands like a mirror; there she fixed her study of divine reading with such intensity, and raised up such frequent turns of prayer and tears and such firm and constant meditation on the future, that she easily made up for any negligence of her remaining time through that very devotion. And because of this, the life of the virgin Scholastica seemed to be joined perpetually with the angelic choirs and the societies of the saints. 

It would be most difficult for me to follow all the deeds of Saint Scholastica, and it is not necessary. Therefore, at last, as she reached a mature age and grew heavy with years, the saint could clearly perceive that her spirit would soon be thinned and emptied from her body. Every year, she used to go to Monte Cassino just once to visit and hear her blessed brother, Benedict. Since she stayed just outside the monastery not far away, she would go to hear his divine words, which for a long time had brought salvation to her and to many other Christians; because she believed she could attain nothing more healthy, she went to him. 

And so, not far outside the monastery gate, Scholastica and Benedict were situated together at the very end of her life. When they had spent that whole day in the praises of God and holy conversation, as the shadows of night were now falling, they took food together. While they were still sitting at the table and the hour grew late during their sacred conversation, the holy virgin asked her divine brother not to leave her that night, so that they might speak of the joys of heaven until morning for her final comfort. He answered her most kindly: "And what is it that you are saying, sweetest sister? Do you not know that it is not permitted for me to stay outside the monastery?" 

But when the most holy virgin heard the words of her brother refusing her, she immediately clasped her fingers together and placed them on the table. She bowed her head into her hands to pray to God. As she lifted her head from the table, such great flashes of lightning and crashes of thunder sounded, and such floods of rain broke forth, that neither the venerable man nor his companions who had come with him were able to move even a foot outside the threshold where they were sitting. 

Indeed, the tears of the holy woman were so powerful with the Lord that they could draw a great rain even from a clear sky. For as Saint Gregory <note>Saint Gregory the Great, who wrote the primary biography of Benedict and Scholastica in his *Dialogues*.</note> writes, there was such a coincidence between the prayer and the flood that it was at one and the same moment that she lifted her head and the rains descended. Then the man of God, realizing that he could not return to the monastery because of the lightning, thunder, and the flooding of the great rain, was somewhat saddened and complained to his sister in these words, saying: "May Almighty God forgive you! Sister, what have you done?" To which she replied: "Behold, I asked you..." <note>The text ends mid-sentence as Scholastica begins her explanation.</note>

**Concerning Saint Brigid, the Scottish virgin. Chapter 138.**

**B**rigid the virgin, the first of that name <note>original: "eius nominis prima"</note>, was by nation Irish or Scottish. <note>In the medieval period, "Scotia" often referred to Ireland, the home of the "Scotti" people, rather than modern-day Scotland.</note> In the times of the Emperor Justin the Elder <note>Emperor Justin I, who reigned 518–527 AD.</note> and the blessed Roman Pontiff, the fourth of that name, she was most famous and distinguished in that region both for her very sharp penitence and for the splendor of all her virtues. However, I do not remember having yet read in what year she died. Nevertheless, her birthday <note>In hagiography, "birthday" (natalitius dies) refers to the date of a saint's death—their "birth" into heaven.</note> is venerably celebrated by the faithful on the first day of the Kalends of February <term>Kalends: the first day of the month in the Roman calendar</term>. Now, Scotland is the homeland of this holy virgin, a certain northernmost portion of England or Britain, which turns toward the Northern part; for it is separated from the English island by certain small rivers and a mountain of no great size. Indeed, in that place during the winter time, the days are so short that the sun scarcely illuminates the earth for three hours.

[Woodcut illustration of a female saint, St. Brigid, standing in a garden, holding a burning lamp in her right hand and a palm branch in her left.]

Therefore, this Brigid, a virgin of this region, was an indelible example of most famous virginity and piety, which she left to posterity with her great radiance. Now, this Brigid was the daughter of Dubthach <note>original: "Daboth"</note>, a most noble man in that region, by his wife Erocha. Even as a small girl, her parents took great care to instruct her from childhood in the study of good virtues. She herself, as a chosen little girl, distinguished from her very childhood by her character, sobriety, piety, and modesty, grew and improved for the better every day. But no one is able to fully enumerate her virtues and the famous deeds which she performed from her childhood until the day of her death. Truly, we shall demonstrate a few of these innumerable things in this place (according to our custom). 

First of all, the virgin Brigid was of a lovely face and beautiful appearance, and was quite graceful in the eyes of all, and famous for her wonderful kindness. Because of this, she was held in great honor among other girls of her age, not only among her own people but among almost all the provincials. While she was taking care of her parents' flocks (for at that time this service alone belonged to the women of that region), she was occasionally sent by her mother, according to custom, to gather butter from the milk of the herds, just as other girls were sent by their parents. Although she—as she was of a most pious mind—had given away all the butter she had curdled to the poor of Christ, she nevertheless brought back a greater quantity of butter than the other adolescent girls at the time requested by her mother. 

When she was of age for a husband, and her parents had decided to join her in marriage, she refused, saying she had chosen perpetual modesty and virginity. After she had professed perpetual virginity in the hands of the bishop, she touched the wood of the altar according to the custom of virgins making their profession; and immediately, it blossomed back to life as a testimony to her life-giving virginity. In this greenness, it continues even until now...

# On Saint Bridget of Sweden, the best matron. Chapter 139.

**B**ridget, or Brigida—the second of that name—was of the Germanic nation <note>original: "natione Germana"; the author uses this broadly for Northern European peoples.</note>. In the one thousand three hundred and seventy-second year from the birth of Christ <note>Historical records usually cite 1373 as the year of her death.</note>, after long and enduring pilgrimages and innumerable deeds of holiness, she returned her excellent soul to God in the hands of the Lord's servants at Rome, on the tenth day before the Calends of August <note>July 23rd.</note>, having most devoutly received the sacraments of the Church.

## On Saint Bridget the Prophetess

Almost all her servants were freed; many of both sexes, both male and female servants, she transformed into brothers and sisters <note>original: "fratres & sorores," referring to her monastic community members</note>. Nor could she long endure the visits of her noble kin or the frequent crowds that sought her out; instead, she changed both her clothing and her life. She dressed herself in the cheapest and roughest garments and gathered many virgins and matrons to her by both word and example. For these women, she desired a single style of dress; they were not permitted to use linen except for veiling the head and wiping the hands. In this manner, she gathered many virgins from various parts of Germany <note>original: "Sermania," likely a transcription error for "Germania"</note> and settled them all together with her in a monastery she had built. She joined them in food, work, and prayer, and among them, she was the first to arrive at any task to be done. By her modesty and example—rather than by fear—she provoked them to prayer and labor. She separated all these women from men as if from serpents, so that no occasion for malicious gossip <note>original: "lingue maledicte," literally "the cursed tongue"</note> might be offered. 

When this Bridget had renounced the whole world, casting aside and trampling upon its delights, she devoted herself daily to prayer, fasting, and reading alongside the others. Being inspired by the Divine Spirit, she built—or rather restored and renewed—several "double monasteries" <note>Monasteries that housed both monks and nuns in separate wings but shared a church</note> for both men and women in Germany, following the example of Saint Basil. In these, although she wished the buildings to be connected, she joined the living quarters in such a way that no one could pass from one to the other except in cases of great and evident necessity. 

She decreed that the church <note>original: "basilicam"</note> itself should be shared, so that the men in the lower part and the sisters separately in the upper part might perform the divine services. She decided that the principal care of these monasteries should belong to the Abbess. To the brothers, she assigned only the divine ministries <note>The performance of Mass and sacraments</note>. She decreed that one of them, who would be called the Prior or Confessor, should preside over the others. She intended these monasteries to have revenues for their support, and she decided that the food and clothing for everyone should be managed by the Abbess of the monastery. Neither the brothers nor the sisters of this order were to presume to leave the monastery except for great and evident necessity, and with the permission of the Abbess herself. 

She also decreed that such brothers and sisters should be consecrated by Bishops. These religious figures were commanded to commonly wear gray garments, along with a cloak of the same color, marked with a red cross on top <note>The distinctive habit of the Brigittine Order</note>. They used hempen fabrics for their garments <note>original: "Cannibusq[ue] p[er] te[m]pa," likely referring to coarse hemp cloth</note>. They all professed the Rule of Saint Augustine, with certain constitutions added by Saint Bridget. Furthermore, Saint Bridget assigned specific numbers to the brothers and sisters. The most holy Bridget herself attested that all these things had been revealed and dictated to her by God. 

This Rule was approved and confirmed by the apostolic authority and special privileges of Pope Urban V and many other Roman Pontiffs whom she had visited. Therefore, the merit of her great devotion, prayer, and intellect was so high in the sight of Almighty God that, through her vigilant study and not without a great gift from God, she deserved—if the accounts are true—to describe future events (concerning the destruction of certain kingdoms) with such clarity that it seems more like a completed fact than a prophecy, much like the holy Daniel. 

By divine command, she came to Rome with a most religious retinue for the sake of devotion. The aforementioned Pope Urban first confirmed the Rule she had begun. Later, when the Pope himself asked her whether he should go to Avignon <note>The "Avignon Papacy" was a period when Popes resided in France rather than Rome</note>, she completely discouraged him. She predicted so calmly to him that if he went, his labors would be in vain and he would soon die, that nothing was known more clearly after it happened than before. She also sent writings to his successor, Gregory XI, urging him to return the Roman Court to Rome entirely, though he did not immediately comply. By these merits, she must certainly be considered most beloved by God, venerable above all other women of her age, and extolled with every praise of holiness; for such a great light of the future could not have shone forth in a heart defiled by sin. The writings of her prophecies are held in no small value by many. Set on fire by the love of Christ, the holy...

# **On Theodolinda, Queen of the Lombards**

->The Kalends of August <note>August 1st</note>: on which day she departed from the world.<-
¶ On Theodolinda, queen of the Lombards. Chapter 500.

**T**heodolinda, the illustrious and great Queen of the <term>Lombards</term> <note>The Lombards were a Germanic people who ruled a kingdom in Italy from 568 to 774</note>, a woman truly most Christian, was the wife first of King Authari Flavius <note>The name "Flavius" was adopted by Lombard kings to claim Roman-style legitimacy</note> and then of King Agilulf, his successor. Around the year of our Lord 590 <note>original: "noningētos supꝛa qngētesimū"—the text likely intends 590, as this matches the reigns of the mentioned rulers</note>, while Gregory the Great presided as Pope in the Chair of Saint Peter, and while Maurice Augustus was ruling as Emperor of the Romans, she shone forth by her noble lineage, her kinship, and her supreme piety. She was also distinguished by nearly infinite and extraordinary deeds; indeed, she won for herself a famous name of perpetual renown for the conversion of all the Lombards to the faith.

[Hand-colored woodcut illustration of Queen Theodolinda. She wears a crown, a red gown with gold detailing, and a blue mantle. She holds a scepter in her right hand. The background features stylized green foliage.]

This illustrious queen was, in the first place, the daughter of Garibald, the excellent and most Christian King of the Bavarians. Bavaria—which was then the kingdom of <term>Noricum</term> <note>An ancient Roman province, largely corresponding to modern Austria and parts of Bavaria</note> under that same king—is a distinguished and noble province of Germany. <margin>A description of Bavaria.</margin> It has the Swabians or the River Inn <note>original: Ennius</note> as its border to the west. To the southern region lies Bohemia and the Danube, which river flows almost through its middle. To the east is the Ecci mountain <note>likely referring to the Enns area or the eastern Alps</note> which separates Pannonia <note>modern-day Hungary and surrounding areas</note> from Bavaria itself. To the south truly are the Curvaca mountains <note>likely the Karawanks</note> or the Italian Alps. Between Austria and Bavaria, the Isar is placed as the boundary. In it today there are many famous cities, of which Salzburg is the metropolis and primary city. 

This Theodolinda, therefore, originated from that province. In her youth, she was of such exquisite beauty that it seemed incredible to all; she was also of a nearly divine and versatile intellect. Furthermore, she was most kind in her person and most pleasing to everyone. Her father, in the flower of her age, joined her in marriage to Authari Flavius, King of the Lombards. In that year, Chilperic, King of the Franks, since he was a most bitter enemy of King Authari, was angered at Garibald because he had joined his daughter to him in marriage. Coming into Bavaria with a large army, Chilperic expelled Garibald from Bavaria and deprived him of his paternal kingdom. Garibald, fleeing with his people, came to his daughter Theodolinda. Authari received him with a joyful spirit, and honored him so much—as if in return for the gift of his wife—that the son-in-law Authari himself did almost nothing in Italy except by Garibald's arrangement.

King Authari, however, survived for only a year after he took her as his wife. Thus Queen Theodolinda herself, during that time with her husband and his nobles and all the soldiers, attained no less glory or praise than she had with her father. For she showed herself equally companionable, approachable, and very kind to all. Indeed, she very kindly comforted everyone—especially the poor, the oppressed, and those destitute of strength—with both word and deed. She was a protector to these; she defended them. Nor did she ever let anyone depart from her presence sorrowful, until she had provided the help requested for their need. Nor could she ever be so charmed by any worldly pleasures that she forgot her subjects. 

After her aforementioned husband died a year later, the Lombard nobles were for a long time in disagreement over the election of a future King. At last they agreed on this condition: that whichever of the Lombard princes this Theodolinda (their most beloved queen) should choose as a husband, they would accept as their king. After expressing her thanks to them, so that she might be seen to have consulted the common good, she chose Agilulf, Duke of Turin, a most warlike man of great prudence and...

**Concerning Theodolinda, Queen of the Lombards** **Leaf 130**

...she chose a man for herself who was outstanding in beauty and declared him king. Therefore Agilulf <note>Agilulf reigned as King of the Lombards from 590 to 616 AD.</note>, having been appointed and hailed as King by the choice of this heroic woman <note>The original Latin uses 'virago,' which in this period was a high compliment for a woman possessing 'masculine' strength or wisdom.</note>, and having recognized the wisdom and magnanimity of his wife, soon entrusted to her almost the entire care of the kingdom. She administered this with great prudence throughout her life alongside her husband and son, in the greatest quiet and peace, and with the love of the citizens and almost everyone. And as long as she presided, she provided many examples of justice against the guilty. 

And although all the Lombards observed the rites of the gentiles <note>original: 'gentilitatis'; here referring to pagan or non-Christian Germanic customs.</note>, she nevertheless, in the midst of such great occupations and despite being surrounded by pagan rites, never wished to neglect divine matters; nor did she cease her fasts and other good works of this kind, which pertained to appeasing divine wrath and deserving His mercy for the conversion of her people. She practiced great and frequent generosity toward all, and especially toward the poor. 

Moreover, King Agilulf himself, her husband, having taken up the kingdom, granted the requested peace to the Khagan <note>original: 'cachano'. While the text says 'King of the Huns,' this refers to the Khagan of the Avars, a nomadic group often confused with Huns by medieval chroniclers.</note>, King of the Huns. Then in the following year, he likewise made terms with Chilperic, King of the Franks, and restored the kingdom to his father-in-law, Garibald, King of the Bavarians, who had been driven out. 

Once the kingdom was pacified, he undertook a war against the Romans and fiercely besieged the city of Rome for a year, inflicting several disasters upon it. From there, moving against the city of Padua (which was constructed only of wood), after he had besieged it for a long time, he finally set it on fire and left it burned and almost desolate. He did the same in the cities of Cremona and Mantua. 

Such, therefore, was the courtesy of this queen and (if I may say so) the natural dexterity of her character toward all things, that she seemed to have easily adapted her way of living to the diverse and even contrary customs of men. For this reason, since she knew she had earned great merit among her Lombards, she almost compelled nearly all of them, by her most elegant and effective exhortations, to <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; it likely refers to the Lombards' conversion from Arianism or paganism to Catholicism.</note>...

### Concerning Theodolinda, Queen of the Lombards

...your [hearts] toward the gleaming grace of eternal light, mercifully bestowed upon you.

I beseech you to abstain from carnal desires which war against the soul <note>original: "carnalib⁹ desiderijs q̄ militāt aduersus aīaz"; a quote from 1 Peter 2:11</note>, just as the living apostle of Christ exhorted his people in his writings. Be as little children in malice <note>original: "Malitia paruuli estote"; a quote from 1 Corinthians 14:20</note>, because the Lord of Glory himself took on the form of human infancy. Clothe yourselves in the armor of justice and the virtue of patience, through which you may gain your souls; for He who is the Redeemer and Redemption of all shall Himself be the strength of all. Walk steadfastly in the way of truth and peace, and let no earthly pleasures hinder you, for heavenly ones are prepared in exchange for them all. 

These and similar lessons Queen Theodolinda taught to all her people, both by word and by example. Thus this most Christian <term>virago</term> <note>The Latin 'virago' here refers to a woman of heroic or masculine strength of character, intended as high praise for her leadership.</note> and most religious lady was the cause of many great benefits for all the Lombards. Furthermore, among her other works of piety, she built at her own expense a most noble monastery in honor of Saint Columbanus the Abbot at Bobbio, an ancient city of Lombardy, with the most magnificent buildings. She also contributed and assigned many estates for the maintenance of the monks. 

She also built several other monasteries and churches—most notably at Monza, in the territory of Milan, a famous and well-populated town. There she constructed from the foundations a most distinguished church in honor of Saint John the Baptist, which she took care to adorn with estates and other riches, as well as many vessels of silver and gold (which still exist today). Because of her example, from that time onward, all our Lombards have taken the most holy John the Baptist, the precursor of our Lord, as their special advocate and protector. 

It is established that she bore only one son, named Adaloald, the successor to the kingdom, by her husband King Agilulph. While he was still a small child, she reigned for ten years after her husband's death. To secure protection for him, she betrothed him to the daughter of Theodebert, King of the Franks, when he was barely four years old. 

Indeed, this most prudent woman took care to make peace not only with all her Lombards but also with all the Italians and other nations. Queen Theodolinda herself was nonetheless always ready in spirit for all noble undertakings, both because of her virtue and the glory of her deeds; however, for as long as she lived, she utterly removed, pushed away, and abolished the matters of war from every side. For not only were her own Lombards led to religion and the love of peace by the justice and modesty of this holy woman, but even the cities of the Roman Pontiff and other neighboring nations—as if a healthy breeze and spirit were blowing from her—began a process of change and imitation. She turned the desires of all toward a holy, modest, tranquil, and peaceful way of life, and toward the cultivation of the Christian religion, nurturing her restless children and peoples. 

Indeed, neither war, nor sedition, nor tumult is found to have occurred in the entire kingdom of the Lombards while Queen Theodolinda reigned. Nor was there any enmity or envy against her, nor any conspiracy of men out of a desire for power. 

As to what kind of death our divine Queen met, I do not recall reading it anywhere. It is certain, however, that all her associates, friends, and many peoples gathered for the funeral rites in public processions and (as I might say) in circles. They followed her with wailing and tears, not merely as attendants to a Queen from the palace, but as if each individual were burying one of their own most dear loved ones. 

Her tomb is said to still stand as a famous site in Monza, in the church of the holy Precursor <note>Saint John the Baptist</note> which she herself built. In that place (as they say), there was for a long time an image of the divine Theodolinda herself; it is said to have remained even until the time of our ancestors, showing that she was heroic not only in spirit but also in her very speech and countenance.
