**FOLIO 132**

## Of Queen Cesarea and Empress Irene

**Cesarea**, the most illustrious Queen of the Persians: a woman truly renowned and exceedingly wise. In the year of our salvation 640—while Constantine Augustus, the third of that name, ruled in Constantinople <note>Constantine III, son of Heraclius, who reigned briefly in 641</note> and Pope Theodore presided in the chair of Peter in Rome—she offered a supreme example of faith to be imitated by all. Although I find no record of her ancestral origins, I find she was a most beloved wife to her husband the King, which is known to have been achieved primarily through her singular goodness.

->[Woodcut illustration of Queen Cesarea standing in a landscape, hand-colored]<-

For this reason, I believe she should be extolled with all the more worthy and outstanding praise, because she fulfilled her devotion more ardently by her own will and through a singular gift of divine mercy, rather than by the prompting of any preacher or teacher. Driven by zeal for the Christian faith, and without her husband's knowledge, she set out from Persia with a few attendants in humble dress. After much labor and danger, she finally reached Constantinople. There, she was received with great ceremony and honor by the Emperor Constantine. 

Remaining there for some time, she was most carefully instructed in the teachings of the Christian religion by most learned and holy men. She finally emerged as a <term>catechumen</term> <note>a convert receiving formal introductory instruction in the faith</note> and a most Christian woman along with all her attendants. The Empress, wife of the Emperor, received her from the sacred font <note>acted as her godmother during baptism</note> with great joy. 

When her husband, the King of the Persians, learned of this, he suffered no small amount of grief. Sending legates from his palace to Constantinople, he humbly petitioned the Emperor for his wife to be returned to him. Augustus <note>a title used here for the Emperor</note> replied that it would be within the Queen’s own judgment whether to stay or depart. Therefore, the legates should ask her themselves. To them, she affirmed that she would never return unless the King himself became a Christian. 

Once the King realized this, he immediately came to Constantinople with a most honorable company of forty thousand Persians in a great and peaceful procession. Received most kindly by Augustus himself, he was baptized not long after, along with all his people. Augustus received him from the sacred font and chose him as a most dear son. After these matters were settled, the King was presented with many gifts and honored with privileges. Bidding farewell to the Emperor and Empress, he returned happily with his most beloved and Christian wife to his country and kingdom.

### Of Empress Irene. Chapter 254.

**Irene**, of Constantinople, the most beloved wife of Leo Augustus <note>Leo IV, known as the Khazar</note>. In the year of our salvation 773—while Pope Hadrian, the first of that name, presided in the chair of Peter in Rome—she shone most brightly through her imperial power, her beauty, and her many vigorous deeds. She was of Athenian origin, born to most noble parents, and was conspicuous for her remarkable beauty. 

->[Woodcut illustration of Empress Irene seated on a throne with two attendants, hand-colored]<-

<meta>This page follows the history of famous women, specifically moving from the Byzantine empress Irene to the legendary Pope Joan. The Latin source text uses many abbreviations (such as 'qʒ' for 'que' and 'cū' for 'cum') which have been expanded for this English translation.</meta>

->**On the Empress Irene**<-

Because Constantine <note>Constantine V, reigned 741–775</note> had summoned her from her homeland in Thrace to his presence, he was greatly delighted by her incomparable beauty and the composure of her manners. He joined her in marriage to Leo <note>original: "leoni seu leo cozario," referring to Leo IV, known as 'the Khazar'</note>, his firstborn son. For this reason, upon the death of her father-in-law Constantine, she succeeded as Augusta <note>A title for the Empress</note> by right of her husband, and she bore a son named Constantine to her husband. Finally, when her husband was removed from human affairs, she administered the empire excellently for ten years alongside her very young son, Constantine.

But when he had grown somewhat older and asserted that the rule was finally owed to him, he removed her from administration for eight years (as some prefer to say). At last, this woman of great spirit—and greedy for power—seeing that she had fallen into discord with her son, seized the youth (who was far too trusting in his own strength) by a certain feminine cunning. Having removed him from power, she cast him into custody. She alone ascended to the throne from which once the entire world received its laws. Having become a famous empress above other mortals, she ruled alone with great glory for five years.

Furthermore, it was brought about by the friends of her son Constantine that, with the help of the Armenians <note>Refers to the Armeniac Theme, a military division of the empire</note>, Irene was deposed from the height of the empire after five years; and her son Constantine, released from his chains, was restored to his father's throne. He, being more mild toward his mother than she had been toward him, and placing much hope in the help and strength of his friends, did not return her to prison. Instead, he ordered her to be kept in the Palace of Eleutherius—which she herself had built—with every abundance of resources. All of her friends, however, were sent into exile.

Yet, when he conducted himself unsuccessfully against the Bulgars, and when the high officials attempted to remove him from power for that reason and substitute his uncle Nicephorus in his place, Constantine was exasperated by anger and broke out into shameful cruelty. First, he tore out the tongues of Nicephorus himself and his brother Christopher. Next, he deprived Alexios, the patrician of Armenia, of his sight <note>Blinding was a common Byzantine punishment to disqualify rivals from the throne</note>, and forced his own wife Maria to take on a monastic habit. He then brought in Theodote, a lady of the bedchamber, as his wife, whom he immediately crowned.

Because of these enormities, the woman Irene—who, although forced to lay down the fortune of empire, had nevertheless preserved a noble spirit—took up the hope of reassuming the principate. If she were to give lavishly to the nobles from the unlocked treasures she had secretly hidden in the palace where she lived in seclusion during her reign, she believed she could make the minds of the leading men favorable to her own claim. When she had drawn them to her opinion with ample gifts, she acted so that those who had deposed her would also capture her son Constantine and deprive him of his sight. Thus this spirited woman reassumed the empire that had once been taken from her. Constantine, however, died from the illness brought on by these events.

Finally, when Irene had ruled for another five years, she was besieged in the Palace of Eleutherius by Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus I, her successor</note>. After he had received the diadem from Tarasios, the Patriarch of Constantinople, and at the persuasion of the patricians Leo and Triphyllius and the treasurer Sycopeus (recently enriched by Irene), it was arranged that he should enter to Irene with humility. He acted with flatteries—though she resisted, having nothing left but that palace in which she stayed—asking her to open all the treasures to him upon his promise to grant her requests. Once these were obtained, the wicked man, having cheated her of his good faith, banished her to exile on Lesbos. There, already an old woman, she ended a sorrowful life.

Others, however, seem to feel differently about the end of this woman. They say that while the mother and son were in discord and depriving each other of the empire in turn, the Romans departed from them and transferred the empire to Charlemagne, then King of the Franks. They say he attempted to bring back into one what seemed to be a divided empire by a marriage to Irene, and that Irene herself had agreed to this. When the patrician Aetios noticed this, he quickly elevated Nicephorus and, by a siege, forced Irene to step down from power and enter a monastery, where she finally grew old.

The Marquis and Griselda lived most happily together in marriage. They saw the children of their children even unto generations and generations. ### Concerning Matilda, the glorious Countess of Lombardy. Chapter 146.

**M**atilda was a glorious, illustrious, and most excellent woman of celebrated genius, the Countess of Mantua and many cities. I profess that I have read in many books that she lived during the times of Gregory VII, the Roman Pontiff, and also of Henry III <note>Though the text specifies Henry III, historical records show Matilda’s primary conflict was with his successor, Henry IV.</note> of the same name; specifically in the year of our salvation 1007 <note>original: "anno... septimo et millesimo"</note>, owing to her most brilliant deeds in many matters. She had as her parents Boniface, a most noble and magnificent citizen of Lucca by birth, and Beatrice, daughter of the first Emperor Henry. Since she was their only offspring, she succeeded her parents in the rule of the cities of Lucca, Parma, Reggio, Modena, Ferrara, and Mantua, and of that part of Tuscany <note>original: "ethrurie"</note> which modern people call the Patrimony <note>The "Patrimony of Saint Peter" refers to the land and sovereign power held by the Pope.</note>. For these reasons, she was held as renowned and famous throughout all Italy. She married, in the flower of her elegant youth, Godfrey, a most powerful man and brother to Richard and Robert, surnamed Guiscard, the illustrious Dukes of Apulia, Calabria, and Campania; through him, she also attained much glory. She therefore commanded her cities together with her husband for many years, from whom, however, she never produced any offspring.

But she waged almost infinite wars, for she was a most invincible <term>virago</term> <note>In the medieval context, a "virago" was a woman who possessed masculine strengths and virtues, such as courage and leadership in battle, without losing her status as a woman.</note> and most prudent. Wherefore, by the decree of the Roman Pontiffs Alexander II and Gregory VII, she deserved to be called "Countess." Indeed, since she seemed born for honor and glory, she also meditated upon, planned, and performed all things above human estimation. First, indeed, when she heard that her kinsman Richard and his son William, strenuous warriors, had occupied certain lands in Apulia belonging to the jurisdiction of the Church, she went there from Lombardy with an army and soon compelled them to restore what had been captured. After these things were strenuously performed, they returned to Rome with the army and were greatly honored by the Roman Pontiff.

Not much later, Gregory VII, the pontiff of the same name, celebrated a great council in the Lateran and wished this Countess Matilda to be present because of her own great wisdom. In this council, he <term>anathematized</term> <note>Excommunicated; a formal curse by the Church excluding someone from the community of believers.</note> Robert Guiscard and the other Normans because they had recently occupied many lands of the Church in the March of Ancona. Therefore, Countess Matilda magnanimously repressed and humbled the power not only of the aforementioned Dukes of Apulia and Calabria, but also of Emperor Henry III, who often exercised his power against the Roman Pontiffs; she forced him to restore those things he had occupied concerning ecclesiastical right. Furthermore, she received Pope Gregory, who was being too fiercely pursued by Emperor Henry, into her town of Canossa in the territory of Reggio, to be protected most honorably. To this place at last Emperor Henry, marked by anathema, came in haste with all his forces. Having seen Countess Matilda's...

FOLIO 135
->Concerning Countess Matilda<-

With great spirit and power, and also with wisdom: immediately having cast aside his royal finery, with bare feet, Henry <note>The text refers to the Emperor Henry IV</note> begged for mercy like a petitioner and a bishop. And when entry had been denied to him, and the winter was most bitter, he remained for three continuous days in the outskirts of the town <note>This refers to the Castle of Canossa</note>, always praying for pardon. At last, primarily at the request of this Countess Matilda, and of Adelaide, Count of Savoy, and the Abbot of Cluny <note>Hugh of Cluny</note>, he was introduced into the castle at the feet of the Pope. When Henry had promised to correct his errors in the presence of those mentioned above, he was absolved by the Pope himself and reconciled to the Church. He took care to establish peace with the Roman Pontiff with great skill <note>original: "maria dexteritate"</note> by means of an oath. And this same Emperor Henry promised to observe complete obedience, and indeed did so through the mediation of this heroic woman <note>term: "virago" — in medieval Latin, this was a term of high praise for a woman possessing "masculine" strength of character or courage</note>, the Countess.

Now, this Matilda was most eager for divine things, and a most ardent defender of the Holy Roman Church, and well-deserving of it. Indeed, relying on her devotion, after Christ and his mother the eternal Virgin, she most courageously resisted whichever shameful and unjust men arose; however, she wished to be present for and bring aid to faithful and honest men. For many princes of the world, and many other Church officials, and several commoners had conspired against the Roman Pontiffs like members of the devil, raising their horns and heels <note>A biblical metaphor for rebellion and pride</note> too proudly against the Church of God, having made a conspiracy among themselves; but Matilda herself took up protection against them all with an unbroken spirit and always maintained it without fail.

Nevertheless, Matilda was pleasing to all for her piety, religion, and justice. Therefore, after the death of Godfrey her husband <note>Godfrey the Hunchback</note>, a little later she took as her husband Azzo, the Marquis of Este, a blood relative of her previous husband and joined to her in the third degree of affinity. Later, when the matter was recognized, since she was a woman of the best and God-fearing conscience, she consulted the Roman Pontiff on what needed to be done; at his persuasion, she sought a divorce from this husband, namely Azzo of Este. Therefore, from then on, Matilda served God and the Roman Church most chastely in prayers and other good works.

For this Countess Matilda was a woman of vast and versatile talent. She learned, whenever there was a need for change, the exercises and opinions that are proper to prudent and good men. First of all, having set aside military matters entirely, she took care to restore the character of her citizens—which had been weakened and entirely corrupted by the negligence and ignorance of past times—into a better form and elegance. From then on, she began to enjoy the company of most holy and learned men, and especially of Anselm, Bishop of Lucca—a man of great erudition and goodness—and also of the great Abbot of Cluny, and many others. By their excellent teachings and advice, among other things, she built almost innumerable churches, and most grand monasteries in various places, which they say numbered one hundred. 

Foremost among these in the territory of Lucca was the monastery of Frassinoro <note>original: "Frisōariū"</note>; in Reggio, the Abbey of Canossa; in Modena, Nonantola; in Ferrara, Pomposa; in Mantua, Saint Benedict <note>San Benedetto Po</note>; and in almost innumerable other places she built various other monasteries which still stand today. She decorated them with the relics of the saints, with most precious gold and silver vessels, and with garments beautiful beyond belief, and enriched them with innumerable estates and lands. 

At last, truly worn out by old age, in the sixty-ninth year of her life—specifically in the year of our salvation one thousand one hundred and thirteen <note>Matilda actually died in 1115; the manuscript reflects a common medieval dating variation</note>—in Bondeno, a town in the Mantuan territory, full of good works, she passed to the Lord. Some say that when this wise and illustrious woman had decided to solemnly celebrate the birth of the Lord <note>Christmas</note> at that same town, which was then famous, Pontius, the Abbot of Cluny, arrived there with many monks for the sake of her grace, and was most reverently received by her. And while he set out to celebrate the night office on the night of the Lord's Birth (even though it was freezing with an immense frost), the Countess herself most eagerly went to him. But while they were performing the divine service, due to the immense frost, her aged limbs stiffened so much that when she returned home, with a fever...

# FOLIO 136
## Concerning Saint Constance, the Christian Empress

It was, therefore, as previously stated, that this Constance was the daughter of William <note>William I (the Bad) or William II (the Good) of Sicily; historically, Constance was the daughter of Roger II and the aunt of William II.</note>, formerly the best king of the Sicilians. At her birth, as many people say, the Calabrian Abbot Joachim <note>Joachim of Fiore (c. 1135–1202), a mystic and theologian famous for his prophetic visions of history.</note>, who was gifted with a prophetic spirit, said to William: "This newborn girl will be the future ruin of his kingdom." 

Stunned and terrified by this foretelling, and having placed his faith in the prophecy, the King began to turn over in his mind with anxious meditation how such a thing could happen through a woman. He saw that it could not happen otherwise than through a husband or a son. 

Taking pity on his kingdom, he decided to follow a plan—if such a thing were possible—to ensure that all hope of marriage or offspring was taken away. He arranged for the young girl to be shut away within monastic walls <note>original: "monasticis clausam clausuris"</note> so that she might promise a vow of perpetual virginity to God. This plan was not to be despised, had it actually been successful. But why do we recount such foolish and weak human efforts against God, who justly punishes the wicked deeds of mortals? Indeed, we are frustrated by a single divine impulse.

# **On Saint Clare of Assisi**

¶ Concerning Saint Clare, disciple of the seraphic <term>Francis</term><note>Saint Francis of Assisi (1181–1226), founder of the Franciscan Order. He is called "seraphic" because of his vision of a six-winged Seraph during which he received the stigmata.</note>. Chapter 148.

**C**lare, a most holy virgin, the daughter and disciple of the seraphic Francis in Christ, lived during the time of the Roman Pope Gregory IX <note>original: "Gregorij pontificis Romani eius nominis nōni"</note>. Around the year of our salvation 1227, in <term>Umbria</term><note>A central region of Italy known as the "green heart" of the country, where Assisi is located.</note>, the most prominent province of Italy, at the ancient city of Assisi, she was held as a woman highly celebrated for her character, the austerity of her life, and her miraculous holiness. Indeed, born in that same city to honorable parents, she was endowed from her tender years with a singular piety; she would take the food intended for herself and most piously distribute it to the poor. As she grew older, having heard of the incredible reputation for holiness of the divine Francis, she immediately went to him to be instructed. Not long afterward, moved by the warnings and examples of the blessed Francis himself, she took up the habit of holy conversion and religion at the church of Saint Damian <note>The small church of San Damiano, which Francis had physically repaired after hearing a voice from a crucifix tell him to "rebuild my church."</note>. There, under a vow of continence and perpetual poverty, she began to lead her life. Soon, many young women, moved by the reports of her holiness, renounced the world and dedicated themselves to Jesus Christ. How much she flourished in humility, patience, contemplation, and other virtues could not easily be put into writing. For instance, she used to wash the muddy feet of the sisters and servants when they returned from outside; and inside the convent, she performed the most laborious tasks of service as if she were a lowly servant girl bought for the purpose, showing herself a prompt helper to all with all her strength. Indeed, her paternal inheritance, which had come to her after her conversion, she quickly sold and most eagerly distributed the money to the poor, reserving absolutely nothing of the price for herself. For she had made such a pact with <term>poverty</term><note>The "Privilege of Poverty," which Clare fought to have officially recognized by the Pope, allowed her community to own no property or possessions.</note> that she wished to have nothing at all except God; for this reason, she would not permit the sisters to reserve anything for the future beyond their daily and necessary food.

She covered her small body with only a simple tunic and a very cheap cloak, so that she seemed to be merely keeping it warm rather than nourishing it, and she afflicted her tender flesh with continual fasts. During the <term>Greater Lent</term><note>original: "Maiorē aut qdragesimā"; the forty-day fasting period before Easter.</note>, she fasted on bread and water alone, tasting a little wine only on Sundays; on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, she abstained from all fish. Furthermore, she frequently afflicted her body with a harsh <term>hairshirt</term><note>original: "cilicio"; a garment made of coarse animal hair worn against the skin as a form of penance.</note> made of cords, and she would stretch herself out on the bare ground or on bundles of twigs to sleep. Her devotion to God was supreme and incredible; being awake almost incessantly, she persisted in prayers with weeping. From this it happened that once, when the day of the <term>Lord's Supper</term><note>Maundy Thursday, the day commemorating the Last Supper of Christ.</note> had arrived, as she—most devoted—revolved in her mind again and again the capture of our Savior, his mockery, and his other shames, she remained so outside of herself that, with unblinking eyes fixed on Christ, she seemed entirely insensible.

When she had lived for forty-two continuous years in wonderful holiness of life—specifically in poverty, continence, and continuous labors—she afterward suffered from a long-lasting illness for twenty-eight years. Finally, as she approached the sleep of death, during which for seventeen days she took absolutely no bodily nourishment—

**¶ On Radegund, Queen of the Franks. Chapter 150.**

[A woodcut illustration of a crowned queen, Radegund, seated on a throne, holding a scepter. In the background, there is a landscape with a castle or city.]

**R**adegund was a noble queen of the Franks and a distinguished virgin, worthy of being remembered. By her "Barbarian" <note>original: "natione Barbara"; the author uses this term in the Roman sense to mean she was from a non-Latin Germanic tribe.</note> origin, she was from Thuringia, a province of Germany. Her father was Berentharius (or Berengarius), a man of noble and honored family among his own people. When Lothair <note>Lothair I (also known as Clothar I), a 6th-century Merovingian King.</note>, King of the Franks, had conquered and overran her homeland, giving it over to his soldiers as plunder, she was taken captive as a young girl as part of the royal spoils. When the King saw her elegance and the beauty of her face, he was greatly pleased. He sent her to the city of Vermandois <note>A region in Picardy, northern France.</note> to be raised and educated. When she reached marriageable age, the King took the young woman as his wife. 

But when the King noticed the firm intention of his new bride to remain a virgin, he was moved by her prayers and kept her as an untouched virgin. Saint Radegund, though she was consecrated to God, feared that she might eventually fall away from her path because she was advancing so much in worldly rank. Therefore, she most eagerly dedicated almost all of her royal resources and wealth to alms for the poor. For whenever any revenue from taxes came to her, she gave away tithes <note>A "tithe" is a tenth part of one's income given to the church or the poor.</note> of everything she was to receive before she even took it; what remained, she distributed to monasteries. Where she could not go in person, she sent gifts through faithful and diligent men, considering any money lost that she had not spent on the poor. 

She also gathered many of the destitute and needy, just as the aforementioned Elizabeth <note>likely referring to Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, a famous queen-saint mentioned in earlier chapters of this work.</note> did, and she very often washed their heads for the sake of Christ and most piously tended to their diseases and sores. Though she was a queen, she served the poor as fervently as if she were a humble servant girl. Amidst royal foods and delicacies, she often ate only beans or lentils, so that you would think she was one of the "three youths" from the Holy Scriptures. <note>A reference to the Book of Daniel, where Daniel and his companions refused the King's rich food in favor of vegetables and remained healthier than those who ate the royal meat.</note> Every night at an unseasonable hour, she would rise from her bed and devote herself to prayer, shedding abundant tears. She considered the hardships she bore and the things she did to be light, fearing only that she might become unworthy in the eyes of Christ, her bridegroom. 

Finally, with the consent of her husband—the most Christian and excellent king—she changed her dress at the monastery of Saix <note>original: "Moninione," referring to her retreat at Saix before moving to Poitiers.</note> under the holy Bishop Medard. Having taken up the holy religious habit, she was immediately consecrated with the sacred veil. A very famous monastery was built by the King at Poitiers <note>original: "Pictauium"</note>, and she was appointed there as Mother and Abbess by the saintly bishop. In that place, she was made illustrious by her abstinence, charity, humility, and other almost incredible virtues. She shone brightly with many miracles both at her death and afterward, for which reason her passing was most glorious. Her anniversary is celebrated with veneration by everyone every year on the Ides of August. <note>August 13th.</note>

### Concerning Blessed Clare of Montefalco

She was a follower of the <term>Augustinian Order of Hermits</term> <note>A religious community following the Rule of Saint Augustine, emphasizing shared poverty and inner spiritual life.</note>. During the time of Pope Boniface VIII and the Emperor Albert, she was most renowned and distinguished for the sincerity of her life, just as her name "Clare" implies. <note>original: "sicut nomine clarissima" — a play on words, as 'Clara' means bright, clear, or famous in Latin.</note>

When she had passed through her childhood years in the secular world and reached the age of twelve, she began to recognize the changeable nature of human affairs. # **Of Blessed Clare and Maria of Pozzuoli FOLIO 139**

By grace, this Clare, an **Augustinian** <note>A member of the religious order following the Rule of St. Augustine.</note>, shone forth not only as illustrious but as a most celebrated woman. Indeed, the Lord cannot deny such grace to anyone who makes themselves worthy of Him. Therefore, by these virtues and merits, and through her ever-watchful gift of prophecy and foresight, she became a most renowned visionary in her own time. Adorned with these merits, at last, in the year of our salvation twelve hundred and ninety-nine, in her own **Convent** <note>The original term "Cenobio" refers to a community of monks or nuns living together.</note> at Montefalco—the very town of her birth—she returned her holy soul to God. 

Concerning the proclamation of her holiness and the testimony of all the aforementioned things, we report this specific evidence, which can be seen with open eyes and which has perhaps never been found in any other saint. For when she had died and her body was opened, a clear and distinct image of the **Crucified Christ** was seen within her heart, along with all the symbols of His passion. Furthermore, in the gallbladder of her body, three small stones were found, all of the same weight. This was a most evident sign of her holiness. Seeing such a miracle, a certain faithful and pious poet sang these verses in praise of the wonder, saying:

<note>original: "Monte sata e falco/virgo sanctissima clara..." The following is a translation of the Latin poem describing the miraculous discovery of the instruments of the Passion inside Clare's heart.</note>

Born of Montefalco, the most holy virgin Clare,
Perfected in the sacred and modest way of Augustine,
Worshipped God with her heart day and night, 
Even unto God Himself. She longed to have felt
The cross of Christ and all his torments; thus, 
When her life’s light ended and her flesh was opened,
That which she had pressed within her entrails was revealed:
In her sacred heart, the **Cross** was seen, and the **Lance** likewise.
Then there was the **Column**, and also every **Scourge**;
Besides these, three small stones were joined in her gallbladder,
The color of which can scarcely be distinguished one from another.
One weighs as much as two, or even as much as all three together,
And yet two weigh only as much as three; anyone may see this.
To this, he adds her fatherland and her home...

Her little body, which is almost divine—and which I myself have seen to this day—remains in no part decayed. Since it still presents a certain appearance of a living person to those who look upon it, it leads everyone into admiration and veneration of her perfection and her holiness.

# **On Maria of Pozzuoli**

...food, and throughout her entire life she always abstained from wine. Among other things, her speech was always very rare and sparing. Womanly occupations were of the least concern to her: no distaff <note>original: "colus"; a tool used in spinning wool, symbolising traditional female labor</note>, no wool-weight, no needle, nor wool-working; but the bow, the javelin, the spear, the helmet, the shield, the sword, and the blade, and other such arms which are commonly used in wars. Very often, indeed, she spent the whole night without sleep; although whenever the necessity of nature compelled her to rest, she would lie on the bare ground or upon her shield, and would lie there just like a disciplined soldier. Finally, whatever time was left over from active duties (as is handed down concerning Hannibal <note>The Carthaginian general famous for his physical endurance</note>), that alone was given to rest. 

Devoted to warlike matters, she always moved joyfully among armed men. And although she took great delight in the company of soldiers, her chief concern was always (a truly admirable thing) the preservation of her chastity <note>original: "pudicitie"</note> throughout her whole life, and of her modesty, which she kept certainly inviolate until the very end. This fact made her more famous and certainly more glorious among mortals, since it was not easily believed that a young woman, living continually among soldiers, could have preserved her chastity and modesty unstained. There were, however, some who tried to undermine this virginity of hers with false rumors; but it was later clearly discovered that all those things had been falsely fabricated. 

Thus, this Maria was more fit for arms and for handling wars than for any other womanly exercises and ornaments. Whence many accounted it a great glory for themselves if the opportunity of joining in combat with her were granted to them, whether in a foot-battle or a mounted one. Since she was a woman of a very strong and robust body, she reported victory from all those with whom she undertook a contest, and she departed from the battle as the victress. She studied the care of her body very little, or certainly not at all those womanly refinements which, if they are superfluous, are rather to be condemned than approved. 

It is well known that she never waged an unjust war; rather, this was her only purpose in entering battles: either for the sake of protecting friends or for defending the rights of her fatherland. So great was the magnitude of her spirit that sometimes even alone, or certainly accompanied by few, she did not fear to face the enemy. And in attacking them, following the example of Hannibal, she would enter the battle first, and when it was finished, she would be the last to withdraw. To the strength of her body was added the memorable genius of a distinguished commander, especially in arranging ambushes by which she might circumvent the enemy. She was seen to be glowing and impassioned no less in the heat of battle than in every other duty of war, equally patient of hunger, thirst, heat, cold, and vigils, and finally of all exhaustion. 

Through these labors and constant dangers, this Maria turned out to be a most fierce woman and most warlike in every part of war. Whence many, moved by this reputation for womanly vigor, were most eagerly drawn from their own country to see her—some led by the miracle of the woman, others to offer their hand in combat and to test their strength and power against her. Among these, Robert, King of the Sicilians <note>Robert of Anjou (r. 1309–1343), also known as Robert the Wise, King of Naples</note>, when he had heard many wonderful and almost incredible things about her virtue, came from his kingdom to see her at Pozzuoli in Campania. 

Francesco Petrarch <note>The famous Italian poet and scholar (1304–1374)</note> also writes as a rich witness. When he had arrived in that place at some time specifically for the sake of seeing her, he saw her both armed and unarmed—a thing unheard of, and worthy of remembrance in all ages and monuments. He also relates that when he was once in the city with a friend and they were walking together in a friendly manner (as happens), he was greeted by her while she was fully armed with a helmet on her head; he believed entirely that it was surely an armed knight, not a woman. But afterwards, when he understood from certain gestures who it was, he immediately climbed with some of his friends upon the higher citadel of that city, so that he might better see her fighting from there. And so he clearly observed that she had reported a most glorious victory and triumph over several very brave men, who had come there from various places for the sake of this very thing. He also relates that when he found her alone...

**FOLIO 140**

**On Baptista Malatesta** <note>Baptista Malatesta (1384–1448) was an educated Italian noblewoman and poet. However, the anecdote following this title describes a woman named Mary whom Petrarch encountered.</note>

When he was at rest, he asked her if she would deign to perform some feat of strength in his presence for his entertainment, so that he might more certainly witness her hardiness. But she, being a most kind-hearted woman and a lady of noble spirit, wished to comply with the wishes of Lord Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374) was a world-famous Italian poet and scholar, often called the "Father of Humanism."</note> himself. She had been very kindly invited, and because he appeared to Mary <note>original: "marie"</note> to be a man of some excellence, she immediately took up an iron bar and a large rock or stone. One after the other, with little effort, she hurled them a very great distance. After throwing them, she very kindly addressed those standing by: "You," she said, "who are men and not women, take up this stone and, if you are able, see if you can surpass my throw by the same distance." But Francesco Petrarch, being struck with amazement when he saw that the woman’s strength surpassed that of the men, declared that he could never have been persuaded that such excellence <note>The word used here implies both physical power and exceptional character.</note> existed in any woman in the world, unless the matter itself had been proven before him.

### On Baptista Malatesta and Joanna of Sicily

...letters; which undoubtedly declare both her elegance and her purity. She also delivered an oration to Pope Martin V <note>Martin V (reigned 1417–1431) was the Pope who effectively ended the Western Schism.</note> in which she wonderfully praised his papacy, which had been desired by all. Through her speech, she followed the joy of his priesthood with the most exquisite praises. So great was the adornment of this oration and such were her insights that she was most magnificently praised and commended by Pope Martin himself. This distinguished woman wrote many other works besides these, which seem to greatly delight both those who read them and those who hear them. 

Furthermore, she was considered a woman of memorable justice, as well as clemency and piety. She was so charitable and gracious toward everyone that she was frequently greeted in letters and other writings by the most learned men of that time, and especially by the most devout priest, Francesco Petrarch. <note>original: "Frāciſcho petrarcha". Note: This is a historical anachronism in the text, as Petrarch died in 1374, before Baptista was born. The author may be confusing her with another member of the Malatesta family or referring to a different humanist scholar.</note> There exists a volume by him in which he greatly encourages her in the pursuit of fine literature. This magnificent woman, Baptista, certainly took no pleasure in expensive or precious clothing, for she said that a woman’s dignity or any honor was not placed in such things. Instead, she devoted all her greatest study to collecting books and to adopting the habits of women who excelled in virtue and in every honesty of character; she believed that the true glory of the entire female sex was placed chiefly in this. 

Indeed, she administered her husband’s principality more correctly and prudently than her husband did himself. Because of these things, it happened that she was always held in the highest honor by everyone; she was cherished by all as the common parent of everyone, as much by strangers as by her own subjects. In her whole life, she produced only one daughter named Elisabeth, who equaled her mother in both beauty and talent, and who was later married to the Prince of Camerino. After the death of her husband, she lived a celibate life in widowhood for several years. Finally, dedicated to the Order of Saint Clare, <note>The Poor Clares, a Franciscan order for women.</note> she spent the remainder of her life in a monastery in Urbino among the assembly of holy virgins. There, through the greatest labors—in which she devoted herself most strictly to the service of religion and the pursuit of the celestial life—she departed from this life with the greatest goodwill and as an example to all. She left behind many memorable teachings and a holiness of life which could serve as a certain guide to all Christians for living rightly and blessedly. For these reasons, this Baptista deservedly comes to be counted by us in this place among famous women.

## Concerning Joanna of Sicily, the illustrious queen. Chapter 152.

**I**oanna, <note>Also known as Joan I of Naples (1325–1382).</note> the first of that name, the renowned Queen of Sicily and Jerusalem, was the daughter of Charles, Duke of Calabria, and the granddaughter of King Robert through his firstborn son. She lived in the same age and time as the aforementioned famous women, Baptista and Mary. She was highly illustrious and famous not only for her origin, power, and noble character, but also for her most robust and invincible heart. In all matters, she was so brilliant and sharp-eyed that no one could have deceived her by any cleverness, but rather only by fraud. For she was long-suffering and very outstanding, as the insults of harsh fortune sufficiently showed in her life.

## **Concerning Saint Catherine of Siena, Folio 142**

So great was the persistence and frequency of her prayer that her knees became as hard as those of a camel <note>This is a traditional hagiographic image. It was famously used to describe James the Just, suggesting his knees became calloused like a camel's from constant kneeling in prayer.</note>. **On Paula Gonzaga**

[Large decorative initial P] Her name is counted among the illustrious women of this work of ours, second to none in the gifts of wisdom and modesty. She was the wife of Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, the Prince of Mantua, an extraordinary woman who possessed the most holy gift of ancient constancy and patience. In the year 1449 after the birth of Christ, she died in Mantua, a distinguished city of Cisalpine Gaul <note>The historical name for the region of Northern Italy between the Alps and the Apennines</note>, leaving behind the great brilliance of her name. 

This illustrious woman had as her father Malatesta, from the famous and very ancient Malatesta family of Pesaro, the prince of the city in the province of Flaminia <note>A region in eastern Italy along the Adriatic coast</note>. She was clearly the most charming and beautiful among the other women of her century. In her face, there was a certain special grace and a truly serious expression. Such a distinguished bearing is surely the best way to draw out the goodwill of the people, which is the chief and firmest defense of kingdoms. 

Truly, she excelled among others of her sex and among women for her singular eloquence; moreover, she was remarkably affable even to great men. She was liberal beyond measure toward the wretched and those destitute of all help. She was greatly moved by the misfortunes of others, to whom she tirelessly brought aid according to their circumstances <note>original: "pro ratione personarum" — meaning she gave appropriately based on the individual's social standing and specific needs</note>, especially those who fled to her for assistance. Because of these noble qualities—more than can be expressed in words—she was most beloved by all her people. 

Everyone always attributed much to her far-reaching and most prudent counsel. She frequently made use of that saying of Plato: "We must realize that we are born not only for ourselves, but for all the human race; part of our birth our country should claim, and part our friends." <note>This is a famous quote from Plato, though notably cited by Cicero in his work "On Duties"</note>. Drawn by these virtues among others, her husband, Prince Gianfrancesco, took wonderful delight in such a wife, as she was so wise, so just, and so beneficial to all. 

Toward the end, when he gave himself over to military affairs, he thought it right to entrust her with the entire administration of his city, relying greatly on her counsel and wisdom. It was her care not only to ensure the best discipline for her citizens—shaping them toward refined and noble character and the best institutions of well-governed cities—but also to ensure that those who were religious men in the city and her lands, but who were living less religiously than they ought, were transferred to a more praiseworthy way of life. 

Thus, she established many temples and monasteries in her city for both women and men, in which religious men and women lived separately and occupied themselves with divine matters, following all holiness of character and integrity of life—the best parts necessary for preparing for the celestial life. This healthy and wonderful discipline, which flowed from the Holy Spirit, is preserved most perfectly and incorrupt in that city to this day. 

Since she herself was incredibly devoted to divine things and omitted nothing that pertained to fostering religion, she used her own goods and resources to restore and complete many collapsed monasteries of religious men and women, endowing and decorating them wonderfully. 

Nevertheless, in order to make this most praised woman, decorated with all virtues, even dearer to Himself, the Lord God finally allowed her to be tested by a most grave illness. This happened in the flower of her age, so that her excellent virtues might appear more and more proven. For she was soon struck with a double hump <note>original: "gibba." This likely refers to a severe spinal deformity such as kyphosis or the effects of spinal tuberculosis, known as Pott's disease</note>: one on the chest and another on the back. Because of these, she was immediately made so swollen and so deformed that her head seemed to be carried upon her chest. Thus she was debilitated in all her limbs. Furthermore, she was beset by pains and by gout <note>original: "podagra"</note>, so that she could not even [bring] her hand to her mouth...

Thus Paula, as illustrious as she was sickly and debilitated in her whole body, devoted herself to religion. She decided to build a place for herself not far from one of those buildings she had ordered to be constructed. There, as becomes a Christian, following a proven way of life, she finally reached the end of her days. This occurred four years after the death of her husband, when she was sixty years old. This excellent end to her life and her outstanding virtue earned this most holy woman a most celebrated name. Furthermore, she was characterized by a perpetual generosity toward both men and women who lacked her resources; nor was her kindness closed to those endowed with virtue and good character. 

It would not be easy in this space to recount her fasts or explain her abstinences, undertaken to repress all harmful desires of the body, nor her constant prayers to the immortal God for her own safety and that of her family—prayers which she sometimes poured out with tears. All these qualities were exceptionally prominent in this illustrious woman. You might say that in this place, the noble matron Paula, through her merits and prayers, made the Creator of all things so well-disposed toward her that He opened the lap of His bounty and compelled many graces to be poured out upon her, both at the moment of her death and thereafter. 

It is recorded that her husband, Gianfrancesco, had six children by this outstanding woman: four males and two females. 

The first of these was **Ludovico**, who succeeded his father in power; he was a prince of his age with no small reputation, learned in literature and practiced in military affairs. 

The second was **Carlo**, a most brave warrior; few were his equal in height of body or certainly in strength, yet he was not without skill in the liberal disciplines or learning. 

He was followed by **Gianlucido**, who was quite sickly and particularly deformed; he survived his father's death by only a few years. 

The fourth son born to them was **Alessandro**, who suffered from the same <term>hunchback</term> and <term>goiter</term> as his mother; he was a very religious man who spent almost his entire life among men of religion, occupied in the praises of God. 

Of the daughters, the eldest was **Margherita**, who [married] Prince Leonello...

**¶ Concerning Ursina, the wife of Guido Torzella. Chapter 156.**

[Large decorated initial U] Rsina, the wife of Prince Guido Torzella of Parma (who possessed many castles), and she herself in that same age, comes to be celebrated with wondrous praise throughout all of Cisalpine Gaul <note>The region of Northern Italy</note>, especially because of her own most famous deeds—both divine and human—performed by her with vigor and marvel. She thus derived her origin primarily from the illustrious and most famous family of the Visconti (who ruled Milan). She was a woman truly outstanding in her beauty, rivaling those who in these lands have achieved the glory of admirable loveliness. Her marriage, according to the fortune of that prince, was celebrated with great magnificence, festivity, and splendor, according to the custom of that people. The Torzella family was sufficiently illustrious. And so this Ursina was an illustrious heroine <note>original: "virago," a term used here to denote a woman of masculine strength and spirit</note>, both in words and deeds; she was approachable, sufficiently kind, and benevolent, and more magnificent than can be described. She was greatly esteemed by her husband, since his character was very similar to her own, and their habits were perfectly matched. She was especially generous as far as her means allowed. Toward young maidens especially, who could not marry due to a lack of resources, she actively performed all duties of piety. She attended the divine mysteries <note>The Holy Mass</note> frequently and devoutly every single day, never missing them. She prayed continuously to the Lord our Redeemer that he might deign to grant her this among other things: that she might be able to rule and govern her people with the greatest peace and praise for her husband. She could hardly bear to look upon licentious women or men who were usurers <note>Money-lenders who charged interest, often condemned by the Church</note>. Most of all, she detested wicked and lost blasphemers of God and the saints; indeed, out of zeal, if the opportunity had been given to her, she would have torn them apart with her teeth. She was, nonetheless, approachable and possessed a great soul for forgiving. She was, moreover, not ignorant of managing domestic affairs, guided by both divine and human examples; and led by these examples, she always kept herself in the highest esteem and good reputation. To all her subjects and friends, but to her husband most of all, she was always most beloved. By these things, she obtained a most famous name in all of Cisalpine Gaul. Of this vigorous woman, many and almost incredible famous deeds performed by her could be written, which indeed I think should by no means be kept silent in this place: those things which Ursina vigorously performed in defending her property and the Milanese princedom or kingdom. For when at one time a great war had arisen between the Venetians and the Duke of Milan, Filippo Maria, the Venetian fleet came up the Po River <note>original: "Heridanus," a classical name for the river Po</note> and attacked and captured Burello, her husband's most well-known castle. Once it was taken, they soon moved with great noise to Guastalla, another town of her husband’s situated on the bank of the Po, where their camp was established. When Ursina learned of this—she was then eight miles away from Guastalla—immediately (like a daughter of Mars <note>The Roman god of war</note>) she drew up all the troops she could find. She put on a breastplate <note>original: "thorax"</note> along with all her cavalry armor, and courageously mounting her horse, she said to her fellow soldiers: "Be brave, my fellow soldiers, and let us go with surpassing strength, for I do not intend to take off these arms I have put on until these enemies of ours have been routed and put to flight by us." Having said this, with no less greatness of spirit than Queen Semiramis of the Assyrians against the Babylonians, she set out to break the siege of her castle...

### Concerning Hortensia and Cornificia leaf 45

**H**ortensia, the daughter of the eminent orator Quintus Hortensius, lived during the time of Octavian Augustus. She was a woman worthy of being extolled with the highest praise, for she not only embraced her father’s eloquence with a lively heart, but also preserved that vigor of delivery in all matters where opportunity required it—a quality which most often fails even among the most learned men.

During the time of the Triumvirs <note>The Second Triumvirate: Octavian, Mark Antony, and Lepidus, who ruled Rome from 43–33 BCE.</note>, a multitude of matrons found themselves burdened with an intolerable financial weight. The state demanded a heavy payment of money from them, yet they could find no man who dared to provide legal protection or advocacy in such an unsuitable matter. She alone dared, with a constant mind, to take up the cause of the women before the Triumvirs. She pleaded the case so effectively with her inexhaustible eloquence that, to the great admiration of those listening, it was as if the sex had been changed and the elder Hortensius had returned to life.

Nor was this excellent work, undertaken by a woman, executed unsuccessfully. Just as she never faltered in her speech nor failed in a praiseworthy demonstration of her legal rights, so too was the desired result granted by the Triumvirs. Indeed, the process moved so freely that a much larger portion of the imposed tax was removed. While a modest silence under a matron’s stole is usually seen as praiseworthy in public, the Triumvirs judged that when opportunity demands it, an eloquent speech should be extolled as its own ornament. After this deed, which brought great glory to Hortensia, the remaining small amount was easily paid by the matrons. What more can I say, except that the spirit of her ancient lineage breathed so much into this woman that she deservedly lived up to the name of Hortensius?

### Concerning the eminent poetess Cornificia. Chapter 58.

->[Woodcut illustration: A woman in a red dress holds a scroll inscribed with "DIVINITY & HUMANITY" and "HE WILL HUMBLE" <note>original Latin on scroll: "DIVINITAS & HVMANITAS" and "HVMILI TABIT"</note>.]<-

**C**ornificia was a most worthy poetess who flourished during these same times. She shone with such poetic skill that she seemed not to have been nourished on Italian milk, but on the Castalian waters <note>Castalia was a spring on Mount Parnassus sacred to the Muses; drinking from it was said to inspire poetry.</note>. She was equal in glory to her own brother, Cornificius, who was himself a distinguished poet. Not content merely with having such a splendid natural talent, she felt the sacred Muses urging her toward the heights of art. She very often set her learned hands to the pen to write Heliconian poems <note>Mount Helicon was the home of the Muses.</note>, having cast aside the distaff <note>The distaff was a tool used in spinning wool, the traditional symbol of domestic female labor.</note>.

She wrote many notable epigrams which were still highly valued in the time of the priest Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 CE), a prominent Christian scholar and translator of the Bible.</note>, as he himself testifies. O, what a feminine honor to have neglected womanly trifles and applied her genius to the studies of the greatest poets! Let those who are lazy and negligent feel ashamed, as well as those who miserably distrust themselves. Such people persuade themselves they are born only for leisure and the bedchamber, and are useful for nothing except the embraces of men and the conceiving and raising of children. In truth, women share in common all those things that make men glorious, if only they are willing to sweat in their studies. By nature's strength—which was not cast down—and through her genius and long nights of study, she was able to surpass the female sex and seek an eternal name through honest labor. This was no common reputation, but the rare and excellent glory desired by even the most gifted men.

XCIX 94
# On Sulpicia and Albumea.

**S**ulpicia, the wife of Lentulus Cruscellio <note>Lentulus Cruscellio was a Roman politician who was targeted during the proscriptions of 43 BCE.</note>, was distinguished during the same era as the two women mentioned above. She acquired an indelible reputation for herself through a nearly equal degree of devotion. 

Her husband Lentulus was proscribed <note>To be "proscribed" meant to be placed on a public list of state enemies whose property was confiscated and who could be killed for a reward.</note> by the Triumvirs <note>The Second Triumvirate: Octavian, Mark Antony, and Marcus Lepidus.</note> during that same political storm previously described. Having secured his safety by a swift flight to Sicily, he remained there in exile and in poverty, his wealth having been seized. When Sulpicia was informed of this, she decided she wished to endure these hardships together with her husband. She judged it unseemly to enjoy joyful honors and a bright fortune at home while her husband faced the bitterness of ruin—a fate from which those other women did not shrink when the opportunity to endure such calamities arose.

However, Sulpicia did not find it easy to reach her husband. She was being watched with the utmost diligence by her mother, Julia, to prevent her from following her husband into exile. But what guards are not deceived by true love? Taking her opportunity, she put on the clothes of a slave <note>original: "servili sumpta veste"</note> and, having deceived her mother and the guards, this noble woman set out. Accompanied by only two little maidservants and two little manservants, she left her native soil and her ancestral home to follow her exiled husband. She did so even though the law did not forbid her—once her husband was led away into misfortune—from entering into a new marriage. 

This illustrious woman did not fear the secret escapes, the tides of the sea, or the Italian mountains as she followed the uncertain tracks of her husband, seeking him through unknown regions until she found him and joined him. She considered it more honorable to follow a husband cast down by fortune through a thousand life-threatening perils than to idle in luxury and peace in her fatherland while he struggled in exile. 

<margin>The admirable love of a wife for her husband.</margin>

Such a judgment truly reflects an illustrious mind, smelling more of a prudent man than a woman. <note>Boccaccio frequently uses "masculine" qualities as the highest praise for women who showed courage or intellectual strength.</note> For one must not always shine with gold and gems; one must not always indulge in elegance; one must not always flee the summer sun or the winter rains and frost. Marriage beds are not always to be cherished, nor must one always spare oneself. Rather, when fortune shifts, one must undergo labors with their husbands, endure exiles, tolerate poverty, and bear dangers with a brave spirit. 

<margin>Note.</margin>

This is the "military service" expected of wives; these are their wars, these their victories, and these the conspicuous triumphs of their victories: namely, to have overcome softness, luxury, and domestic difficulties with honor, constancy, and a chaste mind. From this comes their everlasting fame and glory.

### On Albumea, the Tiburtine Sibyl. Chapter 73.

**A**lbumea, the Tiburtine Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses; the Tiburtine Sibyl was associated with the town of Tibur (modern Tivoli).</note>, was a prophetess and a most distinguished virgin. During the time of Octavian Augustus, she shone with great renown in Italy and throughout the Roman world. She predicted many things to Augustus himself.

# Concerning the Virgin Mary. Folio 46.

[Augustus] consulted her. After a three-day fast, she responded with the words that the divine father Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian.</note> records in the 18th book of *The City of God*, chapter 23, saying: "As a sign of judgment, the earth shall be wet with sweat. From heaven, the King shall come, to remain for future ages." <note>original: "Juditij signuz tellus sudore madescet. E celo rex adueniet p secula futur⁹." This is the beginning of a famous Sibylline prophecy about the Last Judgment.</note> There are twenty-seven of these most beautiful verses, the last of which is: "A river of fire and sulfur shall fall from heaven." The capital letters of these verses yield this meaning: **Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior of the World.** <note>The translator refers to a famous acrostic where the first letter of each line in the original Greek poem spells out "Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior."</note>

When these things had been spoken, and while Augustus was watching, heaven was opened and an immense splendor fell upon him. Looking up toward the sky, he saw a most beautiful virgin standing upon a certain altar, holding a tiny infant in her arms. Upon seeing this, he suddenly heard a voice saying: "This is the altar of the Son of God; worship Him." 

Having heard and seen these things, Augustus, who was standing in his chamber, immediately threw himself to the ground and worshipped God. Because of this, he thereafter forbade anyone from calling him a god. <note>In Roman history, Augustus was the first emperor to be deified, but medieval Christian legends claim he recognized Christ's superior divinity and established the 'Ara Coeli' (Altar of Heaven) in Rome.</note>

**Concerning Mariamne**

<margin>Mariamne is unworthily killed.</margin>

...understood: Mariamne, however, in the course of time, understood what had been most secretly decreed <note>Herod had previously left secret orders that Mariamne should be killed if he failed to return from his meetings with Roman authorities, so she would not belong to another man.</note>. And since she had already conceived a cursed hatred toward Herod on account of the unworthy death of Aristobulus <note>Mariamne’s brother, whom Herod had drowned.</note>, and thinking that she was loved by Herod for nothing but the use of her beauty, she heaped up her anger. She bore most heavily how she herself had twice been unjustly condemned by him; and because she had given birth to Alexander and Aristobulus, boys of conspicuous beauty, she could in no way restrain her feelings. With their impulse working within her, she fell away, so that she denied her bed to the man who loved her. While she spurned him—as if all the lineage of the ancient kings <note>Mariamne was a princess of the Hasmonean dynasty, the traditional Jewish royalty that Herod, as an outsider, had replaced.</note> rose up in her—she attempted with a certain haughty gesture to trample his power underfoot. She did not fear to say openly in his presence that Herod was a foreigner, not a Jew, nor a man of royal offspring, but rather an ignoble Idumean <note>original: "idumeum ignobilem"; Idumeans were forced converts to Judaism, and many Judeans viewed them as "half-Jews" or usurpers.</note>, not worthy of a royal wife—a fierce, insolent, faithless, and wicked man, and a monstrous beast. 

Although Herod endured these things with difficulty, yet because his love prevented him, he dared to attempt nothing cruel against her. At last, as things proceeded for the worse (as some believe), it was arranged by Cypros, Herod's mother, and Salome, his sister—to whom Mariamne was most offensive—that she should be accused to Herod by a suborned cupbearer <note>A servant bribed to give false testimony.</note> of having tried to persuade him to give Herod a love potion she herself had prepared. Or it was claimed that she had sent her most beautiful portrait to Antony <note>Mark Antony, the Roman leader.</note> to provoke his desire for her and fuel his hatred for Herod. When Herod believed these things, and Mariamne's own ill-will toward him gave them credit, he, being angry and kindled with anxious fury, complained to his friends in a long speech. 

With them urging him on, and with Alexandra, Mariamne's mother—seeking to earn the King's favor—he was led to order her to be killed, condemned to capital punishment as if she were plotting the destruction of the royal majesty. She indeed stirred up such noble spirit in herself that, despising death and keeping the beauty of her face whole, she did not weep in any feminine way. She listened in silence to her rebuking mother and looked upon the others weeping with dry cheeks. She went to her death as if to a most joyful triumph—not only without trembling but with a cheerful countenance, offering no prayers for her safety—and received death from the executioner as if it were desired. 

By this unshaken composure, she not only saddened the envy of the savage king, but she also gained more ages for her name <note>Meaning her fame and reputation grew through history.</note> than the weeping Herod could have granted to her immortality through months of his own tears and prayers. But after Mariamne, that charming woman, died, the king's soul burned so greatly that he called out her name again and again. On account of this, he strove to do everything that might bring him some comfort; for he held daily banquets and pleasant conversations, but nevertheless they helped him not at all. He even refused the governance of the kingdom and was so held by griefs that sometimes he even ordered his servants to call Mariamne as if she were alive. 

And while he was so held (as Josephus writes in the fifteenth book of the *Antiquities* <note>original: "Antiquitatum"; referring to the historical work by Flavius Josephus.</note>), a certain pestilential sickness came upon him, which killed many of his friends and gave everyone cause to suspect that it had happened through the wrath of God, namely for the iniquity committed against the most innocent Mariamne. And so the king himself came to worse things, so that at last, like one damned and a fugitive, he chose the wilderness. Worn out by these thoughts and anxieties, he did not survive long, but fell into a most difficult illness. For he was so gripped by a constriction of the throat and a change of mind <note>Likely referring to madness or a loss of mental faculty.</note> that all those things which were accustomed to provide a cure for such a disease were of no use to him at all; indeed, they seemed contrary by the judgment of God. 

Wherefore at last, in desperation, the physicians—since the sickness would by no means cease with the medicines brought, and the king could receive nothing—ordered that he be given whatever he wanted, giving him up in despair of his health. Finally, after he had ordered his mother-in-law Alexandra and his sons born of Mariamne to be killed, and having appointed Archelaus—his son born of a concubine—as his successor, this man, unrestrained by any justice and most unhappy in the judgment of all, at Sebaste this...

**On Agrippina and Pompeia Folio 48**

...she was deprived of it. She, being indignant and provoked with a woman’s fury, threatened that she would snatch away from him <note>Nero</note> the very power she had secured for him. Terrified by these threats, and knowing her to be all too watchful, and—due to the memory of her father Germanicus <note>A beloved Roman general and Agrippina's father</note>—full of the support of friends, Nero tried to secretly kill her three times with poison. But the woman, through her vigilance, avoided the attempts by using antidotes. Finally, when she had escaped the other snares he had set for her death, Nero understood he must act with a more cautious deception. A response was given to him at Misenum by Anicetus, the commander of the fleet and his tutor since childhood, who suggested that a fragile ship could be constructed; if Agrippina were taken aboard, she might perish at sea without suspecting a plot. Since this pleased Nero, he received her as she was coming from Antium, feigning repentance for past hatreds with a false display of filial affection. He took her in his arms and escorted her to her house with great reverence. From there, she boarded the ship prepared for her destruction to go to dinner, accompanied by Creperius Gallus and Aceronia, her freedwoman. While they were sailing through the night, a signal was given to the conspirators, and the roof of the ship, heavy with much lead, fell and crushed Creperius. Then, while the sailors were trying to tilt the ship to its side in the calm sea to capsize it, Aceronia was killed by oars while calling for help for the Empress. But Agrippina, though her shoulder was struck and wounded, finally threw herself into the sea and was rescued by coastal bystanders and brought to the Lucrine Lake and her own villa. From there, she sent word to Nero via her freedman Agerinus that she had escaped. Nero ordered the man to be detained as if he had come to plot against the Emperor’s life. Then Anicetus, Herculeus (a captain), and Obaritus (a naval centurion) were sent to finish her off entirely. When the house was surrounded by Anicetus and her little maidservant—her only companion—had fled, the ministers of death entered. First, Herculeus struck her with a club. Then, when she saw the <term>centurion</term> <note>A professional officer of the Roman army</note> drawing his sword for her death, she bared her belly and cried out that they should **"strike the womb!"** <note>original: "ventrem ferirent"—a famous defiant gesture, suggesting the womb that bore such a monstrous son should be the first to be destroyed.</note> And thus she was killed and cremated that same night with a cheap funeral service and covered with earth. Others claim that Nero inspected her body after the murder and some members he criticized, others he praised, before she was finally buried.

**¶ On Pompeia, the wife of Seneca. Chapter 68.**

**P**ompeia Paulina, the renowned wife of Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the eminent philosopher and orator, was of the Roman nation. Although we lack certain knowledge of her family, she flourished in the fifty-second year after the birth of our Lord Christ, providing the whole world with the best example of most pious marital love toward her husband Seneca. Now, this most celebrated and excellent old man, Seneca, had been accused before Nero as if he were a participant and accomplice in the <term>Pisonian conspiracy</term> <note>A plot led by Gaius Calpurnius Piso to overthrow Nero in 65 AD.</note>. Under this pretext—but primarily because of an innate hatred for his virtues—a way was opened by Nero himself to vent his cruelty upon Seneca. It is thought by some that this was done at the prompting of Poppaea <note>Nero’s wife</note> and Tigellinus (the only ones who enjoyed the Emperor's trust). Thus, a centurion was sent to Seneca to command that he choose whatever death he wished for himself. When Paulina saw that he was girding himself for this execution, she set aside her husband's consolations and, aided by the charms with which he had encouraged her, and moved by the impulse of her most chaste love, she determined to meet death—and that specific kind of death—bravely alongside her most beloved husband. She resolved that as an honorable life had held them together, so a single death should dissolve them together. And so, undaunted, she entered the warm water; and in that same hour, she opened her veins with her husband to pour out her spirit by order of the prince, who felt no [malice toward her...]

¶ **Concerning Saint Petronilla, virgin and daughter of the divine Apostle Peter. Chapter 70.**

Petronilla, that holy virgin and daughter of the divine Peter, the prince of the apostles, is a figure we have rightly judged worthy to present here before other illustrious Christian women. She stands as the primary glory of Christian virginity, for from her extraordinary radiance, much of her renowned splendor has been added to our sacred rites. **Concerning Saint Martha**

...I shall be made whole. When she had finally touched him from behind, and he had turned and

### Concerning Saint Martha and Mary Magdalene

...from her decaying flesh, worms often flowed <note>original: "putrefacta carne sua... vermes effluerent"</note>. With tree branches spread upon the ground and a stone placed under her head for a pillow, she would lie down to rest. She was diligently focused on her prayers, through which she would bend her knees a hundred times during the day and just as many times during the night, according to her custom. She was distinguished by her faith, hope, and charity, and the brilliance of the other virtues. Her table was very often shared with pilgrims and guests as was her habit. Whenever she ceased her divine exhortations, she remained vigilant with frequent works of her hands. Furthermore, the words which she brought forth in her preaching were confirmed by the most exquisite miracles.

Later, while this distinguished apostle of Christ was curing many sick people at Avignon, a certain young man who had perished, overwhelmed by the waters of the Rhone River, was brought to her to be raised from the dead. Seeing him, she was moved, and (with everyone standing by) she prostrated herself on the ground in the shape of a cross and prayed to the Lord with these words: "O Adonai <note>A Hebrew title for God meaning 'My Lord'</note>, Christ Jesus my master, you who through your holy and ineffable mercy raised my brother Lazarus, your beloved, from the dead; you who hold the keys of death and of life; you who command death and it flees; you who call the dead and they rise again. Look down, my most dear guest <note>Martha is often called Christ's 'hostess' or 'guest' because she received Him into her home in Bethany</note>, and look, I pray, upon the faith and the prayers of those surrounding us, and revive this boy, so that those seeing your great powers may believe in you, the one and living Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever, Amen." 

And taking the hand of the dead man, she said: "In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, boy, I say to you, arise!" And with these words said, he immediately rose up alive and unharmed, and he received baptism. 

She knew of her own death long in advance. Finally, when she had been burning with fevers for nearly a year, in the middle of the night before the day of her passing, Christ came to her in a festive manner and said: "Come, my beloved hostess, come and exit the prison of the flesh, and pass into the palace of heaven, for you have received me so often. I will not take away from you the grace of comforting the disconsolate, which I have granted to you by a singular privilege, even after your 'falling asleep' <note>A traditional term for the death of a saint</note>. And those who come devoutly to your tomb seeking the grace of your help, I will undoubtedly hear." 

Afterward, Martha commanded the Passion of the Lord—which she had with her written in Hebrew—to be read to her. While it was being read for the second time, and the reader reached the words: "Father, into your hands I commend my spirit," she surrendered her worthy soul to the Lord. This happened when the thirteenth lustrum <note>A 'lustrum' is a period of five years; she was 65 years old</note> of her whole life was completed, on the sixth day of the week, at the ninth hour—the same hour Christ redeemed the world—on the fourth day before the Kalends of August <note>July 29th</note>, on which day her anniversary is most devoutly celebrated. Great indeed was the brilliance of this woman, to have earned the right to see and touch Him who existed before time, and through whom time was made, who came in the fullness of time, and who had the power to lay down his life and to take it up again. 

There was, nonetheless, another Martha who was a martyr, the wife of Marius, who under the Emperor Claudius obtained the palm of martyrdom along with her sons Audifax and Abachum and her husband.

**About Saint Mary Magdalene**

...ed. For **symbol** <note>original: "symbolum." While we now use "symbol" for signs, in a religious context, it refers specifically to the Creed—the summary of Christian beliefs.</note> in Greek can be called a **contribution** <note>original: "collatio." This refers to the tradition that each of the twelve Apostles contributed one clause to the Creed.</note> or a **sign** <note>original: "indicium."</note> among the Latins. This is because it is what several people bring together into one. Indeed, this is what the apostles did: by gathering into one these words, they collected what each one believed. It is called a **sign** or **token** so that from it one might recognize who was truly preaching Christ according to his established rules. Therefore, when the apostles and all the faithful were about to depart to begin their preaching, they established this sign of their shared mind and faith. Specifically, each one was first to keep the **Creed of faith** <term>Symbolum fidei: The Apostles' Creed, used as a litmus test for orthodoxy.</term> in his heart, and then preach it in his teachings unceasingly and most excellently.
