**Of Saint Sabina**

Sabina, an illustrious and most famous woman among matrons and martyrs, flourished and was celebrated in Rome at the same time as the previously mentioned divine Serapia. She shone brightly with the most distinguished titles and the highest reputation for virtue. Born to a noble and powerful Roman family, she was the daughter of Herod the Metallarius <note>original: "metallarium". This title likely refers to a high-ranking official overseeing the imperial mines or the mint.</note>. Her father joined her—while she was still a young girl of extraordinary beauty and endowed with countless riches—in marriage to the noble youth Valentinus, a patrician. Sabina loved him most devotedly as long as he lived. But when that same and most loving husband reached his final day and died, and she had carried out his burial with royal honors, <margin>Note this beautifully</margin> she was instructed and baptized in the Christian faith by Pope Sixtus <note>Pope Sixtus I, who led the church in the early 2nd century.</note>. Taking up a vow of widowhood as a celestial spirit of modesty, she became an object of admiration to everyone. First, she began to devote herself to thrift and sobriety and to cling to divine fasts; then she applied herself with great effort to sacred meditations and prayers day and night, keeping watch and rejecting superfluous thoughts as an impediment to her holy purpose. 

When she had received the aforementioned most holy Serapia—a traveling pilgrim and most modest woman—into her home with all joy, she saw that Serapia's mind was entirely devoted to divine worship. From then on, Sabina regarded her as a sister and a mother in the heat of her faith. She not only provided for Serapia’s needs from her own resources but, by Serapia's encouragement and guidance, she was kindled to all works of piety, so that she might receive and cherish all of Christ's poor as if they were her own children, always with a cheerful face. Furthermore, she was so warmed and inflamed by the teachings of the Apostle James regarding the endurance of the world's tribulations and passions with an even mind, that she herself began to long for those same trials with the greatest joy. For she often kept that teaching of the Blessed James in her mouth, saying: "What joy we ought to consider it, dearest sister, when we fall into various temptations." <note>A reference to James 1:2: "Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds."</note> Wherefore, even when she was later provoked by blows and many injuries, she nevertheless remained most constant in that same strength of soul; nor did she ever permit herself to be angry at anyone on earth, so persevering was she in the love of Christ.

Finally, after she had gathered the most holy remains of the aforementioned Serapia, celebrated them according to Christian custom, and placed them in her own tomb—which she had built for herself with the greatest adornment—she was immediately accused before the Prefect Elpidius of being a Christian and of giving the martyr Serapia a proper burial. When he furiously ordered her to be presented to him in the <term>praetorium</term> <note>The headquarters or judgment hall of a Roman magistrate.</note>, he immediately questioned her: "Are you Sabina, formerly the wife of Valentinus of most illustrious memory, and the daughter of Herod the Metallarius, that excellent man?" Sabina replied: "I am." And he said: "Why have you forgotten your lineage and preferred to associate yourself with the most impure Christians, whose life is death? Why do you not rather worship the gods whom your ancestors and our <term>Augusti</term> <note>The title used for the Roman Emperors.</note> adored?" To this she replied: "I give thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ, who has deigned to free me, a sinner, through our holy Pope Sixtus and his holy servant Serapia, from much filth and the power of demons. I will no longer be deceived by errors, for I perceive that you are erring by adoring demons, those most wicked deceivers." 

Then the prefect said: "So then, is it not only us, but also our most sacred Emperors who are deceived, adoring demons and not gods?" Sabina replied: "Would that they would adore the God who made all things, by whose nod all things visible and invisible are ruled, and not your foolish or senseless idols of demons; for you and your Emperors are destined to burn together with them." The Prefect said: "By the gods, unless you sacrifice, I will pronounce a capital sentence against you without any hesitation!" Sabina then said: "I will never sacrifice to demons, because I am a Christian; I hold Christ for the true God, and I am his handmaid and worshipper. Although you may command all kinds of torments to be brought against me and threaten me with a cruel death, you will never succeed in making me deny the faith of my Lord Jesus Christ (through whom the heavens are opened to me) for the sake of the short time of this life." Then the Prefect, on the Aventine Hill <note>One of the seven hills of Rome, where the Basilica of Santa Sabina stands today.</note>, pronounced the sacrilegious sentence, saying: "We decree that Sabina, although a Roman patrician, for blaspheming our gods and not obeying the Emperors, be struck with the sword. And all her properties [registered] with public titles..."

# Concerning Saint Cecilia

Her parents <insert>and because of her excellent education in good literature</insert> began to rejoice greatly. Yet she herself, already a most wise young woman, knew that youth often endures many battles of the flesh. **Concerning Saint Cecilia Folio 62.**

She entreated her servants, asking that they might assist her with their prayers and commend her purity to the Lord. But when these things were done, the night came in which she moved into the secret silence of the bedchamber with her husband. And as she was of a famous and lively spirit, and eloquent in her speech, she addressed her husband with these most sweet words: "O sweetest and most beloved young man, there is a secret that I may confess to you, if only you will swear to guard it with total devotion." Valerian swore to her that he would reveal it for no reason and out of no necessity.

Then she said: "I have an angel of God as a lover, who guards my body with exceeding zeal. If he senses even slightly that you touch me with a polluted love <note>The Latin 'poluto amore' refers to lustful or non-consecrated sexual desire</note>, he will immediately rouse his fury against you, and you will lose the flower of your most gracious youth. But if he knows that you love me with a sincere and immaculate love, and that you preserve my virginity whole and unsullied, he will love you just as he loves me, and he will show you his grace."

Moved by her most sweet and wise words, and by her every gesture, her husband Valerian immediately said: "You speak rightly, piously, and holily. But if you wish me to believe your words, show me this angel. And if I prove it is truly an angel of the Lord, I will do exactly as you urge. But if you love another man, I will kill both you and him."

Then the blessed Cecilia said: "If you permit yourself to agree to my counsel, and promise to be purified in the eternal fountain <note>A reference to the 'fons perennis' or the waters of baptism</note>, and believe that there is one God in heaven, living and true, then you shall be able to see him." 

Valerian said to her: "And who will there be to purify me, so that I may see the angel?"

Cecilia answered him: "There is an elder who knows how to purify men so they may deserve to see angels."

Valerian said to her: "And where shall I find this old man?"

Cecilia answered: "Go to the third mile-marker from the city on the road called the Appian Way. There you will find several poor people asking for help from those passing by, for whom I have always had great care. Give them my blessing in my name, saying: 'Cecilia sent me to you, so that you might show me the holy elder Urban, for I have secret matters to bring to him.' When you see him, you will indicate what has been discussed between us. Once he has purified you and clothed you in the whitest garments, come back. As soon as you enter this chamber dressed in them, you will find the holy angel who is also the lover of your deeds, and he will grant you everything you ask of him."

Then Valerian, going forth, found everything exactly as Cecilia had predicted. He reported Cecilia’s words to Urban, who was hiding among the tombs <note>original: 'sepulchris'; likely a reference to the catacombs where early Christians hid from Roman persecution</note>. Urban was cheered with great joy; prostrating himself on his knees with hands outspread, he said with tears: "Lord Jesus Christ, Good Shepherd, sower of chaste counsel, receive the fruit of the seeds which you sowed in your servant Cecilia. Lord Jesus Christ, Good Shepherd, your servant Cecilia has served you like a busy bee <note>original: 'apis argumentosa'</note>. For the husband whom she received like a fierce lion, she has directed to you like a most gentle lamb. He would not have come here unless he had believed. Open therefore, my Lord, the door of his heart with your grace, so that recognizing you as his creator, he may renounce the devil and his idols."

As the holy bishop was praying these and similar things, suddenly an elder appeared before them, clothed in snow-white garments, holding in his hand a book <note>original: 'titulum'; here meaning a scroll or codex</note> written with golden letters. Seeing him, Valerian was immediately seized with great trembling and fell down as if dead. The elder, lifting him up with gentle words, said: "Son, take and read the text of this book, and believe, so that you may deserve to see the holy angel whom your bride Cecilia promised you."

The words of the scripture were these: *One Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is over all, and in all of us.* <note>A quote from the New Testament, Ephesians 4:5-6</note>

The elder, questioning Valerian, asked whether he still hesitated at this. Valerian cried out with a loud voice, saying: "Truly there is nothing under heaven more true that can be believed!" 

Then the pontiff <term>pontifer (Bishop/Pope)</term> Urban, having taught Valerian the whole rule of faith, baptized him and sent him back joyful to Cecilia, clothed in white garments. When Valerian returned, he found Cecilia praying inside the chamber, and standing next to her was an angel of the Lord, having wings with shining feathers and radiating a flaming appearance, and carrying two golden crowns. He gave one of these to Cecilia and the other to Valerian, saying: "Keep these crowns with a clean heart and in—"

# **Concerning Saint Cecilia**

"...keep them with an unspotted body, for I have brought them to you from the paradise of God. And this shall be a sign to you: that they can by no means be seen by others, except by those in whom chastity has been as pleasing as it has been proven to be in you. And therefore, Valerian, because you have consented to the counsel of chastity, Christ the Son of God has sent me to you, so that you may suggest whatever petition you wish." Then Valerian immediately and earnestly prayed that his brother Tiburtius might likewise be saved, for he might perhaps be somewhat stubborn <note>original: "duriusculus," implying he was a bit hard-hearted or difficult to persuade</note> in believing. At length, he too was won over by the arguments of the virgin Cecilia and received holy baptism. A short time later, together with his brother Valerian, he attained the palm of martyrdom. After this, Almachius, the prefect of the city, began to compel Cecilia to offer incense to the gods according to custom. But she said to the officers: "Hear me, brothers: To me, indeed, it is most glorious and greatly to be desired to endure all torments for the name and confession of Christ. But I grieve enough for your youth, which you spend without care, doing whatever is commanded of you by an unjust judge." 

Then they, weeping, begged her not to lose such singular beauty. To them she replied: "This is not to lose youth, but to exchange it: to give mud and receive gold; to give a small and vile dwelling and receive a vast home, built of precious stones." As the virgin continued in this way to discourse upon the kingdom of God and the piety of Christ, more than four hundred of both sexes <note>original: "promisui sexus," referring to a mixed group of men and women</note> believed and were washed in the holy font of baptism. 

Afterwards, when the prefect Almachius again questioned Cecilia as to her status or religion, she stood her ground in that place where even princes were accustomed to tremble. Though the ignorant multitude raised a din of discordant cries and threats, the virgin’s constancy was not broken in the least. Rather, mindful of her salvation and inflamed by the fire of faith in Christ, with a most steadfast heart and a sharp gaze, she was not terrified in any part and answered the prefect wisely and shrewdly that she could in no way agree with him. To her he said: "Choose one of two things: either sacrifice or deny that you are a Christian." 

Smiling, Cecilia said: "O judge, confused by necessity, who orders that I deny I am innocent so that he himself may make me guilty. If you wish to condemn, why do you urge me to deny? If you wish to acquit, why do you wish to inquire?" 

"Lay aside your boldness," said Almachius, "and worship the gods." 

Cecilia replied: "I know not where you have lost your eyes. For those whom you call gods, I and all who have healthy eyes see to be stones, and bronze, and lead." And thus, she ignominiously rejected the judge who wished to calm her with such a lying demonstration of gods, nor could she be induced by any commands to do what was ordered. 

Then, violently enraged, he ordered her to be led back to her house and there to be burned in the heat of the baths. When she had been shut in the heat of the bath for a whole day and night, she remained in perfect health, as if in a cool and rose-filled place, so that not even one part of her limbs failed, even by a sign of sweat. When Almachius heard this, he sent someone to behead her there. When the executioner <term>spiculator: a Roman military term for an executioner or scout</term> had struck her three times and was unable to cut off her head, he left her there half-dead. During the three days that Cecilia survived, she did not cease to encourage the souls of all the women whom she had nurtured in the Catholic faith; to them she divided everything she possessed. 

Then the holy pontiff Urban took away her body and, with all his fellow bishops weeping, placed it most devoutly [in the tomb]. He turned her house (as she had ordered) into a church and consecrated it, where God's blessings abound in memory of the most famous virgin Cecilia. This most excellent virgin suffered <note>in this context, "suffered" refers to her martyrdom</note> on the tenth day before the Calends of December <note>November 22nd</note>, on which day her anniversary is celebrated with worthy honor by all.

**Concerning Saint Martina**                                        **Folio 63**

**¶ Concerning Saint Martina, virgin and martyr. Chapter 84.**

Martina, a Roman virgin and martyr, lived while the prince Severus <note>original: "seuereo pncipe," likely referring to Emperor Alexander Severus (r. 222–235 AD), though some traditions place her under Septimius Severus.</note> was still ruling the Romans. It was in the same year that the aforementioned most holy Cecilia also steadfastly bore her martyrdom for Christ in Rome. Among other Roman women, she was a woman illustrious in her time for her power, lineage, character, and religion. Indeed, many noble deeds of hers are to be written by us in this place. This renowned virgin was the daughter of an exceptionally powerful father (though his name and family are unknown to us) and of a most Christian and pious man. For this reason, we say that she shone more nobly and worthily than the life of the aforementioned virgin Cecilia in this regard alone. Her father was a Roman patrician <term>Patrician: A member of the high-ranking hereditary ruling class in ancient Rome.</term> and three times a Consul. Being foremost a most devoted Christian, he maintained perfect charity toward God and the highest integrity toward men. To demonstrate that he walked without blame in all the commandments and justifications of the Lord, and being most ready for all service to the servants of God, he ensured that this only daughter—as a future bride of Christ—was excellently educated in character, faith, and other justifications, as well as in good letters. <note>The term "good letters" refers to a classical liberal arts education.</note> Being outstandingly learned in these teachings, she soon turned herself toward God. Although she moved among the great crowds of men, she lived as if she were without flesh, showing that she ignored all worldly things. Offering herself to the Lord, she chose with a great soul to place little value on the succession of children or offspring. Then, as she was no moderately learned in good literature, she applied herself with the greatest effort to learning the Sacred Scriptures. And so that she might be able to cut away from herself all worldly anxieties and the source of her faults with the "evangelical sickle," she read through the Gospels of Christ with great fervor, and she stored their teachings in the cellar of her breast according to her capacity. And since she was quite wealthy, she did not seek high things or trust in the uncertainty of her riches, but seemed to hope in the living God. Knowing that mercy was preferred over sacrifices by Christ—as the Lord says in the Gospel: "Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy" <note>original Latin: "Beati misericordes: quoniā ipsi misericordiā cōsequētur," a quote from Matthew 5:7.</note>—she turned herself to works of piety and humility. To grasp that which is the good life, she took care while she lived to store up future treasure for herself through the generous giving of alms. And as is fitting for holy virgins who promise chastity, she displayed the greatest modesty in all her works, not only in words but through good justice and conduct. All her speech was directed toward the destruction of idolatry; for this reason, she was constantly inflamed with a most steadfast heart to fight off enemies and repel their spears in every way. At that time, by the order of the prince Severus, all were being forced to the worship of the gods. But the virgin Martina, despising the prince's command, worshiped Christ in a certain temple. For this reason, she was seized by the pagans and led before Caesar to sacrifice to the gods. But she, with a cheerful face, said to the Emperor: "Enter the temple of Apollo yourself, and let all who are lovers of it see how my sincere, untainted, merciful, and holy almighty God receives my immaculate and most pure sacrifices." Caesar therefore commanded that what was done by Martina be watched with the greatest diligence. But as she prayed, a great earthquake suddenly occurred, so that the whole city was shaken, and the idol of Apollo...

<meta>This page continues the hagiography (biography of a saint) of Saint Martina, a third-century Roman martyr. The previous context would have established her arrest and refusal to sacrifice to Roman gods.</meta>

# **On Saint Martina and Blandina Folio 64**

When a most savage lion was ordered to be released to tear her apart, by a divine gift <note>original: "divino munere"</note> it not only did not harm her, but rather, having cast itself down at her feet, it appeared to worship her. Then, making an attack on the Emperor's kinsman <note>original: "parentem"; this refers to a high-ranking relative or official close to the Emperor</note>, it immediately tore him to pieces. **Concerning Saint Reparata, virgin and martyr. Chapter 88.**

[A woodcut illustration of a female saint, likely Saint Reparata, standing in a landscape. She wears a long robe and a mantle, with a halo around her head. She is holding a closed book in both hands.]

**R**eparata, a most beautiful virgin, endured a glorious martyrdom for Christ in the city of Caesarea in Palestine during that most dangerous persecution under Decius <note>The Decian persecution (c. 250 AD) was one of the first empire-wide efforts to suppress Christianity throughout the Roman Empire.</note>. She drew her origin from the most noble of parents and an even nobler lineage in that city, though their names remain unknown. Indeed, as a young girl, she was remarkably radiant in her physical beauty, her character, her integrity, and her incredible faith. Because of the remarkable sincerity of her mind and body, her constancy, and her great spirit in the presence of the Emperor Decius, the Church has honorably judged that this twelve-year-old girl should be placed among the holy and famous women. 

For when she was twelve years old, she was accused before the Emperor Decius (who was then present in that city) because it was said that she spent day and night in fasts and prayers according to the Christian custom. It was reported that at every moment and in every action she pressed the sign of the cross onto her forehead, and that she denied and despised the gods and goddesses, worshiping Christ who was crucified by the Jews and continually offering sacrifices to Him. She was immediately presented to Decius. 

After he had for some time admired her beauty, her shapely form, her simple attire <note>original: "habitum nulla varietate distinctum," suggesting she wore plain, unadorned clothing rather than the finery expected of her noble status</note>, and her integrity and girlish gravity, he first addressed her with flattering words, saying: "O little child, worthy of every honor! How blessed are the breasts that nursed you, and happy is the mother who bore you. I have learned that since you are born of noble stock, you could join yourself in a most illustrious marriage—if only you will sacrifice to the immortal gods so that you may live."

But she, standing before the prince, her face flushed with a crimson color <note>original: "purpureo respersa colore," literally "sprinkled with purple," a poetic way of saying she blushed with modest dignity</note>, raised her eyes slightly toward the prince and then cast them back down to the ground. With a humble voice but a high spirit, she said: "It is enough for me, O prince, to have lived twelve years if I may deserve to reach that life which knows no end. Cease, I beg you, my Emperor, from speaking such things. For I have indeed always sacrificed, and I do sacrifice, the <term>sacrifice of praise</term> <note>original: "hostiam laudis." A liturgical term referring to prayer and worship rather than a physical offering of animals.</note> to my Lord Jesus Christ."

To which Decius replied: "How many torments await you unless you sacrifice?"

She answered: "I do not fear the punishments which you promise to inflict upon me. For I have decided it is better to die than to worship your gods; therefore, do as you please."

First, lead was brought out, melted in a pot so that it might be poured over Reparata. But as she prayed, it became so cold that the virgin suffered no injury from it at all. Then Decius said: "Bring boiling vinegar, so that the tongue which named Christ may be cooked immediately!" And as he poured it into the delicate mouth of the little girl, she said with a most constant heart: "I drink your vinegar, O Caesar, as if it were a honeycomb. And in this, I am comforted in my Lord Jesus Christ. Indeed, your torments which you order to be brought upon me provide not pain, but refreshment."

When the Emperor saw that the little girl was not shaken by any torments, or by threats, or by the discordant shouts of the unskilled multitude, he said: "O, the hardness of this girl! How..."

Her eunuchs, Protus and Hyacinth, because they would in no way sacrifice to idols and would not yield even after the harshest tortures of the lash, were ordered to be beheaded on the third day before the <term>Ides of September</term> <note>September 11th</note>. Their bodies were carried out and buried in the cemetery of Basilla on the Via Salaria.

# On Saints Rufina and Secunda and Saint Sophia

Then, shut in a filthy and foul place, smoke from burning dung <note>original: "fumus stercorum." The use of foul-smelling smoke was a common torture intended to degrade as well as suffocate the prisoner.</note> was cast in by order of the judge so that they might be tortured by the stench and rot; but by divine power, that smoke appeared to them like the most fragrant incense, and the darkness seemed like the brightest light of midday.

Finally, they were thrown naked into the Tiber <note>The primary river flowing through the city of Rome.</note> with a stone tied to their necks; while they had remained submerged for nearly half an hour, they soon appeared to all clothed in dry garments, singing praises to the Lord.

When this was reported to the judge, Count Arcesilaus ordered them to be led to an island ten miles from the city; there, although they were weak in their sex, they were nonetheless most strong in virtue <note>original: "virtute." This reflects a common theme in early Christian literature where the spiritual strength of female martyrs is portrayed as overcoming their supposed physical or social "weakness."</note>.

Although bonds held their hands—which were dirty from the filth of the prison—behind their backs, their eyes, which the torturers were unable to bind, were raised toward heaven. With tears, they prayed to the Lord in this manner: “O almighty Father of your blessed and beloved Jesus Christ, through whom we have received the knowledge of you...”

# **->About Queen Zenobia<-**

With the Emperor Valerian <note>Roman Emperor from 253–260 AD; he is famous for being the only emperor captured as a prisoner of war.</note> condemned to a shameful slavery and his effeminate son Gallienus languishing in sluggishness, Zenobia—not unmindful of her former hardiness—decided to conceal her **beauty** behind armor and serve as a soldier alongside her husband. Not only this: but it is even believed that she summarized these histories into short **Epitomes** <note>original: "Epithomas"; these are condensed versions or summaries of longer historical works</note>. Because of her heritage, she knew the Egyptian language, and she used it along with her knowledge of Syriac. She also commanded her sons to speak Latin. Why say more? She was indeed so powerful that after Gallienus, Aureolus, and Claudius Augustus were removed, and Aurelian—a man of complete integrity—succeeded to the leadership, she drew upon herself the task of avenging the shame of the Roman name and pursuing great glory. 

For after the Marcomannic war was settled and affairs at Rome were composed, Aurelian undertook an expedition against Zenobia with all care. After many notable wars conducted against barbarian nations on his way, he finally arrived with his legions not far from the city of **Emesa** <note>Modern-day Homs in Syria</note>. Zenobia, having overlooked nothing, had advanced with her army alongside a certain Zaba, whom she had taken as a partner in war. There, a fierce battle for supreme power was fought for a long time between Aurelian and this Zenobia. Finally, when Roman valor appeared superior, Zenobia used flight and retreated to **Palmyra** with her people. 

She was immediately besieged there by the victor. After she had defended the city with wonderful skill for some time, refusing to hear any talk of betrayal or surrender, she was reduced to a great lack of necessary supplies. At this point, since the Palmyrenes were unable to resist the strength of Aurelian's forces—and the Armenians and Saracens coming to Zenobia's aid had been intercepted and defeated by him—the city was captured by the Romans through force of arms. 

From there, as Zenobia fled toward the Persians on **dromedaries** <note>Swift, one-humped camels</note> with her sons, she was followed and captured by Aurelian's soldiers. She was presented alive to Aurelian with her sons. Because of this, Aurelian boasted no differently than if he had overcome a primary leader and the fiercest enemy of the Republic. He reserved her for his **Triumph** <note>A formal victory parade through the streets of Rome granted to successful generals</note> and led her to Rome with her sons. 

Then a triumph was celebrated by Aurelian, featuring the admirable spectacle of Zenobia. In this parade, among other remarkable and noteworthy things, he led the chariot which Zenobia had ordered to be built for herself out of gold and the most precious gems; she had hoped to come to Rome not as a captive, but as the mistress of the world and a victor, possessing the Roman Empire—and in this very chariot she proceeded with her sons. She herself was bound with golden chains on her neck, hands, and feet, and was so burdened with a crown, royal robes, pearls, and precious stones that, although she was of inexhaustible strength, she often stopped, exhausted by the weight. 

Truly, after the triumph was completed, they say she grew old among the Roman matrons in a private condition with her sons, her treasure and furniture having been used up. A possession at **Tibur** <note>Modern Tivoli, Italy</note> was granted to her by the Senate, which for a long time afterward was named "Zenobia" after her; it is not far from the Palace of the Divine Hadrian which is in that place, and which the inhabitants called **Conche**. According to Pliny in the fifth book of his *Natural History*, the royal city of this woman was called Palmyra, located in **Assyria** <note>The author uses Assyria here, though Palmyra is typically associated with Syria</note>. It was distant from Damascus, as he reports, by twenty-seven miles. To this day (as they say), it has been completely leveled.

**Concerning Saint Agnes**

It is not to be doubted that all of Scripture has commemorated this holy virgin <note>original: "sancta virgine"</note>, as when it said: "These are they who came from the warmth of the house of Rechab" <note>This refers to the Rechabites from the Book of Jeremiah, traditionally seen as symbols of religious fervor and asceticism</note>, and as our Lord says in the Gospel: "I have come to send fire upon the earth, and what do I wish but that it burn?" <note>A reference to Luke 12:49, connecting Agnes's spiritual passion to the "fire" of Christ</note>. For this reason, as the blessed Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), a Bishop of Milan and one of the most influential figures in the early Church, who wrote extensively in praise of Agnes's virginity</note> reports: "Her childhood was counted in years, but the maturity of her mind was immense; she was a young girl in body, but gray-haired in spirit; beautiful in face, but more beautiful in faith."

Indeed, so great was her faith from her very childhood that she believed without doubt that God would be powerful enough to fulfill those things He had promised, and for that reason in her hope <insert>her...</insert> <note>The text cuts off here at "spe su-," likely intended to be "spe sua" or "in her hope..."</note>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the martyrdom of Saint Agnes, a 4th-century Roman girl who was executed during the Diocletianic Persecution. This section describes her final prayer, her execution, and a miraculous vision granted to her parents after her death.</meta>

->### **Concerning Saint Agnes FOLIO 75**<-

"What I hoped for, I now hold; what I desired, I now embrace with my hands. You, therefore, I confess with my lips; you I desire with my heart and my whole being <note>original: "totis visceribus," literally "with all my guts," a common medieval expression for deep, internal devotion</note>. Behold, I come to you, the living and true Lord, who lives and reigns with our Lord Jesus Christ your Son and the Holy Spirit, through all the ages of ages. Amen."

Scarcely had the virgin Agnes spoken these words when the fire <note>Agnes had been sentenced to be burned, but the flames miraculously divided and did not harm her</note> was so completely extinguished that not even the warmth of a blaze remained. Then **Aspasius** <term>vicarius (deputy)</term>—fearing a riot of the people—ordered a sword to be plunged into the holy virgin’s throat. And by this rosy end, drenched in the redness of her own precious blood, Christ consecrated her to himself as both bride and martyr.

Because of this, Agnes—in the thirteenth year of her age, on the **twelfth day before the Kalends of February** <note>January 21st, which remains her feast day in the liturgical calendar</note>—lost death and found life, for she loved only the Author of life. At the very hour that Saint Agnes entered the heavens, there was such a great earthquake—despite the sky being perfectly clear—and such storms, flashes of lightning, and thunder, that the greatest part of the insane mob perished.

She was buried by her parents within the city with the weeping of all, and with such mourning as had never before been practiced by the Romans out of piety. While her parents were keeping watch at her tomb with constant vigils through the night, after the eighth day of her martyrdom, in the silence of the middle of the night, they saw an **army of virgins**. They were all dressed in <term>cyclas (robes)</term> woven with gold, passing by in a great light. Among them they saw the most blessed Agnes shining in similar clothing, and at her right hand was a **Lamb** <note>The Latin for lamb is "agnus," a wordplay on her name "Agnes" that became her primary symbol in Christian art</note> whiter than snow. When the parents saw this, they were struck with great amazement. 

The most blessed Agnes, with a cheerful face and a gentle voice, said to them:

"Do not mourn or weep for me as if I were sleeping, after the manner of the pagans. Rather, rejoice with me, because I am not at all dead as you suppose. But if you ever loved me, if you follow my instructions <note>original: "monitis," advice or warnings</note>, do not seem to envy my great glory. For I have here many mothers, sisters, kinswomen, and companions whom I did not know before, with whom I have certainly received the single palm of virginity. Perhaps you pity me because I left the world through so many and such great torments? I rather grieve for your fates, whom the cancer of this world still encloses; whom every day—as if fighting in a battle line—now anger, now greed, now lust, and the various incentives of vices drag toward ruin. But as for me, whose departure was accompanied by a crowd of angels, and whom Christ himself came to meet: rejoice for me! You should instead be burdened for yourselves, who remain longer in this tabernacle of death; for as long as you dwell here, you will be pilgrims away from the Lord. Therefore rejoice with me and again be glad, because no darkness shall take hold of me; rather, migrating from darkness to light, I have received the reward of completed martyrdom as you begin the fire of the path of faith."

**Concerning Saint Emerentiana and Saint Eulalia**

She also possessed noble distinctions of birth and virginity; and although she was not yet a <term>Christian</term> <note>original: "christiana"; meaning she had not yet received formal baptism</note> but was only a <term>catechumen</term> <note>A "catechumen" is a person receiving instruction in the Christian faith in preparation for baptism.</note>, I shall relate only a single, yet most praiseworthy, deed from her life. This will be enough to understand her whole character and to grant her the honor her merit deserves. It happened that the parents of Agnes were burying her most sacred body in a funeral procession according to the Roman custom, followed by a great multitude of her parents, kin, and other friends. While they were doing this, many of the heathens—driven by hatred and enmity toward the Christians—rushed into their midst. They treated them no differently than the most senseless enemies of the Roman Republic. With insolent audacity, they began to throw insults, many reproaches, and even stones at the parents and others who were honoring the holy funeral rites, intending to disrupt the burial service.

While the virgin Emerentiana stood among those mourning, she was immediately moved by a pressing sense of piety. In her great sadness, she forgot her sex, her modesty, and even the mournful garments with which she was covered, for she could not endure what was happening. Instead, she suddenly burst forth into the middle of the crowd and the discordant shouts of the ignorant multitude. With a steadfast spirit, the fire of faith, a bold countenance, and a stern face, she began to threaten them for daring so senselessly to disturb the faithful followers of Christ from their duty of piety. 

Because of this, the insane populace, rising against her in their usual way as if against a detestable race, began to shout out in a tumultuous rush, saying: "Why is this most wicked race not driven out of the city entirely? Let them be cast into the waves or surely crushed by stones!" Turning all their fury upon her, they began to pursue her with stones. But she, with her knees fixed to the earth at the tomb of the most blessed Agnes and her eyes raised to heaven, maintained an unconquered patience until death amidst the loud tumult of the people and the innumerable strikes and wounds from the stones. 

She even said that she was suffering lesser torments than she deserved. Hence, there is no doubt that this virgin Emerentiana was **baptized in her own blood** <note>The "Baptism of Blood" is a traditional Christian belief that those who suffer martyrdom for the faith before they can be baptized by water receive the full grace of the sacrament through their death.</note>, since she was seen to have endured death most excellently while standing firm in the defense of justice for the Lord. At the very hour when the virgin Emerentiana died for Christ, there were great flashes of lightning, thunder, and bolts of fire, because of which it is said a great multitude of the heathens perished. It is said this happened so that henceforth none of the heathens would presume to bring any further injuries upon the tombs of the saints. The parents of Agnes, coming by night with priests to the [tomb] of this holy virgin...

### ¶ Concerning Saint Leocadia of Seville, virgin and martyr. Chapter 98.

**L**eocadia, a virgin likewise of Seville <note>While the text calls her "hispalensi" (of Seville), it immediately identifies her as being from Toledo. Historically, Leocadia is the patron saint and most famous martyr of Toledo.</note> born from the most noble and ancient city of Toledo, lived during the same era as Eulalia. Through her burning faith and remarkable virtue, she provided a joyful example to her contemporaries and to those who came after her. She left behind a beautiful and eternal testimony of faith and constancy. So that her holy and shining name might gleam with special brilliance, we have thought it worthy to record a few details here for the sake of memory. 

When she proclaimed and stood firm in her identity as a most devoted Christian, she was seized in that city by the sacrilegious governor <term>Dacian|A Roman official notorious in medieval accounts for his ruthless execution of the Great Persecution in the Iberian Peninsula.</term> and was immediately cast and thrust into a most foul prison. She was wasted away for a long time by the harsh conditions of her imprisonment. Finally, when she heard of the hard, heavy, and immense tortures and torments suffered by the blessed virgin <note>Saint Eulalia of Mérida, another prominent Spanish martyr mentioned in the previous chapter.</note> Eulalia and the other martyrs, she fell to her knees in prayer. Persisting in her devotion, she surrendered her unpolluted spirit to Christ on the fifth day before the Ides of December <note>December 9th, her traditional feast day.</note>. On this day, her anniversary is solemnly celebrated by the faithful as one who kept her faith whole for God and His Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. We pray to be made sharers in her faith, charity, and perseverance.

# XXXI <note>Chapter 31</note>

## **Concerning Saint Christina**

<note>original: "mortis victricem tandem suscipiet celum"</note>
...at last heaven will receive the woman who has conquered death. In the eyes of myself and all those faithful to Christ, after this world is lost and after the death of this body, all things shall be healed. Indeed, I myself shall rejoice in the wholeness of my limbs, where life shall be troubled by no disease. 

Then, just as they were about to tear her limbs apart, Christina poured forth her prayer in these words: "O Lord Jesus Christ, who lives forever in heaven together with the Eternal Father and are never absent, I beseech you not to abandon me in the midst of this struggle <note>original: "agone"</note>, but stretch out your hand and extinguish this fire which has been prepared for me, so that my tyrannical father may not rejoice over me, your handmaid." 

Hardly had she finished these words when a flame burst forth and killed a thousand men. Then her father said: "Christina, I beseech you, tell me who taught you so many and such great evil arts?" <note>The word "maleficia" here refers to witchcraft or sorcery, which the Romans often accused Christians of practicing when they performed miracles.</note> She responded: "I have already told you that my father is Christ, who taught me to keep the truth and led me from the path of those who wander toward eternal grace." 

Filled with wrath and insane fury, Urbanus <note>Christina’s father, the Roman governor of Bolsena</note> shut her back up in prison, where, by the service of angels, she was not only fed but also cured of every wound. 

At about the silence of midnight, her father Urbanus sent men to drown the virgin Christina in nearby Lake Bolsena with a stone tied to her; but, freed by angelic protection, she was brought safely to the shore in an instant. Then she prayed to the Lord, saying: "Lord Jesus Christ, who does not abandon those who trust in your mercy, I beseech you now do not refuse to show your wonders in me, your handmaid, but command me to be reborn through baptism, so that I may be cleansed from every stain of the flesh and from the spirit of Satan." 

Straightaway a bright cloud descended from heaven and baptized her; and soon a voice followed, saying: "I am Jesus Christ whom you have confessed; I am here now because you called upon me, nor shall I ever abandon you until the course of your life is completed." 

That same night her father Urbanus, by the judgment of God, yielded to nature <note>A common euphemism for death</note>. After his death, a certain Dion, a most great persecutor of Christians, succeeded to his office. When he tried to force Christina to sacrifice to idols and she utterly refused to do so, he immediately ordered her to be thrown into a furnace heated with pitch, wax, and oil. 

But she, looking toward heaven with a joyful face, said: "I sing a hymn to you, and I glorify your holy name, Lord Jesus Christ, who has deemed me worthy to be reborn through the bath of regeneration <term>lauacruʒ generatiōis</term> <note>A theological term for baptism used in the New Testament (Titus 3:5).</note> and the renewal of your most holy name. For I saw your holy angel, by whose help this fire was overcome, so that through your wonders your holy name may be glorified everywhere." Because of this, the fire did not harm her in the least. 

Afterward, she was ordered to throw incense to Apollo, but as she prayed, the idol she was commanded to worship was suddenly reduced to ashes; and the tyrant <note>Dion</note> died instantly. By this miracle, three thousand people submitted their necks to the yoke of Christ <note>A metaphor for conversion</note>. 

And when a certain Julianus had been made his successor, and he himself had commanded the virgin Christina to sacrifice to idols, and she had similarly refused with an unbroken spirit, she was again ordered to be thrown into a burning furnace; but by the power of God she came out from the furnace unharmed, as if from a bath, walking out in magnificent confidence. 

Seeing the virgin's manly constancy, Julianus ordered a Marsian <term>Marsum</term> <note>The Marsi were an ancient Italian people famous for their skills as snake-charmers and healers.</note> to release two asps, two vipers, and two dragons <note>In this context, "dragons" usually refers to very large, powerful snakes.</note> against her. The snakes immediately killed the snake-charmer, but then threw themselves prostrate at her feet. She then commanded them to seek out deserted places. 

Then Christina, with a low voice, said to those standing by: 
<margin>Note.</margin> "My dearest ones, no tree is solid or robust unless it is tested by the assault of constant storms, shaken in its trunk and bent this way and that, and unless the blast of whirling winds often strikes it. For by these very vexations, the tree is tightened and pressed down, and it is more surely strengthened as its roots are fixed. So too am I now, by the biting lashes of this tyrant and the frequency of my torments, better protected, extended, corrected, and strengthened..."

Her holy body was moved to Venice after four hundred and fifty years and is kept in the small city of Torcello. For it is believed that it was brought to that city by Constantius, son of the Emperor Heraclius, who, when he went to Rome, stopped in that place and built a village which he wanted to be called *Constanciacum* after his own name. Returning from Rome, he took her body from Bolsena <note>original: "vulsino"</note> and gave it as a gift to the church of Torcello, where it is kept even to this day.

**FOLIO LXXXII**

**Concerning Saint Fausta and Saint Margaret**

...and makes them immortal—those who, for the sake of his love, strive in the contest <note>original: "agone," referring to the spiritual and physical struggle of martyrdom</note> and conquer. For he himself teaches in his Gospel to worship the creator of the sun and moon with fitting faith; not to admire the elements of bodies, nor other visible things, but to admire only the creative Intellect, who is known invisibly through these things. He taught us to adore him alone: who, penetrating through all things, though he is incomparable, is perceived by the intellect alone. Moreover, he is revealed to us through those things which he has made. He produces, governs, and preserves them, assisting all things invisibly—not only celestial things, but also terrestrial ones—wishing to show the magnificence of his works through these things, even to those who worship false gods.

Upon hearing these things, Eulasius believed; he immediately followed the opinion of Fausta. Then the emperor sent a prefect to punish Eulasius. Having been seized, he then ordered her to be led into a frying pan <term>Sartago: a large, shallow metal pan used in Roman times for cooking, often cited in hagiography as an instrument of torture</term> in the amphitheater, so that he might offer her to be torn apart by wild beasts. But all of them, running up like the tamest dogs, lay down at the feet of the virgin. After this, he commanded many nails to be fixed into her body; then he ordered her to be fried in the pan together with Eulasius. 

While she was placed there in torments, singing with the prophet, she said: *We have become as a wonder to many, and you, Lord, are a strong helper.* <note>Psalm 71:7</note> *They curse us, Lord, and you will bless.* <note>Psalm 109:28</note> *Let those who rise up against us be confounded, but your servants, O Lord our God, shall rejoice in you.* When these prayers were finished, the pan immediately cooled down. Then even that prefect embraced the faith of Christ, and immediately a voice came from heaven, saying: "Come now, you blessed ones, receive the kingdom which your heavenly Father expects for you in exultation, about to return the rewards of your labors." 

Hearing these things with joyful faces—while all the faithful around them were weeping—they themselves were laughing, as if they were not dying but migrating <note>The text emphasizes "migrating" as a transition to heaven rather than a final death</note>; and changing friends, not leaving them, they gave back their spirits to the Lord. 

Then Maximian Augustus, hearing what had happened concerning Eulasius and the prefect, blasphemed his own gods. Recognizing that they now had no power, he proposed from then on to desist from the persecution of the Christians. All the people standing around cried out together: "Great is the God of the Christians, who works great things in all!" And so each one returned to his own home with joy, glorifying and blessing the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. To whom is honor and glory forever. Amen.

Now, Fausta and Eulasius suffered on the twelfth day before the Calends of October <note>September 20th</note>. On that day, the annual solemnity of the holy virgin Fausta is celebrated; her most holy relics are kept with honor in Lucca <note>original: "Luce," referring to the city of Lucca in Italy</note>, in the temple of Saint Frediano. Innumerable things could have been said concerning the life of this holy virgin Fausta—of her strength, her wisdom, and her piety—which we have omitted out of a desire for brevity.

**¶ Concerning Saint Margaret, virgin and martyr. Chapter 105.**

[Decorative initial M containing a crown and the letters M and A]
It is handed down that the most blessed virgin Margaret underwent a glorious martyrdom for Christ at Antioch. However, there is uncertainty among various writers as to what time, or on what day, or under which reigning prince among the Romans it occurred. These variations are not without argument; but setting aside the disagreements of writers, what many believe is the opinion that she suffered instead while Diocletian and Maximian were ruling.

**Of Saint Margaret** [Page 13]

...having suffered. For they say she was the daughter of a certain Theodosius, a chief patriarch of the pagans. It is passed down that she was famous and powerful not only through the wonderful beauty of her body and excellent learning and the abundant holiness of her life, but also in her power against demons. Indeed, the name Margaret <note>The name Margaret is derived from the Greek "margarites," meaning "pearl."</note> was appropriately given to her according to the nature of things: for she was in her nature and life just as her name. For the name "Margaret" itself can signify a precious stone, which contains many virtuous properties within itself. Indeed, from childhood (so to speak), a certain divine force and grace was present in this maiden's soul, which through many things made itself known and seen through her understanding, beyond the senses of her little body, which others perhaps older could not even have thought of.

And when she began to know and be wise beyond her age, she began most religiously to adore and worship Almighty God; and regarding divine matters, as far as she could know them, she considered nothing holier; among other things, she did not cease to cherish and follow the poor with incredible piety for God’s sake. And when she had reached her fifteenth year <note>The text likely refers to the "fifteenth" year, a common hagiographic trope for the start of a saint's trials.</note>, hearing of the incredible struggles of the martyrs—namely, how much blood of the righteous was being shed—filled with the Holy Spirit, she commended and dedicated herself entirely to the Lord above all. 

From then on, establishing for herself a rule for living well and blessedly, turned entirely toward God, she wished to embrace mercy, modesty, and humility, along with all-encompassing chastity. And in every act and word, she resolved to maintain a quiet and placid mind; the presence of God always occurred in her thoughts. She was humble in mind and gentle in her actions, upright only against vices. Indeed, according to the small measure of her ability, she tried to prepare her soul as a temple of God with virtues. For she affirmed that the hearts of the saints are temples of God, just as the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> says: "The temple of God is holy, which you are." <note>original: "Templum dei sanctum est: quod estis vos" (1 Corinthians 3:17)</note>

And since she knew the Lord had said through the prophet: "Upon whom else shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet and him who trembles at my words?" <note>original: "Super quem alium requiescam, nisi super humilem et quietum, et trementem manus meas" (Isaiah 66:2)</note> She held nothing more excellent than humility itself and nothing more lovable, hoping that by this purity alone, virtue could be made most pleasing to both men and God. The maiden Margaret was then following her nurse’s flocks, playing <note>The Latin "lasciviens" suggests youthful, unburdened activity.</note> not far from Antioch. When Olybrius the Prefect, coming from Asia, saw her—remarkable in her beauty and playfulness—he immediately, as a powerful man, sent those who would bring her to him, so that he might take her either as a wife or a concubine. 

But she suddenly began to call upon Christ, saying: "Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, O God, nor my life with men of blood." <note>original: "Ne perdas cum impiis deus animam meam: cum viris sanguinum vitam meam" (Psalm 26:9)</note> "Lest my faith be polluted, nor my body defiled: Send me, I beseech you, my God, a guardian Angel who may direct my senses, so that I may answer the wicked prefect with confidence and wisdom." 

The girl having been seized, she was immediately brought to the prefect. They said, "Most worthy governor, this girl calls upon Christ, whom the Jews affixed to a cross." But the governor ordered her to be presented at his tribunals. Where, when questioned about her name, her lineage, and her worship of the gods, she replied: "My name, magnificent governor, is Margaret. I am noble-born and of a notable lineage. Truly, I call upon and adore Jesus Christ, the Almighty God, who has preserved my virginity pure and inviolate until this day." 

The governor, becoming angry, soon ordered her to be shut in prison. Later, when she could not be persuaded by any promises and flatteries, nor by threats, nor be led astray or deceived into worshipping the gods, he had her suspended in the air and beaten for a long time. And looking up to heaven, she said: "In you, Lord, have I hoped; let me never be put to shame, nor let my enemies mock me." <note>original: "In te domine speravi non confundar in aeternum, neque irrideant me inimici mei" (Psalm 31:1 and 25:2)</note> "Look upon me, I beseech you, your handmaid, and have mercy on me; deliver me from the hands of the ungodly, lest my heart be terrified by the blows <margin>Note.</margin> but send the dew of your grace, so that my wounds may be healed and my pain may rest." 

While she was praying these very things, the executioners beat her for so long that the earth was drenched, turned red by her blood. Then she said: "It is better for me to be humbled by the judgment of heavenly discipline than to be damned with infidelity and its followers, as our Apostle says: 'When we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world.'" <note>original: "Cum iudicamur a domino corripimur: ne cum hoc mundo damnemur" (1 Corinthians 11:32)</note> For it is the strength of Christians...

# Concerning Saint Margaret: Page 83

...as if to be purified by fire and flames in the manner of metal vessels. Then the prefect said, "What is this, Margaret? Why do you disobey us and have no mercy on yourself? Agree with me and worship the gods, lest you perish miserably with the rest." To which the virgin replied, "O wicked and impudent dog! <note>original: "canis"</note> If I were to take pity on my fragile flesh, I would lead my soul into destruction just like yours. But I prefer that this body be exposed to execrable tortures so that afterward my soul may be crowned in heaven. Indeed, he is unharmed whom God corrects with any strike, for He shows Himself as our lover through such chastening. For He Himself said to us: 'Those whom I love, I rebuke and chasten.'" <note>A reference to Revelation 3:19.</note> Enraged by this, Olybrius ordered her to be thrust into a most foul prison. 

There, when she had poured out her prayer, a horrible dragon suddenly emerged from a corner of the prison and swallowed her. However, the sign of the cross which Margaret had traced upon herself grew within the dragon's mouth, so that it immediately split the beast into two parts. Thus the blessed virgin emerged from its belly unharmed. At that very moment, looking toward the left side, she saw Satan standing there in the form of a black man. <note>In medieval literature, demons were frequently depicted as having dark skin to symbolize their association with shadows and hell.</note> When the virgin had seized him, she threw him to the ground, saying, "Be still now, you enemy, most evil beast, and author of Gehenna!" <margin>Note.</margin>

On the following day, the governor <term>praeses<gloss>prefect or local ruler</gloss></term> said to her, "Worship my gods." She replied to him, "It is more fitting for you, magnificent prefect, to worship my God, who is most perfect and most blessed, sufficient unto Himself and to all others. For He is the beginning of all things, He is the middle, and He is the most excellent end. He is most well-known and most manifest through His works. His substance, however, is entirely invisible; nothing like Him can we see or even imagine. Therefore, no material can take on His image, nor can any art imitate Him by sculpting. Yet His works are perceived by all our eyes: namely the heavens, the earth, the sun, the moon, the light, the rivers, the sea, the animals, and the plants, all of which He alone made—not with hands, nor with labor, nor with the help of anyone; but when He willed all things to be well made, they were instantly created. This Lord, O prefect, is the one you and all men ought to follow and certainly to worship; and He is worshipped only through the practice of virtues. Because of this, we have endured adverse fortune much more frequently than other nations, yet even in the greatest dangers we have not wished to abandon this law and this ritual of worshipping the true God. Your demons, however, whom you command me to venerate and worship in the place of gods, we can most aptly prove to be evil enemies. For everything that is good cannot fail to be beneficial, and conversely, that which is evil cannot help but harm. But Saturn and Jupiter, Minerva, and Juno, and your other similar gods, rejoice exceedingly in slaughter and the blood of men; and how then shall these be good gods? Rather, they are wicked and ruinous spirits whom you compel me to adore. Take heed, I pray you, most worthy prefect, of what even your most ancient prophet, Orpheus, sang concerning our true God whom we say we worship, asserting that He created all things in these words:

**Concerning Saint Euphemia**

He is the beginning: the middle also: and the same is the end: <note>original: "Ipe est principium: medium quocqʒ: ꝛ exitus idem"</note>
The voices of the ancients have taught us all these things:
But not to those alone: but to all those who have been seen worthy of this name/ and so
it seems to us that a pious opinion concerning God must be held. And so our law alone has most diligently 
ordained: that which leads us to true piety/ and compels us to have a care for true virtue. By these reasons, however, the prefect <note>The Roman official overseeing the trial</note> was not only not moved to remorse: but was hardened in a greater way/ and compelled her to offer sacrifice/ and when she refused/ he ordered her to be hung up:
and her whole body to be torn with whips/ evidently so that by the bitterness of the pain/ he might make her do what was commanded against her will. But while she remained immovable/ though her skin was already stripped from her flesh/ he ordered her to be drenched with vinegar and salt. And when the virgin Margaret <note>The text here refers to Margaret of Antioch, whose story concludes before Euphemia’s begins</note> had endured even this kind of torment constantly and bravely/ he ordered a vessel full of water with burning coals placed beneath it to be set in the middle/ and he ordered the virgin to be placed in it with her hands and feet bound:
But by the prayer she poured out/ immediately a great earthquake occurred/ and soon a dove coming from heaven/ placed a golden crown on Margaret’s head: and soon a voice followed from heaven/ saying: "Come, my beloved, come into your rest/ and come into the kingdom of heaven/ prepared for you by the Lord on account of your constancy of faith. Blessed are you who loved virginity/ and preserved justice and patience/ because for this reason the crown of the heavenly kingdom is granted and decreed to you." In that very hour it is recorded that about five thousand men, excluding women and children, believed in the Lord. Because of this, Olybrius <note>The Roman governor associated with the martyrdom of St. Margaret</note> ordered them to be beheaded. To her body there was soon a very great gathering of both heathens and Christians. For the sick/ the blind/ the lame/ the deaf/ and the weak, as many as were able to touch the holy body: became healthy and safe from their illnesses and infirmities. Indeed, this virgin Margaret not only attained the glory of holiness because of this martyrdom/ but rather she was held as the principal advocate of women in labor above all other holy virgins, just like a mother/ and temples/ and altars/ and chapels/ and sacred offices were established for her by the public institution of the church. And the sacred ecclesiastical synod established/ that the day of her martyrdom should be celebrated in its own time from year to year on the thirteenth day before the Calends of August <note>July 20th</note>/ with joy and exultation by all the faithful of Christ.

Whether, however, she was Asian or Roman is not sufficiently certain. It is believed, however, rather that she was Roman/ because she had a senator for a father/ born of his wife Thodola. They were indeed believed to be Christians/ when one considers their distinguished piety

<meta>This page appears to be a theological discourse or a passio (martyrdom account) concerning Saint Euphemia, likely a translation or commentary on a Greek original. It contrasts Christian cosmology with various pagan philosophies (Epicureanism, Platonism, and traditional polytheism).</meta>

# Concerning Saint Euphemia

...she wonders, intending to see him in his own works. As our Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> says: "For the invisible things <note>original: *invisibilia*; quoting Romans 1:20</note> of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made: and also his eternal power and divinity." That is, we are drawn from the vastness of the visible creation toward the unity of the invisible Creator. 

But we, separated from worldly wisdom—which attributes all things to chance—are lifted up by divine meditations. Through his help, we are set apart from those who claimed either that matter has always existed and wished for God to be merely a craftsman <term>artificer (artificem): a reference to the Platonic Demiurge who shapes pre-existing matter rather than creating from nothing</term> of things; or from those who worshipped these very elements as gods. 

Or you—who introduced families of gods categorized by sex, by age, and by parts, as if they were some common rabble <note>original: *plebem*; implying the pagan gods were a lowly, unruly crowd compared to the one God</note> subject to the senses—we, being set apart by the Holy Spirit and raised to higher things, living the true life (that is, possessing true wisdom), are free from this folly of yours. For we remember that the world was made from nothing by God, and that all living creatures were brought forth <note>The Latin abbreviation *pocū* is likely *procreata* or *producta*</note> by the power of the creative Word...

<summary>This page presents a theological defense of Christian monotheism, quoting St. Paul to argue that the invisible God is known through His creation. It rejects pagan concepts of a "craftsman" god, elemental worship, and the personified Greek/Roman pantheon in favor of creation ex nihilo.</summary>

-> # Concerning Saint Lucy <-

<margin>note</margin>
"Whoever wishes to be perfect: sell all that he has and give to the poor, and follow me." 
<note>original: "Qui vult perfectus esse: vendat omnia que habet...". A reference to Matthew 19:21.</note> 
And again: "You cannot serve God and <term>mammon</term>." <note>original: "māone" (mammonae); mammon refers to wealth or material greed.</note> Therefore, having set aside the necessities for her life, Lucy 
reserved nothing more for herself, along with her mother Eutychia. From where did this fervor come, if not from the love 
of God? From where came this tireless meditation on the law of Christ, if not from a desire for Him who gave the 
law? And so, nearly all her goods were distributed among the poor of Christ by the virgin Lucy. 
Then, Lucy was accused before the consul Paschasius by her betrothed, specifically on the grounds that she was a 
devout Christian and was living contrary to the laws of the emperors. When she had been summoned to him, Paschasius 
interrogated her, saying: "What is this superstition of yours?" Lucy replied: "I am indeed most worthily 
a Christian, Consul, and from Christian teachers I have learned to live by a triple rule: namely, piously, 
holily, and justly—so as to love Almighty God with the most fervent worship, and to cling to virtue and love my neighbor with the most fervent charity." "Indeed, Paschasius, you can certainly observe by many 
arguments that we Christians love God most worthily. For among them, perpetual chastity 
is maintained; there is no mention of swearing oaths; lies, hatreds, and other vices are far from 
us. And so that they may be seen to cling to virtue, they neglect money and wealth (as you have seen 
me do); they despise glory and hate pleasures; they are constant, severe, and 
great of soul even in the midst of torments for God; and countless other things of this kind. 
Furthermore, you can very clearly infer how great the charity of Christians is from their benevolence, fellowship, 
and equity. The religion of Christ produces men of this sort; indeed, it has set before all the works 
of virtue, from which liberty arises and is confirmed. For the cause and those things which belong to our liberty, 
and the nature of the body, and those things which happen externally, is God, by whom all things that exist are produced." Then 
Paschasius said: "These things are vain and superstitious. Only adore the immortal gods 
and sacrifice to them." To which she replied: "A true and immaculate sacrifice before 
God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation, and to keep 
oneself immaculate from this world. <note>original: "Sacrifitium verum...". A quotation of James 1:27.</note> As for you, do whatever you wish, but I will 
perform those things which shall be for my salvation. For even if you threaten lashes and slaughter, 
I shall not hesitate to cry out: sharpen the sword! Bring fire! Cut my little body 
to pieces, and burn it all! The stars will sooner descend to the earth, and the earth 
ascend into heaven, than you shall hear anything false from me." And when many things had been said back and forth, 
Paschasius ordered <term>procurers</term> <note>original: "lenones"; men who managed brothels.</note> to come, who were to provoke the virgin into lust. 
But when they began to try to drag the holy virgin away to the brothel, the Holy Spirit 
fixed her with such great weight that she could not be moved at all—even when magical 
arts were applied, and many pairs of oxen. Then Paschasius said: "What logic is this, 
that a delicate girl, pulled by a thousand men, is not moved at all?" To which she replied: 
"Even if another ten thousand were brought by you, they would hear the Holy Spirit speaking through me: 
'A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.'" <note>original: "Cadent/ a latero tuo mille...". A quotation of Psalm 91:7.</note> Upon 
hearing this, the judge became more and more insane and began to be tormented; and with a terrible voice and a 
barking sound he pursued her, insisted, urged, compelled, and threatened to strike her, and 
dragged her, unvanquished and protesting, to judgment. The virgin said to him: "Why do you torment yourself, 
most wretched Paschasius? Why do you tremble with paleness? Why are you torn apart by different emotions? If

# Page 81

## ## Concerning Saint Dorothea

[Woodcut illustration of Saint Dorothea standing in a landscape, holding a lantern or censer in her right hand and a basket of flowers/fruit in her left. A small church is visible on a hill in the background.] <note>The basket of flowers and fruit is Dorothea's primary attribute, referring to the miracle where she sent roses and apples from paradise to a skeptical lawyer named Theophilus.</note>

**D**orothea, a glorious virgin, in the three hundred and tenth year after the birth of Christ, in the city of Caesarea in Cappadocia, under the tyrant Maximinus <note>Maximinus II (reigned 308–313 AD), a Roman Emperor known for his fierce persecution of Christians.</note>—while the Roman Pope Miltiades presided in the seat of Blessed Peter—earned a glorious triumph through martyrdom. She was indeed born of noble Roman blood, having Dorus the senator as her father and Thea as her mother, both of whom were most Christian and wealthy parents. From these two names, the name Dorothea was given to her. <note>original: "Dorothee" — The author highlights the etymology combining her parents' names, Dorus and Thea, to form "Dorothea," which means "Gift of God."</note>

These most noble people, fleeing the most savage persecutions of the tyrants, left behind all their estates and countless other castles and most proud houses, and traveled to the kingdom of Cappadocia with a great deal of money. Furthermore, while they were there, they brought forth this daughter of wondrous beauty, who shone so brightly among others with such unseen beauty that you would believe she surpassed all other young maidens of that kingdom in loveliness; indeed, you would judge her a celestial image rather than a mortal one. Moreover, she emerged as distinguished in her exceptional education and excellent character. At that time, Maximinus was exercising his tyranny in those Eastern regions, and Maxentius, the son of Maximianus, had seized the same in Rome. Indeed, just as they were partners in tyranny, so they seemed to imitate one another in their crimes, so that you would not know to whom the palm of wickedness should most especially be given. From this, they stirred up more vehement and heavier persecutions against the Christians than others had. For Maximinus was, among other things, a public enemy of all equity, and a destroyer of modesty, honesty, and justice—the most infested persecutor and enemy of the Christians above all others. Against them, he exercised such cruelty that he hastened to surpass all his predecessors in wickedness. 

Nevertheless, they were very often overcome not only by men but even by women who, set on fire by the word of God and the heat of faith, were indeed seized as women, but were crowned as brave men in the contest of martyrdom. In the midst of these storms, this virgin Dorothea, although she possessed a most beautiful face and other limbs of her body, nevertheless studied to be even more beautiful in her religion, her spirit, and the honesty of her life. And what is greater: that which seemed beautiful and decorous to men, she decided—by the judgment of her own healthy mind—to consecrate to God rather than dedicate to human use; that is, she resolved to persist in perpetual virginity for the sake of God. 

But Maximinus, who was defiling things both divine and human with his lust and cruelty, having learned only of the beauty of this holy virgin and not of the merit of her proposed virginity, set his mind to polluting and violating her. When it was discovered, however, that she was a Christian—which, according to his edicts, seemed to make her more a subject for punishment than for his lust—he was placed in a state of ambiguity and began to seethe, not knowing which way to turn. But where his mind was in doubt, the lust that dominated him more widely took hold. While the virgin was waiting to be snatched away to punishment for the sake of martyrdom, he solicited her through secret messengers to commit an act of debauchery. 

She replied that it was a crime for her to defile the temple of her body, which she had once and for all consecrated to the best and greatest God, with the contagion of idols and lust. Therefore, she was indeed more ready for death than to sin in the sight of her God. But she said to the cruel tyrant that it was not fitting for anything flattering or soft to be offered, nor was it worthy for those fierce minds—which daily... <note>The text breaks off here as the page ends.</note>

LXXXVIII

### **On Saint Catherine**

Let it be known that although the royal riches were taken away and the kingdom appeared to stand without any king, the royal title of the ancient Ptolemies <note>The Ptolemaic dynasty ruled Egypt from the death of Alexander the Great until the Roman conquest.</note> remained for certain in this same family of the **Lagidae** <term>Lagidae: another name for the Ptolemaic dynasty, named after Lagos, the father of Ptolemy I</term> until the time of this King Costus. And in this manner, I would believe without a doubt that Costus himself, the father of the divine Catherine, was called "King," just as we have seen explored in many kings of our own age. These men are called kings of a kingdom even when that kingdom is in the possession of another—as we have the example in the **Kingdom of Jerusalem** <note>During the Crusades and long after, many European monarchs claimed the title "King of Jerusalem" even when they did not control the city.</note>. 

But we must return to the virgin Catherine. Therefore, this virgin was a woman more illustrious than the other women of the city of Alexandria in her origin, power, character, and education in her time. If we wished to search back through the endless line of her parents, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, we would not stop until we came through innumerable ancestral kings to **Ptolemy Philadelphus** <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus, the 3rd-century BC ruler famous for sponsoring the Library of Alexandria and the translation of the Hebrew Bible into Greek (the Septuagint).</note>, the greatest king. From such an ancient lineage, so many good things emanated.

Thus, when her father King Costus was taken away by an early death (while she was still a young child), and since she was his only daughter, it happened by law that she became the heir to his innumerable riches. As she grew in both age and wisdom, she began to adore and worship Almighty God most religiously. From this, she considered nothing more holy than charity and piety, pursuing Christians with an incredible love. She was especially studious of learned men and grave, holy persons, from whom she always desired to hear or learn something excellent. And because she gloried in the fact that all things existed in God alone and in the same Jesus Christ, the Redeemer of all—whom she proposed to herself as a model for her own formation and learning—she always placed Him before herself through every practice of piety, as if she were constantly seeking something new from Him. 

Therefore, she followed Him in every institution of her life (not like **Cleopatra**, who was the talk of the whole world) <note>Cleopatra VII is often used in medieval literature as a "bad" foil to Catherine's "virtuous" Egyptian queen archetype.</note> and clung to Him according to the example of the Prophet who says: *It is good for me to cling to God* <note>original: "Mihi adherere deo bonum est" (Psalm 73:28)</note>. She imitated Him in all things as a true worshiper of Christ. She utterly despised the sects of the gentiles and wonderfully embraced and continually labored over the Christian religion and the Scriptures. 

Furthermore, she was more prudent than can be believed and was steeped in all the **liberal arts** <term>liberal arts: the traditional curriculum of grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy</term> and was distinguished in the speech of almost all languages. 

At that time, **Maxentius** the tyrant, the son of Maximian—who from the beginning had pretended to be a worshiper of the Christian faith to catch the favor of the common people—was a most wicked man and very fond of the magic arts. He had traveled from Rome to Alexandria with his whole household and his wife to visit his colleague, the tyrant Maximinus. When he had arrived and been received with great honor, he decreed according to custom that a solemn sacrifice be celebrated for the gods, to which he also forced all the Christians who were found within the city. 

At that time, the virgin Catherine was eighteen years old. When it was reported to her that Maxentius was present in the temple along with an innumerable multitude to sacrifice to the gods, she was inflamed with zeal for God. Fortifying herself with the **sign of the cross** <note>original: "Crucis signaculo"</note>, she wished to go there with a respectable company of her people. There she found many of those who professed Christian doctrine weeping together. And so, she addressed the Emperor with these words: 

"Why, O Caesar," she said, "do you destroy such a vast multitude in such great folly and the vain error of idols? Return to your senses at last from this foolishness and recognize the Lord, who created this world and all things that are in it by His word alone. It is He who redeemed the human race from eternal death with His own blood; to Him belongs perpetual honor, and to Him glory is owed forever and ever. Neither..."
