# **Concerning Saint Barbara**

She said to her parents: "What do these images mean for themselves?" The parents responded: "Child, <note>Latin: *infans*. Though Barbara is a young woman, her parents address her here as a child or one who is 'speechless' in the face of divine mystery.</note> what are you saying? You see that these are not the likenesses of men, but they are gods, for it is commanded that they be adored for that which is unknown and that which is least perceived." To them, the girl replied: "Were they then once men, these whom we now worship?" Both parents said they were. But she, as she was a young woman of the greatest spirit, was moved for a short while by a natural instinct; and now, as if awakened from a certain lethargy and (so to speak) from a deep sleep, with the eyes of her mind somewhat opened, she considered that God and the power of God must be a saving force for the world. To seek Him, she first raised her mind to heaven, contemplating the beauty of the celestial bodies. Marvelling at them, she judged that there were not many gods, but one God, who had made and ruled all these things entirely. And when she was drawn by an ardent desire into the knowledge of the true God, she began to read through and study the pagan <term>philosophers</term> <note>While we think of philosophers as scientists or thinkers, in this context, they were also viewed as spiritual investigators seeking the first cause of the universe.</note> with great effort and accuracy. Among them, she noticed a very great dispute and contention regarding the true God; and she had even learned from those same philosophers that a certain vain superstition had taken its beginning among the ancients, which, as if a source of all evils, had established a multitude of gods. It had persuaded people to sacrifice victims to them, to perform solemn rites, to set up statues, and to build temples—even though these had previously been the graves of men, but, being built more magnificently, they had been called by the name of temples. From this, she judged the <term>religion of the ancients</term> <note>Meaning the classical Roman and Greek pantheon of gods.</note> to be more like the fables of poets than true religion. And when she perceived that these things had no truth in them, she despised all those idols of her ancestors with a great voice of the heart. But when she also turned herself to investigating the <term>theology of the poets</term>, <note>A traditional classification of theology that dealt with the myths and stories told by poets like Homer or Hesiod.</note> she learned from Hesiod and Orpheus, the best of poets, that she should not doubt that all things in the world emanated from one God and are contained by His power. This was especially according to the opinion of <term>Orpheus</term>, <note>A legendary Greek poet and musician. In the Middle Ages and Renaissance, Orpheus was often viewed as a "proto-Christian" who had discovered the truth of the one God through nature.</note> who in certain poems said that all things were governed by divine power in this manner:

<margin>Verses of Orpheus</margin>

->You who cultivate virtue, give your ears only to my<-
->words: and direct your minds:<-
->To the contrary, you who despise the holy laws: from here<-

¶ And so the virgin Barbara, when she had received such a pious opinion concerning the one true God from the poet and theologian Orpheus, immediately—just as it is well known that the Father <term>Aurelius Augustine</term> <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a famous convert who also searched through various philosophies before finding Christianity.</note> did—after many wanderings through the errors of her ancestors, she began to travel about, not only through the city streets and squares, but through all of Asia and Egypt, seeking the true husband of her soul.

<summary>Saint Barbara rejects her parents' idols and, through the study of philosophy and the poetry of Orpheus, deduces the existence of a single, all-powerful Creator. Inspired by this discovery, she begins a spiritual journey to find the true God, paralleling the intellectual struggle of Saint Augustine.</summary>

# Of Saint Barbara, Folio 92

...for whom she did not fear to die; she judged it worthy to die so that she might forever cling to His love. <note>The "love" referred to here is that of Christ, whom Barbara has chosen as her spiritual bridegroom.</note> Then, word was brought from **Alexandria** to **Nicomedia** <note>Nicomedia was a major city in the Roman Empire, located in modern-day Turkey; Alexandria was the intellectual capital of the Christian world at the time.</note> that the wisest of men was in Alexandria, **Origen** by name <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was a famous early Christian scholar and theologian known for his immense learning.</note>. **Concerning Saint Barbara**

<meta>This page continues the hagiography (biography of a saint) of Saint Barbara, focusing on her trial and public defense of her faith before the Roman authorities.</meta>

# Concerning Saint Barbara Folio 93

Therefore, sitting before the tribunal, Marcianus <note>A Roman provincial governor traditionally associated with the martyrdom of Saint Barbara.</note> ordered Barbara to be brought to him. Looking at her, he said, "Why, beautiful girl, do you hand yourself over to this kind of death? Offer a sacrifice to the gods, and you shall depart unharmed. But if you neglect to perform this: know that you must be killed by various and most bitter torments."

To him she replied: "Listen to me, Governor Marcianus: the gods whom you urge me to adore are not gods, but the worst of demons. Leaving heaven, they descended to earth so that they might commit murders, sexual immoralities, and countless other evils. For they did not teach modesty or justice by their example; instead, some rejoice in obscene pleasures, others in brawling, and others in hunting. 

But my Lord Jesus Christ (whom I love and worship with all my heart), as the true God, did not encourage wars or fights like your Minerva—whom you falsely call a goddess—but instead urged peace and total tranquility among men. Nor do various hunts with dogs please him, as they please your <term>Diana the Huntress</term> <note>The Roman goddess of the wild and the hunt, whom Barbara contrasts with the peaceful nature of Christ.</note>..."

<summary>This page records the interrogation of Saint Barbara by the governor Marcianus, featuring her bold critique of Roman deities like Minerva and Diana in favor of the peace of Christ.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the life of Saint Barbara and introduces the life of Saint Anastasia. The previous page detailed the trials and ultimate execution of Barbara by her own father, Dioscorus.</meta>

**On Saint Anastasia**

...trace. And so, the blessed virgin Barbara suffered <term>martyrdom|The act of dying for one's faith</term> on the day before the Nones of December <note>December 4th</note>, the very day on which her annual feast is celebrated. After her death, her spiritual father, a religious man named Valentine, collected her remains. Carrying them into the city and preparing them with fragrant spices, he buried them with reverence. At her tomb, all those who suffer from any lingering illness receive health, to the praise and glory of Almighty God, to whom belongs honor and glory forever and ever, amen. 

However, whether this virgin Barbara suffered under the tyrant Maximinus is a matter of doubt for many, and even for me. Since the great teacher <term>Origen|A prominent early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD)</term>, to whom she had sent letters, flourished during the time of the Emperor Alexander who ruled the Romans around the year 230 of our salvation, I would rather say she suffered under the Emperor Maximinus Augustus, rather than that tyrant Maximinus <note>The author is likely distinguishing between the Emperor Maximinus Thrax (reigned 235–238) and the later, more infamous persecutor Maximinus Daza (reigned 308–313)</note>. 

From that "Phaethon-like" <note>original: *phetonitica*; an allusion to the Greek myth of Phaethon, who was struck from the sky by a thunderbolt</note> lightning strike upon Dioscorus—whereby Dioscorus perished, struck and burned as if by the sun's chariot—a custom grew: whenever we see a flash of lightning, we immediately cry out, "Saint Barbara, pray and intercede for me!" I am well aware that she has performed many other miracles in similar circumstances, but it would be a long task to commit them all to writing now. Her most holy body was later translated <note>The ritual movement of a saint's body from one location to another</note> to Venice; it is now reverently preserved in a marble sarcophagus in the Monastery of the <term>Cruciferi|The "Cross-bearers," a religious order</term> in a chapel dedicated to her name.

### ¶ On Saint Anastasia the Martyr. Chapter 111.

[Woodcut illustration of Saint Anastasia standing in a landscape, wearing a long robe and cloak with a halo, holding a small ornate vessel in her right hand. In the background are hills, trees, and a small church on a hill to the right.]

**A**nastasia, a most noble Roman matron, was a devoted worshiper of the Divine Majesty. An example of untainted purity and immense piety for all religious women, she underwent a glorious martyrdom for Christ in Rome under the Emperor Diocletian. For these reasons, she acquired a double portion of praise: first, because like a diligent farmer, she had sown the good fruits of piety throughout her life; and finally, because she watered the garden of her merits and virtues with the shedding of her holy blood. 

She was the daughter of Pretextatus, an illustrious Roman nobleman and pagan, and her mother Fausta, a Christian. When she reached adulthood, her parents joined her in marriage to Publius, a Roman patrician of equal nobility. Because of her virtues and piety, she was greatly troubled by this husband. Through her paternal inheritance, Anastasia was quite wealthy, so much so that her vast income perfectly matched the high status of her family. She was excellently instructed and taught in the Divine Scriptures by Saint <term>Chrysogonus|A Christian teacher and martyr who acted as Anastasia's mentor</term> (who was later a martyr for Christ). She was so constantly intent upon these writings that, as if trying to satisfy a great hunger, she pored over the Gospels and the Epistles of Saint Paul without ceasing. From this constant reading and meditation on the Holy Scriptures, she learned that Christians should not put their hope in "the uncertainty of their riches," but in the living God, who provides all things abundantly for everyone. Understanding that the wealthy must be rich in "good works" and ready to share, she determined to "store up for herself a good treasure for the future," so that she might lay hold of that which is the truly good life. She knew well that she had received great riches not so that she might consider herself blessed by them alone, or use them wickedly...

<summary>This page concludes the story of Saint Barbara, explaining the origins of her patronage against lightning, and begins the life of Saint Anastasia, a noble Roman woman dedicated to scripture and charity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the hagiography of Saint Anastasia, specifically detailing her transition from a wealthy noblewoman to a clandestine servant of the imprisoned Christians in Rome.</meta>

# On Saint Anastasia Folio 94

...she should use her goods neither to despise the poor, nor to consider them an instrument for her own pleasure, nor to think she would ever lose them. Therefore, since she had read the Apostle Paul saying, "He who sows faithfully shall also reap faithfully," <note>original: "Qui fidēter seminat, fidenter et metet"</note> and again, "God loves a cheerful giver," and also having read the Prophet saying, "I made both the poor and the rich, and I have equal care for all," she was set on fire by the Divine Spirit. She said within herself: "Since God cares for all, who should fear that his inheritance might be diminished, when it is being shared at God's command? Fear, Anastasia," she said, "fear rather lest you become lukewarm, barren, and unfaithful in good works, and at last be found utterly destitute and helpless. Do not fear, I say, that it will be difficult to enter the kingdom of heaven, provided you are humble, provided you are generous, because for this you shall be called most blessed. You shall feel no want because of this, neither in this age nor in the future. Therefore, give to the poor so that you may **lend to God** <term>lend to God: the text uses "fenereris," implying a spiritual form of usury where charity to the poor is a loan that God pays back with interest in heaven</term>; consider God your debtor. Feel that mercy is placed before all sacrifices for the one who shows mercy, for the Lord says: 'Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.' <note>Matthew 5:7</note> Namely, you also shall obtain glory and rest." <margin>Her great humility.</margin> For that reason, she decided not to feel herself a rich woman, nor to show any sign of her nobility, but covered in a humble garment, she went out daily with only a single little maidservant to visit the sick and to look upon those banished to prison for Christ. She fed them and others who were hungry, clothed the naked, took strangers into her home, and indulged in other works of piety. With the hope of an eternal reward, she lent to Christ in the person of the poor, who said: "Whatever you have done for one of these, the least of my brothers, you have done for me." And although she was constantly watchful in these things after the example of Martha, <note>Martha is the biblical figure representing the active, working life of service.</note> she nevertheless also set aside for herself a certain number of hours in which she wished to devote herself to divine and spiritual progress. 

When this was reported to her husband—namely, that she, accompanied by only one maidservant and in cheap clothing, was going around to the prisons in the manner of the Christians and supplying them with necessities—he immediately shut her up in a very narrow and foul prison. He did this so that even her food was taken away, so that once she was killed by this treatment, he might seize her very extensive estates. Fearing, however, that she might die because of this, she sent mournful letters to her father and teacher, Chrysogonus, <note>Saint Chrysogonus was a martyr and Anastasia's spiritual mentor.</note> in these words:

✠ **Anastasia to the holy confessor of Christ, Chrysogonus.** <margin>The Letter.</margin> Although my father was a worshiper of idols, my mother Fausta always lived most Christianly and chastely, and she saw to it that I became a Christian while still in my cradle. After her death, I took up the yoke of a sacrilegious husband. By God's mercy, I have avoided his bed by **feigning illness**, <note>A common motif in early Christian virgin-martyr stories where women used various means to preserve their chastity within forced marriages.</note> and day and night I embrace the footsteps of our Lord Jesus Christ. And since that man is exhausting my inheritance (from which he gains his status) with unworthy and shameful idolaters, he has also handed me over to a most heavy custody as if I were a witch and a sacrilegious woman, so that I suspect I shall lose my physical life. Nothing remains but that, having lost my spirit, I succumb to death. In this death, although I glory in the confession of our Lord Jesus Christ, my mind is nevertheless greatly crushed because my riches, which I had vowed entirely to God, are serving those who are alienated from God and are shameful. Therefore, I pray you, man of God, that you would instantly beseech the Lord that He either bring Publius <note>Publius is the name of her husband.</note> to His faith, if He foresees he will come to it; or if He foresees that he will remain in this perversity of unbelief, that He command him to give place to His worshippers. It is better for him to breathe his last than to deny the Son of God and hinder those who confess Him. For Christ is my witness: if I am set free, I will cling to the footsteps of the saints and exercise the care of all more solicitously than I began. Farewell, man of God, and remember me. 

When Chrysogonus had read this letter and offered prayer with many confessors, he wrote back in this way...

# On Saint Anastasia

**A Letter.** ¶ To you, tossed about by the storms and whirlwinds of the world: Christ, walking swiftly upon the waves, will soon arrive; and with a single word of His command, He will subdue the spirit of the devil blowing against you. 

Endure patiently, and as if you were placed in the middle of the sea, believe that Christ is coming to you; and turning to yourself, cry out with the prophet <note>A reference to King David, traditionally considered the author of the Psalms.</note>, saying: "Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise Him, the salvation of my countenance and my God." <note>original: "Quare tristis es anima mea..." from Psalm 42 (or 43 in modern numbering).</note> 

The evidence of the seeds of the divine gift is proven when earthly things are taken from you and heavenly things are bestowed. For God extends His favor to these extremes so that what He provides may not seem worthless to us. See that you are not troubled by the fact that hardships are brought upon you while you are living a holy life. 

For you are not being deceived, but tested. Your defense is not that which you think can be maintained through human means. Hear the scripture saying: "Cursed is the man who puts his hope in man. And blessed is the man who puts his hope in the Lord." <note>original: "Maledictus homo qui spem suam ponit in homine..." from Jeremiah 17:5–7.</note> Take care, he says, strongly and watchfully...

<summary>This page contains a spiritual letter of encouragement to Saint Anastasia, using the metaphor of a storm at sea to represent her worldly persecutions. It quotes the Psalms and Jeremiah to remind her that her suffering is a divine test and that true hope lies in God rather than human aid.</summary>
